en: A bookseller came and said, "I request you to annotate this book. I opened it and saw that it was Master Shizhi Xiaogong’s commentary on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
It is divided into ten sections, all of which explain the scriptural text; by the ninth section, thirty-six questions are posed.
Answer: Although my own commentary on the meaning of "light" (*ābhāsa*) actually applies to various sutras, I could not bear the restlessness [of others].

During the intervals between my other duties, I corrected the errors of the Japanese annotations and published it. Furthermore, the *Siming Jiaoxing Lu* (Record of the Teachings and Practices of Siming), *Lebang Wenlei* (Classified Writings on the Land of Bliss), and *Shishi Tonglan* (Comprehensive Survey of Food Offerings) compiled by Shi Zhi have already circulated in the world; now this book has also emerged as a matter of course. It is merely a play of words.
Is it not that Master Xiao’s intention toward others has remained undiminished?
On an auspicious day at the beginning of the twelfth lunar month in the eighth year of the Genroku era (the year of Yi Hai), I,
the monk Ruhai, currently residing and studying at Fǎlún Jǎngsì on Gāomiàoyúnshān in Lower Province, respectfully record this.
The Illuminating Commentary on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Volume One (including the preface), composed by the Śramaṇa Zongxiao of Shizhi in Siming. The Preface states:
Although this sutra belongs to the category of Vaipulya and cannot be compared to the finest cream (*amṛta*), those who receive and uphold it are numerous; thus, it is... [text continues]
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is peerless in its magnificence; however, having been transmitted from India to the East, it underwent successive translations across various dynasties by five masters.

Including the intermediate versions, there were six different recensions. That which is currently transmitted is the oldest extant version, translated by Master Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang dynasty.
Yet, how is it that this has circulated separately outside the canon (*zàngwài*)? Former sages did not understand the differences between these textual lineages.

For the most part, the original texts were conflated and altered to complete the translations attributed to Dharmarakṣa; furthermore, through successive transcriptions, errors arose where characters were mistaken for one another, resulting in discrepancies across various editions and registers.
Consequently, there are instances of missing passages and lengthy interpolations, as well as variations in meaning and orthography.

Since the source texts themselves were not uniform, there was no standard by which to choose between them; thus, those who read and recite these scriptures often find their eyes clouded amidst such confusion.

There are many such works; I, this humble person, now respectfully consult the catalogs of sutra translations throughout the successive dynasties. First, I present the sequence and volume divisions of the texts;
next, I describe the five chapters and three sections of the Tiantai school’s exegesis of the sutras and the sequential arising of its various parts.

Thereafter, I investigate and examine the combined editions of the Dragon Canon and the separate circulations among human hands, taking the *Tiantai Wenzhu* (Textual Commentary) as my guide and further employing the interpretations of various masters.
I have recorded all variations, discrepancies, and errors in the annotations and provided a uniform punctuation system;
furthermore, I have systematically analyzed remaining doubts regarding phenomena and have appended explanations on the cultivation of objects and contemplations to clarify them.

May each person thus be able to manifest the Great Luminous Treasury inherent within themselves, thereby avoiding the reproach of one who counts another’s jewels while remaining poor. Once these ten sections were completed, they were arranged in ascending order.
The title for this scroll is *The Illuminating Commentary on the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*. Alas! How could the meager light of a torch suffice to assist the soaring brilliance of the sun and moon?
Yet, as the Great Teaching is resplendent and its light necessarily illuminates even the smallest crevice, my humble and insignificant aspirations cannot remain hidden.
Written on the first day of the long month in the year of Gengxu during the Shaoxi era of the Great Song, by the Bhikṣu Zong.
Xiao respectfully prefaces this work in six parts: first, the translation of the volumes; second, the general purport of the five chapters; third, the division of the text into three sections;
fourth, the sequential arising of the various chapters; fifth, the correction of errors and misconceptions; and sixth, the phonetic transcriptions and glosses.
Seven: Indicating the punctuation and reading; Eight: Annotating the phenomena and characteristics; Nine: Resolving remaining doubts through discernment; Ten:
Revealing the cultivation of the object of contemplation.
One: The Section on Translation and Volumes.
Now, translation is the throat and collar of Buddhist study and the primary head for the interpretation of the Dharma.
This is because our Buddha was born in the kingdom of Kapilavastu and established his teachings throughout the Five Indias;

the languages and scripts of those five regions all originated when the Brahmā of the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended to become the human race at the beginning of the kalpa, and thus they differ from the [language] of this land.

Because the characters created by Xie [Xiè] differ from those used elsewhere, it was necessary for a monk from India to bring them so that each could be translated into the vernacular (Huáyán) before they were fit for recitation and propagation.

This is precisely the intent behind the fact that, throughout the three dynasties, the "Monastic Histories" (*Sēngshǐ*) and the "Ten Categories of Monastic Regulations" (*Shíkē xuǎnfó*) both place translation at the very beginning.
This scripture exists in an Indian original (*fànběn*); here in this land, some have been translated individually while others have been compiled through combination.
There are six versions in total.

First, the Dharma Master Dharmakṣema, a śramaṇa from Central India, translated one work in four fascicles consisting of eighteen chapters during the Xuanshi era of the Northern Liang dynasty under the reign of Juqu Mengxun; it was titled *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.

The *Jingmai Yijing Tujì* (Record of the Translation of Scriptures by Jingmai) states that when the Master of Prophecies (*Chanshi*) was translating the scripture, he remarked that its chapters and sections were incomplete;
this is precisely that original ancient translation of the old scripture which serves as the basis for the version currently in circulation today.
The second was the śramaṇa Yaśakūṭa from Central India; "Yaśakūṭa" translates as "Treasury" (Chēngzàng).

Together with Jñānakūṭa, he translated one work in five fascicles during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Later Zhou dynasty, titled the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* (Jīn guāng míng jīng), also known as the *Suvikrāntavikrāmi-parivarta-mahāprajñā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
Zhi Sheng’s *Shìjiào lù* states that these five fascicles do not constitute a complete translation.
However, the version based on the *Xiṃ* manuscript has been further augmented with the "Chapter on Life Span" (*Āyus-pramāṇa-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on Mahāprajñāpāramitā-devī.

Thirdly, the *Sūtra of Golden Light for Kings* (*Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra-rāja*), consisting of one volume in seven fascicles and twenty-two chapters, was translated by the Śramaṇa Paramārtha (translated as *Zhēndì*) from Western India, at the imperial decree of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, in the first year of the Dàqīng era.
The *Nanshan Neidian Lu* states that this edition adds four chapters to the translation by Paramārtha (Chen):

namely, the "Chapter on the Differentiation of the Three Bodies," the "Chapter on the Extinction of Karmic Obstructions," the "Chapter on the Dhāraṇī of the Most Pure Ground," and the "Chapter on Fulfilling Vows by Relying on Emptiness.
With these four chapters added to the eighteen chapters of Paramārtha’s original version, it becomes twenty-two chapters in total.
The Śramaṇa Jñānagupta from Northern India—translated as Zhìdé (Volition-Virtue)—together with Dharmagupta, translated one fascicle titled the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra:
Silver-Lord Dhāraṇī Chapter and Chapter on Entrustment* during the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Great Sui dynasty.
The *Shìjiào lù* states that the translations by the three masters Paramārtha, Jñānagupta, and [Jñānayaśas] are all...
These two qualities are not present [in the current version], yet they exist in the Sanskrit manuscript examined by the Master; therefore, they have been translated here.
In the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Great Sui Dynasty, the Śramaṇa Baogui of Daxingshan Temple reviewed the previous four translations.
Finding their texts redundant, he took the translation by Dharmakṣema as his base text, drawing from various other versions to eliminate redundancies and supplement omissions.
These were compiled into one work in eight fascicles. At that time, only this single manuscript was retained for inclusion in the canon, while all other duplicate versions were eliminated.
Therefore, the *Shijiao lu* states: "Master Gui [used] the eighteen chapters of the prophetic version;
Yaśas continued with the *Ayuṣparyanta-parivarta* and the *Mahāpratisarā-devī-parivarta*; Paramārtha translated four chapters; and Zhìdé translated two chapters."
In total, twenty-four chapters and eight fascicles were compiled into the work titled *The Combined Edition of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*. Its own preface states:
"This translation of the sūtra is now complete.
In the first year of the Zhengsheng era, the Śramaṇa Yijing of Qi Prefecture in the Great Tang personally traveled to the Five Indias and returned to the River [region].
Luo Feng, by imperial decree of Empress Wu Zetian, translated one volume consisting of ten fascicles and thirty-one chapters, titled the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
Compared to previous translations, the wording of this text is somewhat more extensive;
yet upon investigating its meaning, it is largely the same, differing only slightly.
The above six versions consist of five translations; because the *Combined Version* (*Hebu*) was not translated from Sanskrit, it is excluded from the current canon.

Thus, three versions remain extant. According to the Great Canon (Tripitaka) of Lake [Hangzhou] and Fuzhou, two versions are preserved: first, the *Combined Version*, located in the section marked "Hua" (化);

second, the *Suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (or *Suvikrānta-rāja-sūtra*), located in the section marked "Zhang" (場). Although there are only these two versions, they in fact comprise all five translations.

Because the *Hebu* (Combined) edition subsumes all versions, there are three [editions]: first, the separately circulated version outside the canon, which is the ancient translation by Dharmakṣema that I am now explaining;

as the *Tianzhu Taidiao Mulü* states: "The four-fascicle *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* translated by Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang was circulated separately in the world and never entered the canon. This is it.
Someone asked: "Since there are already various translations in the canon, for what reason do you only lecture on and recite the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (Chen-jing)?
I shall now extend my explanation through two points. First, Master Zhi was active during the Chen and Sui dynasties; he passed away in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era [597 CE].

Since the translations produced under the Tang dynasty did not yet exist at that time, it is likely he had not seen them either. Therefore, the reason he lectured only on the *Śālistamba-sūtra* is surely because, among all..."

In the translation of meanings, there is neither fixed adherence nor total disregard for the two [aspects of form and meaning]. This sutra began with the Northern Liang dynasty and has passed more than a thousand years;

its flourishing recitation and the resulting spiritual responses and realizations have been manifold. It cannot be that this was not a translation by a *śāstra-mahāyāna* (a master of prophetic revelation);

surely it must be that above it accords with the Buddha’s intent and below it accords with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings. Thus, Shen Qing of Beishan said: "The Northern Liang was a minor state, yet observe how the Holy Master [Dharmakṣema]..."

The prophetic declarations (*vyākaraṇa*) translated by [Dharmakṣema] show that his country was no small one. As the Book of Chu states: "The state of Chu has no treasures; only the good is its treasure.
These words, though simple, I personally deem wise.
[The general purport of Chapter Two and Five.]
The National Preceptor Zhizhe of Tiantai realized the *dhāraṇī* of universal integration and extensively expounded the three great commentaries on the *Lotus Sūtra*.

While he provided definitive exegesis for the entirety of the sacred teachings of his lifetime, although he did not provide detailed, separate analyses for all other sūtras, his general discussion of the principles of the Great and Small Vehicles, the partial and the perfect, and the provisional and the real, is already exhaustive. Fortunately, this master also once gave a separate lecture on this [present] sūtra.

Since Master Xuánzàng’s commentary has been widely circulated, I have now composed this explanation of the scripture’s title, summarizing his text to serve as a foundation for students’ hearing and reflection.
Xuánzàng’s preface states:
"This *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is so profoundly deep and immeasurable that even the realm of great empty space cannot serve as a metaphor for it."
How could its height and breadth ever be exhausted, even by weighing it against mountains or counting its drops against the oceans?
It is the realm where all Buddhas traverse and where Bodhisattvas practice. Named "Golden," it surpasses all other jewels;

taking the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) as its essence, its meaning is the adornment traversed by the Tathāgatas, and it takes as its primary principle the profound and wondrous merits of the Bodhisattvas, shining forth brilliantly.

The hearts of all the devas were filled with joy; they regarded it as the King of Sutras by name, which gathers and encompasses all scriptures, and is constantly protected and sustained by the four Buddhas of the four directions. It is likewise so for all the three periods of time and the ten directions.
All Bodhisattvas from every other quarter pay remote homage to it, while the Four Guardian Heavenly Kings personally shed tears as they extol it, and all the devas do the same.
Covered by the majesty of Heaven and the spirits of Earth, moistened by the fertility of the Earth, augmented by great eloquence, supplemented by wisdom and merit,
and enriched by precious wealth— should anyone hear this, they will be able to contemplate the unsurpassed, subtle, wondrous, and profound meaning;
they shall open the gate of the ambrosia and enter the city of ambrosia, causing all sentient beings to partake of that ambrosia.
With the sword of wisdom, one tears asunder the net of afflictions; the torments of the three miserable realms are removed, and all states of existence are utterly withered.
To state the essential point: every unprecedented phenomenon in all the worlds appears in full manifestation.

Venturing to rely upon this meaning, I wish to set forth these words, hoping that even a drop may enter the ocean, or that birds heading toward the mountains may truly rely upon a single fragment of opportunity.
"Uniform" refers to the color yellow. If one wishes to examine the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*) of the title at the beginning of this sutra:
first, "Golden Light" constitutes the name; furthermore, there are five aspects: (1) showing the general and specific [meanings]:

all sutras spoken by the Buddha consist of words and letters, which is the general sense, whereas the three characters "Golden Light" are the specific sense, as the means of accommodation and transformation differ; (2) clarifying the translation...

The Sanskrit term *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is translated as follows: *suvarṇa* is translated as "gold" (*jinpōpo*), *prabhāsa* is translated as "light" (*kō*), and *uttama* is translated as "supreme" or "brilliant" (*mei*).
Regarding the three terms as metaphors, ancient masters used the three characters for "Gold," "Light," and "Supreme" to represent the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*) or the Three Heavens;
however, Tiantai extensively refuted this interpretation and subsequently established his own "middle way" approach.

Ten sets of three dharmas are used to explain the three characters—namely, the path (*mārga*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), nature (*prakṛti*), prajñā, bodhi, the Mahāyāna body, nirvāṇa, and the virtues of the Triple Gem.

These ten dharmas encompass the beginning and the end; their meaning contains both the direct and the reverse, as well as the horizontal and the vertical, pervading all analogies for the three dharmas.
Only thus can they accord with the intent of the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā* of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*).

Regarding the establishment of the title: although most of the preceding analogies were drawn through inferential reasoning, establishing the title based on the actual text is what makes it truly intimate and appropriate;

thus the Preface states that this is "the king among all *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* sūtras. To establish the name at the very beginning is therefore most effective. Fifth, as for the designation based on its essential nature:
the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is worthy of veneration and preciousness, hence it is called "Gold" (*suvarṇa*); it is quiescent yet eternally illuminating, hence it is called "Light" (*prabhāsa*).

Great Compassion is able to bring great benefit; "Luminous" (*prabhā*) is itself the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, a Dharma-gate that is the very essence of reality, rather than borrowing worldly gold as a metaphor for the Dharma.
Question: The ancients said that this sutra derives its name from a metaphor. Why do you now deviate from that to rely strictly on the literal text? Answer:
It is not that I am now following the literal text to the point of subverting the metaphor; rather, if one were to stubbornly cling to the metaphor, it would in turn subvert the meaning.
Regarding the words and their meaning, there are two approaches that must both be preserved: for those of dull faculties, one uses analogies to illustrate the Dharma;

for those of sharp faculties, the Dharma itself serves as the analogy. As the text below states: "Within this very scripture, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, one attains the vision of me," and it further says:
"Out of great compassion for those of dull faculties... [For] those of dull faculties cling to the stump or to the finger.
To benefit others, one need not point specifically to individual instances (the above is from the *Xuánwén*).

For example, when the former masters of the Tiantai school first explained the title through the five meanings of "interpreting the name" (*shìmíng*), they analyzed the titles established according to the seven categories to determine their respective orientations.

Most said that this sutra is named after a single metaphor (*dānpì*) to establish its definitive meaning; however, there are those who explain it as being named after a single dharma (*dānfǎ*) without losing the metaphorical aspect.

It was solely the Dharma Master Siming who understood this; thus the *Shiyiji* states: "One should know that the three characters of this sutra’s separate title indicate it is a discourse on the Dharma, not a parable.
It describes the Tathāgata wandering within the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*, dwelling in this samādhi and then proclaiming:
'This is the King of All Sutras, the Golden Radiance. Is this not a direct pointing to *dharmatā*?"
The title is *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, not "the Dharma-nature is like gold and light.

Regarding the metaphors established in the subsequent text, one interpretation holds that various masters explained *suvarṇaprabhāsa* as referring to worldly objects; in fact, they did not understand the perfect integration of dharmic characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
The Great Master, wishing to demonstrate that the ocean of *suvarṇaprabhāsa* contains all dharmas in harmonious completeness, followed the interpretations of those masters.
Using three characters as metaphors to fully illustrate the ten sets of three dharmas is insufficient, for the analogies employed do not encompass all aspects of the dharmas being compared.

Although these metaphors follow the intent of others to clarify the dharmas, they fail to accord with the fact that the title of this sutra represents the dharmas themselves rather than a metaphor. Therefore, I shall subsequently provide two interpretations based on the text itself:

one according to the literal phrasing (*fu-wen*) and one according to the essential substance (*dang-ti*). This serves to refute those who argue that the metaphors are remote and distant from the meaning; instead, one must rely upon the sutra and approach the dharmas directly.

Regarding the question of whether the single dharma (ekadharma) established by the Four Ming [Masters] is intended to be comprehensive or partial, I maintain that *Shiyi* (The Omissions Supplemented) profoundly grasps the profound intent of the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning of the Text) concerning the principles of "affirmation" (*zong*) and "negation" (*duo*).
Specifically, it is said that while the Tiantai [Master Zhiyi] first employed affirmation, the ancient masters extensively elaborated on the meaning based on their own interpretations;

however, their analogies for comparing other things were incomplete. Subsequently, through negation, they returned to the text to show that the single dharma is to be understood as the very essence of the phenomenon itself.
The fixed title is established based on the text as "Approaching.

Second, the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is the essence; this essence is the primary substance of this single sutra. If this sutra is taken according to its meaning, it has the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) as its essence;

if taken according to the text, it has the dharma-nature as its essence. While the term "dharma-nature" is general, here—[it refers to... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on a Buddhist scripture, likely concerning the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* or a similar Mahāyāna text. The translation reflects the technical terminology of Chinese Buddhist scholasticism.)

The Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) entered by the Buddha constitutes its essence. This essence is the destination toward which all various practices converge, just as the myriad stars revolve around the North Star or as the ten thousand streams flow toward the Eastern Sea. Therefore, one should know that the Dharma-nature is the primary essence of this sutra;
the interpretation of the "essence" (*tattva*) in the *Liturgy for Paying Homage* is identical in intent to the "Dharma-nature" of this sutra. Thus it is said, "The Tathāgata..."

That which is the sphere of its activity is the dharma of ultimate nobility; furthermore, "essence" (tī) has the meaning of "bottom" (tala), for one who attains this essence reaches the source and the very bottom;
furthermore, "essence" has the meaning of "penetration," for one who attains this essence penetrates all different names and distinct explanations.
The thesis is that the constant fruit of the three bodies is the essential core; "thesis" (zong) here means the vital point.

This sutra specifically employs the Buddha-fruit as its essential core because the *dharmatā* is profoundly deep and subtle-miraculous; if one wishes to manifest it, it cannot be accomplished except through the fruit.
One should know that the fruit is the pivotal key for manifesting the essence—just as when the main rope is pulled, the mesh of the net becomes orderly. As the Sutra says: "Śākyamuni Tathāgata..."
The lifespan attained by Śākyamuni is the person who has realized the fruit; the measure of that lifespan is the dharma of the fruit.

That the person who realizes the fruit accords with the dharma-nature (dharmatā) is such that the four Buddhas, when severing doubts, raised up Mount Meru and weighed it against a scale, yet none were able to know its quantity.
This clarifies that while the eighty years are impermanent, even their permanence cannot be known—how much less can one know that they are not [permanent]?
If one does not rely upon the fruit [of Buddhahood] to explain that permanence is neither [simply] permanent nor impermanent, this meaning is difficult to clarify;
therefore, the three bodies as the fruit of permanence constitute the essential core of this sutra.

Fourth, its function is to extinguish evil and give rise to good. "Function" refers to efficacy; because this sutra extinguishes evil, it is said to possess power, and because it gives rise to good, it is said to possess efficacy.
Because it is good, it is said that this is used as a partial illustration; suffering is the evil fruit, while the three poisons are the evil causes.
Since the evil causes are not eliminated, the evil fruits do not cease. Therefore, the Sage first causes the elimination of the evil causes, which is why the "Chapter on Repentance" comes first.
Happiness is the good fruit, while repentance and praise are the good causes. Because evil is extinguished and good arises, the "Chapter on Praise" follows.
The subsequent "Chapter on Repentance" eliminates evil without failing to produce goodness; the "Chapter on Praise" produces goodness without failing to eliminate evil;

the "Chapter on Emptiness" guides one toward the accomplishment of eliminating evil and producing goodness; and from the Four Heavenly Kings downward, the protection and circulation of the sutra are all instances of producing goodness and eliminating evil.
Therefore, the power and function of this sutra consist in the elimination of evil and the production of goodness.
The *Vaipulya* (fangděng) sutras of the five directions constitute the teaching-as-appearance (*jiaoxiang*). "Teaching" refers to the words spoken by the Sages for the sake of those below;
"appearance" refers to the analysis of similarities and differences. Regarding the teaching-as-appearance of this sutra: if one establishes it as *Prajñā*, the timing differs;

if one enters it as the convergence of the three [vehicles], the flavor is distinct. According to the sutra, there was once a bhikṣu who recited and chanted the Mahāyāna *Vaipulya* scriptures. Once...
If one asks whether the Vaipulya (fangděng) is not indeed a textual category, the teaching of the Vaipulya is common to those of the three vehicles.

If this is so, then according to the principle of the five flavors, it should be subsumed under the flavor of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Regarding the principles elucidated in the four *piṭakas*, it is included within the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*.

Regarding the principles elucidated in the four teachings, it corresponds to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-naya*). Within the Shared Teaching, one may discuss that which "retains the distinct" (*bié*).
The *Mingyuan* (Exposition on Illumination) has already explained at length that this sutra belongs to the latter part of the Vaipulya (fangděng),
referring to the *Prajñāpāramitā* as having already extensively expounded emptiness (*śūnyatā*). As for its current classification as Vaipulya,
it was grouped with the preceding [texts] by the compilers because their thematic affinities were identical.

The *Shiyiji* (Records of the Supplementary Omissions) presents the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*) as follows: "Profound" (*xuan*) refers to that which is obscure and subtle, difficult to perceive;

"meaning" (*yi*) refers to the depth of the principles and their underlying causes. Within this profound and subtle meaning there are five layers: first, the names that can express the beginning and end of a scripture;

second, the essence (*svabhāva*) invoked by those names; third, the principle (*tattva*) of that very essence; fourth, the power and function (*vṛtti*) established by that principle; and fifth, the scope—both general and specific—of these four verbal teachings.

The Great Master [Zhiyi], having investigated and extracted these five meanings to explain this single title, intended for students to first understand the purport of the sutra before examining the text, thereby enabling them to cultivate wisdom and practice. This is the cause for upholding the Dharma at the site of enlightenment;

arising from stillness and in accord with the Buddha’s mind, he expounded these profound meanings. Therefore, it cannot be compared to those who rely on obscure realization or merely follow the literal text.
And thus it was spoken. ○ Third,
as for the threefold division of the text,

my ancestors followed the distinct method of interpreting the scriptural text established by the Dharma Master Dao’an of the Eastern Jin dynasty, dividing it into the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Circulation.
In the *Tri-skandhaka-sūtra*, the [sections on] arising and ceasing serve as the basis for the "wondrous seal" (*miao qi*) established by [Paramārtha];

thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* by Vasubandhu became the standard rule. (The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* states: Formerly, during the Later Qin, Emperor Yao Xing issued an edict for a monk to lecture on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.

However, the monk merely read the text aloud without any structural divisions. The Emperor said: "I have heard that the Buddha-way is profound and mysterious, and the purport of the sūtras is deep and esoteric. How can it be explained so directly, with almost no chapters or sections? The monks had no response, and the report spread in all four directions. At that time, Master An of Xiangyang heard of this and sighed, saying: "How is it that...")

Our school likewise received this censure; therefore, we examined the *Āgama* section, regardless of its size, establishing it according to the three stages of introduction, main body, and circulation. From this point onward, the treatises began and concluded with these divisions. When the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang dynasty translated the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*, the text indeed stated:

"The sūtra contains three parts in total: first, the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, the section on what is expounded in the holy teaching; third, the section on practicing in accordance with the teaching.

This sufficiently demonstrates that the assertions of [Dao]an were implicitly in accord with the sūtras and śāstras. Regarding Tiantai’s adherence to those established rules, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-vyākhyāna* states: "Whether a sūtra is large or small, it is customarily divided into three sections. This refers to what is called the three [sections] of this sūtra.
Regarding the divisions:
first, the introductory section (*nidāna*) comprises one chapter and a half. The commentary on the sutra states: "This sutra consists of four fascicles and eighteen chapters;

the manner of dividing them has varied since ancient times... (and so forth). Now, following the traditional division from "Thus have I heard" up through the *Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*, it concludes with the "Assembly of Devas and Nāgas."

The introductory section of the Śraddhālakṣaṇa Bodhisattva’s chamber consists of three parts: first, the sequential introduction, also called the general introduction (*sūtra-pūrva-nimitta*), which comprises the five elements beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*);

second, the narrative introduction, also called the specific introduction (*viśeṣa-pūrva-nimitta*), which extends from "At that time, the Tathāgata was dwelling in the immeasurable and profound *dharmatā*" up to "the chamber of the Śraddhālakṣaṇa Bodhisattva. This is the relevant passage.

Within the text of the sutra, there are seven distinct sections: first, the section on the Tathāgata entering meditative concentration; second, the section describing seventeen chapters of the sutra text;

third, the section on Faith-Mark harboring doubts; fourth, the section on the ten kinds of auspicious omens; fifth, the section on Faith-Mark expressing his doubts; sixth, the section on the four Buddhas quelling those doubts;

seventh, the section on the assembly of devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings; and eighth, the section on the three introductory prologues, beginning with [the Buddha] emerging from his chamber.
However, the extensive and solemn matters are contained within the seventh section below.
Second, the Main Body of the Teaching (*śarīra-bhāga*) consists of three and a half chapters of scripture, from "At that time, the four Buddhas, amidst the great assembly...

down to the end of the *Śūnyatā-parivarta*, which constitutes the Section of the Correct Exposition. This section contains four sub-sections: first, from "At that time, the four Buddhas... down to... [end of fragment].

1. The Chapter on Life Span (Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta) establishes the doctrine of permanence to reveal the essence; 2. The Chapter on Repentance (Pratikarman-parivarta) specifically discusses the function of eliminating evil while also concurrently producing goodness;
3. The Chapter on Praise (Stuti-parivarta) specifically discusses the function of producing goodness while also concurrently eliminating evil;
4. The Chapter on Emptiness (Śūnyatā-parivarta) leads to the perfection of both producing goodness and eliminating evil.

The third part, the *Pravartana* (Circulation) section, consists of thirteen chapters from the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" (*Caturmahārājakāyika-parivarta*) through the end of the scripture; these are all texts for circulation.

There are seven sections in total: first, from the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" through the "Chapter on Vaiśravaṇa" (*Saṃjñeya-parivarta*), it clarifies how the Heavenly Kings make vows to exhort and encourage human kings to widely propagate this [scripture].
This further comprises five parts: first, the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings," which explains how the power of the heavenly deities protects those who request [the teaching].
Second, the "Chapter on Great Eloquence," which pledges to augment the eloquence of the speaker; third, the "Chapter on Merit," which pledges to enrich the petitioner with material wealth;
fourth, the "Chapter on the Earth Deity," which pledges to benefit the place of the petition and the site of the discourse with the essence of the earth;
fifth, the "Chapter on Vaiśravaṇa," which pledges to establish security through martial prowess for those who petition, speak, and listen. This is the second [section].
Chapter Three: "The King of Men Who Widely Propagates the Sūtra and the Heavenly Kings Who Assist and Protect," which explains the correct doctrine and the skillful gathering [of the assembly].
Chapter Four: "The Spirits and Deities Who Guard and Protect upon Hearing the Sūtra," which clarifies the heavenly deities and terrestrial spirits who provide protection.

Chapter Five: "The Bestowal of Prophecy," which certifies that the merit of hearing the sūtra is not in vain. Chapter Six: "The Flowing Water That Cures Illness," which cites the power of hearing the sūtra in the past.
The seventh chapter, "Praising the Buddha," elucidates how the benefits of extolling the Buddha’s Dharma are profound and weighty. The commentary states:
"The Prologue" refers to that which is about to bring benefit;
"The Main Body" refers to the discernment of the Way according to the needs of the audience; and "The Circulation" refers to...
"Flow" (liú) refers to downward pouring; "continuity" (tōng) refers to being unobstructed.

This is intended so that the waters of the True Dharma may flow from now on, following the vessel of the Holy Teaching, without being blocked in future ages. When the sutras speak of what are called superior, middling, and inferior words—all being excellent—this is precisely the meaning of these three divisions.

Someone may raise this doubt: "For what reason is the introductory section (*nidāna*) included within the 'Chapter on the Duration of Life' (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*)? The commentary explains this as follows: "This is the standard pattern for all sutras.

For example, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, there is no separate 'Introductory Chapter,' and the introduction is contained within the main discourse; in the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the main discourse is contained within the introductory chapter;
and in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the introductory section is included within the main body. All sutras are like this; why should this one alone be an exception?"
Those who are confused about the intent of this sutra likely do so because the four Buddhas sever doubts in isolation;
thus, the introduction is cited within the section on the Lifespan (*āyuṣpramāṇa*), and based on this meaning, the chapters are divided unevenly. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-vyākhyā* states:
"The 'Radiance' chapter and the 'Introduction' are identical in content. This was a chapter-title established by the translator and was neither composed by the Buddha nor [authorized by] Ānanda.
It was recorded at the time of the difficult compilation.
○ Fourth, the Arising of the Various Chapters:
The three major divisions of the preceding outline constitute the general framework from beginning to end of this sutra; now, following the *Wenju*, they are restated.
The sequential arising of these eighteen chapters follows the order of the text;
that it unfolds in this manner clearly demonstrates that every chapter of the Tathāgata’s teaching has its own underlying cause and purpose.
Regarding the "Introductory Chapter": The Dharma does not operate in isolation, but arises by depending upon conditions.

Desiring to expound the life-span of the three bodies, the two kinds of emptiness, and the repentance and praise [of the Buddhas] to guide and benefit all sentient beings, the Tathāgata, after having preached the *Prajñāpāramitā*, descended to Vulture Peak.

There, he surveyed the capacities and conditions of the assembly and perceived that they would inevitably harbor doubts concerning his own lifespan. Thereupon, he entered into the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), and upon emerging, he recited twenty-seven verses in advance.
Because the text of the seventeen chapters is introduced here, the "Preface Chapter" (Nidāna-varga) is placed at the beginning.

Once the Tathāgata had finished his narration, the conditions of the disciples and the Buddha’s response coincided; thus, those with faith and wisdom recognized the Buddha and entered meditative absorption.

Furthermore, upon hearing in various sūtras that the Buddha had told Māra he would enter parinirvāṇa, doubts arose as to how the Buddha could say that by practicing non-killing and giving food, one gains longevity.

Regarding the statement that the Buddha’s life span was eighty years: when one contemplates this meaning—that the Buddha proclaimed his entry into extinction at age eighty—one is moved to reflect on how the four Buddhas entered the chamber, using a drop of water as a metaphor for a mountain, a grain of dust for the earth, and so forth, to illustrate the vastness of Śākyamuni’s lifespan.
This causes the faithful practitioner to deeply penetrate the Dharma-body and Reward-body, fully awakening to the three bodies as one essence; therefore, the "Chapter on the Lifespan" is placed next.

Although his marks of faith have already removed doubt and he has permanently ascended to dwell upon the stage of perfection (*pariniṣpanna-bhūmi*), he considers how the three bodies (*trikāya*) and the lifespan of the inherent nature-virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) possessed by all sentient beings are realized.

Desiring to overturn and shatter the obstacles of delusion for such beings and to manifest the power and function of the Sūtra, his marks of faith accord with his former vows; he enters the "Dream-like Samādhi" and in a dream beholds a golden drum.

On the following morning, after reciting the Verses of Repentance for Non-arising (*anutpāda*), he went before the Buddha and presented his petition once more so that the fourfold assembly might hear it;
having heard it, they practiced, and through practice, they realized [the truth].

Thus, there is the Chapter on Repentance (*Pratikramana-parivarta*). After Xinxiang had finished presenting his repentance, the Tathāgata, seeking the source by tracing the flow, spoke of his previous life as a golden dragon.
The Venerable One praised the Dharma King with verses, praying that in future lives he might dream of a golden drum at night and speak of it as it truly is during the day;
since today’s fruit has indeed fulfilled this vow, this "Chapter of Praise" was composed to recount these events.
The chapter on Repentance is dedicated exclusively to destroying evil, while the chapter on Praise is dedicated exclusively to generating goodness.

If these two were not accompanied by emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they would both fail to achieve their purpose; for one wishes to use the two types of emptiness—of phenomena and of persons—to guide and perfect repentance and praise, thereby manifesting the power and function of the sutra.
Therefore, the Buddha briefly expounds the Chapter on Emptiness here.

The Buddha’s exposition of the first three and a half chapters of this sutra, which elucidates the Path according to the capacities of those present, being thus concluded, the Four Heavenly Kings heard it and their hearts were filled with both sorrow and joy.

Thereupon, they respectfully addressed the Buddha six times, exhorting the king to widely proclaim this sutra so that the people of the realm might enjoy peace and security, and so that it might circulate without obstruction; hence there is the chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings.
Although the Four Heavenly Kings protect and circulate [this teaching], if there were no one capable of expounding it, this Path would ultimately not flourish.
Therefore, the Goddess of Eloquence, by means of her original spiritual power, vowed to augment those who speak and those who listen with wisdom and eloquence;
hence, there is the "Chapter on the Great Goddess of Eloquence."
Even if the speaker and the listener possess eloquence, if they lack the provision of the four requisites, it will be difficult for them to settle their bodies and devote themselves to the Way.
For this reason, the Goddess Śrī provides them with wealth and treasures so that they may be fully supplied with what is needed;
only then can the Great Teaching flourish. Therefore, the "Chapter on the Goddess Guṇavatī" is spoken.

Once the benefit for those who preach and listen has been fully realized, if the realm should become unstable and famine, pestilence, and various evils arise in competition, the flow of the Dharma will be obstructed.

Thereupon, the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā, by the power of the protection of the Dharma, will cause the essence of the earth to well up as rich, fatty moisture, so that the hundred grains may flourish in abundance and the five fruits may grow luxuriantly; from this, people will come to delight in practicing the giving of wisdom.
Out of deep faith in the Triple Gem, this first chapter on the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā is presented.
As for the General Vajrapāṇi (Candraprabha), his original ground is profound and remote;

he is a true Bodhisattva who, seeing this sutra, has circulated it through expedient manifestations as a ghostly form, commanding the twenty-eight divisions with valor and martial prowess, and guarding [the Dharma] day and night.
To protect those who preach, recite, and chant, so that all their evils may be extinguished until they encounter a Buddha and attain the path of Bodhi,
there is the Chapter on Vajrapāṇi (Sanzhi).
All the devas and spirits have together made a solemn vow to ensure that human kings do not forget the entrustment of our Buddha.
One should govern the state and family with the True Dharma so that it may circulate from this point forward without obstruction.
Because the Buddha wished to exhort the kings of men with this, he spoke the "Chapter on Righteous Discourse.
Now that the Buddha has already expounded the Righteous Discourse to assist the family and state, the fourfold assembly remains unaware of the supramundane right view.

Moved by this, the Buddha recounted how, in the past, he had accumulated merit as King Saṃcita, who renounced the precious jewels of the four continents to offer them to the Jewel-like Samantagambhīra (Bao-ming) so that he might hear the sutra.
Subsequently, for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, he occupied the positions of a Wheel-turning King, a Brahmā, and Śakra.
Now, having attained the body of the True Dharma, he cites the past to verify the present; therefore, he proclaims the "Chapter on Saṃcita."
The retribution for hearing the sutras is such as this; the merit of listening to the Dharma is repeatedly extolled.

For this reason, the great Bodhisattvas, through their unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*), manifest themselves as deities, dragons, the sun, the moon, rivers, and other spirits by means of skillful means (*upāya*). They propagate the teachings throughout the world to benefit those who lecture upon and recite them;
hence there is the category of ghosts and spirits.

The "Praise by Ghosts and Spirits" chapter provides benefits only for the present; however, because it is intended to cause those who hear this sutra to swiftly attain the higher stages and thereby demonstrate that the propagation of the sutra is not in vain,
the narrative describes how the three great bodhisattvas and ten thousand devaputras attained the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*) upon hearing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
and how the Buddha bestowed predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) upon them— hence there is the "Chapter on Bestowing Predictions."
The tree deity suspected that the various devaputras had descended briefly to listen to the Dharma and would immediately receive their predictions of enlightenment.

The Buddha then explained their past causes: in the past, there was an elder named Jālin who cured the illnesses of the multitude; the "Jālin" referred to was actually his son, Jalavāhana, who saved the fish.
This was the Buddha’s remote narration of the causal origins; for this reason, he spoke of the chapter on "Curing Illnesses" together with the others.
Having finished explaining the distant precedent, the proximate cause shall now be proclaimed. The Buddha himself declared: "In the past, when I was a son of the Water-Holder, my name was Jalavāhana.

Once, arriving at a desolate marsh, I saw ten thousand fish on the verge of death. Unable to bear seeing them writhing in agony, I gave rise to a *saṃnāha-citta* (the mind of armor) and provided them with water and food, while teaching them the causes and conditions of their existence.
By the merit of hearing this in the morning, they were fortunate enough to die that very evening."

Having already established a great karmic affinity in his previous life when he was born as a result of his retribution in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he attained awakening upon hearing [the teaching] but once today;
because this answer was spoken for the sake of the tree deity Vardhamāna, there is the "Chapter on the Elder’s Son Jalavāhana."

As the Tathāgata was about to conclude his teaching of this sutra and the transmission of the Way, he feared that those who propagate the scripture might be stingy with the Dharma or stingy with wealth, and thus unable to sacrifice their bodies for the sake of the Dharma.
Therefore, by means of his supernormal power, the Buddha caused the great earth to tremble, causing the Stūpa of the Original Being (Sattva) to emerge.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One arose, paid homage to the tree deity, and inquired from him regarding the past deeds of renunciation. The Buddha then recounted the former sacrifices.

In all cases where one feeds a tiger with one's own body, it is a vow to seek the subtle and wondrous Dharma-body; because this Jātaka story serves as an exhortation for disciples who are greedy and stingy, there is the chapter on "Sacrificing the Body.

The Buddha taught this single sutra so that it would be good from beginning to end—perfect in its commencement, middle, and conclusion—and thus three times the Bodhisattva moved the Buddha to respond.
Because the grace of the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma and his deliverance of sentient beings is so profound, they praise the World-Honored One’s true merits with one voice and in unison;
therefore, the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha" is appended at the end of this volume.
V. Distinguishing the Correct from the Erroneous:
This scripture has been in circulation for a long time, and its textual corruptions are particularly numerous.

Upon examining the canon and conducting a comparative study, I found that only the eight-fascicle *Guangming* (Radiant Light) version contained within the *Hebu* (Combined) collection was attributed to Dharmarakṣa’s translation; yet it contains several discrepancies. This is likely because the text was revised by various masters.

The translation has been revised to this extent; now, in order to establish the correct version, I have cited more than twenty passages from the *Samyuktāgama* to corroborate it using the doctrinal texts of the Tiantai school.
By examining the wording and verifying the facts, I have restored the ancient edition.

Since Master Zhizhe lectured only on the *Ekottarāgama* and did not see the *Samyuktāgama*, other discrepancies were either based upon commentaries and records or inferred through specialized reasoning; provided that [the corrections] remain within these bounds...
In principle, it may well be fortunate that one should not discard the words because of the person.
Regarding the character *zài* (in) in the *Zhǔwángshè Dàchéng Hé bù zhù zuò zài zì bié xíng chàn běn*, some versions use *zài* based on the *Hé bù*.
The *Guānjīng Shū* states: "To stay for a short time is called *zài*; to remain for a long duration is called *zhù*; these are merely provisional expressions."

The *Vimalakīrti Record* states: "At the beginning of all sūtras, the two characters 'dwelling' (*zhù*) appear; their names differ but their meaning is the same, and the translators have selected them accordingly.
Thus, although it is said that the names differ while the meaning remains the same, one should know that this sūtra originally used the character "dwelling" (*zhù*).
Therefore, the commentary says: "'Dwelling' refers to the Buddha as the person who dwells, and the royal city as the place where he dwells. Based on this, the [textual] decision is made.
The character "讖" (chan) is originally the character "住" (zhu).
Under the phrase "each and every one [is] angry and disputing," this was omitted during the translation; because people do not believe it, Tiantai has already supplemented it.
Those who read this sutra must know this, which is why the commentary states: "each and every one is angry and disputing."
These two phrases should be present; they have either been omitted during translation or were originally concise in the sacred text.
For internally, there is mutual strife and contention, while externally, everyone lacks faith. These two points constitute a violation of the precept against false speech:
having previously deceived others with untruths, one is now constantly deceived and provoked to anger; having previously spoken without substance, people [now...]
Those who lack faith [should know that] cause and effect are manifest. *Fèn* (忿) is pronounced with the *fěn* (粉) radical; it means resentment and anger.
"Extensive and solemn practice" (*guǎngbó yánshì*) follows the *Yánjìng* (嚴淨) recension of the *Hébù* (合部); there are also those who follow the *Hébù*. The commentary states:
because it is adorned with various merits, it is called "solemn practice. Since Tiantai relied upon the *Yánshì* recension for his lectures...
Upon verifying the original text of the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), the reading "the words are correct" is the authentic one.

As for the phrase "gazing upon the Honored Countenance without momentarily averting the eyes," since this phrase does not exist in the original prophecy and is likewise missing from the combined edition, it should be understood that these words belong to the compilers of the sutra; were they removed, the preceding sentence would remain abruptly truncated.

If one maintains these two phrases, one’s sincerity will become manifest; moreover, since both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Bhadracarī-praṇidhāna* maintain them, it is evident that these two phrases must not be omitted from this scripture.

For instance, while the *Tianzhenjinhebu* (The Combined Edition of the Heavenly True Gold) reads "just like true gold," the separately circulated *Chenben* (Prophecy Text) or [other versions] read "just like heaven."
"Gold is entirely indeterminate. The commentary on the *Śāstra* explains: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* compares temporal iron to temporal gold;
temporal gold to ocean gold; ocean gold to nāga gold; nāga gold to Jambudvīpa gold; Jambudvīpa gold to the gold of the Four Heavenly Kings;
and so on in succession up to the gold of the sixth heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin. It is compared thus.
The gold of the Buddha’s body is like the gold of the sixth heaven, which is as common as iron compared to it; thus, the gold of the Buddha’s body surpasses all else.
Once, when the Buddha entered a city, he emitted a golden light that illuminated the ground. A woman prostrated herself, and her golden hairpin fell to the earth, yet she could not see it.
Only after the Buddha had departed did she find it. According to the current text, if one were to say it is like natural, refined gold...

Regarding the phrase "like celestial gold," there is no sense in which the gold of the Buddha’s body surpasses it; one should carefully examine its meaning and take "just like pure gold" as the correct interpretation.

The *Fahua jing ceyao* (Essentials of the Lotus Sutra) states that the character "jiao" (校) is correctly written as "jiao" (鉸), which the *Guangyun* defines as "decorative clasp" (*zhuangjiao*), referring to gold.
It is a jade ornament. Furthermore, it is like when Emperor Xuan of the Han dynasty once bestowed a carriage with a black canopy upon Huo Guang and had it entirely adorned with gold fittings;
the characters "yan" (verify) and "jiao" (examine) there are incorrect.

It is just as the *Guofo hebu* (Combined Sections on Passing the Buddha) was made into the *Yufu bixing chan* (Separate Prophecy on Encountering the Buddha), where "guo" (passing) and "yu" (encountering) are not fixed; one should know that they are interchangeable.
The character "zi" (字) is a corruption of "dao-bi" (刀筆); the intended meaning of the scripture is likely that it is just as the Buddhas of the past have accomplished.

Regarding the phrase "the subtle and wondrous spoken [teachings]" (所說微玅), some versions of the *Biexing chan* (別行讖) read "hearing the subtle and wondrous" (聞說微玅), while the *Hebu* (合部) version also uses the character "wen" (聞).

Now, observing the intent of what has come from above and below, the character "suo" (所) is taken as correct; this refers to what is called "correct mindfulness and contemplation," which is the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate taught by all Buddhas.
In the *Hebu* (Combined) edition, it is also rendered as "laoju" (牢固), while in the separate *Xingchan* (Practice) edition, it is written as "laoju."

Regarding "firm" (*kaṅkha*), it is said here that "firm" (*kaṅ*) is itself "solid" (*kha*), and "solid" (*kha*) is also "firm" (*kaṅ*). If one intends the meaning of "securely fastened," this is not the case.
In antiquity, when prisons were constructed, those of the Yin dynasty were called *Yǒulǐ*, those of the Zhou dynasty were called *Língyǔ*, and they were also named *Láo*.
One should know that the stagnation of sentient beings within the three realms of existence is like a prison; thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All sentient beings..."

To dwell amidst the turbidity of afflictions within the triple world is precisely what is meant by being imprisoned in the fortress of suffering. This sutra likens the bonds of birth and death to a net;
furthermore, the subsequent phrase "firm and solid" (*láo*) likewise corresponds to the hardships of a prison.
While the Buddha’s words contain many layers of meaning, the character *láo* (firm/solid) is taken here as the primary sense.
Regarding the phrase "like a mass of molten gold," the *Praise of the Buddha* chapter uses the character 鎔 (*róng*) for both instances; here, however, the character 融 (*róng*) is used.
While it carries the meanings of "convergence," "clarity," and "luminosity," it ultimately does not convey the sense as effectively as 鎔 (*róng*), which refers to the casting of pure gold.
This is used to compare the excellence of the Buddha’s golden body, whose radiance is like that of cast gold, as described in the *Sutra of Forty-two Sections*.
The postscript states, "Gold becomes even more radiant when melted," which is precisely the point.

Furthermore, since this sutra also contains expressions such as "like casting a gold ingot" and "like refining pure gold," these passages serve as proof that the character in question must be read as *róng* (melted).

In the *Kongpin* (Chapter on Emptiness) according to the separate edition of Baoshen’s translation, there is either a prose section at the beginning of this chapter along with two lines of verse which state:
"At that time, the Buddha further spoke a verse for the Bodhisattva, the Earth Goddess Bhadraśrī.
Furthermore, at the end of the chapter, there are four lines of verse which state: "With a joyful heart, he practices giving, his mind free from..."
"Cherishing the contemplation that the nature of phenomena is empty is the unsurpassed wisdom"—who among those who see such scriptural passages would not doubt their authenticity?
Now, by examining the *Hebu* (Combined) edition, we know that these were added by later retranslators;

Master Gui’s version should instead belong to the *Shiloujiachen* (Śīlabhadra) edition. It is likely that the text from the *Hebu* edition was indiscriminately appended to the separately circulating *Shiloujiachen* edition.
Some have claimed that the two ancient records—the *Gushan* and *Huguo*—both state that later generations falsely added [these verses], which is incorrect.
Now, examining the commentary, it explains this chapter by stating there are forty-five lines of verse, with nothing else provided as an interpretation.
Verifying the original *Chen* manuscript, it is evident that these did not originally exist; they should therefore be excised.
I shall now explain that there are two versions of the *Bie xing chan* (Separate Practice Prophecy): one reads "Now I" (*jin wo*) and the other reads "I now" (*wo jin*).
When combined into a single edition, it is titled *Jin wo*. This discrepancy often arises due to the combined version. The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "I shall now explain" (*wo jin yan shuo*), "explain" (*yan*) means to expand, which is the opposite of brevity. Following this interpretation, we should take "I now" (*wo jin*) as the correct reading.
This should be integrated with other translations.

Regarding the phrase "arising through the conjunction of these three" (*saṃnipāta*) found in this chapter—wherein it is said that this [text] exists through the conjunction of the final causes and conditions of conceptual construction (*parikalpa*)—the various prefectures of Zhexi (Zhejiang) have altered the characters used for recitation to "generated characters" (*shēngzì*). Here, we shall now follow [the standard].
The commentary states: "The two phrases, 'arising through the combination of causes and conditions of deluded thought,' clarify the object of the provisional contemplation (*jia-guan*).
As for the original text [of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*], one should not arbitrarily alter it.

Regarding the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, some versions write it as *Pílóuhé* (毗樓合), and even within the combined editions, the character *liú* (留) is used; this is according to the Chinese phonetic transcription."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and various sūtras frequently use the term "Vilou," from which we know that both characters [of "Vilou-le-che"] are transliterations of the Sanskrit sound,
differing only in their light or heavy tonal weight. Now, examining the commentary, which translates "Vilouleche" (毗留勒叉) as "Increasing" (增長),
we know that the character "Liu" (留) is the original form in this sūtra.
"Planned to go and punish" (*gui wang daofa*) means that the various provinces were in accord with this prophecy. Alternatively, it is said "personally went" (*qin wang*);

this was altered by later generations who saw that the state had instances of a personal military expedition (*qinzheng*). The character *gui* (planned) in the *Siming Ji* (Records of Siming) is taken as "regularly planning and seeking.
To "take by means of the Dharma" (*yi fa qu zhi*) is to "punish" (*daochu*). The precedent in the *Zhuan* (Commentary) states: "When there are bells and drums, it is called 'punishing' (*daofa*)."
This refers to military expeditions; alternatively, some editions read "punishment" (*fá*), meaning to humiliate or exact a fine as atonement, which is not the intended meaning of the scripture.

Regarding the phrase "the realm over which one rules" (*shēn suǒ wáng lǐng*): in certain versions of the *Chèn-běn* (Prophecy Text), it is written as "the realm over which one rules and leads" (*shēn suǒ wáng tǒng lǐng*).

However, even the combined editions lack the character "leads" (*tǒng*). Here, "wáng" is pronounced as *bà*, referring to a hegemon (*bà-wáng*). As the *Guó-yǔ* states: "A hegemon (*bà*) is a 'grasper' (*bǎ'); he grasps and holds the feudal lords."

The meaning conveyed by the character "King" (王) alone is already sufficient; if the character "Govern" (統) is added, the wording becomes redundant while the principle is diminished, such that both the word and its significance become inappropriate.

Furthermore, regarding the Mother of Ghosts (Kumbhakarṇī), she is accompanied by five hundred ghost-children as a single group acting as her sons; in a separate version of the *Chenben* (Prophecy Text), these are referred to as "son-ghosts."
Regarding the designation "Son of Heaven" (兒子), it is based on the *Hebu* (Combined Edition). If people do not see the *Hebu*, they will claim it is an error of the scribe's brush.
Now, it is said that the original *Chen* (Prophecy) text was "Son of Ghosts" (鬼子); subsequently, because the *Hebu* existed in a re-translation, the distinction arose.
If one says "Son of Heaven," it is a title used in relation to the Mother; if one says "Son of Ghosts," it is a description based on his appearance. They are one and the same.
When consulting both [the *Vinaya*] and the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-vaibhāṣika* (Piniye) in detail, one should take the "Ghosts' Child" (*Hārītī*) as the correct standard.

Her original name was the Yakṣiṇī Prahlāda; because she later gave birth to five hundred ghosts who devoured the men and women of the royal city, they called her Hārītī, which translates as "Mother of Ghosts. As for the term "five hundred sons," it refers to the children of this mother.
To name him "Son" (putra) or to use a specific title for the child emphasizes both the literal meaning and the underlying intent.

If one says "Demon-Son" (rākṣasa-putra), the term "demon" refers to his physical form, while "son" is a designation relative to his mother; thus, it implies that a demon-mother gave birth to a demon-child, much like the common proverb: "dragons beget dragons, and phoenixes beget phoenixes."

Regarding the phrase "hearing this fragrance," the *Combined Edition* (Hebu) reads "hearing this wondrous fragrance" (*miaoxiang*), while the *Separate Recension of the Prophecy* (Biexing chanben) also has "wondrous fragrance.
One should follow the *Combined Edition*. It should be understood that this chapter consists of two sections concerning the human kings' offering of incense; this is the latter section.

As for the first instance where the fragrance pervades the celestial palaces, there are two [instances]; the "wondrous fragrance" here refers to the incense canopies extending vertically through both above and below.
In the subsequent section concerning the fragrance pervading the ten directions, it says that various fragrances not only pervade this [world], but even reach the Buddhas;
when recording what they smell, it states, "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, also smell this fragrance," which likewise connects the upper and lower realms.
In this context, if one were to say "smell this wondrous fragrance," there would be a discrepancy between the upper and lower sections; therefore, what is used here is as follows.
It is not grasped.
That fragrance pervades the three thousandfold great thousandfold world system, including ten billion suns and moons.
This scripture states that within the great thousandfold world system there are nine such sets of ten billion; this is an error in the translation, as the commentaries and records do not explain why.
To begin with, I shall first indicate their number and subsequently point out their distinctions. The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

"One thousand sets of the four great continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the desire-realm heavens, and the Brahma-worlds, are called a 'small chiliocosm' (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*). The commentary explains:

This means that one sun and one moon, illuminating the four continents, constitute a single world-system. One thousand such suns and moons, along with one thousand Mount Sumerus, [constitute a small chiliocosm].
A thousand of the six heavens of the desire realm, covered by one second dhyāna heaven, is called a small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*).
The verse further states: "A thousand of these small chiliocosms is called a medium chiliocosm. The commentary explains: "These 'thousands' refer to the aforementioned small chiliocosms;
when a thousand such small chiliocosms are accumulated and covered by one third dhyāna heaven, it is called a medium chiliocosm."
The *Chān jiè yě sòng* (Verses on the Thousandfold World System) further states: "A thousand times this [thousandfold world] constitutes a great trichiliocosm;
all of these undergo formation and destruction simultaneously. The commentary explains: "This 'thousand' refers to the aforementioned intermediate chiliocosms.

By accumulating one thousand of these intermediate chiliocosms, and covering them from above with a single heaven of the fourth dhyāna, it is called a great trichiliocosm (*mahāsāhasralokadhātu*). Within this [great trichiliocosm], there are one thousand heavens of the third dhyāna."

A million [worlds] constitute the second dhyāna heaven, and ten billion constitute the first dhyāna heaven; because these are accumulated threefold to form a "great" unit, it is called a "trichiliocosm.

This does not mean that there is another "great trichiliocosm" outside of this one. This great trichiliocosm remains for twenty kalpas of increase and decrease, and it is destroyed by the three great calamities over twenty kalpas of increase and decrease;
therefore, it is said that they all share the same formation and destruction. Next, I shall clarify why this is not the case.
According to the *Gantong zhuan* (Account of Spiritual Resonance), Nanshan asked the Heavenly King Wei: "I have heard that in three thousand lands there are suns, moons, and Mount Sumerus;
some say there are ten billion, while others say there are a hundred billion or a thousand billion. Which of these is correct? The Heavenly King replied:
"The sutras clearly state that there are a hundred billion transformation bodies of Śākyamuni Buddha. How could it be only one hundred?"
Regarding the first point: it is merely that the terminology has become corrupted and abbreviated over time;

taken as a whole, ten thousand *koṭis* of suns, moons, and Mount Sumerus constitute the measure of one great trichiliocosm (*mahāsāhasralokadhātu*). Furthermore, the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* states:

"Both the sūtras and śāstras refer to a 'great trichiliocosm' as 'one hundred *koṭis*,' yet these do not accord with various systems of calculation; this is an error in translation. Moreover, [the commentary] explains:
Kāśyapa’s *Fangzhi* states that from the four continents up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are ten billion locations, all of which are governed by the Buddha’s transformation.

According to the three preceding texts, if one calculates the number of great trichiliocosms (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*) precisely, if one says there are one hundred billion, it is still short by nine hundred and ninety billion.
What the *Vaijayanta* Heaven calls "one hundred parts" refers only to one part of this total; the remainder is as follows.
Upon examining the thirteenth fascicle of the newly translated *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is also stated that there are twenty-two tiers of great trichiliocosms;

the hundreds of millions of words and meanings therein are entirely identical to the present text. Alas, when the Sanskrit manuscripts first arrived from the West, the journey was vast and the languages were profoundly different, such that the principles could not always be fully conveyed. This was the case even with Master Dao’an in the past.
This refers precisely to what is called "the five losses to the original" and "the three difficulties" in the translation of scriptures. According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*,

the *Lokadhātu-vibhāga* (Qishi jing), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, and the *Śākyamuni-dig-vyavasthāna-sūtra*, which explain the orientation of the great trichiliocosm and the dimensions of the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*),
there should be four [types] of large and small Iron Ring Mountains corresponding to the ten billion Great Iron Ring Mountains and Small Iron Ring Mountains.

The differences between them are merely that the texts vary in their detail and clarity regarding what is explicit or implicit. For now, I shall cite a passage from a worldly scripture to illustrate this:
it states that the center of the four continents is Mount Sumeru; outside the mountain are eight tiers of mountains; beyond these eight mountains is the salt ocean;
and beyond the ocean is a mountain, namely the Iron Rim (Cakravāḍa), which encircles the four continents—this is called one "world-system" (*cāturdvīpaka*).
When the lands reach this measure and number one thousand, surrounded by an iron wall, it is called a small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*).
When those small chiliocosms again reach one thousand, surrounded by an iron wall, it is called a medium chiliocosm (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*).

When those medium chiliocosms again reach one thousand, surrounded by an iron wall, it is called a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*). Regarding these four layers of Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) above:
Regarding the division into large and small, the first and second layers are designated as "small," while the third and fourth are designated as "large.

If one discusses their numerical values, the first "small" layer contains a thousand *koṭis*, the second and third gradually decrease, and the fourth contains only one. Such are the quantities of these large and small units.
How could this sutra and the *Avataṃsaka* be considered identical in scale when both are simply termed "one hundred *koṭis*"? Furthermore...
According to the verses of the *Abhidharmakośa*, the Lesser Cakravāḍa Mountains are three hundred and twelve and a half yojanas high.
However, according to what was shown by the deity Vaiśravaṇa in the *Gantong zhuan*, regarding the four tiers of the Cakravāḍa Mountains:

the first tier reaches up to the Yāma Heaven, and so on, with each successive tier reaching up to the Ābhāsvara Heaven; thus they increase twofold in height, while their circular circumference serves to obstruct [the light].

Because the fierce Vairambha winds from other directions blow down the original Mount Sumeru, the Sanskrit term *Cakravāḍa* translates as "Wheel-Encircling" (*Lunwei*), for this mountain resembles a chariot wheel. Originally there was no word for "iron";
the translators established the name based on the fact that the substance of the mountain is iron.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, ten billion heavens of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception correspond to one great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).

Regarding the intermediate chiliocosm (*dvisāhasramadhyamasāhasralokadhātu*), there is one thousand second-dhyāna heavens at its summit, each covered by a fourth-dhyāna heaven. This demonstrates the vast extent of both the environment and the inhabitants of the fourth dhyāna.
Thus, the *Zhulin* states: "The first dhyāna is like a village; the second dhyāna is like a district; the third dhyāna is like a prefecture; and the fourth dhyāna is like a province."

If one reaches the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) from a [single] world-system, and it is not the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), its width is fourfold that;

thus we know that above the Great Trichiliocosm there is only a single Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. Why then does this sutra speak of ten billion Heavens of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception?
How could they be so many? Now it is said that the number "ten billion" is an error; it should read "hundreds of thousands of millions" (koṭīśatasahasra), as has already been explained above.

The statement that there is only one [level] from the fourth dhyāna up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) reveals that the retributive fruits of the fourth dhyāna and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception are particularly sublime, and that their environments and inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) are vast and expansive.

However, if one considers the great trichiliocosm, wherein each contains thousands of billions of Mount Sumerus, and upon each there are form and formless heavens, then the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception likewise consists of thousands of billions; it is simply that the physical forms of those beings are subtle.
Because the primary and secondary worlds interpenetrate one another without hindering each other’s perception of their own scale as being that of a great trichiliocosm,
the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that one hundred or one thousand gods of the Yāma Heaven may gather together upon the stalk of a single lotus flower without it becoming cramped;
furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that sixty gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven sit upon a single [seat].
The meaning is that the needle-point listening to the Dharma does not create any obstruction; this is what is intended.
Former masters’ commentaries all failed to see this passage, and their claims that it was an error in the sutra cannot avoid being mere empty fabrications based on citations.
The "Immeasurable Great Saṃghāta" section is identical to this separate recension of the *Xiṃ* (Prophecy) text;
alternatively, the reading "Heavenly Multitudes" is incorrect, for this text describes the assembly gathered in Jambudvīpa to hear this sūtra, and thus does not encompass the celestial classes.

In the "Chapter on the Accumulation of Goodness" (*Śubhasaṃcaya-parivarta*), there is also this phrase: "tears flow down crosswise. In the *Combined Edition* (*Hebu*), it is uniformly rendered as "flowing crosswise" (*héngliú*).

In the separately circulated version of the *Prophecy* (*Chànběn*), it is mostly rendered as "flowing intermingled" (*jiāoliú*). Now, examining the three commentaries by Gushan, Siming, and Huguo, they all employ the character "crosswise" (*héng*).

Regarding the interpretation of the meaning, since the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* was also translated by Master Chàn (Paramārtha), it is likewise referred to as "flowing crosswise"; thus, the *Wénxuǎn* (Selection of Refined Literature) [also adopts this].
Wang Can’s *Fu on Ascending the Tower* says: "Grieving that my old hometown is cut off, my tears fall crosswise beyond restraint.
Some might argue that Buddhist scriptures should not employ the conventions of secular literature;

yet they fail to realize that the translation of Sanskrit into Chinese (Hua) was precisely intended to accord with the classics and histories in order to guide the sentiments of sentient beings. How could it be appropriate for the language of the common streets to interfere?
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (寶軸耶雜華) is called the "King of Writings" for its profound thought and deep talent;

it is a scripture of the recent scholastic tradition that adopts the character "jiao" (交), following an old corruption. The pronunciation of "ti" (涕) is "ti" (體); it refers to the fluid from the nose.
"Limbs and joints are relaxed and at ease. "Lí" (肢) is the same as "zhī" (肢); some versions read it as "zhī" (支), which is incorrect. Some versions read "tiē" (體) for "jié" (節);
following the *Hébù* (合部) and the *Xījì* (新記), we take "jié" (節) as correct, because the "Kōngpǐn" (空品) also speaks of "limbs and joints" (*zhījié*) as hands and feet.
According to the *Yǎ* (爾雅), "yí" (怡) means joy; it describes an appearance of harmonious gladness. "Jiě" (解) is pronounced *jiāmài* (佳買); it means to loosen or expand.
[The section] on Dispersion.
Regarding the "Chapter on Mahāprajñāpāramitā-devī," some original editions are titled "Chapter on the Deity Mahāprajñāpāramitā.

This title is also absent from the *Combined Edition* (Hé-bù), which suggests that the word "deity" (*shén*) was likely added later by someone who saw the term "deity" within the body of the scripture. Master Xián stated that the term "merit" (*gōngdé*) also appears within the scripture.
As for the question of why the name of the Deva is not also included in the catalog, it is known that this cannot be done.
Regarding *Bāraṇī*, the *Hebu* (Combined) edition renders it as *Sāraṇī*; in the separately circulated prophetic manuscript (*chǎnběn*), the two characters are not fixed.

This must have resulted from a re-translation of the *Hebu* edition where "Bā" was changed to "Sā," thereby causing the discrepancy. As for mantras, they are esoteric speech and do not admit of deletion or addition.
May the reader take note of this.

Regarding the characters for "fan" (fān) and "canopy" (gài), the erroneous use of the character for "banner" (fān) in the sutras and śāstras has long been established; however, Jingxi Zhanran corrected it in his *Fuxingji* (Supplementary Notes on the Practice of the Path).
