Thus, that text states: "The character 'fān' should be written as 'fán,' which is the general name for a banner or ensign. This is found in the sutra.

Regarding the character for *fan* (幡): the *Shuowen Jiezi* defines it as "cloth for wiping a writing brush. However, since the ritual implements of the Buddha-dharma resemble banners and flags, one must use the character *fan*. [Recite:
*Namo to the Śākyamuni Tathāgata, whose body is adorned with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas,* etc. This...
In the commentary on the scriptural text of this section, the "Kings of Men" pay homage to the Triple Gem: Śākyamuni Buddha is the Buddha; the subtle and wondrous torch of Dharma is the Dharma;
and the Great Eloquence of Merit is the Saṃgha. Regarding the phrase "at that *nayuta*," two characters were lost during the translation period;

they should be supplemented according to the "Chapter on the Good Collection," which states that the body attains a golden hue adorned with the hundred blessings. This is also found in the "Chapter on Sacrificing the Body" as subtle and wondrous.
In the "Chapter on Praising the Dharmakāya Adorned with a Hundred Blessings," the World-Honored One’s body is described as being adorned with a hundred blessings.

These three passages cited here sufficiently demonstrate that the term "hundred blessings" is missing from the current text; alternatively, one may substitute "ten thousand practices" or "concentration and wisdom.

As explained in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra), these may be designated as "wisdom adornment" in terms of teaching (*jiao*) and "merit-adornment" (*pu-de*) in terms of practice (*xing*).

This refers to what is called "ornamentation" (*vyūha*). One should know that if two characters were omitted here, then the eighteen characters from "Namo" (*namas*) downward would form a single sentence, rendering them all superfluous.

This is an example of how Xie Lingyun, together with the two masters Yan and Guan, revised the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, making various additions and deletions. I address you, future worthies: herein, in truth...
One must not fail to know that the two characters "bai fu" (hundred blessings) are missing [in some versions].

The *Shenming Biqiu Hebu Zhongyi* (The Compendium of Re-translations by the Bhikṣu Shenming) reads "Baozhì Biqiu"; here, "zhì" is pronounced with the *tu* and *jian* finals (*zhì* = *tu jiàn qiè*), meaning "full.

According to the *Dazang Suixian Jingyin Ji* (Record of the Pronunciations of the Scriptures in the Great Canon by Section), one translation calls him "Baoshi Biqiu"; here, "shi" is pronounced with the *zhi* and *shi* finals (*shi* = *zhi shì qiè*), meaning "to place."

Furthermore, "Most Victorious" (*Parama-jaya*) is translated as "Jewel Accumulation" (*Ratna-kūṭa*). "Accumulation" (*kūṭa*) means a "heap. If one minutely examines the three characters above, their phonology, etymology, and terminology differ while their meaning remains the same.

However, the ancient *Chen* (Prophecy) manuscript reads "Jewel Darkness" (*Ratna-andha*). "Darkness" (*andha*) implies obscurity and depth; compared to the three preceding translations, its meaning is vastly different.
Moreover, after the *Chen* translation, various masters vied to translate the name; they must have certainly understood that "darkness" (*ming*) [refers to the profound].
The characters were not yet approved; Confucius said, "It must be that names are rectified. I have therefore named this work *Shenwei* (Profound Rectification);
let those who understand it examine it closely.

Regarding the "ear-rings" (*er-dang*) in the *Tianguan* (Celestial Crown) and its various apocryphal versions, they are generally written as "ear-rings," but here I follow the standard of the Four Ming Monastery.

The *Zhìhùguó* (Wisdom Protecting the Nation), the *Sānjì* (Three Records), and others all state that the correct form is *ěr* (pronounced as in *rúzhì*); the *Cāngjiépiān* (Cangjie’s Lexicon) states that "to *ěr*" means to have pearls in the ears.

The *Zhou Lǐ* (Rites of Zhou) says, "the crown has *ěr* [pearls] on the back and *jué* [jewels]. The *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states, "piercing the ear and applying a pearl is called a *dāng* [ear-ornament]. The *Wénxuǎn* (Selections of Refined Literature) mentions "presenting bright *dāng*s from Jiangnan."

It was intended that these sentient beings should combine the characters *he* (合) and *bu* (部) to form the character *he* (合), yet the separate edition of the prophecy (*chanben*) had instead produced the character *jin* (今).

Master Rong collated and verified the texts, adopting the character *ling* (令) as the new record and taking the character *jin* (今) as the original. He then explained that "jin" is a term used for summoning;
however, he took the character *ling* (令) as the correct meaning of the scripture, explaining that it signifies each of the heavenly kings addressing one another, saying, "Let this be so."
Sentient beings who hear this Dharma shall attain immeasurable majesty and virtue.
May they be free from calamities and forever depart from all suffering (two lines). *Tāhe pāhe* (and so forth, four lines); *Canda canda* (and so forth, four lines).

Regarding the above three sections of the scripture, the presence or absence of the wooden printing blocks, as well as their opening and closing [in circulation], are uncertain; I have now examined them.
The sub-commentary (*shu*) divides the verses of this chapter into six sections totaling one hundred and two and a half lines.

The fifth section, beginning from "Mahābrahmā Devendra," consists of forty-nine and a half verses; these cite how listening to the sutra can bring about deities and dragons, thereby exhorting practice.

The *Huguo* (Protecting the State) and *Gushan* (Island Mountain) commentaries both state that there are versions of the text where [the phrase] "many shall be free from calamities and misfortunes" and so forth is expanded.
Regarding these two lines, furthermore, the four lines beginning with *dodhākhe* and *padhākhe* were all added falsely by later generations. Now, an objection is raised:
"If these six lines are excluded, there would be only forty-eight lines; why then does the structural analysis of the commentary lack half a verse?
The *Xinji* (New Record) states: "If the four lines beginning with *caṇḍa-caṇḍa* are combined to form three lines, then..."
One must exclude the four phrases beginning with "Muchu" (須除) and "Duoxi" (多醯), and retain only the two phrases "Cun" (存) and "Wuzaihuo" (無災禍);
only then will there be forty-nine and a half lines of verse. Now, the objection is raised:

if it is as you say, then there would be only forty-nine lines and one phrase, not even completing half a line; moreover, how could one face-to-face fail to recognize that Tiantai [uses] "Zhantuo" (旃陀)? "Zhantan" (旃檀).
The passage beginning with "Ta" and so forth is an explanation of the meaning through the fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*);

as for what is now being explained, one should preserve the two phrases "to cause there to be no calamities or misfortunes" and so on, for they were originally present in the *Chen* manuscript, though they are absent from the *Hebu* (Combined) edition—this must have been deleted during the time of a subsequent re-translation.
Next, the four phrases beginning with "Duoxie poxie" and so forth are present in the *Hebu*, yet these are merely the texts of later masters produced during a subsequent re-translation.
Because people did not understand this and erroneously incorporated it into a separate version of the *Viniścaya-sūtra*, I have now removed it.
Furthermore, I have expanded the three phrases concerning Caṇḍa and Caṇḍālī into four phrases, following the Tiantai interpretation which states:

"The Sanskrit term Kaurava-danti translates into Chinese as 'Warrior Unconquered. Since Tiantai follows the expanded translation for the name, how could he possibly combine the four phrases back into three?"
Having made this demonstration, it finally accords with the forty-nine and a half lines of verses divided into sections in the commentary (*shu*).
Furthermore, one must know that the combination of four lines into three is itself a text from a re-translation of the combined version;

here, following the Tiantai tradition which exclusively adheres to the version by Huichan, we follow the expanded explanation. Those who do not understand this will simply claim that worldly people are deluded.
To interpret this as "opening and closing" is incorrect.
The name *Weidu* (違駄) is pronounced with the second character *duō* (駄) as *hé* (賀); alternatively, some editions of the sutra write the first character simply as *wéi* (韋).
According to the two biographies, the *Gantong* (感通) and the *Linggan* (靈感), when this deity first met the Master, he introduced himself as Wei Kun (韋琨). *Wéi* (韋).

"Xing" (Surname) is Yu, and "Kun" (Name) is Kun; thus, the character for "zi" (courtesy name) must omit the "chuō" radical. In the two phrases "transmitting the beginning and end" and "wasting the courtesy name," it simply refers to General Wei.

Regarding the two phrases "delighting in intimacy" and "delighting in the immeasurable," there are original texts where the character "ài" (delight) is written as "shòu" (receive), both featuring the "dāo" (knife) radical.

This was an error in the original manuscript; now, according to the combined editions of all sections, both instances are written as the character "ài" (love). If they were written as the character "shòu" (receive), then the two instances of the character "yuè" (joy) would necessarily have to be pronounced with an entering tone, which certainly does not accord with the intent of the scripture.
"Bi-pu" (馝馚): "bi" is pronounced as *biǎo* (蒲結切) and "pu" is pronounced as *fén* (馚乏聞切). This describes the appearance of fragrance being abundant and pervasive.
Some editions of the sutra read "fu-fu" (馥馥); the *Xinji* (New Record) states that both describe the profusion of fragrance and are interchangeable.
However, I maintain that if they were truly interchangeable, later editions of the sutra would lack standardization; therefore, this is incorrect.

Regarding the immeasurable merits described above, the *Shu* (Commentary) states that the twenty-seven lines of verse beginning from "From among all sentient beings" onwards concern how listening to this sutra can bring peace and happiness to the land.
However, both the separately circulated *Chen* (Prophecy) edition and the *Xinji* (New Record) contain twenty-seven and a half lines of verse.
The *Xinji* claims that the first line is redundant; yet, upon examining the *Hebu* (Combined Edition) and the *Zuisheng* (Most Victorious), it is found to be complete.
Since both sūtras contain these two lines, they cannot be considered redundant; I shall now expand upon them by presenting two interpretations.

First, it is possible that when Tiantai was lecturing on the *Prophetic Sūtra* (Chenben), there were originally twenty-seven lines of verse, and later, when the combined edition (*Hebu*) was retranslated, two lines were inserted therein.

Alternatively, someone may have extracted these lines from the combined edition and included them in a separate recension of the *Prophetic Sūtra*, thereby resulting in this "extra" portion. Second, it is possible that these two lines were added by the commentator (*shu*).
In the text of the "Middle Section," one half of the characters following the word "practice" (*xing*) is missing.

Regarding the phrase "cultivating according to characteristics" (*suixiangxiu*), some editions combine it with the subsequent section, while others treat it as a separate heading; the two versions of the *Chen* manuscript do not agree.

Now, following the explanation in the *Siming Ji*, [it is understood that] "possessing wondrous roots of goodness" (*miaoshangen*) is a distinct designation for the remote causes and conditions, whereas "cultivating according to characteristics" is...

Regarding the phrase "separately indicating the present causes and conditions" (*biē biāo xiàn yīnyuán*), since this refers to the present causes and conditions, it certainly cannot refer to what has already been done or what is yet to be done;
thus, it is correct to adopt the character *yǐ* (以).
As for the "harmonizing of the six great elements to form the four great elements," the *Bie xing chèn běn* (別行讖本) may either follow the *He bu* (合部) version or follow the *Si da* (四大) version.
Now, it is said that the original *Chen* (prophecy) text fundamentally consists of the six *dà* (greats); thus the commentary explains: "The six *dà* are the six hollow organs (*fù*).

As for the fact that the ancient manuscript was incomplete, it is surely because the scriptures were suppressed by former dynasties and their texts were severed and lost amidst the dust of warfare.

Subsequent generations failed to collate and publish them, resulting in their incompleteness—much like how many portions of the *Shi* and *Shu* among the Six Classics were lost during the fires of the Qin.

At the end of certain manuscripts of the *Bie xing chan* (Separate Translation of the Prophecy), there is sometimes a chapter titled "Entrustment" (*zhulèi*). People have been unable to determine whether this exists or not.

Now, consulting the *Yijing tuji* (Illustrated Record of Translated Scriptures) and the *Shijiao lu* (Record of the Buddhist Teachings), both state that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* translated by Dharmakṣema consists of eighteen chapters in four fascicles;
thus, the text as it actually stands contains no chapter on Entrustment. Therefore, the *Siming ji* (Record of Siming) says: "In the world, there are those who add a chapter on Entrustment."
The fact that it has been divided into nineteen chapters in successive editions is an instance of erroneous attachment.

Although the two translations by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavara of the Sui dynasty and the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Tang dynasty both include a chapter on "Entrustment" (*pàizhù*), a comparison with their respective translations reveals that the "Text on Entrustment" found at the end of the present version translated by Dharmakṣema is entirely different in style from them. This must have been a later person’s imitation and plagiarism of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
I entrust this private compilation to be circulated alongside [the scriptures]. By adding brass to gold and hemp to silk, who among men lacks the discernment to reach such a state?
If people can excise these corruptions, then the holy teachings will become pure and correct.

Some may doubt, asking: "Since the *Zhìdé* (Yìjìng) translation already contains the chapter on 'Entrustment' (*parindanā*), why did the Master Dharmakṣema not translate it from the original Sanskrit manuscript?

Now, I shall resolve this through three points, the first being brevity.
That this scripture may be abridged is due to the fact that its primary doctrine—the discernment of the Path according to the needs of the audience—is contained in the first fascicle.

From the section on the Four Heavenly Kings downward, the entire text belongs to the *pariṇāmanā* (entrustment) section, wherein various devas repeatedly vow to propagate it, and the Tathāgata earnestly issues words of entrustment.
Although the *Anuparīndanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Entrustment) could have been omitted, it was retained as appropriate for the occasion.

This sutra was translated during the Northern Liang dynasty under the reign of Juqu Mengxun. At that time, the Buddha-dharma had only recently been disseminated, and people did not yet have deep faith;
because the original text was extensive, Master Daorong (Chen) selected the essentials and abridged it for translation.

This is similar to how Master Kumārajīva, when translating the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, reduced the text by ten times for those of inferior intelligence—abridging nine parts out of ten. Although three translations still remain incomplete, I have examined them.
The *Combined Edition* in eight fascicles and the Tang translation in ten fascicles reveal that Master Dharmakṣema’s version was abridged;

this is also evident from the *Record of the Translation of the Scriptures*, where Dharmakṣema himself stated that the chapters and sections of this sutra were still incomplete. Tiantai also remarked that the foreign manuscript still contained much more.
Furthermore, although it is said to have been deficient and extensive, my Patriarch’s commentary has already established its definitive form, and it has long been upheld by the fourfold assembly.

According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*, four types of translation are established: first, translating the characters but not the phonetics, such as the divine mantras in various sutras;
second, translating the phonetics but not the characters, such as the *svastika* on the Buddha’s chest; third... [text truncated]
Regarding the translation of both sounds and characters: if the scripture itself consists purely of Chinese words, it is said that neither the four types of sounds nor the characters are translated.

If this refers to the title of the scripture, it is indeed so. However, in order to establish the four propositions in this tradition, the fourth point merely states that "sounds and characters are not translated," because there have already been explanations regarding the presence or absence of translated characters and meanings throughout ancient and modern times. Thus says Wang Jing.
The Duke was pleased with the explanation of the characters, saying: "The subtlety of the creation of these characters is not unique to this land alone;
it is like the two characters *ou* and *a* in the Buddha-land. *Ou* signifies 'existence,' therefore it is written to the left; *a* signifies 'non-existence,' therefore it is written to the right.
Furthermore, that they are inscribed upon Buddhist scriptures (*fanjia*) is because the Buddhist sutras serve to refute those of the non-Buddhists (*waidao*).
Regarding this principle, as stated in the *Myōraku* (The Wondrous Joy): "In all the scriptures of the non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Regions, 'A' and 'U' are placed at the beginning;
because they take 'existence' and 'non-existence' as their fundamental tenets, the Buddhist scriptures establish the two characters 'Ru' (如是, *evam*) and 'Ni' (不是, *naivam*) to refute those [views].
Only by relying on the Buddha-dharma and departing from the views of existence and non-existence does one truly [attain it]."
This is the True Path.
The *Jingang kanding ji* (Record of the Collated and Determined [Meaning of the Diamond Sūtra]) states: "The Sanskrit term is *sūtra*, or *sūtraka*, or *sūtrānta*;
these are all variations of the Sanskrit sound according to regional dialects. It is correctly called *sūtra*, which is translated as 'thread' (*xian*), because in India..."
The term *sūtra* refers to four realities; these four are: holy teaching (*āgama*), mat (*kaṭhina*), rope (*rajju*), and thread (*sūtra*).
This is because in that region [India], when people offer flowers to the Buddha and place them upon a table, a fierce wind blows them away;

they therefore string them together with thread. Furthermore, it is observed that in this region [China], the holy teachings are able to uphold the Buddha’s words so that nothing is lost, just like a thread.

Because it threads together the flowers [of the teachings], it is designated by the term "sūtra" (line/thread). Since this region does not value the name for "thread," it is translated as "jīng" (sūtra).
This thus secretly accords with the "mat-sūtras" of that region while simultaneously conforming to the "jīng" of the Confucian and Daoist traditions here.

Nevertheless, although both sides are thus accorded with, they cannot avoid being confused with one another; therefore, the two characters "yùdǐ" (desire-bottom) were added to translate it as follows: [Sanskrit: *sūtra*, Chinese: 欲底經].
The *Qifang* (契方) is able to distinguish it from the scriptures of this region; thus, both the Chinese and Sanskrit versions are complete.

"Beiliang" (北涼) was the dynastic name during the period of illegitimate rule in Longyou (隴右). Since the chaos of the Yongjia era (永嘉), when the Central Plains were devastated and various barbarian tribes settled there, there were generally sixteen kingdoms throughout China, and Beiliang was one of them.
The *Neidian lu* (內典錄) states that the Emperor’s surname was a compound clan name.
The name Juqu was originally Mengsun; he was a Lu-shui Hu from Yuan-Lingsong whose ancestors served as the Left Grand Juqu of the Northern Xiongnu, taking this title as their clan name.
Mengsun was widely read in various histories and had some knowledge of astronomy. After killing Duanye, he styled himself the Governor of Liangzhou.
He subsequently defeated Juqu Noutan at Qiongquan and, seizing the momentum, entered Guzang, where he proclaimed himself the King of Western He.
The king was from Longxi; during the fifth year of the Long’an era of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, the *xinchou* year, he styled himself Northern Liang.

During the Xuanshi era, he translated sūtras and śāstras, widely propagating the Buddha-dharma. Since the master Daomeng had resided in this country and transmitted these teachings there, it is designated by the name "Northern Liang."
The Tripiṭaka Dharma Master—referring to those who master the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras—is called a "Dharma Master" because he propagates these three teachings.

Since no person is born knowing everything, who can remain without doubt? If one has doubts yet does not follow a teacher, those doubts will never be resolved.
Tánwúchèn (also transcribed as Tánmóchèn, which translates as "Abundant Dharma") was a native of Central India.

He entered the monastic order at the age of six and could recite ten thousand words daily from memory. Initially, he studied the Hīnayāna, but later encountered the White-Headed Meditation Master (Báitóu Chánshī), who instructed him in the Mahāyāna.
It took ten days of debate before he finally realized its great principles. The *Shìjiào lù* states that Master Chèn...
Once, while accompanying the King of Central India into the mountains, the king became thirsty and could find no water. The Master recited a mantra, and water gushed forth from a parched rock.
He then said, "It is by the power of Your Majesty’s benevolence that this spring has been produced from a withered stone.

Thereafter, the King’s attitude toward the Master gradually grew distant. The Master said, "I shall now summon a dragon with my mantra and place it inside a jar to cause a drought; the King will surely request me to release it."
A dragon informed [the King] in secret; the King became enraged and dispatched men to arrest him. Daśabala then took with him such scriptures as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and fled to Kucha.
Because Kucha was largely devoted to the study of the Hīnayāna and did not believe in the Mahāyāna teachings, he subsequently traveled to Guzang and stayed overnight in a guesthouse.
Fearing that he might lose the original texts of the scriptures, he placed them under his pillow and fell asleep. During the night, a divine being suddenly pulled the Master down to the ground.
For three nights in succession, thieves came; suddenly, a voice was heard from the air saying, "This is the Tathāgata’s treasury of liberation;

why do you use it as a pillow? Thereupon, he moved it to a high place. The thieves returned again but were ultimately unable to lift it. Realizing that the Master was a holy man, they all came to pay their respects and offer thanks.
When Juqu Mengxun heard his reputation, he immediately issued an edict summoning him to perform translations. He remained in Liang for seven years.
In total, he translated twenty-three sections of sutras and treatises comprising one hundred and forty-eight fascicles.
Later, when Emperor Taiwu of the Northern Wei heard of the Master’s spiritual arts, he dispatched an envoy to invite him. Daoxun feared that Daorong would devise a stratagem for the Wei court;

his suspicions having suddenly shifted, Daorong then took his leave to return to the West. Just as he was about to depart, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying: "My enemies have arrived; though you are many..."
The Sage could not save him; by the time Chen reached his destination, forty li away, Xun had secretly dispatched an assassin to kill him.
Those who heard of it sighed in grief, all lamenting that the propagation of the Dharma was so fraught with such hardship.
The *Liji* (Book of Rites), in its "Institutions of the King" (*Wangzhi*), states: "The people of the five regions have different languages and unequal desires;

their intentions must be conveyed and their wishes must be communicated. Those from the east are called *ji*; those from the south are called *xiang*; those from the west are called *didi*; and those from the north are called *yi*.
That we now use the term *yi* to refer to interpreters of Western languages is likely because during the Han dynasty, there was frequent interaction with the northern tribes."
The translator was also proficient in Western languages (Sanskrit). At that time, when the Buddha-dharma arrived, he was commissioned to translate it;

for this reason, Buddhist scriptures are all referred to as "translations" (*yi*). The *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song* states: "The word 'translation' (*yi*) means 'to change' (*yi*).
It refers to using what one possesses to exchange for what one lacks. To illustrate: when an orange tree is transplanted from its native soil, the orange transforms."
Although the *jiji*, the orange, and the tangerine differ, their pungency, fragrance, leaves, and trunks are no different;
just as the *nyagrodha* tree of the Western Regions is the willow of the Eastern Lands (*Dongxia*), such that though their names differ, the substance of the tree is one.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states that the Sanskrit term *varga* is translated here as "chapter" (*pin*). The *Shu* (Commentary) explains that "chapter" carries the meaning of "category.
Within this text, sentences and phrases are grouped into *vargas* according to their thematic affinity, much like the five sections and seven clusters in the Vinaya.

The *Xinji* (New Record) notes that "thematic affinity" is a metaphorical expression used to clarify "affinity"; it refers to the affinity of "climate" or "season," which is equivalent to "species" or "type. As for example: [text follows].
The differences between the twenty-four qi of yin and yang constitute the distinctions among their various types. The *Xici* states:
"Things with similar directions group together, and things of the same kind cluster. Mencius says: "Therefore, all things that belong to the same category are generally similar."
"Buddha" is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "The Awakened One" (*buddha*). It is said that he is called "Awakened" in contrast to those who are deluded and ignorant.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because he can awaken himself and also awaken all sentient beings—like waking from a dream or like the blooming of a lotus—he is named Buddha.
The *Vajra-si-yuan* states: "Who does not awaken? Who is able to awaken? It is the essence itself."

The same applies to the term "Buddha," which is uniform and singular throughout. One should know that although the word "Buddha" is used here as a general title, it actually serves to summon a specific individual;
it refers exclusively to Śākyamuni, the teacher of this particular sutra.
He resided in the great city of Rājagṛha; this city was located in the kingdom of Magadha and was the place where the Buddha wandered for alms and performed his transformative teachings.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Sanskrit language it is called Rājagṛha-kalpa, which in this [Chinese] language means 'King’s Abode City.
In the past, there was a king named Tiara (Tianluo) who had no son. While out hunting, he encountered a female lion; as the retinue dispersed, the king had intercourse with her."
When the moon was full, he suddenly came to the palace and gave birth to a son; spreading the false rumor that it was a gift from Heaven, he raised him as his own son.
Because there were dark spots on his feet, he was called King Pāda-lekhaka (the Spotted-footed King). Later, upon succeeding to the throne, he took a delight in eating meat.

When the cooks suddenly ran short of supplies, the king took recently deceased infants to serve as food. The king found them delicious, and the cooks hunted for them daily without ceasing, causing grief and resentment throughout the entire kingdom.
The minor kings of the thousand small nations raised armies to depose their sovereigns and establish them in Mount Qi;

the various rākṣasas assisted them as ghost-kings, vowing to seize a thousand kings to sacrifice to the mountain deity. They had obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine kings, lacking only Puming, whom they finally captured.
Puming begged to be allowed to return home to practice giving before returning to face death. Bozu asked the king about this.
Because he had been able to hear the sublime Dharma, he praised the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) extensively and reviled the act of killing.
Upon hearing the Dharma, Aśva-pāda immediately realized the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Thereupon, each of the thousand kings took a drop of his blood and two strands of his hair, and together with Aśva-pāda, they made a vow before the mountain deity to establish a residence within the five central mountains as a great kingdom.
For this reason, it is called Rājagṛha (the King’s Abode). Furthermore, when the common people built houses within the five mountains, they were burned seven times;
they considered themselves to have little merit, while the King possessed the power of merit such that his own dwellings were not burned.

The multitude deliberated and said, "Our houses have been made into the King's Abode. Because they were thus spared from burning, it is called Rājagṛha. Moreover, after Aśvajit attained the Way, he pardoned the thousand kings here.
The name of the place is "King’s Pardon" (Rāja-kṣānti); the scriptural tradition merely borrows it for the term "dwelling.
Regarding the phrase from the *Lotus Sūtra* concerning Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain: in the Sanskrit language, Gṛdhrakūṭa is translated as "Vulture Peak";

this is because its summit resembles a vulture, and furthermore, because vultures, having finished eating corpses in the Śītavana charnel ground to the south of the mountain, would come to roost there.

Because the mountain is ancient and because it is a place where holy seers and divine spirits dwell, the *Xiyu ji* states that its Sanskrit name is Gṛdhrakūṭa, which in the Tang language is translated as "Vulture Peak" (*Jiufeng*) or "Vulture Terrace" (*Juitai*). Its former designation, "Qishajue," is a corruption.
This peak rises prominently from the southern slope of the northern range; since vultures have nested there and it resembles a high terrace, it is so named.

The void and the emerald green reflect one another, their colors distinguished by depth and lightness. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is the dwelling place of all Buddhas of the three periods.
Even if the great trichiliocosm were to be consumed by fire at the end of the kalpa, I would remain here eternally to preach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings.
It is only because the fetters of sentient beings are so deep that they do not see me. (Gṛdhrakūṭa: *gṛdhra*, vulture; *kūṭa*, peak.)
"Surpassing all bodhisattvas"— the character *guò* (過) is read with a departing tone (*qùhū*), meaning "to transcend" (*yuè*). In the following passages—

"surpassing the fragrances of all devas," "surpassing the night until dawn," "surpassing the king of bees," "standing above the knees," "surpassing the human eye," "surpassing all Tathāgatas," "surpassing and surpassing the immeasurable," "surpassing this day," "having passed this night"— [these uses] do not exceed the capacity of one's own person.
"Exceeding humans and exceeding the calculation of kalpas," with the thirteen characters "exceeding" (過) all pronounced as a departing tone (去呼).
The commentary on the *Sūtra-king of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa* states: "If one takes the words as the sūtra, it constitutes the three kinds of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya);
if one takes the principle as the sūtra, it constitutes the three kinds of ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); if one takes the union of words and principle as the sūtra, it constitutes..."
Regarding the three kinds of Middle Way: if one speaks of other truths, it is a sūtra but not a king;
if one speaks of the Middle Way, it is both a sūtra and a king, attaining mastery among the nine kinds of sūtras. This passage from Tiantai is obscure and concise, making it difficult to perceive.

Previous masters have offered interpretations numbering in the dozens. Zhiyi’s *Fahua Wenju* (Record of the Lotus Sūtra) explains this through the true [aspects] of the Three Teachings—Tripitaka, Shared, and Distinct.

Regarding the conventional truth, there are three types of true and conventional [truths]: those that connect the Perfect with the Shared, those that connect the Perfect with the Distinct, and those that correspond to the three teachings of the current school.

The essence of these three types of middle way is established by Zhiyi as being the Middle Way itself. Although Zhiyin of Siming established this, how could it withstand the "whale-swallowing" critique of Master Yue of Xiachuan?
Thus, the *Yibian* states: "That which was established by Siming is, for the first [type], like the seventh [case]; for the second, [it is like] the second."
Later, it seems that [the teachings] were investigated and scrutinized according to the five periods and three vehicles; yet neither approach is appropriate.

The "Seven" (seven periods) lacks the designation of the "Middle Way," while the "Five and Three" (five periods and three vehicles) lacks the name of the "Tripitaka. Whether advancing or retreating, there is no fixed standard—where, then, are the rules?

However, Siming [Zhiyuan] used the "Seven" and the "Two Truths" to interpret and harmonize the King of Sutras (*Prajñāpāramitā*); herein the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* is fully present, and both the partial and the perfect are subsumed, which perfectly accords with the Vaipulya [teachings].
The principle of universally benefiting the four types of capacities is the sovereign power that governs this King of Sutras;
if one can pray for the removal of the calamities of Xiachuan, then the Way of Siming will naturally shine with brilliant light.
Regarding the Buddhas of the East, Akṣobhya; the South, Ratnaketu; the West, Amitāyus; and the North, Svarasvati:

the *Mahā-śāstra* states that among the four directions of Jambudvīpa, the east is the beginning of enumeration because it is where the sun first rises, and furthermore, because the east is the direction of spring.
Nevertheless, these four Buddhas are identical in their superior transformation because they shared the same causal practices. As the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* says: "Beyond..."
In the past, there was a Buddha named King of Emptiness (*Śūnyarāja*). After he entered parinirvāṇa, there were four bhikṣus who practiced together but broke the precepts.

Later, they entered a stūpa and, by contemplating the Buddha image with intense focus, attained the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*. The Buddhas appeared before them and bestowed prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), declaring that they would all attain Buddhahood in the four directions.
In the east, in the world-realm of Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavyūha*), their Buddha’s name shall be Akṣobhya. In the south... [text continues].
In the world Fanghuānxǐ (Square Joy), the Buddha’s name is Bǎoxiàng (Jewel Mark). In the western world Ānlè (Peace and Bliss), the Buddha’s name is Wúliàngshòu (Immeasurable Life).
In the northern world Liánhuāzhuāngyán (Lotus Adornment), the Buddha’s name is Wéimiàoshēng (Subtle and Wondrous Sound).

Regarding the title *Sūtra of the Supreme Drum-Sound*, the *Record of Protecting the State* states that "Drum-Sound" is named after a metaphor.

The *Qinhou* (Kindness and Intimacy) chapter of the *Cangjie Pian* says it means "affection"; the *Shiming* (Explanations of Names) says it means "intimate," referring to how they support one another.
The *Suoyin Ji* (Record of Investigating the Hidden) says that "kindness and intimacy" refers to the six types of kin. The *Hanshu* (Book of Han), citing Ying Shao, states: "To serve the six kin..."
It is said that the "six relations" consist of father, mother, elder brother, younger brother, wife, and son.
Regarding "malevolent stars and calamitous anomalies," the *Sūtra on the Distances* states: "Malevolent stars" refers to when Venus (Mars) moves in disorder or when comets suddenly appear;
"calamitous anomalies" refers to irregular seasonal signs such as wind, rain, snow, and frost. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that in the Sahā world there are eighty thousand...
When the four thousand calamitous transformations and the twenty-eight great malevolent stars appear in the world, they can give rise to various kinds of disasters and anomalies.
Zhang Wujin’s commentary states: "Malevolent stars" does not refer to the evil of being wicked or cruel, but rather to the evil of bringing about misfortune.
The celestial phenomena all receive the refined vital energies of the Four Great Elements and the Five Phases; when these energies stagnate and fail to circulate freely, [disasters arise].
The Buddha’s compassion arises because acting contrary to one's nature brings forth calamities in response; as the *Suyin ji* states:

"If one can inwardly contemplate the Dharma-nature and realize that the root of transgression is empty, regarding Buddhas and sentient beings as equal within one's own mind and giving rise to compassion for the entire Dharma-realm, then what need is there to worry that the portents of malevolent stars will not be extinguished?"
The *Zhongxie Gudao Shu* (Exposition on the Various Malevolent Arts and Sorcery) states: "Human malevolence, ghostly malevolence, and dharma malevolence are called the 'various malevolences.

Dharma malevolence refers to the scriptures of all non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*), while sorcery (*gudao*) refers to poisonous ghosts. The *Siming Ji* (Record of Siming) explains this through its literal meaning: it is when other ghosts inflict poison and harm upon people;
according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "sorcery" (*gu*) refers to worms within the abdomen. The *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* states that greed and resentment constitute [this malevolence].

When the sins of humans reach their limit, they encounter insects that take form, becoming known as *gudu* (poisonous spirits). To understand this is to realize that the three poisons of one's own mind constitute the *gudu*, which can harm the Dharma-body and the life-force of wisdom.
The *Yin Yun* (Phonetics of the Great Canon) states: "To harm others through incantations and arts is called the way of *gudu*.
The *Sheng Jing* (Sutra on Birth) says: "There was a person who specialized in practicing the rites of *gudu*; he served a deity and gained the favor of a wealthy man."
Finding no one willing to give her in marriage to him, he sought a wife in a foreign land. The woman had originally served the Buddha and practiced compassion;
she converted him, leading him to eventually cease [his former ways]. The *Jiǎngshù Dǐngshān Jì* states:

"Poisonous snakes devouring one another—when the stronger transforms into a *gǔ* (demon/pestilence)—enter the human belly to act as food, such as *gǔjiǔ* (demon-wine) and *gǔ* (demons). The *Yànxián Lù* records that people in the south raise golden-colored [snakes].
They feed on *shu-jin* (silk brocade) and take its excrement, placing it in food and drink to poison people; once people die, the silkworms rejoice.
They can cause people to become wealthy, yet they are extremely difficult to dispatch. Neither water, fire, nor blades can harm them;
however, if one places much gold and silver among them and dispatches them, when passersby see them, they will take them, and the silkworms will immediately follow along.

This is called "marrying the gold silkworm. The *Yutang Xianhua* (Idle Talk from the Jade Hall) states: Yu Gou of the Zhongshu [Secretariat] was afflicted by *gu* poisoning for which no medical treatment could be found.
Incidentally, a practitioner of pinning and cauterization passed by his door and said, "I too have once suffered from this;

"Please do not eat it early; I shall come. Once he arrived, he ordered [the snake] to open its mouth and took up a bell to wait for the moment.
Just as the snake settled, it suddenly slipped away. The next day, he waited as before with the same bell and struck the snake;
it was red in color, like a hairpin-staff, and measured two inches in length. He immediately ordered fire to burn it, and thus it was eliminated.
The *An-yeh Tóuhuāng-lù* states: "In Xīnzhōu there is a medicinal herb called Jí-cái (Ji-cai), which cures *gǔ*-poisoning with incomparable efficacy.
It is called 'Jí-cái' because in the past, when a man encountered poison, he had a slave named Jí-cái who obtained this medicine;
thus it was named after him. Its appearance resembles that of peony; those who encounter poison secretly seek out two or three inches of it and mince it finely."
Add a small amount of licorice and decoct it for consumption; if one induces vomiting, the ailment will be cured. This is recorded exactly as in the *Dàpíng guǎngjì*.
Regarding the account of seeing a bad dream while lying down, the *Sū* states: "The mind-spirit is hidden and subtle, yet karma manifests within it; thus one sees things that are disagreeable.
The *Guǎngyùn* defines a dream as the wandering of the spirit during sleep. The *Fāzhēn chāo* cites the Vinaya, stating: "Sleeping with a distracted mind..."
There are five faults: first, bad dreams; second, the failure of the devas to provide protection; third, the mind not entering the Dharma; fourth, failing to contemplate the signs of light;

first, the "true dream" (*zhengmeng*), which occurs without any external stimulus and is a peaceful dream occurring spontaneously; second, the "startled dream" (*emo meng*), which is a dream resulting from being startled; third, the "thoughtful dream" (*simeng*).
1. The dream of things thought of while awake; 2. The dream of things spoken of while awake; 3. The joyful dream, which is dreaming with joy; 4.
The fearful dream, which is dreaming with fear. One should know that among the six types of dreams in the *Zhouli*, the "correct dream" (*zhengmeng*) is the only one that is auspicious;
it is a prior omen of good or evil. For this reason, the ancients established the office of the Diviner of Dreams.
In later generations, officials abolished this practice, likely because the people of the world had become so corrupt and deceitful that they frequently engaged in false pretenses.
One should bathe and purify oneself thoroughly. The *Jiqian* (Explanations of the Text) states: "Discussing bathing in general, all forms of washing are termed *guàn* (盥).

However, discussing them specifically: washing the hands is called *guàn*; washing the feet is called *xǐ* (pronounced *xiān*); washing the head is called *mù*; and washing the body is called *yù*. This is according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*.

It is said that "washing" (*mù*) means bathing the hair. Mencius said: "Even if one is an ugly person, if they observe the fasts and purify themselves by bathing, they may sacrifice to the Supreme Deity.
Regarding the host of *yakṣas*, the *Vimalakīrti-vyākhyā* states: "*Yakṣa* is translated here as 'light and swift. There are three kinds: first, those on earth..."
The first two dwell in the void, while the third resides in heaven as a servant to the devas. Because of their evil and poisonous nature, they receive the retribution of a yakṣa;

yet because they cultivated the vehicle in the past, they have seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma. Since they once gave elephants and horses as offerings, they are able to fly through the air. The *Chanyi chao* states:
"The new translation is 'Yakṣa,' which translates as 'valiant and robust' (yǒngjiàn), capable of soaring through the sky; the old translation was 'quickness' (jié)."
This spirit is the one who, at the time the Buddha first attained enlightenment and turned the wheel of Dharma, transmitted the sound [of the teaching] to the Brahma Heaven; it is this very ghost.
Now, in this Dharma assembly, we summon and invite it by transmitting talismanic edicts to be presented to the Supreme Emperor. This is precisely the name and reality of this deity;
it must be addressed as the "Swift and Efficient Spirit-Messenger."

Regarding the Nairañjanā River, the *Xiyuji* states: "Traveling four or five li southwest from the monastery of the Śīlabhadra Ācārya in the kingdom of Magadha, one crosses the Nairañjanā River to reach the city of Gayā.

The eight classes [of beings] who show reverence are: first, devas; second, nāgas; third, yakṣas; fourth, gandharvas;

fifth, asuras; sixth, garuḍas; seventh, kiṃnaras; and eighth, mahoragas. These constitute the eight classes. Regarding what are called "humans and non-humans," some say that the *kiṃnara* has a single horn on its head;
thus, the *kiṃnara* is a "human-non-human" (*manuṣyāmanuṣya*). This is the meaning of Avalokiteśvara.
The *Śāstra* states: "We do not here adopt the interpretation that 'human and non-human' refers specifically to the Kinnaras; rather, this is a summary of the eight classes [of beings].

The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* asserts that all eight classes are called "humans and non-humans," or alternatively, that "humans" refers to the assembly of humans and "non-humans" refers to the assembly of non-humans.
For instance, after the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* has enumerated the eight classes, it concludes by saying: "the assembly of humans and the assembly of non-humans."
The *Yi Lengyan Jijie* states: "Among the six realms of existence, with the exception of the human realm alone, the remaining five realms are all designated as 'non-humans' (*amanuṣya*).
Furthermore, beneath each of the Four Heavenly Kings, two classes of spirits are governed, which together constitute the Eight Divisions (*aṣṭa-gaṇa*)," and so forth.

The *Weimo Sushu* explains that the meaning of the "Eight Divisions" involves many interrelated points, precisely because of the various discrepancies presented above; thus, "division" (*bu*) refers to...

This is because empty space is unobstructed and universally encompasses the ten directions; therefore, they are called the ten voids.
"Joyful and delighted" (*huān xǐ yuè yù*): "delighted" (*yù*) is also "joyful" (*xǐ*); these are merely cross-referenced definitions within the classics.

The *Lǐjì* (Book of Rites) says, "Man is the heart of Heaven and Earth; he is the refined essence of the five elements. The *Zhuāngzǐ* says, "That which is honored through non-action is the Way of Heaven;
that which is burdened by action is the Way of Man. In Sanskrit, this is *puruṣa*, which is translated here as "human."

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that "human realm" (*mānuṣya*) is named for the cessation of the mind; this means that among the six realms of existence, one is able to cease [afflictions] and exercise patience.

The translators, finding it cumbersome, omitted the remaining characters. *Bodhi* means "enlightenment," *sattva* means "mind," and *mahāsattva* means "great being."
