"When a bodhisattva first resolves to attain enlightenment, they vow to deliver all beings; they are able to endure the tasks of accomplishing the path, remaining unshakable and indestructible—this mind is called *sattva*.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* states: "There are three great matters for which it is named Mahāsattva: first, number..."

First, "Great" (Mahā) refers to being immeasurable; second, "Virtue" (Sattva) refers to dwelling in the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna); third, "Activity" (Sattva) refers to being able to pacify the afflictions of sentient beings.
Alternatively, the sūtra translates it as "Bodhisattva" (K'ai-shih), meaning one who develops the faith of sentient beings.

Ancient translations rendered it as "Noble Being" (Gao-shi), meaning one who has transcended ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). The *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Pitaka) translates it as "Awakened Sentient Being" (Jue Youqing). It is also...

It is said that regarding the name "Great Courage" (*Mahā-vīrya*), the *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Since the names of Bodhisattvas are thus rendered with inconsistent translations, they should be retained in their Sanskrit forms.

The name is called "Faith-Aspect" (*Śraddhā-lakṣaṇa*). The *Sūtra of the Supreme Victory* names him "Wondrous Banner" (*Citra-dhvaja*), while the *Record of Protecting the Nation* states that "Wondrous Banner" is established by way of metaphor.

Regarding the term "faith-sign" (*śraddhā-liṅga*), Chengguan’s Commentary states: "The 'sign of faith' refers to the signs within the household of faith that exist during the stage of the path of semblance (*sādṛśya-mārga*).
As stated in the passage below, 'one sees a person who resembles a Brahmin,' this indicates that while the conditions for the stage have arisen, one knows it is not yet the true [stage].

Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the true and the semblant stages, the stage of Samantabhadra is adjacent to the ultimate honor; since the sign of faith is described as 'semblant,' I do not yet dare to make a definitive judgment."

Regarding "short-lived" (*āyuṣya-parītta*): the *Shu* (Commentary) states that "life" (*śou*) refers to vitality (*ming*). That which is obtained as retribution—the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)—which maintains continuity without interruption, is termed "life.
The *Jing yinyi* (Meanings and Phonetics of the Sūtras) states: "Life is also vitality; though not distinct, they are divided:
'life' takes the name for a single period [of existence], while 'vitality' takes the portion of a person's birth. These are merely different names."
Regarding the "Eighty Years" in the *Fangbian* (Section on Eighty) of the *Yupian*: "Fang" means correct or beginning. The commentary states that there are three grades of worldly lifespan:
the lower grade is forty years, the middle grade is eighty years, and the upper grade is one hundred and twenty years. The lower grade is premature death; the upper grade is extreme old age;
and the middle grade is neither too young nor too old. The Buddha’s proclamation of his extinction at eighty signifies abiding in this middle grade. Xinxiang did not... [text ends]

Because one forms such an interpretation, doubt arises. Thus, if we follow the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou), the Buddha was born in the year Jia-yin of King Zhao’s reign and passed away in the year Ren-shen of King Mu’s reign; his lifespan was only seventy-nine years.
As for all the sūtras and śāstras that state the Buddha’s lifespan was eighty years, these merely speak in terms of a general approximation.
First, regarding non-killing, the *Sūtra Commentary* states: "Now, life is that which all sentient beings cherish together;
to seize and harm it is a great suffering, while to pardon and release it is joy. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The sin of killing can cause sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
Later, if they are born among humans, they will receive two kinds of retributions: first, [they will have] much..."
Regarding the second [of the two causes of illness], namely a short lifespan, Liang Zhou Yong wrote in a letter to He Yin:
"Among the greatest of transformations, none surpasses death and birth; among that which life holds most dear, none surpasses one's vital essence (xing-ming).
This vital essence is of the utmost urgency for others, whereas flavors may be regarded as something that can be deferred for me. Those who read these words should be moved to reflection."

Second, regarding the "Chapter on Bestowing Food and Flowing Water," it says: "I am now able to provide food for these fish; in future ages, I shall bestow the food of the Dharma. The Commentary states:
"As for 'food,' that which is obtained through the *upādāya-vipāka* (retributive environment) sustains life, while its loss brings death.
A hundred flavors and sweet syrups are food of the retributive environment; one's own flesh, marrow, and bones are food of the *pratyātma-vipāka* (primary retribution). This...

All these matters concern the *sūtra* on giving, which speaks of the "Dharma-food": namely, the flavor of mundane dharmas, the flavor of supramundane dharmas, and the flavor of the supreme among supramundane dharmas.

Regarding the ten great numbers, such as the *koṭi*, *nayuta*, and *asaṃkhyeya*, within immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of *kalpas*, it is said in the *Avataṃsaka*: [The passage continues with the enumeration of the ten great numbers.]
*Asaṃkhyeya* (阿僧祇): immeasurable, boundless, limitless, incomparable, incalculable, ineffable, inconceivable, unfathomable, unspeakable, unspeakably unspeakable.
*Koṭi* (俱胝): in the Sanskrit language, this translates as "hundred million" (*billion*). *Nayuta* (那由佗): this translates as "ten billion.
*Asaṃkhyeya* (阿僧祇): this translates as "innumerable. According to the *Suanjing* (算經), Huang Di invented calculation.

The Dharma totals fourteen levels, namely from one to ten: (1) hundred, (2) thousand, (3) ten thousand, (4) hundred million, (5) billion, (6) ten billion, (7) hundred billion, (8) trillion, (9) ten trillion, (10) hundred trillion, (11) quadrillion, (12) quintillion, (13) sextillion, and (14) septillion. From the number ten thousand upward, there are three methods of calculation:
the lower method multiplies by ten at each step, the middle method multiplies by one hundred at each step, and [the upper method follows its own progression].
The higher grades increase by doubling; the extensive enumeration of numbers in Buddhism, as clarified in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, refers to fifty-two numerical units:
one is the beginning of counting; ten ones make ten; ten tens make a hundred;
ten hundreds make a thousand; ten thousands make ten thousand (*ayuta*); ten ten-thousands make a *lakṣa*; ten *lakṣas* make a *niyuta*; ten *niyutas* make a *prayuta*.
One *lakṣa* makes one *koṭi*; ten *koṭis* make one *madhya*; ten *madyas* make one *ayuta* (also known as *nayuta*)...
[and so on] until ten *balañcas* make one *asaṃkhyeya* (the *asaṃkhyeya* being the fifty-second number at the end of the sequence).
Furthermore, in the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra*, Prince Siddhārtha compared his calculations with the great mathematician Aṣvajit.
The son then stated that one hundred makes a thousand (and so on), up to a hundred thousand million *rājas* being called a *daśa-gulpha*.
Even if one enters such a system of calculation, one can fully know the weight in *jin*, *liang*, and *zhu* of even Mount Sumeru; those who require it should consult that text.
The Sanskrit term *kalpa* is translated in the Qin language as "differentiation of time periods. The *Zhulin* states that *kalpa* is an Indian [term].
The designation for recording time is like the era names (*nengo*) of this region.
Even to the point of filling and satisfying hungry sentient beings with one’s own marrow, bones, flesh, and blood—the *Shūki* (Commentary) states:

"Regarding 'marrow, bones, flesh, and blood,' when viewed from the perspective of that [other being], they constitute one's own; yet through the inference of wisdom, they are not one's own," as in the case of a prince feeding a tiger.
The Śibi king’s sacrifice for the dove involved the flesh of his parents’ bodies, not his own; his "own body" refers to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Observing the precepts constitutes the skin, and so forth, up to the subtle and wondrous wholesome mind which constitutes the marrow."
The *Tianjian liuli guyuan zhucun* states: "That which is deep blue yet appears reddish is called *gàn* (紺). The character *yǎng* (佯) is pronounced *yú cháng* (余常);
it means 'weak' or 'faint. Among the five colors of the world, this hue is not prominent; the deep azure of heaven is seen only in Buddhist scriptures."
It is like the pure land inhabited by the Tathāgata. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that a land where there are no sentient beings of the five turbidities is called a "pure land.
The *Zhulin* says: "A world that is bright and pure is termed 'pure'; that which is pure in its habitation is termed 'land' (*bhūmi*)."
It is made exclusively from celestial garments (*devavastra*) as its seating mat; the various devas wear robes weighing six *zhu*, which is said merely to describe their lightness and fineness.
Eight *zhu* constitute one *zi*, and twenty-four *zhu* constitute one *liang*. According to the *Zhangfu yi* (Ritual of Official Attire), the sitting mat serves as the seating mat.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Ten Recitations Vinaya) states that the shape of the seating mat is the same as that of a woolen rug or mat.

Regarding the lion throne (*siṃhāsana*), the *Record of the Western Regions* states that the imperial throne of the kings of India is even more lofty and expansive, inlaid with pearls and gems, and is called a "lion throne.
This is like the "dragon bed" (*longchuang*) used by rulers here in this land. Since the Buddha is the Dharma King, he sits upon this throne.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "Is the lion throne created through the Buddha’s transformation (*nirmāṇa*), or is it substantially existent?"
"Is it made of gold? "It is not something that truly exists. It is named after the seat upon which the Buddha—the lion among men—sits.
For the lion is the peerless and fearless leader among four-footed beasts, capable of subduing all others;
the Buddha is likewise so.
In Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, upon the summit of the Great Snow Mountains in the Western Regions, there is Lake Anavatapta from which four rivers flow.
To the east, the Gaṅgā River—also called the *Gangā*—issues forth from the Silver Elephant’s Mouth;
this is translated as "Heavenly Arrival" (*Tianlai*), for it descends from the peak of a high mountain as if arriving from heaven. This is the lake.
Its southern branch is called the Sindhu River, translated here as the "River of Verification. Its western branch is called the Sītā River, translated here as the "Cold River.
Its northern branch is called the Vakṣu River, translated here as the "Blue River," which reaches this land and is known by the name Yellow River (*Huanghe*).
The *Jīng yìnyì* (Phonetic and Semantic Commentary on the Sūtras) states that the sands of the Gaṅgā River are white and as fine as flour.
If one scoops water flowing with a hand and grasps it too tightly, the sand will come out along with the water.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body can know the number of grains of sand in the Ganges. Yet the same treatise also says that there are great rivers in Jambudvīpa that even exceed the Ganges in volume;
for what reason does the Buddha always use the sands of the Ganges as a metaphor? Answer: The Ganges... [text truncated]

The sands of the Ganges are more numerous than those of other rivers, which are not so; furthermore, because the Ganges is where the Buddha sat, where he traveled, and where his disciples constantly saw him, it was taken as a metaphor.
Moreover, all the scriptures regard it as a river of merit and auspiciousness, for if one enters its waters to bathe, all stains of sin are removed;
since people revere and serve this river, it was chosen as a metaphor.

It rained celestial flowers. The *Xu seng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks) records that during the Renshou era of the Great Sui dynasty, a śarīra stūpa was constructed by imperial decree in Xinzhou.
It was moved by the descent of celestial flowers filling the sky; people obtained half a he (a measure of capacity) and presented it as an offering to the Emperor.
At that time, there was a Brahmin monk named Jñānagupta in the capital, to whom the Emperor immediately sent an inquiry as to what the celestial flowers were like. He replied, "They are heavenly..."
The flowers resembled thin mica; if they were blown by the wind, they did not fall to the ground, and even when they did fall, their radiance was extraordinary and surpassing.
The Emperor then secretly mixed fine mica and heavenly flowers together in a single casket and summoned his ministers to examine them.
None among the multitude could distinguish them. He summoned Nāgārjuna again to inquire, and Nāgārjuna identified the heavenly flowers and withdrew the mica for the Emperor.
He was deeply moved by this.
Regarding the celestial music, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "Within the Heaven of Sovereignty (*Īśvara*), there is a celestial maiden named Good Mouth (*Suvaktrā*).
From this woman’s mouth, sounds constantly emerge that correspond to hundreds of thousands of kinds of musical instruments. The *Chuiyu ji* states:
Regarding "nữ-lạc" (female music), the *Cāngpí* states: "Jì refers to beautiful women; because one uses beautiful women for musical entertainment, it is called 'jì-lè' (female music).
Based on this, "jì" must correctly be written with the radical for "woman" (女); both "jì" and "jì" [with the radical for "hand"] are incorrect.
"All sentient beings" (*sarvasattva*): the character *zhòng* (all/mass) was originally pronounced with a departing tone, but in modern speech it is treated as level-toned;

"all" signifies their great number. In Sanskrit, it is pronounced *sattva*, which translates here as "sentient being. The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-samānārtha-sūtra* states that "sentient being" has the meaning of a combination of mental feeling and perception (*saṃjñā*), arising from the conjunction of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and so forth. The *Āgama Sūtras* state: [The text continues with further scriptural citations regarding the nature of sentient beings.]
At the beginning of the eon, when beings descended from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, men and women were born together with those of high and low status; thus they were called *sattva* (sentient beings).

This is an explanation based on the very first instance. If one says that sentient beings exist by gathering the various aggregates (*skandha*), this is according to the explanation of receiving retribution.
If one says they take birth in various places, this is according to the explanation of saṃsāric wandering. This concludes the section translated by the Dharma Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.
Both the sūtras and the śāstras refer to them as "sentient beings" (*sattva*) in order to distinguish them from "insentient things" (*asattva*).
Nevertheless, even though there is this terminology used for distinction, if one considers it in light of the three preceding meanings, both [the literal and the technical senses] are lost.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the Buddha abides in the dharma of non-duality and is thus able to manifest supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

The commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra* explains: "Spirit" (*shen*) signifies the unfathomable; "power" (*li*) signifies efficacious function. Unfathomability refers to the profoundness of the natural essence, while efficacious function refers to the greatness of the power of transformation.
In the *Śākyamuni-pūrvayoga-sūtra*, "Śākya" is translated as "Capable Benevolence" (*Néngrén*); in the *Munigati-sūtra*, "Muni" is translated as "Silent Stillness" (*Jìmò*).

"Capable Benevolence" is his clan name (*gotra*), and "Silent Stillness" is his personal name (*nāman*). The clan name derives from benefiting sentient beings, while the personal name derives from acceding to the principle.
Because he benefits sentient beings, he does not abide in *nirvāṇa*; because he accedes to the principle, he does not abide in *saṃsāra*. This was the prediction of Dīpaṃkara.

To harmonize with the events of his miraculous birth, our Buddha took birth within the Śākya clan; "Śākya" may be translated as "Capable of Writing," which, when translated as "Confucian," means "Capable of Confucianism.

Alternatively, it is translated as "Straight Forest" (Zhílín), because when King Ikṣvāku, the Buddha’s progenitor, banished his four sons to the Snow Mountains, they later returned to the Straight Forest;
their virtue became like a bustling market, and they grew into a powerful nation from that point onward.
Consequently, he took Zhilin as his surname; furthermore, the title of the "Chapter on Names" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was translated as "Crossing Wujiao.
Guo Pu’s commentary on the *River Rhapsody* states: "Wujiao is located beyond the eastern sea, at the place where the waters of the ocean pour forth."
The *Mahā-māra-śāstra* states: "In the Sanskrit language, Māra means 'life-taker' (*prāṇahara*) or is translated as 'slayer' (*ghātaka*);
this refers to the deity Pāpīyān. This person, having obtained good benefit by relying on the Buddha-dharma, later turned back to inflict destruction.

The *Loutan jing* (Kāṣāya-puṇḍarīka-sūtra) states: "The palace of Māra is six thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth; it dwells between the realms of desire and form. This is recorded in the *Benxing ji jing* (Saṃyukta-ratna-sūtra).
The *Biographies of the Buddha* (*Fó jì*) states that when the Buddha attained enlightenment, all the Māras, including Pāpīyas, came to the Buddha’s dwelling and were entirely subdued;

this is explained in detail in that sūtra. The *Fǔxíng* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*) says: "In ancient translations of sūtras and śāstras, the character for 'Māra' was written with the 'stone' radical.

Since the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, it has been held that because Māra can afflict people, the character must have the 'ghost' radical. Dictionaries of word definitions state that the character for 'Māra' originated from the Śākya clan."
The character "diǎn" (典) now generally retains two meanings: if it refers to "robbing life," it follows the meaning of *māra* as a demon;

if it follows the corruption [of the sound], it follows the meaning of "stone. Thus, the *Loutan jing* (Lokadhātuparivarta-sūtra) states: "It grinds and destroys jealousy, just as a stone grinds and destroys merit.
Therefore, if one says that Emperor Liang Wudi was the first to change the character from "mo" (魔) to "diǎn" (典), one must consider that many of the scriptures were produced during the Liang dynasty.
Regarding the question, "Why were the previous translations all derived from the *guǐ* (鬼) [radical]? the answer is: later generations changed them to use the [correct] characters for writing.
The "Assembly of Brahmā" (*fànzhòng*) refers to the assembly of the eighteen Brahmā heavens. In Sanskrit, *brahma* is translated as "pure" (*qīngjìng*).

This is because the deities of this class are not defiled by the dust of desire. As the *Zhēnzhènglùn* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct) states: "The character for 'Brahmā' originally did not exist in this land."
Since the Buddhist scriptures were first translated by ancient translators, this term was employed to transcribe Indic sounds;
it was not until Li Gēhóng that this character was first collected in his *Zìyuàn* and defined as "pure," and later, when Lù Fǎyán of the Great Sui dynasty incorporated it into the *Qièyùn*,
it finally became a standard character of this land.
*Śramaṇa* is sometimes called *sāṃmāna*. Fan Ye’s *Hou Han Shu*, "Annals of Sacrifices to Heaven and Earth," states: "In the language of Han, *śramaṇa* means 'one who has stilled the mind' (*xīxīn*).
One who shaves the head, leaves home, severs worldly attachments, washes away desire, and returns to non-action (*wúwéi*) is such a person.
The *Ruiying Jing* says: "Because one who has stilled the mind reaches the fundamental source, he is titled a *śramaṇa*. Alternatively, it is said that *śramaṇa* translates as "destitute" (*fá*).
The *Dàodà jīng* (Great Sutra on the Path) states that one who severs all deprivations, severs all [erroneous] paths, and cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path is a *saṃgha*.
The *Sēngshǐ lüè* (Brief History of the Sangha), citing the Nanshan school, says: "The term *śramaṇa* is a title shared by both ordinary beings and sages.

Since followers of heterodox paths in India are also called *śramaṇas*, it is necessary to explain the etymology of the word to distinguish [the Buddhist practitioner] from them; thus, the two types are referred to together as such."
This refers to the designation of one's rank, locality, and clan name.
Among the four Brahmin clans of India, the Brahmin is one of them. As the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Collection of Past Deeds) records in a verse spoken by the Buddha:
"Pure and free from a mind of flattery or crookedness, abiding always in right concentration within and without. Thus it is said.
One who practices the various pure conducts (brahmacarya) is called one of the Brahmin caste. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:

"Brahmin" is translated as 'one with external intent' (*wai-yi*); these are individuals of noble learning in the external tradition who have been passed down through successive generations. It is also translated as 'Pure Conduct' (*jingxing*);
they are the distant descendants of Brahmā, and their own kind claim to have been born from the mouth of Brahmā."

The *Zhulung Shuyiji* (Record of Extraordinary Accounts by Various Dragons) states: "A water-huixi transforms into a *jiao* after five hundred years; a *jiao* transforms into a dragon after one thousand years;
a dragon transforms into a horned dragon (*jiaolong*) after five hundred years; and another five hundred years later, it transforms into a *yinglong*.
The *Guangya* states: 'One with scales is called a *jiaolong*; one with wings is called an *yinglong*; one with horns is called a *qiaolong*; and one without horns is called a *chilong*.'"
The *Longfang* (Discourse on Dragons) states: "One who has not yet ascended to heaven is called a 'coiled dragon' (*panlong*). The *Yuannmingbao* (Encompassing the Original Mandate) says:
"The dragon is the yang within yin; therefore, when it rises, clouds emerge. The *Guotu* (Map of the Encompassing Earth) says:

"On Mount Longchi, the four sides are high and there is a pond in the center, seven hundred li square, where the various dragons dwell. The *Shuowen* (Explanations of Characters) says: "The dragon is the chief among the scaly creatures; it can manifest in the dark."
It can manifest as bright, small, large, long, or short; at the spring equinox it ascends to heaven, and at the autumn equinox it enters the rivers.
Master Baopuzi said: "There are naturally occurring dragons, and there are those transformed from silkworms.
In Buddhist terminology, *nāga* is translated as 'dragon. According to the *Sūtra on the Storehouse of Mount Sumeru*, there are five kinds of dragons:"

The *Jingyaoji* (Essential Collection of Various Sutras) states: "Among the dragon-elephants, dragon-snakes, dragon-horses, dragon-fish, and dragon-frogs, the dragon-snake is their primary category, while the others are secondary categories;
thus we know that the dragon-snake is the foremost among the five types of dragons. The *Guanyinyi shu* (Commentary on the Meaning of Avalokiteśvara) states:
"There are four kinds of dragons: first, those that guard the celestial palaces; second, those that raise clouds and bring forth rain."
The three [kinds of dragons] are: those that break through rivers and open channels; those that guard the treasure-trove of the Wheel-Turning King;
and as the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states, there are five kinds of suffering for dragons, namely: at birth, at sleep, at sexual union, at anger, and at death.

Within a single day, their skin and flesh fall to the ground three times, and hot sand clusters around their bodies. The *Nanda Sūtra* states that dragons have three sufferings, the first of which is...
1. Although one may eat food of a hundred flavors, the very last mouthful transforms into a shrimp or a frog. 2.

A handsome man and a beautiful woman who become husband and wife immediately transform into two snakes entwined together. 3. One who has strayed from the Path finds scales, sand, and stones spread upon their back;

as these grow within them, the pain reaches their very heart. The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Origin of the World) states that dragons encompass all four modes of birth—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—and there are dragon kings among them.
The Sūtra states: "In the past, dragons were among humans; they served as great fields of merit and received great blessings and virtue.

Yet, because they did not observe the precepts and fasts, they now undergo the retribution of evil suffering and cannot escape the peril of the *garuḍa*. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Dragons are included within the realm of animals.

Their primary retribution (*vipāka*) resembles that of snakes, yet their secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna*) consists of palaces made of the seven treasures, which are equal to those of the devas; they are also capable of transformation."
His appearance was upright and handsome. His human discipline was lax, yet his spiritual vehicle was urgent; upon hearing the Dharma, he awakened to the Way.
Regarding ghosts and spirits, the *Shizi* says: "The celestial deity is called *ling* (spirit); the terrestrial deity is called *qi* (numen); the human deity is called *gui* (ghost).

The *Yi Zhuan*, "Xici," says: "Essential qi forms things; the wandering soul constitutes transformation. Thus one knows the nature and conditions of ghosts and spirits. The *Book of Rites* says: [as cited above].
In the manifest there are rites and music; in the hidden there are ghosts and spirits. The *Guang hongming ji* states:
"Ghost" (*gui*) means "to return," that into which death enters; "spirit" (*shen*) means "numinous," the source of form. Ghosts are inferior to humans, being limited to the evil realms;
spirits surpass the realm of form, universally encompassing the various states of existence. Because the mind possesses numinous wisdom, it is called "spirit. (From the *Dīrgha Āgama*).
The *Hanyan* states: "All dwellings, streets, lanes, mounds, and burial sites are inhabited by ghosts and spirits; they are all named after what they rely upon. The *Fuxing* commentary says:
"Formerly, there was a man named Sun Zhan who adhered to the 'no-ghosts' theory. Suddenly a guest arrived, and their conversation turned to the ghosts and spirits of the world.
The guest’s arguments were exhausted, whereupon he changed countenance and said: 'Ghosts and spirits are something that the sages and worthies of both past and present have agreed upon.'"
"What do you mean, sir? I am not a ghost. Suddenly, he changed his form and vanished.
Regarding the *Gandharva*, the *Fahua ju* states: "In Sanskrit, *gandharva* translates as 'smelling fragrance.
This deity takes fragrance as its food; it is also translated as 'fragrance-aggregate' because its body emits a fragrant scent. (*Ongyō gisho*)

It is said that the gandharvas are the deities of secular music for Śakra; they dwell within the Vajra Cave on the southern side of Mount Sumeru, and whenever Śakra desires to perform music, their hearts are moved.
The term *asura* is rendered in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as "Āxūlún" (阿須倫), or alternatively as "Āsùluó" (阿素洛) or "Āsūluó" (阿蘇羅);

these are all variations in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* translates it as "Non-Gods" (*fei tian*), meaning that although this class of beings is included within the heavenly realms, they are largely deceitful and lack the majestic virtue of true gods, much like a person who commits evil deeds is called a "non-human. (*Avataṃsaka-sūtra*)
The *Yinyi* (Explanations of Pronunciations and Meanings) states: "Asura" is translated here as "form resembling that of the devas. The old translation, "non-drinker of wine" (*bujiu*), is erroneous.
This is because the Sanskrit term *sura* is translated as "wine," and its pronunciation is close to *asura*; thus, the error arose.

Now, since various scriptures clarify that Asuras are already subject to the precept against intoxicants, there is no contradiction in translating it according to its meaning. One should know that the claim that Asuras do not drink wine is [a misunderstanding of this].

There are two meanings: first, they formerly observed the precept against drinking alcohol; second, seeing the devas drink the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), they gathered flowers from the four continents and placed them in the great ocean to brew wine.
However, due to the karmic power of the fish and dragons, the flavor of the wine could not be perfected; for this reason, they abstained from alcohol.
Furthermore, it is because they are the opposite of being handsome. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that when an asura gives birth to a daughter, she is extremely beautiful.

The case of one who was about to give birth to a son but [the child] was immediately ugly refers to this. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* speaks of the four types of asuras: those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, and transformation.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that asuras consume a hundred flavors, yet the very last mouthful turns into green mud.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that asuras dwell in the hollows of Mount Sumeru or within the salt ocean. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on Practice) says: "Asura..."
His mind was obscured by crookedness; he envied the virtuous and resented their conduct.

*Kālaṃjara* (迦樓羅) is translated here as "Golden-Winged Bird" (*garuḍa*). The *Linggan Chuan* (Record of Spiritual Resonance) states that when these winged birds spread their wings while dwelling on Mount Cakravāḍa, they span three hundred and thirty thousand *li*;
when they coil their bodies, they are six thousand *yojanas* long; and with a single beat of their wings, they fly [vast distances].
Traveling thousands of *li* from one Iron Ring Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*) to traverse a great ocean, he consumes hundreds of dragons daily and also devours a dragon king.
Leaping into the clouds and mists for tens of thousands of *yojana*, he looks down upon dragons whose lifespans have ended;
he coils his body and enters the sea, and before the waters have closed, he seizes the dragon and emerges. The *Buddhadarśana-samādhi-sūtra* refers to this as the "Winged Bird" (*Suparṇin*).
When he who has lived for eight thousand years is about to die, the various nāgas emit poison so that he finds no way to eat.
He passes through the Vajra Mountains, across the ocean, and through the earth, yet cannot pass the wind-circle; he surges up from the opening and returns to the Vajra Mountains.

This occurs seven times in succession until his life ends. Fire then arises and strikes his heart, forming a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi). Once the nāga obtains this jewel, it immediately becomes...
Regarding the term *garuḍa*, the *Huayan yinyi* (Meaning and Pronunciation of the Avataṃsaka) states:

some say it is translated as "the great-throated bird," while others translate it as "the one that emits cries of bitter suffering upon eating. This is because when this bird seizes a nāga for food, it first swallows it into its throat and then regurgitates it;
the nāga, still alive, utters cries of bitter suffering due to the excruciating pain.
The *Kinnara-hua-yen-yin-yi* (The Meaning of Terms in the Kinnara Avataṃsaka) states: "Kinnara" is translated as "Doubting Deity" (*yi-shen*).

This refers to a deity whose appearance resembles a human, yet has a single horn growing from its head; those who see it give rise to doubt, wondering, "Is this a god or a human? Therefore, it is called the "Doubting Deity.
It is also translated as "Hesitant Man" (*you-yu zhang-fu*), because its form is like a human while its mouth resembles that of an ox. Thus it is made so.

Because those who see him are filled with hesitation, the old translations render this as "God of Song and Music" (from *gīta* and *vādya*) or "Artisan" (*śilpin*). He dwells amidst the mountains of the Ten Jewels.
Regarding the *Mahoraga*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "Mahoraga is translated here as 'Serpent God' (*māhura-ga*), also called 'Earth Dragon.
Being legless and moving on its belly, it is the temple deity of the world that receives offerings of human blood; all such sacrifices enter the serpent's belly."
Because his precepts were lax, he fell among the spirits and ghosts; because he was prone to anger, insects entered his body and devoured him.

Because he had previously practiced a small amount of giving and humble respect, he received offerings from people. Because his practice was urgent, he encountered a Buddha, heard the Dharma, and attained the Way.
The number of drops in all waters can be known. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata illuminates the mundane and supramundane dharmas;
knowing their fundamental causes and how they emerge according to their conditions, he knows even the number of drops of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The weight of all the Sumeru mountains can be known. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that the heart of the four continents is Mount Sumeru;

"Sumeru" is also called "Sumeru," which translates as "Wonderfully High. It is called "wonderful" because it is composed of the four precious substances, and it is called "high" because it rises above the seven golden mountain ranges.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Its depth below the water is eighty thousand [yojanas], and its height rising above [the water] is likewise."
It is said that this Mount Sumeru is eighty thousand *yojanas* high and likewise as deep within the waters. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"There are phenomena that can be measured, yet because one’s power is inferior, one cannot measure them.

For example, the weight of Mount Sumeru and the number of drops in the ocean water—these the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas can know, whereas the gods and people of the world cannot. (From the *Han shu*, *Lüli zhi*).
What is called "weight" (*quan*) consists of the *zhu*, *liang*, *jin*, *jun*, and *shi*. These are the means by which objects are weighed and distributed evenly to discern lightness and heaviness.
It originated from the weight of the *huangzhong* pitch-pipe: one *yu* (a dry measure) holds twelve hundred grains of millet, which weigh twelve *zhu*;
two *zhu* make one *liang*, twenty-four *zhu* make one *liang*, sixteen *liang* make one *jin*, and thirty *jin* make one *jun*.
Four *jūn* make one *shí*. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "Eight *zhū* make one *zí*, and twenty-four *zhū* make one *liǎng*.
The measure *liàng* is pronounced with a level tone (*píngshēng*) and refers to calculating or measuring.

Regarding the number of dust particles that can be known across the entire great earth, the *Dacheng Dapiposha Lun* (Mahāyāna Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states: "The Buddha and the Bodhisattvas of the Dharmakāya are able to know [the atoms of] Jambudvīpa..."

The number of motes of dust within Jambudvīpa is already inconceivable, let alone the sands of the Ganges. Furthermore, the *Lun* (Treatise) states that there are large, medium, and small motes of dust:
the large are motes of drifting dust visible to the naked eye; the medium are those seen by the various devas; and the small are those seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) of the sages.
When observed with the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*), they are found to be non-existent, because their true nature (*dharmatā*) is empty. Thus it is said: "Bha."
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that atoms (*paramāṇu*) are so minute that they cannot be broken or burned.

The thirteen-fascicle *Saṃyukta-agama* (or *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*) records that when Prince Siddhārtha competed with the great mathematician Aṣvajit in calculating numerical methods,
he calculated the number of atoms within one *yojana*, and even those contained within Jambudvīpa, which is seven thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth.
He knows the exact number of *yojanas* in the length and breadth of these four continents, down to the number of atoms, as well as all the numerical values within the great trichiliocosm;
as the text is extensive, it is not recorded here, but those who require it may consult it.
Regarding the phrase "generating the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," the *Huayan yinyi* (Meanings and Pronunciations of the Avataṃsaka) states:

*An* is translated as "without" (*wu*); *uttara* is translated as "above" (*shang*); *samyak* is translated as "correct" (*zheng*); *saṃ* is translated as "equal" (*děng*); and *bodhi* is translated as "awakening" (*jué*).

Taken together, it is called "Unsurpassed Correct Equal Awakening. Regarding the character *nu* (in *anuttara*), in the classical texts and histories of this land, its original pronunciation is the *qiè*-rhyme *nùgòu*.
According to the Sanskrit pronunciation, it should be a retroflex (入聲) sound; thus, the character *nòu* found in the *Guǎng yùn* as appearing in Buddhist scriptures is correct.

As for the character *miǎo*, while its radical and rhyme in the dictionaries were originally *héngjiǎo* (橫角切), in Buddhist sutras it is borrowed as *mílüè* (彌略切). Those who pronounce this character often err.
According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gāosēng zhuàn*), five reasons are established for not translating [Sanskrit terms]; the fourth is "conforming to antiquity" (*shùngǔ*).
If one were to translate it, "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" could indeed be rendered as "Unsurpassed Perfect Enlightenment.
However, since the time of Kāśyapa Mātanga, the Sanskrit sounds have been preserved; thus, later translators followed this precedent and never changed it.
The *Zhao Lun* states: "The Way of Bodhi cannot be schematized or measured. It is high and without superior, vast and without limit; it is deep and without bottom, profound and without end."
It is called the Way (*dharma*) because it can be measured as being vast enough to encompass heaven and earth, yet subtle enough to enter the Avīci Hell.

Regarding the term *chánmó* (懺摩) in the *Chànhuì pǐn* (懺悔品), this is translated as "repenting of transgressions. The *Sì míng jì* states: "In the scripture, the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are listed side by side;
Tiantai [Zhiyi] explains *chán* (懺) as 'subduing' (*fú*) and *huì* (悔) as 'repentance,' etc. This is an example of skillful preaching of the Dharma."
One should not hold one's account based on the literal glosses of the vernacular or Sanskrit terms. According to the commentary, there are three types of repentance for this sutra:

first, the *dharmakāya-pratideśana* (repentance through ritual practice), which consists of purifying the mind morning and evening for seven days and seven nights; second, the *nimitta-pratideśana* (repentance through signs), which is to behold Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra at one’s place of practice;
and third, the *pañca-skandha-vihāra-vipaśyanā* (contemplation of the house of the five aggregates). All [of these] must be observed.

Emptiness and quiescence are themselves the repentance of non-arising; because these three meanings are perfectly present, one is able to extinguish all evils, wash away the three obstructions, and manifest the power and function of the sutra.
Regarding the dream of the golden drum, the *Commentary* states: "To dream of a golden drum is to enter the 'dream-like samādhi' (*yathāsvapna-samādhi*); furthermore, it is to enter contemplation."

Regarding "as in a dream," the *Chūkan yōroku* (Record of Emerging from Contemplation) states: "The *yūmū samādhi* (dream-like samādhi) contemplates all phenomena as empty, like a dream that has no reality;
only the Buddha is without dreams. In the causal stage, there are [dreams]. Regarding this, Gushan says: "This is a metaphorical expression to represent the Dharma;

it is not an actual dream. The *Josenshiki* (Record of Aiding Propagation) states: "Those in the four fruits and the pratyekabuddhas still have dreams; only the Buddha is without dreams. This is because...
Because there are no habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), Zhuangzi said: "The True Man of antiquity does not dream while sleeping.

While this statement seems similar [to the Buddhist view], it is nonetheless true that the appearance of the golden drum in a dream is not the same as the Buddha’s state of being without dreams; yet it is also not the same as falling back into seeing evil dreams while lying down.
This is consistent with what follows below regarding King Bimbisāra’s dream of the precious wheel, the Bhikṣu Dharmamitra, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra on Dreaming of Becoming a King*—which seeks the twelve dream-kings—is something those who examine it will fully understand.

As for its form, it is "shu" (姝), pronounced with the *chū* rhyme of the *Shī* (詩) character; the *Mao Shī* says, "The quiet woman is *shu*," and its commentary states that *shu* refers to beautiful countenance.
The *Fāngyán* says that in the states of Zhào, Wèi, and Yān, people called what was excellent "*shu*. The sub-commentary (*shū*) explains that "*shu*" carries a profound sense of superiority.

Great Meaning. Regarding "retinue" (*parivāra*) as explained in the *Shuowen*: "retinue" (*juan*) means to look back upon; according to the *Guangyun*, "class" (*shu*) means category. To look back upon one's own kind is called a "retinue.
In the *Miaoxuan*, five kinds of retinues are clarified: first, the retinue of the principle-nature, which refers to all [sentient beings].
1. Those who are kinsmen by the natural disposition of sentient beings (*dharmatā-yukti*), which is spontaneous like that of father and son;

2. Those who are kinsmen by karma, meaning those with whom one has previously planted seeds and established a connection; 3. Those who are kinsmen by aspiration, meaning those who are drawn along by the power of their vows; 4.

Those who are kinsmen by supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), meaning those who assist the Buddha in his transformative activities through supernatural faculties; 5. Those who are kinsmen by response (*nirmāṇa*), meaning those who have shattered ignorance.

Regarding those who attain the Dharma-nature body and should be born in the Shared Residence, the *Fǎjiàn qìqiān* (Sub-commentary on the *Fǎjiàn*) states: "When the Buddha preaches the Dharma, it necessarily reaches those conditions [who] receive the Way;

like a child receiving the physical body bequeathed by its parents, they grasp this to form a body and become of the same nature as the Buddha. Because this nature is one of intimate affection, they are called 'retainers' (*juàn*);
because they mutually obey and submit, they are called 'subordinates' (*shǔ*. The *Fǎhuá jù* (Sentences of the *Lotus Sūtra*) states: "'Surrounding' means moving in a circular procession."

Regarding "dignified demeanor" (*vīryāpatha*), it signifies the movement of the four gates. The *Chanyi chao* (Explanatory Notes on the Rituals) states: "To go around completely is called 'encircling' (*wei*); to sit all around is called 'circumambulating' (*rao*).

As for striking a drum with a mallet (*baofu*), the pronunciation of *baofu* is close to *yóu*. The *Shuowen jiezi* states: "A *baofu* is the handle for striking a drum; it is also written as *fú*. The *Erya* [explains it similarly].
It is said that the *bāqiú* (枹遒) is a tree that is gnarled and deformed; Kuo Pu’s commentary states this refers to trees with dense roots, branches, nodes, and joints that are knotted and rugged.
The *Shiben* (世本) says that Yi invented the drum and struck it with a mallet (*fū*). The *Dajing* (大經) states:
"The drum depends on the hide, depends on the person, and depends on the mallet; through their harmonious combination, sound is produced."

"Having awakened from the dream": *wù* (寤) is pronounced with the *wǔ* (五) and *gù* (故) finals; it means to wake up from sleep or a dream. Some versions of the sutra write this as *wù* (窹), but the *Guǎngyá* states that this is a name for a hearth, which is incorrect.

"Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet": The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks, "One should say 'to pay homage' (*lì*); why does one say 'to prostrate one's head and face at the feet'? The answer is that regarding the human body...
The head is noble, for it is where the five emotions reside and is situated at the very top; the feet are the most base, treading upon impure places and situated at the very bottom.

Because the noble is used to honor the base, one provides them with reverent offerings. Furthermore, the treatise states that there are three kinds of salutation: the lower salutation is the bow (*yī*); the middle salutation is kneeling (*guì*);

and the superior salutation is the prostration with the head to the ground (*jīshǒu*). As for the prostration with the head to the ground, it consists of placing both the head and face at the feet [of the recipient].
Therefore, within the Buddha’s Vinaya, it is said that the junior monk grasps both feet of the senior monk with both hands and pays homage by prostrating with his head to the ground.

Regarding the etiquette of reverent salutation, it is stated: "In this land [of China], when performing a respectful salutation, bowing from afar is considered weighty; in India, however, bringing the physical form close to the object of veneration is regarded as the ultimate expression of reverence.
Thus, when Ājñātakauṇḍinya had not seen the Buddha for a long time and came to pay his respects, he covered the Buddha’s feet with his face.

"Three circumambulations to the right" (*pradakṣiṇa*): "Circumambulation" (*zào*) carries the meaning of going around completely; the character is also written as *zhe* (迊), though in the sūtras and śāstras it is frequently corrupted to *zā* (匝).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When making offerings according to the Dharma, one must necessarily circumambulate to the right. The *Record of the Western Regions* (*Xiyuji*) states: "One may circumambulate once, twice, or three times;
the specific number requested by the mind is not fixed. The *Sūtra on the Five Precepts* states: "The three circumambulations symbolize respect for the Three [Jewels]."
The Venerable One has extinguished the three evils, destroyed the three poisons, and emerged from the triple world. The *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"When the Buddha first appeared in the world, an emanation-body descended from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven to transform [beings]. Upon arriving, it circumambulated to the right; having completed the circumambulation, it paid homage.

This is the origin of this circumambulatory salutation (*pradakṣiṇa*). Regarding the meaning of this rightward circumambulation, former sages have offered two explanations: one says that it is from oneself... [text truncated]

Regarding the phrase "turning from the Buddha’s right side toward the east and then north," if one cites the precedent, it means turning from the right side of the Buddha, baring the right shoulder, with the right knee touching the ground.
One version states: "From the Buddha’s right side, facing west, he turns north. This explanation is found in the *Nanshan Guijing Yi* (The Nanshan Ritual for Paying Homage), which states:
"Since the scriptures and the Vinaya enjoin that one must circumambulate to the right, those who circumambulate a stupa to the left are possessed by spirits."
In order to cause the practitioner to accord with the celestial seasons, one faces west and turns toward the north; this is observed in the monastic community.
However, within this specific dharma, one instead turns east and then north to perform the circumambulation.

Having witnessed the tracks of Indian Brahmin monks gathered in the capital as they performed their walking meditation and circumambulations, I observed that they all turned from the northwest toward the northeast to accord with the path of the heavens. Thus it is.
Regarding the sun and moon, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that the palace of the Sun Deity emerges again from the east, circumambulates Mount Sumeru to the right, and sets in the west;
the *Zhulin* (Forest of Pearls) explains this in the same way. There are further texts on the matter that cannot be recorded in full. (And so forth.)

"Clear" (*míng*) exceeds the sun; "exceeds" (*yú*) is the same as "surpasses" (*yú*). In the *Guǎng yùn*, it is pronounced with the *qiè* (rhyme) *róngzhū*; the *Máo shī* says, "Let none exceed my village.
The *Zì lín* states that "to exceed" (*yú*) means to "transgress" (*yuè*).

*Dāna* is translated here as "verses of collected gifts" (*jishi song*), meaning that by means of few words, many meanings are bestowed upon those who recite and uphold them.

Regarding the etymological explanation of "hell" (*diyu*): "hell" (*yu*) means "hardness" (*que*); it refers to the hardness of human sentiments and deceptions. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states that it is called "earth-hell" (*diyu*).
Because they exist beneath the earth, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If one possesses nine thoughts of passion and one thought of the Dharma, one descends into the wheel of fire;

if light, one is born in the *Avīci* hell with intervals, and if heavy, one is born in the uninterrupted *Avīci*. If one is purely passionate, one enters the *Abhisaṃskāra* (or *Arbuda*) hell of the Earth.

Furthermore, if within the sunken mind there is slandering of the Mahāyāna, violating the Buddha’s prohibitions, speaking deceptive and false teachings, vainly coveting offerings of faith, and unworthily receiving respect—these five [factors lead to such retribution].

Regarding the question: "If one commits the ten evil acts, one is reborn in the Avīci Hell of the ten directions; since the hells are insentient (non-sentient), how can they move? The *Zongjing* states:
"The answer is that this is induced by the karmic power of sentient beings, causing those undergoing punishment to perceive these things for themselves.
For example, during the kalpa of formation, although the wind is insentient, it is nonetheless capable of forming the kalpa. (*Yang Wengong Tanyuan*)
Someone raised a doubt, saying that the Buddhist teachings on suffering in hell involve periods that are far too long. I replied:

"The Vinaya texts mention banishment three thousand *li*—the distance is vast—and a period of three years—this duration is indeed long. Yet at the very moment one first commits the offense, it is merely a single thought."
The *Mahāpreta-śāstra* states: "When hungry ghosts approach rivers or streams, water-deity guardians strike them with iron staves;
even if there were no such guardians, the water would naturally dry up. Or, if it should rain from the heavens, it transforms into fire.
The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "Those with seven emotions and three thoughts sink beneath the water-wheel and are born at the boundary of fire, taking birth as hungry ghosts for a hundred [eons]."

The *Qianjie Miaoxuan* (The Profound Mystery of a Thousand Kalpas) states that there are three types of hungry ghosts (*preta*). The heavy class are those whose hunger-fire blazes with fierce flames while they are cut off from even water and gruel;

the middling class are those who wait for people to wash away pus, blood, excrement, and filth; the light class are those who occasionally obtain a single meal, yet are further driven and coerced to fill rivers and block seas.
Furthermore, the *Zhenglilun* (Treatise on the Correct Principle) clarifies that there are nine categories of hungry ghosts, namely those who receive offerings of food.
Regarding the invocation in the ritual texts, the term *chù* (畜) is used;
the *Fǔxíng* (輔行) states that the character *chù* applies generally to all [animals], allowing for six categories. The phonetic transcription is *jiū xǔ liù xiàng jiū sān qiè*.

If one follows the reading *chǔ*, it refers to the "six domestic animals": oxen, horses, chickens, pigs, dogs, and sheep. Based on this, however, the realms of rebirth (*gati*) are not fully encompassed; the new *Póshā* (婆沙) [Abhidharma]... [is more comprehensive].

The character for "animal" (*tiryag-yoni*) consists of the radical for "form" (*rūpa*) and the radical for "horizontal. It is called "horizontal birth" because their bodies are mostly horizontal in their movement;

the radical for "form" signifies that their physical bodies are predominantly horizontal, while the radical for "horizontal" signifies that their mental intentions are not upright. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Those with much passion and little wisdom flow into horizontal birth;
the heavy become the furred masses, and the light become the feathered tribes. The *Amṛtarasa-śāstra* states: "The lifespan of animals may be as short as a single *tala-prahāra* (a finger-snap)."
Their lifespans vary, ranging from half a day or a full day, up to a year or even an eon (*kalpa*).
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that there are forty billion different types of animals. Within the *Mahāvibhāṣā Śāstra*, they are subsumed under three categories:
those that roam by day, those that roam by night, and those that roam both day and night; furthermore, there are distinctions among those dwelling in water, on land, and in the air.
Regarding greed, hatred, and delusion, the *Sushu* (Commentary) states: "The greedy mind is like the ocean receiving streams; it never reaches fullness. The hateful mind is like fire with added fuel;
it grows ever more intense. The deluded mind is like glue that binds and freezes water. The *Fajie Cidi* (Gradual Order of the Dharma Realm) states:
"If one uses a deluded mind to pursue all objects that accord with one's desires, seeking them without satiety, this is [greed]."
If the poison of greed, through a deluded mind, gives rise to anger toward all objects that conflict with one's feelings, this is the poison of hatred.
If, being deluded regarding all phenomena of principle and fact, one fails to understand due to ignorance and falsely gives rise to various perversions, this is the poison of delusion.
*Zhiguan* states: "The three poisons delude the mind; in a single thought-moment, they give rise to eight types of sharp and dull afflictions associated with the body."
From the eighteen *anusayas* up to the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśas*), they dwell in the hells;
"to dwell" (*chu*) means to be at ease. As the *Mao Shi* says, "Do not let me dwell in the imperial palace," and the commentary states that "dwelling" (*chu*) means peace and security.
*Mièng-huǒ-yán-chì*: *yán* (from the rhyme category *qiān-zhān*) means "heat" and "to burn. The *Shuōwén* states: "Yán is the flame rising above fire.
*Chì* (from the rhyme category *chí-shì*) means "flourishing" or "intense.

"Flowing through various hardships" (*liú-zhuǎn-zhū-nàn*): *zhuǎn* (from the *Guǎngyùn*, rhyme category *zhī-liàn*) means "to flow and revolve," which carries the sense of successive eddies and whirlpools.
Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of the Hero of the Present Age* states: "The Tathāgata’s ten powers are heroic and fierce;

he roars the lion's roar to crush the armies of Māra, causing them to know that the six teachers do not possess the lion's roar. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "The Great Hero, the Fierce World-Honored One" (New Record).

It is said that the most refined and outstanding among plants and trees are called "heroes" (ying), and the most exceptional among herds of beasts are called "bulls" (xiong). The Tathāgata is likewise;
because his power is able to subdue Māra and restrain externalists, he is called the "Hero of the World" (Shixiong).
The Honored One among two-legged beings, who is endowed with merit and wisdom, is called the "Honored One among Two-legged Beings. A new commentary states:

Among all beings—whether two-legged, four-legged, or many-legged—the Buddha is the most honored; yet he is specifically termed the "Honored One among Two-legged Beings" because, among all classes of beings, those with two legs are considered noble, namely humans and devas.
Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* explains the title "Teacher of Gods and Humans" by stating that among all sentient beings, only...
This is because both devas and humans can give rise to the bodhicitta and attain the fruits of the Three Vehicles.

Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Supreme Kindness of Parents* states: "A human being receives a body from their parents; for ten months they are carried in the womb, and for three years they are nurtured and cherished with constant care.
Only then can one lift the head and wear hair. How could one suddenly disregard their kindness and turn one's back on their righteousness? Devas [are no different].
Though the earth is vast, it cannot cover this person; though the ground is thick, it cannot support this person. When such a person’s life ends, they will fall directly into hell.
Such a transgression must be confessed and repented.
Regarding the term "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*) as used in the *Guǎngyùn*: "ordinary" (*fán*) means not being one. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Those who have grasping and attachment are called ordinary persons," meaning those who give rise to a mind of craving by grasping at form and so forth. The *Mahātejas-dhāraṇī Sūtra* states:
"Because they are deluded within birth and death, transmigrating and dwelling in an incorrect path, they are called ordinary persons. The *Buddha-nature Sūtra* states:
Ordinary worldlings take the view of a self-identity as their nature.
They are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance. Regarding the character *fù* (覆): its phonetic components allow for three pronunciations—first, *fú* (方福切), meaning "to examine";

second, *fú* (扶富切), meaning "ambush troops"; third, *fù* (敷救切), meaning "to cover. Here, "shrouded by darkness" (*àn fù*) should be understood in the sense of "covering," which corresponds to the third pronunciation, *fù*.

It should be pronounced with the *jiù* (救) tone when calling it; as for the character "fù" (覆) appearing in various sutras, many people mispronounce it. I request that you correct this based on the three meanings mentioned above.

Regarding the character "jìn" (近) in the phrase "associating with evil friends," it should be pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). The *Guǎngyùn* defines it as "to attach to"; if it were pronounced with the entering tone (*shàngshēng*), [it would not accord with the meaning].

Thus, "to train" (*xùn*) implies compulsion, which certainly is not the intended meaning of the scripture. In the subsequent passage, "to draw near" (*qīnjìn*)—whether to non-sages or to evil friends—is difficult to maintain;
one should draw near with love and joy, and both instances of "draw near" (*qīnjìn*) should be read with a departing tone.
Regarding the calming of the mind disturbed by afflictions (*kleśa*): afflictions are turbid and vexing phenomena that disturb the mental spirit and cause the mind to suffer vexation;
this refers to the sharpness or dullness of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). As the Master Deshan stated in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*:
"The dharma of afflictions is a malady common to both the clergy and the laity. When the administration is vexed, the state is in chaos; when the mind is vexed, the intention is in chaos."
When water is clear, fish and stones can be seen; when the spirit is clear, inverted perceptions can be recognized.
If even those who study with clarity and simplicity still find themselves distracted and troubled, how much more so for one in a state of chaos—how could such a person attain the Way?

From these causes, stinginess and envy arise; "stinginess" refers to being parsimonious with wealth, while "envy" refers to being jealous of wealth. The *Yùpiān* states that to contend over beauty is called "jealousy.
The *Chuīyùjì* says: "To possess wealth yet be unable to bestow it is stinginess; to cause others' minds to give rise to feverish distress is envy."
"Jian-chǎn zuò è" (奸諂作惡): "Jian" (奸) is pronounced with the *gǔ* and *yán* rhymes; it means private [deeds] or deceit. "Chǎn" (諂) is pronounced *chǒu yǎn*;
it means flattery or crooked fawning. The *Sāncāng* states: "Deceitful speech is called chǎn"; that is, using clever words and a pleasing countenance to crookedly seek to please others' intentions.
The *Yìjiào jīng shū* (Commentary on the Śrīmālā-sūtra) says: "To seek after someone's intentions and speak words accordingly is called chǎn. Thus, his speech was sycophantic.
Such a person’s mind will surely be crooked.

Furthermore, the *Sūtra on Rebuking Lust through Female Beauty* states: "Female beauty is the shackle and fetter of worldly people; like moths rushing into water, they bring about their own scorching ruin.
Though the clash of spears and arrows may reach them, they accept it with a willing heart. It is like a stagnant pool of clear water."
Tidal dragons and sea-monsters dwell therein; golden mountains and precious caves are the abodes of lions. When family life is discordant, it destroys the ancestral line and ruins the clan;
this is truly a hidden malice. If one can abandon it, it is like breaking a yoke and shedding shackles.
The *Commentary on the Forty-two Sections Sutra* regarding Mount Gu says: "Sensual desire can swallow up the roots of goodness and bring calamity to one's body and life."
It is like the jaws of a tiger! Indeed, Xia perished because of Mei Xi; Shang was lost because of Da Ji; Zhou declined because of Bao Si;

Jin fell into chaos because of Li Ji; and Wu was defeated because of Xi Shi. Moreover, when states and nations throughout the world reach such ruin, none of it does not stem from their female beauty—how much more so for a single family or a single person?

To slander the True Dharma (*saddharma*). [In the] *Guǎngyùn* (Extended Rhymes), the sound of "fěi" (誹) is given as *fēi*; it is also pronounced with the *fāngwèi* (方味) cut, meaning *fèi*. To render it with the third tone (*shàngshēng*) would be erroneous.

The *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) states: "If a person, with an unwholesome mind, were to constantly revile and abuse the Buddha throughout an entire kalpa, their transgression would still be light.
However, if a person uses even a single evil word to disparage those, whether lay or ordained, who read and recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, [the transgression is far greater]."
The phrase "the sin is extremely heavy" indicates that the offense of slandering the Dharma is more grave than the offense of slandering the Buddha.
"Prideful arrogance and negligence" (驕慢放逸)—in the *Guǎng yùn*, "prideful arrogance" (*jiāozì*) means self-indulgence; it is also written as "pride" (*jiāo*). The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"Pride (*māna*) is the elevation of the mind toward others; pride (*māna*) arises from being stained by one's own qualities. The *Fǔ xíng chú* explains: "To boast of oneself is called pride (*māna*); to look down upon others is called arrogance (*māna*). Thus, the former is greater.

The Sūtra states: "A bodhisattva may give rise to great arrogance because of experiencing pleasure, or arrogance because of preaching the Dharma, or arrogance because of diligence, and so on, even up to arrogance because of noble status and wealth."
Abiding in the ten stages (*bhūmi*), as extensively explained in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-alaṃkāra*, these are the so-called Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*),

the Stage of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the Stage of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), the Stage Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*), the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*),

the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), and the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). That which is collectively termed "stage" (*bhūmi*) refers to the Middle Way as the ground that sustains all wholesome dharmas.

Furthermore, regarding the ten kinds of precious jewels that serve as the feet and base, there are two interpretations in the commentary: first, taking the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as the feet and the precious jewels;
here, "precious jewels" refers to the causes of the ten stages, which are noble, and the various stages themselves are the precious jewels. The ten stages are the fruit.
Because they are the foundation of the [Bodhisattva] path, they are called "feet. The ten perfections (*pāramitā*) are the feet of the ten stages (*bhūmi*);

thus, with *dāna* (generosity) as the foot of the first stage, if the foot of *dāna* is fulfilled, one enters the first stage, and so on, until if the foot of *prajñā* (wisdom) is fulfilled, one enters the tenth stage.
Regarding these ten perfections, they are formed by adding skillful means (*upāya*), vows (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and wisdom (*jñāna*) to the six perfections.
Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "In the world there are three realms of existence (*bhava*): first, the realm of desire; second, the realm of form; and third, the formless realm.
'Existence' (*bhava*) refers to all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*); it is the Buddha’s teaching that karma which can cause future rebirth [is what constitutes existence]."

Furthermore, it is called "existence" (bhava) because it possesses meaning and because it arises and ceases; thus, it has the sense of being existent. Moreover, that which falls within the truths of suffering (duḥkha-satya) and its origin (samudaya-satya) is existence.
Now, if these three types of existence are explained in detail, they constitute twenty-five existences. As the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) summarizes in verse:
The four continents, the four evil destinies, The six heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma heavens, The four dhyānas and the four formless realms—[these] are not [included in the three].
Contemplate the five *anāgāmins*.

Regarding the sequence of the factors of the Dharma-realm—the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), and factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*)—it is said that faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are called "faculties" because they can produce wholesome dharmas, and they are called "powers" because they can eliminate the five hindrances;

thus, while the names are the same, their functions differ. "Enlightenment" refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), the first of which is the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*).

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)—namely, (1) the factor of mindfulness, (2) the factor of investigation of phenomena, (3) the factor of energy, (4) the factor of joy, (5) the factor of tranquility, (6) the factor of equanimity, and (7) the factor of concentration—are collectively termed "factors of enlightenment" because they are the constituent parts of the awakening that reaches the fruit. As for the "path," it refers to the Eightfold Noble Path:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
The reason *samādhi* and *abhijñā* are collectively termed the "Right Path" (*samyak-mārga*) is that they both depart from deviation and error, leading to the Right Path to Nirvāṇa.
Regarding *dhāraṇī*, the *Mahā-śāstra* clarifies that its nature is wisdom (*prajñā*).

It is translated as "total retention" (*saṃgraha*), because it gathers various wholesome dharmas and maintains them so they are not lost or scattered—just as a complete vessel holds water without leaking. Furthermore, it is also translated as... [text ends]
It means to restrain and maintain [the mind], to prevent evil from arising, and to maintain goodness so that it is not lost. The *Myōraku-ki* states:
"Dhāraṇī is the seed of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable secret mantra."
The Flower Adornment Mantra for Dispelling Fear, which can eliminate all fears of sentient beings, consists of five aspects:

namely, fire cannot burn it, poison cannot affect it, blades cannot wound it, water cannot sweep it away, and smoke cannot suffocate it. The fire of greed does not burn it; the poison of hatred does not affect it;
the blade of delusion does not wound it; the flow of existence does not sweep it away; and the smoke of discursive thought and reflection does not suffocate it.
It cannot be defiled or harmed.

One remains far removed from the ten unwholesome actions and practices the ten wholesome ones. The Sutra in Forty-two Sections states: "Sentient beings perform good through ten matters and likewise perform evil through ten matters;
these are the three evils of the body—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—and the four evils of the mouth... [the text continues with the remaining two evils of the mouth].
The three evils of the tongue are harsh speech, false speech, and frivolous speech; the three evils of the mind are envy, anger, and delusion.
These ten that do not accord with the Noble Path are called "evil. If one repents them and returns to the ultimate principle, they become the ten virtuous actions.

As the Great Sūtra says: "Regarding the ten evil dharmas, there are superior, middling, and inferior grades: the superior leads to rebirth in hell, the middling to rebirth as an animal, and the inferior to rebirth as a hungry ghost."

The karma of the ten wholesome deeds is certain to lead to rebirth among humans or devas. There are four types of lower births: the lowest birth is in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru); the middle birth is in the Western Continent (Aparagoyānī);
the superior birth is in the Eastern Continent (Pūrvavideha); and the most superior birth is in the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa).

Regarding the stabilization in the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), the *Yingluo jing* (Adornment Sutra) clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes refer to those from the first stage, the Abode of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādabhūmi*), through the Abode of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmiparikarmabhūmi*).

The stages of practice—namely, the stage of birth in a noble family, the stage of perfection in skillful means, the stage of right mind, the stage of non-retrogression, the stage of youthful truth, the stage of the Dharma prince, and the stage of consecration—are collectively termed "stages" (*vihāra*). Specifically, these refer to the stages of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavahāra*);
however, in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), they constitute the inconceivable middle.

"Attaining the Ten Powers (daśabala-bhagavat)": according to the *Erya*, "dai" (逮) means "to reach" (*ji*); according to the *Fangyan*, in the region east and west of the Guanzhong area, "to reach" is called "dai.

The Buddha is endowed with ten kinds of powers as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: the power of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), the power of karma, the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the power of the faculties (*indriya*), the power of aspiration (*chanda*), the power of nature (*dhātu*), the power of the path leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*), the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛti-jñānabala*), the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-jñānabala*), and the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*).

The term "power" (*bala*) used as a general designation for "exerting one's full strength" refers to having attained the application of knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), which cannot be overcome or destroyed.
All wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) are dedicated (*pariṇāmanā*); summarizing all sūtras and śāstras, the so-called dedication does not exceed three types:
namely, dedicating phenomena toward principle (*dharma-tattva*), dedicating causes toward results (*phala*), and universally bestowing one’s own merit upon sentient beings.

Upon examining the *Tiantai Dashijiao yi* (The Meaning of the Four Great Teachings of Tiantai), it states that the six realms (*ṣadgati*) are perilous and difficult. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "A realm (*gati*) is called 'arrival' (*prāpti*), and it is also called a 'path' (*mārga*).

This is because the path of the causes of those wholesome and unwholesome karmas can transport one to the place of birth; it is also so called because, by relying on the karma created, one proceeds toward that place of birth."
Therefore, "destiny" (*gati*) carries the meaning of "tending toward," as the karma one has created tends toward [rebirth in] the heavens and so forth.
From the perils of the six destinies down to these various difficulties, there are in total fourteen instances of the character *nan* (peril/difficulty).
The Commentary states: "If one takes it as the 'difficulty' of 'easy versus difficult,' this refers to evil coming to obstruct the good, thereby making the good difficult to accomplish."
Furthermore, if "難" (nàn) is taken as the "obstacle-difficulty," then it is difficult [to reconcile] with the concluding summary following "善" (shàn).

Since it says, "Thus, these various difficulties," this refers to the difficulty of obstacles. If that were the case, all fourteen instances of the character "難" would have to be pronounced with the departing tone (nàn).

It is difficult to associate with evil friends. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Fǎzàng zhuàn*) states: In the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, there was a white elephant. When the state had a criminal, they would only allow the elephant to trample him to death.

Later, a fire broke out in the elephant stable and spread toward the monastery. A bhikṣu recited a verse from the *Dhammapada*: "By doing good one is born in heaven; by doing evil one enters the abyss.
Upon hearing this, the elephant’s heart became compassionate. Subsequently, when it was time for the criminal to be executed, the elephant allowed him to pass unharmed.
The King asked why it no longer caused harm, and the wise minister replied, "This elephant has heard the Dharma, which is why it acts thus. We should now move it closer to the slaughterhouse;
upon seeing the killing there, its malevolence will surely intensify. The King ordered it to be moved, and indeed its cruelty became even more extreme.
This is like the proximity of good or evil friends, as red dyes turn silk crimson and black ink turns it black. The *Shiji* records the story of Mengzi’s mother and her three moves.
The underlying intent of the passage regarding "transference" (*xi*) is also the same as this.

In the phrase "encountering no difficulty" (*wunan*), both instances of the character *nan* (difficulty) are pronounced with the departing tone (*qùhū*); thus, by being "without difficulty," one actually "creates difficulty. The *Shū* (Commentary) states:
"For example, those of the Two Vehicles who dwell in emptiness, claiming for themselves that they have no further evils and no longer advance to seek Bodhi—they are precisely such people."

Regarding "encountering a favorable time," the *Nanshu* (Commentary on Difficulties) states: "For example, people at the beginning of a kalpa, those in the northern continent (*Uttarakuru*), who exclusively experience pleasure, as well as those in the present day who dwell in wealth and nobility, do not cultivate the Path; these all constitute 'difficulties' because they encounter a favorable time."
The *Mahāpuṇya-saṃskāra-durghaṭaka-śāstra* states: During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were two brothers who left the household life to practice the Way.

One maintained the precepts and engaged in meditation and recitation, while the other extensively sought to cultivate merit. As a result of their respective karmic retributions, one became a white elephant, while the other remained as a monk.
One day, the monk entered the city to beg for food; failing to obtain any, he saw the king’s white elephant well-provided with sustenance and addressed it, saying:
"I and you both have faults; therefore, the elephant does not eat. The elephant keeper, being afraid, questioned him. He replied:
"This elephant was my elder brother in a former life. I did not give him alms. Although he has now attained the Way, he cannot obtain food through begging.
Because he merely cultivated merit, his reward is abundant and sufficient. The elephant heard my words and thus did not eat. This was from the ancient Xianshou school.
A master of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* composed a verse: "Merit must be cultivated and not neglected; wisdom must be studied and not omitted.
One who has wisdom but lacks merit is an Arhat whose offerings are meager. One who has merit but lacks wisdom is like an elephant adorned with necklaces of the seven treasures.
Merit causes the sprouts of goodness to grow; wisdom overturns evil and perversity. When both merits and wisdom serve as adornments, one attains perfect enlightenment."

It is also difficult to encounter a Buddha. While the *Xingqi xing jing* (Sūtra on Arousing Practice) recounts the story of the talkative young girl who danced with a basin on her belly before the Buddha, saying, "You previously had relations with me and caused me to become pregnant;

now I am near my time of delivery, yet you do not know my suffering," the Lord of Devas, seeing this injustice, immediately transformed himself into a mouse, entered her garment, bit the basin, and caused it to fall. At that moment, the great earth shook.
If a young girl moves [the image], she immediately falls into the Avīci Hell; this illustrates the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
Its golden radiance is like Mount Sumeru; the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* explains that Mount Sumeru has four peaks composed of four jewels:
gold in the east, lapis lazuli in the south, silver in the west, and crystal in the north, each manifesting its color according to the majestic power of the jewel.
The *Xianyu Kong* (Manifestation of Emptiness) and the *Da Lun* (Great Treatise) state that certain external texts claim Mount Sumeru is composed entirely of pure gold;
when sentient beings cast themselves into it, their color becomes indistinguishable from it.

Long heels, long fingers, round and straight body, full shoulders, neck, arms, hands, and feet;

Regarding the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*), the *Fajie Cidi* states: "The primary marks are general, while these secondary marks are specific. If one lacks these secondary marks, one is not fully perfected.

The zither has five strings, symbolizing the Five Elements (*pañca-dhātu*). The largest string represents the ruler, being broad, harmonious, and warm;
the smallest string represents the minister, being clear, tranquil, and orderly. Kings Wen and Wu added two more strings to embody the bond between ruler and minister.
