The *Shangshu Dazhuan* states: "In ancient times, the Son of Heaven was necessarily attended by four ministers:
the one in front was called the *Yi*, the one behind was called the *Cheng*, the one on the left was called the *Fu*, and the one on the right was called the *Bi*.

When the Son of Heaven had a question and there was no response, he held the *Yi* accountable; when [the matter] could be recorded but was not recorded, he held the *Cheng* accountable. If governance is upright yet not perfectly so, the fault lies with the *fu*; if it is capable of being exalted yet is not, the fault lies with the *bi*. These four officials are specifically charged with remonstrance and protest.

The Buddha addressed the Earth Goddess Dṛḍhā Bhadrā, explaining the meaning of the term "addressed" (*gào*): to command from above is called "addressing";
it means to awaken, to cause one to realize and understand the intent of one's own mind. According to the *Guǎng yùn*, "to address" (*gào*) means to inform.

The commentary states that he addresses the Earth Goddess because the Earth Goddess presides over this great earth, and all the practices of the Bodhisattvas are based upon it; furthermore, this deity possesses a long life.

The strength of the evidence for the realization of the meaning of the past, future, and present is like that in the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Śrī-samudgata-sūtra*), where the Buddha said to Māra:
"I have accumulated merit and cultivated virtue until I have now attained Buddhahood. Māra asked, "Who can serve as witness?
The Buddha then pointed to the earth with his hand and said, "Only the Earth Deity knows me. Thereupon, the Earth Deity surged forth to bear witness. This is what is addressed here.
The testimony of the Earth Deity Gai-zheng Longzun (Kṣitigarbha Nāgarāja) proves that his past praise of the Buddha was not in vain.
The *Soyin ji* states that the Earth Deity summoned her by the name "Good Woman Deity" (Śubhavyūhā) as a way of extolling her excellence.
He is named King Golden Dragon (Suvarṇavabhāsa). This king was the previous incarnation of King Śraddhālakṣaṇa. The commentary states:

Regarding the colors of bees, emeralds, and peacocks, none can serve as a metaphor for its brilliance. The *Yuhengzhi* of Guangxi states:
"The peacock dwells in the lofty trees of high mountains and descends to bathe on the seashore. The female has no tail; the male’s tail is several feet long and produces three [eyes]."
At the end of the year, its tail begins to grow, shimmering with gold and green and spreading out like a brocade wheel;
the common people call this "the courtship," which lasts from dawn until noon. When people gather to watch, they cannot stop cheering as if in competition.

Its tail sheds once at the end of the year, and it grows back again in summer and autumn. Examining its form, it is clearly of the same class as the pheasant and the chicken, yet it is called a *què* (wagtail).

I have not yet fully understood this. His teeth are fresh and white, like white jade or snow. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Tathāgata’s mark of forty teeth is such that they are neither coarse nor fine;
they do not protrude nor recede. Those who do not know [this] say there is not even a hair’s breadth between them. What does "keqiu" (珂丘) mean?
The *Qièyù piān* states that *ke* (kē) is a stone second only to jade; it is also a type of agate that is as pure white as snow.
One source says that *ke* belongs to the class of conch shells and grows in the sea.
Its eyes are long and wide; the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says, "His eyes are pure, long, and wide like blue lotuses. The *Liezi* says there are those with long [eyes].
Regarding "short" (*duan*), Bo Ya said that "long" (*xiu*) refers to length. The length of flesh is determined by human agency; the length of a person's stature is determined by Heaven.

If one explains the character *xiu* (修) according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "to adorn" or "to refine," pronounced *shisaiqie* (師咸切), signifying the decoration of fur upon the body forming patterns.
This differs greatly from the phonetics and definitions of the two preceding characters.

In this sutra, with the exception of the phrases "his eyes were wide," "his eyebrows were long and fine," "his arms were long and hung down," and "the rest were all well-adorned," all other instances are [described as] "well-adorned" (*su-alaṃkṛta*).
Regarding the mark of his tongue being broad and long, the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra* records that the Buddha said to the five sages: "In the past, I once spoke for the sake of humans..."
Lying is not the speech of an immortal; this is not so. At that time, the World-Honored One extended his tongue from his mouth until it reached both ears and then both nostrils.
He then withdrew his tongue and licked it himself, covering his entire face. Having covered it, he withdrew it again. A passage in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"The tongue of a person of merit reaches the nose; the tongue of a Buddha of the Tripiṭaka reaches the hairline; the most supreme [tongue]..."
The Sūtra says: "His tongue covers the face and extends even throughout the great trichiliocosm.
The *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* says: "When the Buddha was first born, the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows was one foot five inches long;
during his period of ascetic practice, it was ten feet four inches long; and upon attaining Buddhahood, it became one [fathom] long."
It is fifteen feet in length, and both its interior and exterior are hollow like a tube of white lapis lazuli.
From the initial arousal of the bodhicitta, through all the various stages of practice, up until the entry into parinirvāṇa—all these are manifested within the hair-tuft.
This hair-tuft is situated between the two eyebrows, symbolizing the Middle Way.
At the very moment of his birth, the Buddha emitted a great light from his body that illuminated all the worlds, including the devas, māras, and brahmās.
Each of them spoke to one another, saying: "How is it that a sentient being has suddenly appeared here, emitting the light of great wisdom to tear asunder the net of the darkness of ignorance?
(From the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*, on the Buddha’s first birth and the emission of light from his body).
Question: What is meant by "constant radiance"? Answer: The Buddha’s body is surrounded on all four sides by a radiance of one *zhang* each;
this mark was present from the very moment the Buddha was born. Question: For what reason is the constant radiance only one *zhang*? Answer:

Although the bodily radiance of all Buddhas is immeasurable, because of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) of this evil world, the Buddha manifests a radiance of only one *zhang*. If sentient beings possess sharp faculties and merit, then the Buddha...
He manifests immeasurable light. It is like a lion;
the text says *huó* (虓), which refers to a lion. The "Account of the Western Regions" (*Xiyu zhuan*) in the *Hanshu* states:

"In the kingdom of Wuyi there are lions that resemble tigers, are a pure yellow color, and the hair at the tips of their tails is as large as a peck-measure (*dǒu*). The *Erya* states: "The *suānmí* is like [a lion]..."
The *Lianmao* (the Leopard-Cat) devours tigers and leopards. Guo Pu’s commentary states that this is the *siṃha* (lion). It originates from the Western Regions;

during the reign of Emperor Shun of the Han dynasty, the King of Shule came to present a lion. The *Tianzi Zhuan* (Annals of the Lord of Heaven) states that the *suanni* (leopard-cat) runs five hundred li in a single day.

The *Luoyang Qielan Zhi* (Record of the Monasteries of Luoyang) states that during the Later Wei, the Kingdom of Persia presented a lion, and Emperor Zhuang addressed his attendants... [text continues].
Zhongli said, "I have heard that when a tiger sees a lion, it must submit; let us seek one out to test this.

Thereupon, he issued an edict to the prefectures and counties near the mountains to capture tigers and bring them in. At that time, two tigers and one leopard were presented from Shan County and Yang County;
upon seeing the lion, they all closed their eyes and did not dare to look at it.
The Chapter on the Well-Assembled Branches of the Śāla Tree further states that one should offer *śāla* flowers; in Sanskrit, *śāla* is translated as "firm" (*dṛḍha*).
This tree stands in the city of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas, where the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa beneath it.
Its flowers resemble lotuses and its fruit resembles a jar; its sweetness is like honey. (Continued from the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*, by Huijiao).
The *Shichuan* records that according to the *Jingnan Ji*, during the Yongkang era of the Jin dynasty, a tree suddenly grew beneath a monk’s quarters;
it sprouted again every time it was cut down, much to the wonder of the community. They left it there without pruning, and within ten days its trunk had grown as tall as the ridgepole.
The monks moved their quarters to avoid it. In summer, white flowers bloomed, which no one could identify. Later, an Indian monk saw them and...
Shedding tears, he said, "The Buddha entered nirvana beneath this tree; it is because I reflect upon its past significance that I weep.
The tree remains there to this day and is a wonder of the region. At the beginning of the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, Anxi presented branches of the śāla tree, stating:
"In the four prefectures under my jurisdiction, there is one called Baluona which is closest [to the capital]. There, there is a śāla tree."

Surpassing ordinary grasses and trees, it does not merely stop at deterring evil beasts; with its towering trunk, it feels no shame before the pine and cypress, and with its spreading shade, it bears no comparison to the peach and plum.
Recently, I dispatched an envoy who obtained two hundred branches of this tree.
If they are permitted to take root in Changle Palace and unfurl their tips in Jianchang Palace, how magnificent this would be! This is recorded in the *Taiping Guangji*.
"A halo one *xun* [in diameter]"—He Cheng’s *Zaoyao* states: "Eight inches is called a *zhi*; three *zhi* is called a *wu*;
five *zhi* is called a *mo*; six feet is called a *bu*; seven feet is called a *ren*; eight feet is called a *xun*; ten feet is called a *zhang*; sixteen *zhang* is called a *chang*.
Furthermore, the *Xiaoya* states: "Four feet is called a *ren*; double a *ren* is a *xun*; double a *xun* is a *chang*. Observe this.
The *Buddha-samādhi Sūtra* states: "The body of Śākyamuni is one zhang and six chi in height, and his halo is seven chi in diameter.
Regarding the term "buddha-field" (*buddhakṣetra*), the *Fuxing* commentary notes that it should properly be called *kṣetra*, which translates as "field" or "soil";
this refers to the realm governed by a single Buddha. Śākyamuni takes the trichiliocosm as his single field.
Regarding the expression "long flagpole and golden *kṣetra*-staff" (*dīrgha-dhvaja-suvarṇa-kṣetra*) found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* concerning the Buddha-lands:
this refers to using the *kṣetra*-staff (the central pillar) to represent the place of residence, rather than referring to the actual field or territory itself.

As for the word *yōng* (傭): its form is slender and round like the trunk of an elephant king; it is pronounced *chōngróng* (丑容切), with the alternative reading *tōngróng* (通容). According to the *Guǎngyùn*, *yōng* means... [text fragment].
It is upright and well-proportioned. Wan Zhen’s *Nanzhou Yiwuzhi* (Record of Strange Things from the Southern Regions) states: "The body of the elephant is twice that of an ox;
its eyes do not exceed those of a pig; its trunk is six or seven feet long and as thick as a human arm."
He heard the profound and subtle sound of the repentance ritual. According to the *Erya*, the southwest corner of a room is called the *ao*;

Guo’s commentary states that it refers to a hidden, secluded, and deep interior space. Because Xinxiang directly heard the Buddha preach the Repentance Ritual for the Non-arising of Dharmas (*wusheng li chan*), it is described as the "profound and subtle sound."

Regarding the term *biè* (莂) in "receiving the prediction (*jìbiè* 記莂)": the *Huayan jing yinyi* (Sutra of the Flower Ornament’s Phonetic Commentary) states that the character *biè* (莂) is correct; however, the *Jingyinyi* (Sutra Phonetic Meanings) states that the character *bié* (別) is correct.
These two explanations are contradictory. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "In 'receiving the prediction,' *biè* means to branch out or to distinguish.

Lexicons mostly use the character *bié* (別); here, following the *Fuxing*, [the character *bié* is adopted]. (Note: The character *biè* [莂] is a rare variant; the standard form is *bié* [別], meaning "to distinguish" or "to separate," which aligns with the context of a "prediction" being a specific designation.)

Because the essence and the function are mutually pervasive, the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of both "bestowing a prediction" (*授記*) and "receiving a prediction" (*受記*). "Receiving a decision" (*受決*) and "receiving a prophecy" (*受莂*) are used interchangeably.

"Bestowing" (*授*) has the meaning of giving; "receiving" (*受*) has the meaning of obtaining; "prediction" (*記*) refers to recording a matter; "decision" (*決*) refers to determination; and "prophecy" (*莂*) refers to discernment.

It is like the great ocean, fully endowed with precious jewels. The *Loutan jing* (Ratnakūṭa-sūtra) states that within the vast sea there are seven kinds of counterfeit jewels and one hundred and twenty kinds of genuine jewels.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that at the bottom of the sea there are four great natures of treasure that are extremely fierce and hot, capable of shrinking the waters of the hundred rivers:
the first is called Sūryagarbha (Sun-Treasury), the second is named Vigatarasa (Free from Moisture), and the third is Jvālā (Flame).
Its light pervades the four quarters without exception. Furthermore, there is a precious jewel named "Universal Gathering of All Jewels";
if this jewel were present, even if the world were consumed by the fires at the end of an eon, it could not cause even a single drop of this ocean water to diminish.

The *Commentary on the Chapter on Emptiness* states that there are four kinds of emptiness: the emptiness of entering emptiness by extinguishing form, which is the Tripitaka Teaching (*zangjiao*); the emptiness where form itself is emptiness, which is the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*);

the emptiness of entering emptiness by extinguishing extremes, which is the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*); and the emptiness where extremes themselves are emptiness, which is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

This sutra encompasses all these teachings and should therefore possess all four kinds of emptiness; however, the fact that it here specifically designates "emptiness" refers exclusively to the emptiness wherein extremes are themselves empty.
... (and so forth). The mind is like a magical illusion, galloping through the six sense-objects. The *Miaoxuan* says: "The mind is like a phantom or a flame; it has only a name, which we call 'mind.
When one speaks of its existence, no material substance is seen; when one speaks of its non-existence, thoughts and conceptions arise once more."
Because it cannot be conceptualized through the categories of existence or non-existence, the mind is called "sublime. The *Miaoshu* (Sublime Commentary) states:
"Even if the eyes and ears do not encounter external objects, the mind still pursues past recollections; thus it is said to 'gallop about,' like a person sitting idly while racing across the world."
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Thus, these six—your current eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—are the intermediaries for thieves who plunder the family treasures.
The *Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra* states: "Because they can damage the life of wisdom and injure and destroy the Dharma-body, they are called 'thieves'."
Regarding the "mechanism of karma," the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "It is like a wooden puppet; if the wedge is absent, the body falls apart and cannot move.
The *Huguo ji* (Record of Protecting the State) explains: "Mechanism (*ji*) refers to the subtle impulse that can trigger action, while 'joint' (*guan*) refers to the articulations.
It moves by means of a person [as its operator]; karma serves as the mechanism, and its substance is like a wooden doll."

The *Dìshuǐhuǒfēng Qǐngguānshìyīn Jīng* (Sutra on the Earth, Water, Fire, and Wind Invoking Avalokiteśvara) states: "You should now contemplate that the nature of earth is not solid; the nature of water does not abide; the nature of wind is without obstruction;
and the nature of fire arises dependently upon causes and conditions. The *Zēnghuī Jì* (Record of Increasing Radiance) comments:

"Earth, water, fire, and wind are the provisional four great elements (*mahābhūta*); if they were the true four great elements, they would be the natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion. (*Lengyan Jíjiě*) [End of quotation].

Regarding why the four elements are collectively termed "great" (*mahābhūta*), it is established based on their activity that they are called "great" because there is no place where these four great elements do not exist.

This is like the analogy of four snakes sharing a single basket; the commentary explains that this clarifies that while the basket is the same, the natures of the snakes differ, as some possess venomous stings.
The meaning of "afflictions as harm" is the same [as the following]. A great sutra states that the body is a casket; the body sustains the four great elements just as a casket holds snakes.
When the casket breaks, the snakes depart; when the body perishes, the elements vanish. The Great Sutra says:
"Suppose there were a king who placed four venomous snakes in a single casket and ordered a person to look after them. If he were to cause even one snake to become angry with me..."
When they were about to execute him, the man fled in terror. They immediately dispatched five *caṇḍālas* who followed him with drawn swords.
Behind them was another man who hid his sword and feigned intimacy; the man did not trust him and threw himself into a village settlement, whereupon he sat down upon the ground.
At that moment, a voice from the sky proclaimed: "Tonight, six great bandits shall come. The man was struck with fear.
Terrified, he abandoned his path and encountered a river whose waters were swift and turbulent; he immediately gathered grass and wood to make a raft and crossed the current.
Having reached the other shore, he was secure and free from harm. The Bodhisattva is also like this:
he contemplates the body as a chest, the four great elements as snakes, the five *caṇḍālas* as the five aggregates (*skandhas*), and deceitful intimacy as craving—the empty village.
The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are the six thieves; the external six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are the river; the afflictions (*kleśa*) are the sea; the raft is the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*);
reaching the other shore is arriving at *nirvāṇa*.

The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are venomous snakes. According to the *Guǎngyùn*, "wán" (蚖) is pronounced with the first tone and the rhyme *guān* (五 官 切), meaning a venomous snake. According to the *Yùpiān*, "wán" (蚖) is pronounced with the second tone and the rhyme *yúyuán* (魚 袁 切), referring to a *rājila* (a type of lizard or chameleon).
Regarding the *yuán* (crawling lizard), Cui Bao’s *Gujin Zhu* states: "The *yíngyuán* is also called *yī*; the larger ones reach three feet in length and are dark purple-black in color.
They are skilled at bewitching people but do not speak; they possess poison. The *Dajing* says: "The four snakes harm people, yet they do not fall into the various evil realms;

the four great elements harm people, yet they are certain to fall into the three miserable paths. The commentary states: "Snakes have venomous stings; one should [therefore] take [the elements as a warning]."
Wu Guan’s intent in composing this scripture is precisely this:
the two elements of fire and wind ascend, which are yang; the two elements of earth and water descend, which are yin.
As for the "two directions" mentioned for each, this refers to correlating the four great elements with the four cardinal directions.
Wind is in the east, fire in the south, earth in the west, and water in the north. The east and south belong to Yang and ascend; the west and north belong to Yin and sink downward.

The *Sijiming* (Record of the Four Clarities) states: "The correspondence of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) with the four directions reveals that the internal four great elements possess the natures of the four directions.

That the ascending and sinking of the four directions serve as evidence for the [contradictory] characteristics of the [great] elements is precisely because the internal and external are fundamentally one."

This refers to the mutual influence between the primary and secondary realms (*niṣyanda*). The two natures of mind and consciousness are restless and never still; as the *Abhidharmakośa* states, they are collectively termed "mind" (*citta*), while that which deliberates is called "thought" (*manas*) and that which discerns is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Mind, thought, and consciousness—these three are one dharma with different names. Regarding their enumeration, it is called "mind" because it accumulates.
Birth is *citta* (mind), discrimination is *manas* (intellect), and subsequent discernment is *vijñāna* (consciousness). Regarding the two natures:
both mind and consciousness each possess the two natures of good and evil. As for "restlessness" (*zào*), it is pronounced *jiào* (qìe);
in the *Zhou Yi*, it is said that "Zhen represents restless movement. The *Lun Yu* states: "When speech has not yet reached its expression, it is called restlessness (*zào*). (Commentary).
This refers to being unsettled.
Good daughter, you should contemplate all phenomena in this way. The commentary states that the "good daughter" is the Bodhi-tree goddess (*Bodhivṛkṣadevatā*).

When the Buddha preaches the Dharma, there must be one who responds and upholds it; he entrusts [the teaching] to one person to instruct the multitude. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "As if for the sake of a single person..."
The same applies to the multitude.
Birth and death are boundless, revolving without ceasing. The *Inga-kyō* (Sūtra on Cause and Effect) states: "Sentient beings circulate through the five realms;
when one body perishes in death, they receive another body. Birth and death are immeasurable, like cutting down all the grasses and trees under heaven."

If one were to attempt to calculate their number, even one's own physical body could not exhaustively enumerate them. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Because humans eat sheep, when the sheep dies it becomes a human;
when the human dies they become a sheep. Thus it continues through ten lifetimes and so forth, dying and being born again and again, devouring one another in mutual succession.
These evil karmas arise together and persist until the end of the future. You owe me my life, and I shall repay you with your debt."
Throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one constantly transmigrates within the grass huts of birth and death.
It is said that the physical forms and environments of the three realms and six paths are governed by yin and yang; as the two energies swirl and circulate, karma rides upon them.
Now, when sentient beings create good or evil, they correspond to these two energies: those who are pure ascend and, being turned by the cycle, form the three wholesome states.
When the path is turbid, one sinks downward; when turned, it forms the three evil realms.
The abode of the five aggregates is entirely empty and quiescent when contemplated. As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The King is the mind-king, and the house is the house of the five aggregates.
If the mind-king constructs this house, then by contemplating the five aggregates, they are seen as the dharma-nature; in that dharma-nature, there is no longer feeling or perception.
Regarding the statement that "the consciousness of formations is itself nirvana, the ultimate emptiness which analyzes the five aggregates," the *Xixuan* (Analysis of the Profound) says:

Form (*rūpa*) takes obstruction as its essential meaning; sensation (*vedanā*) takes experiencing as its essential meaning; perception (*saṃjñā*) takes conceptualizing and establishing [mental images] as its essential meaning;
formations (*saṃskāra*) take shifting, flowing, and creating as their essential meaning; and consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes discerning and distinguishing as its essential meaning.

"Opening the gate of the ambrosia and displaying the vessel of ambrosia"—in more than twenty places throughout this sutra, whenever "ambrosia" (*amṛta*) is mentioned, it invariably refers to the ultimate path of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).
This is because our Buddha, in accordance with worldly conventions, spoke of the provisional and the real to reveal the underlying principle; thus these words were spoken.

Now, first I shall explain them according to their phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and subsequently I shall interpret them according to their doctrinal meaning (*artha*). Regarding the phenomenal characteristics: [to the] east...

The *Shenyijing* (Classic of Divine Marvels) by Fang Shuo states: "Beyond the western and northern seas there is a person two thousand li tall, with a lifespan of eight thousand years, who drinks five dou of 'celestial wine' daily.
Zhang Hua’s commentary notes: "Celestial wine is dew. The *Ruiyingtu* (Illustrations of Auspicious Responses) states:
"When the color of the dew is thick and sweet, it is called 'sweet dew' (*ganlu*). When a ruler bestows virtue and wisdom, sweet dew descends upon his plants and trees. (From the Jin dynasty).
The *Zhongxing Shu* states: "When sweet dew descends, the aged receive honor, and thus the pine and cypress trees receive it;
when the worthy are revered and the multitude are welcomed, the bamboo and reeds receive it. Sweet dew is the moisture of benevolence; its congealed form is like fat, and its flavor is like syrup.
Sweet dew is also called 'Heaven’s Wine' (*tianjiu*). The *Shiyiji* states: "On Mount Kunlun there is sweet dew; when one gazes upon it..."
Its color was like vermilion; when applied to wood or stone, it became as bright as frost and snow. When contained in precious vessels, it was like sweet syrup.
Regarding the sagely virtue of a sovereign, the *Book of the Later Han* states that in the seventeenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming, sweet dew descended upon Yuanling.
Furthermore, in the autumn of the first year of the Yongkang era of Emperor Huan, auspicious trees grew in Wei Commandery and sweet dew descended.
The *Record of Mount Lu* states that during the Taicheng era of the Liang dynasty, Dharma Master Xi was lecturing on the *Guanming Jing* (Sutra of Immeasurable Life) in a forest.
For three days, sweet dew (*amṛta*) drenched the trees; consequently, he established a *śīla-maṇḍala* within the woods, which was named the "Amṛta Maṇḍala.
The commentary by Fayi explains: "Amṛta is the divine medicine of immortality belonging to the various devas; those who consume it have long lives and [vigorous] bodies."

The "tranquil power" (*anala*), the "great body," and the "light" are used as metaphors for the Buddha’s qualities of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*): permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*).

This is an interpretation based on using the four meanings of *amṛta* (ambrosia) to illustrate the Buddha’s four virtues. The *Shiqian* states: "The gate of ambrosia refers to the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) which is eternally abiding;
it is like celestial ambrosia, the medicine that prevents death. This is an interpretation based on taking the principle itself as the gate.
The *Miaole ji* states: "The true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the ambrosia (*amṛta*), and the various teachings are the gates.

This explains that, in terms of the teaching, the teachings serve as the means of access (*nirvāha*), while the ambrosia of the true aspect is the object accessed. Thus, although ambrosia is but one, its application varies according to the text;
it may function as either the subject or the object, appearing in various forms such as a city, a vessel, a chamber, or a flavor. Buddhas and patriarchs exercise their sovereign mastery over these.
Is this not what is meant by saying that there are many gates to skillful means (*upāya*) in its application?
Blowing the great dharma-conch: in India, at most Buddhist assemblies, the blowing of the conch is frequently used to alert the multitude; this is as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*:
"Blowing the shell to signal the time. Furthermore, when the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to blow the conch, the bhikṣus immediately emerged from their meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
The *Jiàngǒng chuánshuō* states: "The *bèihǎi* is a marine crustacean. The *Shénzhì bǔzhù* adds:
"The *hǎibèi* is the same as the great conch (*mahāśaṅkha*), capable of holding a *shēng* or a *dǒu*; it is blown to keep time for music.

It originated among the Southern Barbarians, but today it is still used in the *shuǐlù fǎhuì* (Water and Land Assemblies) in Shǔ. The Bodhisattva Mahākāruṇika holds a precious conch in his hand; this was praised by the ancient masters."
It is said: "Upon the seat of the Dharma, one long blows the great Dharma-conch; its single sound, fierce and majestic, pervades the Sahā world.
One strikes the Great Dharma-drum. "Drum" (*gu*) shares the same phonetic root as "to strike" (*gu*), though its meaning differs from the former.
The *Shi Ben* states that the Yi people fashioned the drum and struck it with a mallet. The *Zhou Yi* says, "It is stirred by thunder and lightning," which indicates the symbol it represents.
Furthermore, the *Rituals of Zhou* states: "Use the thunder drum (*leigǔ*) for divine sacrifices; use the spirit drum (*lingǔ*) for sacrifices to the soil (*shèjì*);
use the road drum (*lùgǔ*) for offerings to the spirits (*guǐxiǎng*); use the great drum (*fēnggǔ*) for military affairs; use the long drum (*gāogǔ*) for labor services;

and use the advancing drum (*jìngǔ*) for the orchestration of metal instruments. The *Records of the Grand Historian* states: "In the past, when the Yellow Emperor was at war with Chiyou, he consulted with Qibo. Qibo said: 'Chi..."
Yu was the essence of the sea; he feared only the sound of gongs and drums. One must advance the army with the drum and halt the army with the gong—only then can victory be achieved.
Thus, the Yellow Emperor employed this stratagem and secured victory; for this reason, it is still used in military law today. The commentary states:
"Beating the drum to solemnize the multitude and lead them forward is like the Buddha preaching the Dharma to urge on those who are deep in their practice."

The *Yusheng fayu shu* (Commentary on the Rain of the Supreme Dharma) states: "When the seasonal moisture descends once, flowers and fruits flourish; this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, which increases the Path and brings beings to maturity.
The *Dajing* (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra) says: "The unsurpassed Dharma-rain falls upon the field of your body, causing the sprouts of the Dharma to grow.

The *Chanyi chao* (Exegesis of the Meaning) explains: "The first character 'yu' (rain) is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*). 'Yu' here means 'to descend. The *Mao Shi* (Book of Odes) says: 'The snow falls thickly,' and the *Zhuan* (Commentary) states..."
That which descends from above is called rain. This subsequent scriptural passage describes the raining down of various celestial flowers and the raining down of fine powdered incense.
It is able to rain down the unsurpassed; that is, it rains down the *mandārava* flowers of the heavens.

It rains down immeasurably, and immediately thereafter it rains down the seven treasures everywhere, raining down exquisite celestial lotuses. Furthermore, it rains down celestial flowers and forty thousand pearls.
The *Yíngluò jīng* (Adornment Sūtra) further describes thirteen types of rain: it rains various flowers, it rains various fragrant flowers, and it rains tears of lamentation.

These thirteen instances of the character "rain" (*yù*) are all pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*), while the others are all pronounced with the entering tone (*shàngshēng*). The *Weimiao fǎcháng shū* (Commentary on the Subtle Dharma Banner) states: "The Samādhi of the Dharma Banner rises high above all practices, like soldiers looking toward their banner. This explains [the significance].
The inscription states: "Banners and flags are for the purpose of signaling commands. The *Sūtra of the Collection of Original Deeds* (*Lalitavistara-sūtra*) says:
"When Prince Siddhārtha attained the Way and subdued all demonic adversaries, he erected the banner of victory."
One relinquishes all that is held dear: limbs, joints, hands, feet, head, eyes, marrow, brain, and beloved wife and children.
The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva’s mind is still not satisfied by giving external objects; only when he gives his own body is he fully satisfied.

This is as in the case of King Bhaiṣajyarāja in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, who burned his own body. For while people do not consider it a favor when they receive external objects, they do so when they receive his very body.

Furthermore, the *Śāstra* clarifies three kinds of giving: the gift of food and coarse material goods is called "inferior giving"; the gift of clothing and precious objects is called "middling giving";

and the gift of one's head, eyes, blood, flesh, kingdom, city, wife, and children is called "superior giving. Only by means of such distinctions can one truly cause [the recipient] to be moved with awe.
From the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" in the *Qishi jing* (Sutra on the Arising of the World), the "Chapter on the Four Kings" states:
On the eastern flank of Mount Sumeru, forty-two thousand *yojana*s above the earth, at the summit of Mount Gandhamādana, lies the city of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
It is six hundred *yojana*s in length and breadth, surrounded by sevenfold walls, railings, rows of trees, and towers.
One contemplates the gardens adorned with the seven treasures and so forth; the city walls where the three Heavenly Kings reside in the south, west, and north are all as previously described.
The *Ekottarika-āgama* states: "At the midpoint of Mount Sumeru are the Four Heavenly Kings.
When they are first born, they are spontaneously born upon the laps of the gods. Furthermore, there are spontaneous precious vessels containing the hundred flavors."
Having eaten and drunk, they grow large; their height is half a *li*, and their clothing weighs half a *liang*.
They take fifty human years as one day and night, thirty such days as one month, and twelve such months as one year.
One human eighteen thousand years constitutes one of their years; thus, their lifespan is five hundred years. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "All worlds..."
Those who dwell between [the realms] do not seek the permanent abode and are unable to relinquish their affection for wives and concubines;
because their minds do not stray from lustful desires, they purify themselves until clarity arises. After their lives end, they are born among the Four Heavenly Kings.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the Four Kings are the subordinate generals beneath Śakra.
The *Fourfold Record of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa* states: "In the Western lands, the north is considered the upper direction.
Because his residence faces mostly east, the north is designated as his left. Therefore, this chapter first lists the Northern Heaven. The *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"The Northern Heavenly King protects the northern continent of Uttarakuru and also concurrently protects the other continents; he dwells on the Crystal Mountain to the north of Mount Sumeru."
Regarding the two spirits, Duta and Ling: one is named Yakṣa and the other Rākṣasa.
The *Jīngyìnyì* (Phonetic and Semantic Commentary on the Sūtras) states that Vaiśravaṇa is also called Vīpa; his original name was Kucira.

Once, while the Buddha was preaching the Dharma, the King [of the North] donned a *kāṣāya* robe and entered the assembly. Everyone was astonished and said to one another: "He is a śramaṇa! He is a śramaṇa!"

From this point on, the śramaṇa was consequently called Vaiśravaṇa. The *Lotus Sūtra* states that "Vaiśravaṇa" is translated as "Various Hearings" (*vividha-śruta*) or "Much Hearing" (*bahu-śruta*), meaning that this king possesses great merit and his fame is heard everywhere.
The *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha* states: "One should fashion an image of the Northern Heavenly King, wearing various celestial garments, with the left arm extended."
Holding a spear that touches the ground, his right hand is bent at the elbow as he supports a Buddhist stūpa; the spear is eighteen feet long.

According to the *Táng lìxiàng yí* (The Ritual for Standing Images of the Tang), this king was clad in full golden armor and stood with his feet upon the shoulders of a woman, beneath whom clouds were formed to support him;
some say this woman is his mother. To his left and right, the eight classes of supernatural beings (*aṣṭavidha-gaṇa*) are arrayed.
The various spirits of wind, water, lightning, and thunder have their son, Kiṇāliśa, who follows them before and behind along with ninety-one sons.

Regarding the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Ti-tou-lai-tuo): *Dhṛta* is pronounced with the *zhà* and *chē* initials; the *Fahua jing* (Lotus Sūtra) states that *Dhṛtarāṣṭra* is translated as [the Guardian of the East].
Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Holding the Nation) is also called Anmin (Peaceful for the People); he derives his name from the land he protects.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the Heavenly King of the East protects Pūrvavideha and also other continents; he dwells on the northern peak of Mount Sumeru, made of yellow gold, and presides over two classes of spirits:
first, the Gandharvas—translated here as "Incense-Seekers"—who are the musicians of Śakra, the Lord of Devas.
He is also named Pūtana, which translates as "Foul-Smelling Ghost" or "Ghost Who Governs Fever. The *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha* states:
"The Holder of the Nation (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) extends his left arm downward, grasping a sword;
his right arm is bent forward with the palm facing upward, holding a precious jewel from which light radiates, signifying his role as a deity who rewards the virtuous and punishes the evil."
The *Youyang zazu* states that in Chang’an there was a temple called Chiguo Temple, which had several *huai* trees planted before its gates.
One day, one of them was cut down for use as firewood; upon each slice of wood, a majestic image of a Heavenly King (*devaputra*) appeared, perfectly formed.
Regarding the Dharma-phrases of the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Virūḍhaka" is translated as "Increase" (*vṛddhi*).
This means that this king protects and sustains the land, causing the roots of goodness in others to increase. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"King Virūḍhaka protects and sustains Jambudvīpa in the south, while also overseeing the other continents; he dwells upon the lapis lazuli terrace at the southern side of Mount Sumeru."
He leads two spirits: the first is named Kumbhāṇḍa, which translates as "Jar-shaped" or "Resembling a Winter Melon," referring to a spirit that causes nightmares and bewitchment;
the second is named Pīli-ta, which translates as "Grandfather," being the lowest rank among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
The *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha* states: "The left hand of King Virūḍhaka extends downward with a sword grasped in it, while his right hand..."
He held a spear with its tip planted in the ground; this manifestation of majestic courage was intended to subdue the wicked and cause roots of goodness to flourish, and thus it became his name.
According to the *Linggan Zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance), one day a celestial deity came to Master Nanshan’s room, moving about as if a human being.
The Master asked, "Who is it? He replied, "Your disciple is the fifteenth son of the Heavenly King of the South."
Zi Zhang said, "The Emperor has ninety-one sons, each possessing heroic strategy and divine martial prowess, and each protects his own capital.
Why do you not manifest yourself? Tian replied, "My disciples have distinct complexions and features that would alarm the hearts of the multitude;
it is sufficient for me to discuss matters with you alone. (And so forth.)
Regarding the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, the *Ting shi zhoutian zhuan* (Biographies of the Devas of the Thunder-Master) states that he is also called Virūḍhaka;
this is translated as "Diverse Speech" because he is able to produce various kinds of speech. He is also translated as "Evil Eye" and "Broad Eyes.
Because this king fixes his gaze with wrathful majesty to cause the wicked to disperse and protects the people, he has attained [this name].
Because of this title, this sutra states that he constantly observes and protects with his pure divine eye, which surpasses that of human eyes.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The King Virūpākṣa protects the western continent of Aparagoyānī, as well as other continents.
He dwells on the western silver terrace of Mount Sumeru and commands two classes of spirits: the first is named Piśāca, which translates as 'eater of essence.'"

The Qi-ghost is also known as the Poisonous Dragon. The *Peacock Sūtra* states that the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa is a great dragon king who has immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dragons as his retinue.
The *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha* states that the Heavenly King of the Western Quarter holds a spear in his left hand and grasps a red rope in his right hand.
Both rose from their seats; the *Qulǐ* states: "One rises when requesting the lesson (*yè*) and when requesting further instruction (*yì*. The commentary notes:

"This is out of reverence for the teacher and respect for the Way, similar to the practice today of tucking up one's robes and stepping forward to request instruction. 'Lesson' refers to a chapter or scroll;

'further instruction' refers to when, after receiving an explanation, one finds it insufficient and desires the teacher to explain it more clearly. Such protocols for advancing to inquire are observed both in this land and in the Western Regions.

All are the same. Regarding the practice of baring one shoulder, the *Yiguang Guanzizai Pusa Yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of Avalokiteśvara) states: "In foreign lands, baring the shoulder is regarded as an act of reverence;

exposing the right shoulder indicates convenience for holding offerings and expresses the ritual of a disciple serving his teacher or performing labor. Thus, they regard baring the shoulder as a mark of respect. In this land [China], however..."

Baring one shoulder is considered an act of arrogance; however, in antiquity there was Xu Jia, who bared his flesh and prostrated himself before Zhang Lu, exposing both shoulders—thus, it is not invariably an act of arrogance.
(The account of Xu Jia and Zhang Lu is found in the *Shiji*; the *Ouyi Zhixu’s Commentary on the Meaning of the Four-Ming Avalokiteśvara* cites this in detail.

The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* asks: "At what time should one bare one's shoulder? The Buddha replied: "One should bare one's shoulder at the time of making offerings, so as to facilitate the performance of tasks."
Therefore, when acting as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), one must bared the right shoulder to manifest the appearance of a field of merit;
thus, whenever one makes offerings, it is precisely the time for seeing the Buddha and prostrating to him, and the time for attending the midday meal, meditating, and reciting scriptures.
The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) clarifies the dress of the people of India, stating that men wrap a cloth around their waists and bare the left shoulder, while women...
The *Guījìng yí* (Ritual of Reverent Return) states: "Nowadays, various śramaṇas universally wear short-sleeved tunics (*biānróu*) that barely expose the shoulders;
they then cut these tunics into two pieces to serve as the 'exposed shoulder' (*biāntàn*) for the three robes.
This results in the loss of both name and meaning."
Regarding the various texts concerning the ritual of *hukui* (kneeling), there are generally four different names for this practice:

first, it is called *hukui guijing yi* (The Ritual of Hukui for Reverent Homage), which states that because the manner of reverence among the Hu people preserves its original conditions, it is termed *hukui*.

Second, it is called *hukui*, as the *Zhulin* (Pearl Forest) explains: "Hukui" means kneeling with the left and right knees alternately placed upon the ground. Third, it is called... [text fragment ends].
Regarding "qiào-guì" (standing on tiptoe): the *Guǎng yùn* states that "qiào" means to lift up or to be precarious;

lifting one foot while standing makes the body precarious. Fourth is "cháng-guì" (kneeling for a long time). The *Xīyù jì* explains that among the nine modes of etiquette in India, the sixth is named "cháng-guì.
The *Fāng yán* states that in the regions between Dōngqí and Běiyān, they call kneeling "cháng. Based on this, the character should be written as "cháng" (長); however, these four...
Regarding the term "huzui" (胡跪): if one says it means simply kneeling on one knee, that is not entirely accurate; let us further examine its characteristics.
The *Fuxing* (輔行) states that the ritual of *huzui* involves three points being raised and prominent.

The *Zhulin* (珠林) explains that *huzui* is synonymous with *huo-gui* (互跪), meaning the left and right knees are alternately placed upon the ground. As for *zhang-gui* (長跪), it refers to standing upright with the feet together and the hands clasped at the chest.
Regarding the etiquette of reverence: because monks are men of sturdy constitution, the rule was established for them to kneel alternately (mutual kneeling).

Because nuns are women of weak physique, rising would cause them fatigue; therefore, they are required to kneel with one leg extended (long-kneeling). Furthermore, the *Vinaya* states that while nuns must kneel alternately, the Buddha permitted long-kneeling.
The *Jigui zhuan* explains that "long-kneeling" consists of resting both knees upon the ground and supporting oneself by standing upright on both feet.
Question: Since the *prāñjali* (palms joined) posture is the kneeling gesture of nuns and women, why does this chapter also refer to the Four Heavenly Kings as being in the *prāñjali* posture?
Answer: Although the Buddha’s regulation of the *prāñjali* posture was specifically restricted to nuns and women, that restriction was further extended to encompass all four assemblies.

The *Commentary on the Meaning of Avalokiteśvara* (*Guānyīn yìshū*) states: "In this land [of China], clasping the hands signifies respect; in foreign lands, joining the palms signifies reverence. The hands are originally separate at both sides;
now they are joined as one to signify that one does not dare to be distracted, but maintains a focused mind and single-minded devotion. The *Zhulín* states:
"In the Vinaya, it is said that one should with single-mindedness join the ten fingers and palms to make offerings to the Lion of the Śākyas and bow in prostration."

To present oneself with reverence means to restrain the mind so that it does not scatter; therefore, one is made to join the palms with a single-minded focus. Nowadays, many people join their fingers while leaving the palms apart, or join the palms while leaving the fingers spread. This is truly because their minds lack concentration. It would be better to have the fingers spread while the palms are joined than to have the palms joined while the fingers are spread. Master Zhuan’an composed a verse on this: The hands are joined to signify the joining of the mind; If the mind is scattered, the hands are of no use. Better to have the fingers spread than the palms parted; It is far better to have the palms joined than the fingers spread. Thus, one should always maintain a focused mind. Even if one’s life were to end at once, One would not regret having failed to practice. If one can cultivate the Way in this manner, One will surely attain liberation from birth and death. The Buddha’s teaching is vast and profound, Yet its essence lies in this single principle. If you can practice with such earnestness, You will surely realize the fruit of Buddhahood. Do not let your efforts go to waste; Strive diligently without ceasing. If you do not practice now, When will you ever find the opportunity? If you wish to escape the cycle of rebirth, You must first sever the bonds of desire. If you wish to transcend the world, You must first abandon worldly attachments. If you wish to attain the Way, You must first subdue your own mind. If you wish to see the Buddha, You must first purify your own nature. If you wish to understand the Dharma, You must first extinguish deluded thoughts. If you wish to reach the ultimate truth, You must first sever the roots of ignorance. If you wish to uphold the teachings, You must first practice the precepts with purity. If you wish to propagate the Dharma, You must first possess wisdom and eloquence. If you wish to be a true disciple, You must first follow the example of the Buddhas. If you wish to be a true teacher, You must first embody the virtues of the sages. If you wish to be a true friend, You must first offer guidance to others. If you wish to be a true leader, You must first act with integrity and justice. If you wish to be a true spouse, You must first be faithful and harmonious. If you wish to be a true child, You must first be filial and respectful. If you wish to be a true elder, You must first be kind and patient. If you wish to be a true younger sibling, You must first be obedient and humble. If you wish to be a true neighbor, You must first be helpful and supportive. If you wish to be a true citizen, You must first obey the laws and regulations. If you wish to be a true human being, You must first cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action. If you wish to be a true deity, You must first practice the four immeasurable minds. If you wish to be a true Bodhisattva, You must first vow to save all beings. If you wish to be a true Buddha, You must first fulfill the three bodies of enlightenment.
