third, the suffering when, during the nāgas' diversions, the garuḍas enter their palaces and seize their young to devour them. This pool is free from these [afflictions].
Regarding the three calamities: if a bird conceives the thought of flying there, its life immediately ends; therefore, it is called the Lake of No Heat-Affliction (*Anavatapta*).
Furthermore, according to the *Huayan He lun* (Compendium on the Avatamsaka), it is also translated as the "Cooling Lake" (*Qingliang chi*).
Sāgara Dragon King—also called Sāgaro or Sāgata; this translates as "Salt Sea"—is the eighth of the concentric oceans outside Mount Sumeru.
A passage in the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The Sāgara Dragon derives its name from the sea where it dwells.
Formerly it was said that he was named after his country; he originally resided in the Great Ocean of Wisdom (*Prajñāpāramitā*), though his current trace is found in the vast blue ocean.

The *Zhujing yaoji* (Essential Collection of Various Scriptures) states that Bhagala is a king of snake-dragons (*nāgarāja*) and thus belongs to the primary lineage, whereas others are all collateral lineages.
Furthermore, this dragon palace contains the scriptures spoken by the seven past Buddhas.

In the past, when Nāgārjuna harbored pride regarding the Buddha-dharma, this dragon took pity on him, led him into the palace, opened a casket of the seven precious gems, and showed him [the scriptures].
Regarding the profound Vaipulya sutras, Nāgārjuna studied them for ninety days yet still could not finish them;

he himself stated on the title page that what he had read was ten times greater than all the [sutras] in Jambudvīpa. As for the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, it was at that time exhaled from the tip of the Great Being’s nose and transmitted to the world.
This is recorded in the *Biography of Nāgārjuna* (contained in the "Zhòu" case of the Tripitaka).
Regarding those who uphold, read, recite, explain, and preach [the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*], the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* itself clarifies five kinds of Dharma-preachers:
first, upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, explaining; and fifth, transcribing. The *Vajraśāstra* by Bodhisattva Asaṅga states:

"To 'uphold' means to receive the words; to 'maintain' means to maintain the meaning. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies six kinds of Dharma-preachers: one upholds [the teaching] by virtue of the power of faith.

To maintain and examine the text through the power of mindfulness is "recitation" (*pāṭha*); to retain it without forgetting is "chanting" (*svādhyāya*); to proclaim and explain it is "exposition" (*vibhāṣā*).
Since the scriptures of the Sages are difficult to understand, they must be explained. To receive and uphold [the teachings] is the mental action (*manas-karma*);

recitation, chanting, and exposition are the vocal action (*vāk-karma*); and writing them down is the physical action (*kāya-karma*). The Dharma is the rule and the teacher is the craftsman; the Dharma does not propagate itself.
Among humans, those who have mastered the five kinds of scriptural transmissions are all called "Masters" (shī).

Regarding the frequent occurrence of epidemics, the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Epidemic" (*yì*) means that the people are all afflicted by disease; furthermore, it is a homophone for "service" (*yì*), as the pestilential vapors of ghosts move about, serving and afflicting people without ceasing.
The commentary to the *Lüshi Chunqiu* notes: "On the first day of the last month of the year, drums were beaten to drive away epidemics and miasmas."
The ghosts of these [deceased] are called *zhuchu* (expelling-removers) and are also termed *nǎo* (driving away). The *Lunyu Shu* (Commentary on the Analects) states:
"The *nǎo* is the expulsion of pestilence ghosts. Because the qi of yin and yang is not regulated, pestilence ghosts follow and bring about calamities;

therefore, the Son of Heaven dispatches the Fangxiang officers, who have eyes made of gold and hats of bear skin, making the sound of 'nǎo-nǎo' with their mouths to drive away the pestilence ghosts. (1)
Three times a year, one performs this rite according to the *Liwei* (Ritual Patterns): "Gao Yang had three sons who were born inauspicious; they departed to become pestilence spirits (*yi gui*).
Two dwelt in the waters of the Yangtze River and wrought havoc; one dwelt in the corners and recesses of human dwellings and delighted in startling small children.
Therefore, in the first and twelfth months, the sacrificial officials are ordered to perform the *nano* (exorcism) to search the rooms."
It is for driving away the pestilence-demons. *Nǒ* (儺) is pronounced with the *nuò* and *hé* finals.

Regarding the appearance of comets as anomalies, the *Han shu*, "Treatise on Astronomy" (*Tiānwén zhì*), states: "The various forms of *qiāng*, *chán*, *bàng*, and *huì* [comets] differ, yet their calamities are one and the same;

there will inevitably be the destruction of a state and the chaos of a ruler, leading to drought, famine, and violent epidemics. The *Han shu yìnyì* (Explanatory Notes on the Pronunciation and Meaning of the Han Shu) identifies these as "demon stars" (*yāo xīng*).
It is said that the *bṛhaspati* star, the comet (*ketu*), and the long star are also called *cāṇūra*. The *Erya* states: "The comet is the *cāṇūra*. Guo Pu’s commentary says:
"It is also called *bṛhaspati*, meaning its form is *bṛhaspati*-like, resembling a broom or a comet. Regarding the etymology:
it is also similar to scattered hemp, hence it is named the "hemp-comet" (*ma-ketu*). The Great Scripture says: "For example, like a black moon, the comet appears at night."
Having briefly emerged and then vanished, sentient beings, upon seeing this, conceived the notion that it was an ill omen. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"The comet is the breath exhaled from the mouths of the hundred-fathom asuras and yakṣa hosts, who desire to harm sentient beings, manifesting light."

Regarding the falling of shooting stars, the *Xingshuo* (Discourse on Stars) states: "To vanish without leaving a trace is called a 'rushing star' (*bēngxīng*); when the luminous traces are connected, it is called a 'shooting star' (*liúxīng*).
Furthermore, "descending from above is called a shooting star; ascending from below is called a 'flying star' (*fēixīng*).

The *Erya* states: "A rushing star is a *zhéyuē*. Guo Pu’s commentary identifies this as a shooting star. The *Yifanyao lue* (Essentials of Translating Sanskrit) refers to it as a "boiling star" (*fèixīng*).

This refers to a falling star. On the twenty-ninth night of the fifth month of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a great falling star as large as a jar or a basin that pierced through the Big Dipper and fell;

countless smaller stars followed it, and all the celestial bodies shook until dawn, when they finally ceased. Thereupon, King Xiang passed away. In the tenth month, the Tibetans entered Longyou and plundered.
Countless beings were killed.

The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) indicates that the five stars—the various lunar mansions including Venus, Mars, Mercury, and the Wind Star—are called the five great pacifying stars (*pañca-vināyaka-tārāḥ*), each manifesting its own transformations;
these constitute the second calamity within the kingdom. The *Qi yao tu* (Chart of the Seven Luminaries) states:
The Eastern Wood-essence is Jupiter (Suìxīng); the Southern Fire-essence is Mars (Yínghuóxīng); the Western Metal-essence is Venus (Tàibáixīng);
the Northern Water-essence is Mercury (Chénxīng); and the Central Earth-essence is Saturn (Zhènxīng).
The Northern Dipper is also called Tiānguān and Běijí; it is the seat of the Zǐwéi Heaven. Mèngkāng’s commentary on the "Treatise on Astronomy" in the *Hànshū* states:
The essence of the five planets disperses into sixty-four transformations that cannot be fully recorded in chronicles.
When two suns appear simultaneously, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) enumerates seven kinds of terrifying calamities; the first of these calamities states:
"When the sun and moon lose their proper courses and the seasons run contrary to their order, there may arise a red sun, a black sun, or two, three, four, or five suns."
Or there may be solar eclipses where the sun loses its light, or the solar disc appears with one, two, three, four, or five concentric halos;
when such calamitous portents as these occur, one should preach the *Prajñāpāramitā* to avert them. The *Huainanzi* states:
"In the time of Emperor Yao, ten suns rose simultaneously, scorching the grain crops and killing the plants and trees so that the people had nothing to eat. Yao then sent Yi to shoot them down."
On the ninth day, all nine [suns] descended together; the myriad people were filled with joy and installed Yao as the Son of Heaven. Zhā Ān once remarked:
"In the second year of the Jianxing era of Emperor Min of Jin, the solar disc fell to the earth, and three suns were also seen following one another from west to east.
The *Heluo Ji* states: "During the Sui dynasty, Li Mi incited a rebellion; while the husband was away, the wife was widowed, and when the father went out, the son..."
The hundred rivers boil and surge; ten suns rise simultaneously.

Regarding the term for the eclipsing of the sun and moon, some editions of the sutra use the character *bo* (博), which is incorrect. The *Guxiang Chao* states that while both the classics and histories use the character *shi* (食), the *Shuowen Jiezi* uses *shi* (蝕);
we now take *shi* as the correct reading. The *Shiming* explains: "When the sun and moon are deficient, it is called *shi* (eclipse)."
It gradually diminishes and wanes, like insects eating the leaves of trees and grasses. The *Tianwen zhi* (Treatise on Astronomy) of the Former Han states:
"When the sun and moon lose their brilliance, it is called a *bo* (thinning/eclipse). Zhang’s commentary says: "The loss of light by the sun and moon is called *bo*. Wei Zhao says:

"The arrival of a pneuma that presses upon them is called *bo*; the resulting deficiency or gap is called *shi* (eclipsing). The *Ji fang yizhuan* (Book of Changes Commentary by Jing Fang) says: "When the sun and moon appear red or yellow, it is a *bo*. Some say it is not so.
When the sun and moon intersect and eclipse each other, it is called a *sūrya-candra-uparāga*. The *Boluozhi* states: "When the qilin fight, the sun and moon are eclipsed;
when the whale dies, a comet appears. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "Sentient beings with evil karma share a common delusive perception, whereby they subsequently see solar and lunar eclipses.

The commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "In the world, there are those who claim there is an eclipse once every six months. The *Shujing* (Book of Documents) says: "This is precisely due to the movement [of the celestial bodies]."
The phases alternate every six months as yin and yang mutually govern one another; thus, there are these eclipses. The Sūtra says it is caused by the Asuras.
Furthermore, the calculations of yin and yang state that because Rāhu and Ketu invade the sun and moon, eclipses occur.
The *Shi-de-zhi-gui* (Exposition on the Pointing to the Three Virtues) explains: "Thus, on the first day of the seventh month in the twenty-first year of Duke Zhao of the *Zuo Zhuan*..."

When there was a solar eclipse, Duke Gong asked Zizhang, "What causes calamity and fortune? He replied, "The two solstices and the two equinoxes (the summer and winter solstices, and the spring and autumn equinoxes):

when the sun undergoes an eclipse at these times, it does not constitute a disaster. This is because in the movements of the sun and moon, at the equinoxes they follow the same path, and at the solstices they pass each other.
At any other time, it would indeed be a disaster. Now you say that 'yin and yang govern each other,' which refers to these two [solstices and equinoxes]."

This is because they share the same path. Furthermore, Du Yu, following the theories of the calendrical experts, stated that during the full moon, the sun’s light reaches out from afar to seize the moonlight, hence there is a lunar eclipse;
when the sun and moon meet, the moon suddenly obscures the sun, hence there is a solar eclipse.

Regarding eclipses having upper and lower limits and varying heights, and the fact that the solar disc remains visible while its center is eclipsed, this is because the mutual obscuration is so dense that the solar rays [are blocked].
"When 'overflowing' and 'all exhausted' correspond exactly, they are mutually eclipsed by intervals of sparseness.

According to the *Baihutong* (Comprehensive Discussions on the White Tiger), "When there is a solar eclipse, one should beat drums at the altar of the earth to attack it with yang to rebuke yin. Someone asked, "What about a lunar eclipse?
He replied, "One should beat bells; that would be appropriate."
White and black, evil rainbows appear repeatedly. The *Yuánmìng bāo* says: "The intersection of yin and yang produces rainbows and halos;

rainbows and halos are the essence (*jing*) of yin and yang—the male is called the rainbow (*hong*), the female is called the halo (*ni*). The *Tōngzhàn* says: "When the qi of yin and yang harmonize, they form rain;
when they are enraged, they form wind and thunder; when struck by baleful qi, they disperse to form rainbows and halos. The *Éryá* says:
The *dìdòng* (rainbow) is called *yú*; the *dìdòng* is the *hóng* (rainbow). The *ní* is called *qiè'èr*. The commentary states: "The *ní* is the female *hóng*.
This appears in the *Li sao*. *Qiè'èr* is its specific name; this appears in the *Shizi*. The *Yierya Yinyi* states: "When two appear and are bright and flourishing, it is the male;
the male is called *hóng*. When they are dim and obscure, it is the female; the female is called *ní*. *Ní* is also written as [霓]."
The *Níyuèlìng* (The Calendar of the Rainbow and Moon) states: "When yin and yang are not in harmony and the order of marriage is lost, this vapor is produced.

The *Yǎnkǒngtú* (The Diagram Evolving from Confucius) says: "The *ní* (rainbow) is the essence of the Dipper (*dōu*); when the Dipper loses its proper course, it casts forth the *ní*. This explains that the scattering of stars constitutes the rainbow and *ní*.
Li Linfu said: "Ten days after the Qingming festival, the rainbow first appears; this is one of the seventy-two seasonal signs (*qīshí'èr hòu*)."
The "Zhong" (Central) is one of the five seasonal omens. Mencius said, "It is like those in a great drought looking for clouds and rainbows.
Zhao’s commentary states: "When it rains, the rainbow appears; therefore, during a great drought, people long to see it. The *Chunqiu Qiantanba* says:

"If the five colors arrive in succession and shine upon the palace halls, there will be matters of war and weapons. Various military manuals state: "A solar halo accompanied by a white rainbow [portends conflict]."
Regarding those who travel from within the capital to the provinces, the *Shenshen ji* (Records of Searching for the Divine) states:
Chen Ji, a local official in Baqiu, Luling, had a wife named Qin who remained alone at home.

She constantly had a man appear, wearing a crimson robe that shone with brilliant colors, meeting her by appointment in the mountain streams. Unaware of their mutual attraction, Qin later became pregnant and gave birth.
The son was like a human being with abundant flesh; when he returned home, Qin was afraid of him and placed the child in a basin.
Whenever Ji stopped, wind and rain would immediately arise. A neighbor saw a rainbow descend into his courtyard, seized the child, and departed.

The *Tàipíng guǎngjì* states that during the sixth month of the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Wei, while staying at Mount Shouyang, he suddenly saw a late-afternoon rainbow descend to drink from the mountain stream.
After a long while, she transformed into a woman. When the Emperor saw that her youthful appearance was extraordinary, he questioned her;
she replied, "I am a celestial maiden. The Emperor desired to take her by force, but her expression was one of extreme distress.
He ordered his attendants to embrace her, whereupon she let out a sound like that of bells and chimes, suddenly transformed into a rainbow, and ascended to heaven.
The great earth shakes and a great sound resounds. The *Rituals of Zhou* states: "When the Yang is submerged and cannot emerge, and the Yin is pressed down and cannot ascend, there is an earthquake.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says that there are three causes and conditions for the earth to shake:
first, the earth rests upon water; the water rests upon wind; and the wind rests upon space. When a great wind arises, the water [is stirred].
When water is disturbed, the earth shakes. Second, it is because śramaṇas who have attained the Way and divine, wondrous devas manifest as responsive miracles.
Third, when I become a Buddha, the earth shakes before and after [the event]. The *Huayan He Lun* (Treatise on the Harmony of the Avataṃsaka) clarifies that there are four causes for an earthquake:
first, the attainment of the Way by the great assembly; second, the appearance of wise persons; third, calamities occurring in the three worlds; and fourth, the attainment of the Way.
The *Huānxi Tàipíng Guǎngjì* states that during the Later Han dynasty, Zhang Heng constructed a seismograph cast of bronze.
It was eight feet in diameter, with a domed cover shaped like a wine jar (*jiǔzūn*). Inside stood a central pillar (*dūzhù*) connected to eight lateral arms equipped with levers and mechanisms.
On the exterior were eight dragon heads, each holding a copper ball in its mouth, while below were toads with their mouths agape.

The mechanism for orally transmitting these [omens] was hidden within a vessel; if there was an earthquake in the east, the "Eastern Dragon Ball" would fall, and the others followed this pattern accordingly.
One day, a dragon triggered the mechanism but the earth did not shake, and everyone marveled at its lack of efficacy.

After several days, however, the Governor of Longxi reported that an earthquake occurred at the same time as the ball had fallen when the mechanism was activated; only then did people begin to believe it.
One should appreciate the subtlety of what they have produced.
Violent winds and heavy rains occur almost every day. The *Erya* states: "A wind that overturns wheels is called *tuai*";
the commentary notes: "A violent wind blowing from above is called *biao*"; the commentary further notes: "A violent wind blowing from below is called *biao*. When the sun rises and there is wind...
Regarding "violent" (bào), the commentary states: The *Shijing* says, "The wind is constant and violent. A torrential rain is called *dōn*.
The commentary notes that today in Jiangdong, the torrential rains of summer are called *dōnyǔ*. This is what is meant in the *Lisao*:
"Let the whirlwind lead the way, and let the *dōnyǔ* sprinkle the dust."

When grain and rice are extremely expensive and there is famine and starvation, the *Erya* states: "When the five grains do not ripen, it is called *ji* (famine). The commentary notes: "The five grains do not come to fruition.
"When vegetables do not ripen, it is called *jin* (scarcity). The commentary notes: "All edible grasses and greens are collectively termed 'vegetables' (*shu*).

When these do not ripen, it is called *jin*. "When fruits do not ripen, it is called *huang* (desolation). The commentary notes: "Fruits are the seeds of trees. "Successive famines are called *jian* (repeated). The commentary notes: "A continuous succession."

"The harvest has not ripened. This refers to the *Zuozhuan*, which states: "Now there is yet another successive famine. The *Guliangzhuan* states: "When one grain fails to ripen, it is called a 'deficiency' (*qian*);
when two grains fail to ripen, it is called a 'famine' (*ji*); when three grains fail to ripen, it is called a 'scarcity' (*jin*); when four grains fail to ripen, it is called a 'distress' (*kang*);
when five grains fail to ripen, it is called a 'desolation' (*huang*). The *Xu xian zhuan* states: "In the Three Rivers region, there was hunger and starvation; there was a blue..."
The Boy in Robes said, "If the people of the world weary of and abandon the five grains, the Earth Official will collect their spirits.

You should lead one another in prayer and repentance to the Father of Grains and the Mother of Silkworms; thus shall there be abundance. The *Shuyiji* states: During the reign of Emperor Xuan of the Han dynasty, there was famine in the regions of the Yangtze and Huai rivers.
Heaven rained grain for three days, and two thousand *qing* of grain fields were recovered in the territories of Qin and Wei. An audience was requested to view this.
The *Yinsu* (Commentary on Sounds) states: "The Sage being far away is 'hunger' because one does not hear the Way; being near is 'satiety. Lacking right wisdom is 'hunger';
lacking the factors that aid the Path is 'famine.

Regarding the term *lüè* (plundering) in the phrase "enemies and bandits plunder and rob," the *Suoyinji* (Record of Pronunciations) cites the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian), where the character *lüè* is pronounced with the initial *lì* and the final *shàng* (i.e., *lüè* as *liè*). This means to seize or take away by force. Furthermore...
The *Zishu* states that "chao-lüe" (抄掠) is pronounced as "lüe" (略); following the *Yupian*, both pronunciations are accepted.
"Lüe" (掠) refers to plundering—that is, seizing property by force.
Just as the various Brahmā heavens expound the *Discourse on Transcending Desire*, the following clarifies three types of discourse, namely the non-Buddhist scriptures of India.
Regarding those who advocate for the existence of desire, there are the four Vedas. The Maṇḍūka Sūtra states: "The first person was named Brahmā, who created one Veda.
Subsequently, the White-Pure Rishi transformed that one into four—namely, the Hymns (Ṛg), the Rituals (Yajur), the Chants (Sāman), and the Exorcisms (Atharvan).
Later, through the gradual increase by figures such as Puṣya, Śuka, and Sunetra, they reached twelve hundred."
The six types of Vedas all clarify matters concerning Brahmā; because they lead to liberation from the defilement of desire, they are called the "Brahmā-discourse on the transcendence of desire.
Śakra Devendra’s various excellent discourses refer to the Indian Vyākaraṇa-śāstra, which is also called the "Discourse on Exposition" (or "Grammatical Discourse").
Pāṇini composed various treatises on grammar; among the texts that are the foundation of worldly writing, there are none whose sounds he did not master.

Possessing the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), he censured worldly dharmas and praised the life of renunciation. Although these are non-Buddhist treatises, they contain no erroneous teachings.

Regarding the discourse on the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) of the *ṛṣis* and celestial beings: the Buddha possesses six supernormal powers, namely, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), mastery over psychic powers (*ṛddhividhi*), and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Because the *ṛṣis* and celestial beings of India today lack the exhaustion of outflows, they are said to possess only five supernormal powers.
This is because what they cultivate yields only the temporary reward of long life; once that karma is exhausted, they fall back into the three realms of existence. Such is their doctrine.
These are the three treatises of Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, and Lokāyata. Sāṃkhya is translated here as "Enumeration" (Śuǔlùn), for it asserts that all phenomena arise from enumeration;
it was composed at the beginning of the kalpa by the Sage Yellow-Head (Kapila).
Vaiśeṣika is translated here as "Excellence" (Shènglùn), meaning it is superior among all treatises; it was composed by the non-Buddhist heretic Ulūka. Lokāyata... [text fragment]

"Vā" (婆) here translates as "asceticism" (*duṣkara-caryā*). This refers to a treatise composed merely by name regarding the times of the appearance of those who transcend the world, which serves to make the mind tranquil.
Zhuangzi said: "The way of governing the right side is to nourish wisdom (*jñāna*) with tranquility; one is born without..."
"To act with knowledge" means to nourish tranquility through knowledge; when knowledge and tranquility nourish one another, harmony and order emerge from one's nature.
The commentary states: "Tranquility arises from knowledge, which is why it can achieve stillness; knowledge relies on stillness, which is why it attains truth.
When knowledge and tranquility nourish each other, the principle of spontaneity emerges, harmonizing with the nature of Heaven."
The teeth are white and stainless like the root of a lotus. The *Erya* states: "Hé (lotus), fúqú (water-lily). The commentary provides alternative names:

it is called *fúróng* (hemp-rose) in the Jiangdong region; its stem is called *qiā*, its leaf *xié*, and its root *mì*. The commentary notes that the "stem" refers to the white, fleshy part below the surface within the mud.
Its flower is *hàn-dàn*; its fruit is *lián*—which refers to the seed-pod—and its root is *ǒu*, which is found within [the pod].
The commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra* states that the "depth of wisdom" (*jizhi*) is also the center of the medicinal seeds of enlightenment.
Regarding the boundless ocean of Dharma-water, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "His ocean of wisdom is profound, like the great sea. The *Guǎnzǐ* says:
"Water that emerges but does not flow is called an abyss (*yuan*). The *Wénxuǎn* says: "How deep! The layered abysses," with the commentary stating: "Layered..."
"Yuan" refers to the ocean.
Regarding the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel appearing on the soles of his feet which are level and full, the *Fenbie gongde lun* (Treatise on the Differentiation of Merits) states:

"The Buddha’s body is adamantine and free from all outflows; when he walks, his feet remain four inches above the ground, yet the patterns of the thousand-spoked wheel manifest upon the earth beneath his feet."
The various insects below [the earth] shall remain safe for seven days; if their lives should end, they shall all be reborn in the heavens.
The *Record of the Western Regions* states that within a monastery in the city of Pāṭaliputra in the kingdom of Magadha, there is a large stone upon which are the twin footprints left by Śākyamuni.
They are one chi and eight cun long and six cun wide, both bearing the thousand-spoked wheel with its rim and ten [spokes].
The patterns on the stone consist of finger-marks, lotus flowers, swastikas, fish, vases, and jeweled swords.
Long ago, when the Tathāgata was proceeding north toward the city of Kuśinagara to enter parinirvāṇa, he looked back at the kingdom of Magadha and stepped upon this stone, saying:

"I leave this footprint here to show sentient beings of the final age; may those who see it give rise to faith and extinguish their transgressions. More than a hundred years later, there was King Aśoka.
He protected and defended the Triple Gem and moved the capital to a great city; beholding these relics, he subsequently constructed a palace-city where he personally made offerings constantly.
Later, various kingdoms vied to lift and transport them back, yet none were able to move them. Furthermore, there was a non-Buddhist who chiseled through them, but they reformed themselves overnight;
subsequently, King Śaśāṅka destroyed the Buddha-dharma, yet after he had chiseled them, the patterns and colors remained as before.

It was subsequently moved and cast away into the Ganges River, whereupon it immediately returned to its original location; this occurred eight times in succession until it could no longer be destroyed.
During the Great Tang Dynasty, the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang personally traveled to India, beheld this sacred site, and drew a map of it to present upon his return.
Emperor Taizong received the report and issued an imperial decree to have it engraved for circulation; today, it is still being re-engraved at Yanqing Monastery in Siming.
It remains so.

The webbing between his toes is like that of a goose king. According to the *Yùpiān* (Lexicon of Jade), "màn" (縵) is pronounced "mòdàn" (莫旦); it means a large pattern. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The mark of the webbed fingers and toes of the Tathāgata is like that of a goose king; when he spreads his fingers, it appears, and when he does not spread them, it does not."
There are those who say that the marks of a Buddha are not fixed, but vary according to the preferences of sentient beings;
thus, some do not value the webbed fingers and long toes, claiming they are like the webbed feet of waterfowl and inconvenient for performing tasks, such as wearing gloves.
For example, when the Bodhisattva Mili Lili of Jibin had webbed fingers, his father considered them a deformity and cut them off with a knife. Such is their view.
If one is attached to the Buddha, he does not appear.
The true *dharmakāya* of the Buddha is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to objects, like the moon reflected in water.
The Great Sūtra clarifies the eight kinds of self-mastery, and the eighth is that the Tathāgata pervades all places, just as empty space pervades all. As for this empty space—
The nature [of reality] cannot be perceived; the Tathāgata is likewise truly invisible. Because of his sovereign power (*vaśitā*), he causes all to see him. The *Miaoxuan* (妙玄) states:

"In the distinct and perfect teachings, the response to conditions is such that the water does not rise upward and the moon does not descend downward; yet in a single moment, the one moon appears universally in all waters.
The Buddhas do not come, and sentient beings do not go; it is through the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness that they are seen."

Regarding this matter, the *Chiyu ji* states: "The moon must rely upon space; space is a metaphor for the Dharmakāya, the moon for the Saṃbhogakāya, the reflection for the Nirmāṇakāya, and the water for the four types of capacities.
Just as a jewel tree produces precious gems, this section of the sutra establishes three metaphors to reveal the wondrous scripture.
Regarding the three items—first, the single precious tree; second, the pure water; and third, the casket—the *Shuji* (Commentary) does not explain them.

Only the National Preceptor Huguo (*Huguo Shi*) attempts to correlate them with the Three Contemplations (*sanguan*), yet even he knows nothing of their actual facts. I shall likewise not adopt his interpretation.
As for the so-called "precious tree," the *Xianyu jing* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish) states that there was once a prince who entered the sea to gather treasures, unaware [of his surroundings].
When their provisions were exhausted, a tree spirit happened to tell them, "If you pray to this tree, it will cause people to immediately obtain food,
drink, clothing, gold, silver, precious jewels, and the like. The Prince prayed to it and indeed obtained food, drink, and precious treasures, thereby escaping the peril.
It is like a casket held entirely in one's hand. The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "If one desires various treasuries of jewels, one should seek the Bodhisattva’s Jewel Casket in Hand.
An ancient hymn of praise says: "The jewel casket is held in the hand by the Treasure-Holder;
Pointing to the hidden store, it causes people to know it. Long buried, the white jade is stained with dust; Suddenly excavated, its clear light emerges from the foundation."
Within the parrot-cup, jade filaments are held; upon coral branches, golden twigs are attached.

Were it not for the Bodhisattva’s assistance, there would have been no end to this wealth, status, and arrogance. The *Gujin zhu* (Ancient and Modern Notes) states that the *qié-téng* was made of bamboo;

Upon hearing this, the Four Kings felt a mixture of sorrow and joy; their tears flowed profusely down their faces.

"Remaining years today are exhausted for you; let us together sprinkle [libations] before the western wind. Now one might wonder:

The character *ti* (涕) is pronounced *tǐ*; "involuntary" (*héng*) means they flow across [the face] without restraint.

Regarding bedding and medicinal requisites, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that "bedding" refers to items such as quilts and covers. The *Zhangfu yi* (Ritual for Robes) notes that the three robes of a bhikṣu are also termed "bedding.
The *Shisong lü shi chao* (Commentary on the Ten-Recitation Vinaya) says: "To sustain one's life, [requisites] should not exceed [the fourfold division];
'medicine' is a general term, yet it must consist of four types. The first is 'timely medicine' (*kālabhaiṣajya*); the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states there are five kinds of *pūjā* [or *puṣpa*]."
"Kṣetra" (ni) here is translated as "proper food," referring to parched flour, rice, dry drinks, fish, and meat.

The five kinds of *khādaniya* (five types of solid foods) are here translated as "improper food," referring to branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and finely ground meals; these are restricted to being eaten from sunrise until noon.
Second is "medicine for the improper time" (*akālabhaiṣajya*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "All beans, grains, and wheat, when boiled, [their heads...]"
The juice from uncrushed [grains] may be drunk. The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states: "Fry rice until it is charred black, add this to the medicinal decoction, and ferment it to make a gruel;
this is also called 'non-timely' (vikāla). The *Caturvargika-vinaya* speaks of eight kinds of gruels:
namely, those made from pears, sour jujubes, sugarcane, *bhallātaka*, grapes, *śāluka*, and so forth. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that these must necessarily be strained."
If the dregs are clear like water, it may be consumed; however, if there is turbid liquid mixed with the food, drinking it even swallow by swallow constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
This [permission] applies to eating from dawn until the second watch of the night. Third, regarding the seven-day medicines, the *Caturvarga-vinaya* states:
"Butter, oil, fresh ghee, honey, and rock sugar—these five kinds, well-known to the world, may be used as both food and medicine."

The *Mahādeva-śāstra* states that sugar syrup may also be accepted for seven days; it further notes that Śāriputra, suffering from a wind disorder, was instructed by his physician to consume five kinds of fats:
those of bear, brown bear, pig, donkey, and fish. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that these medicines are pure and free from the odor of "timely" food;
they are to be accepted at one time and consumed for seven days. As for the four types [of medicines], the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* specifies they are medicines to be taken for as long as one lives.
Regarding black pepper (*marica*), long pepper (*pippalī*), *harītakī*, and so forth—these medicines are taken immediately after meals and may be consumed by a sick bhikṣu for the rest of his life.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "Those things unfit to be considered food—namely all salty, bitter, pungent, and sweet substances—are called 'medicines for as long as one lives' (*yāvaj-jīvika-bhaiṣajya*).
Someone asked: "If one drinks tea after the meal has concluded, to which category of medicine does it belong? [The answer was: "Since it is both bitter..."
The absence of the "qi of food" (wúshíqì) refers to medicines taken for the duration of one's life.

The *Mahāvaipulya Tathāgata-arthasiddhi-samyak-saṃbuddha Sūtra* states that regarding the "Arhat" (Yīnggòng), all humans and devas should offer various kinds of incense, flowers, and necklaces as worship.
Based on this, the character "yīng" (應) should be pronounced with a level tone (*píngshēng*). In the past...
Cien (Ci'en) also reads the character "dang" (當) with a level tone, explaining it as meaning that [the Buddha] is worthy of receiving offerings from others;

however, according to Tiantai’s interpretation, he says that the name "Excellent Field of Merit" (良福田) corresponds to the meaning of "Worthy of Offerings" (應供), and thus "dang" should be pronounced with an departing tone.

Nevertheless, these ten titles are the common names for all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time; the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* provides an extensive explanation, dividing them into eleven phrases.

That "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*) is a summary of the preceding ten [epithets]. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the titles "Unsurpassed Being" (*Anuttara-puruṣa*) and "Charioteer of Men" (*Puruṣa-damya-sārathi*) are combined into a single title;
when added to "World-Honored One," they constitute ten [epithets]. Although the sūtras and śāstras differ in this regard, each has its own significance.
However, whichever one one wishes to read according to one's inclination is acceptable. The *Fahua xuanyi* states that "non-falsity" is the name [of the World-Honored One].
The Tathāgata is the excellent field of merit, named Arhat; he who knows the dharma-realm is named Samyaksaṃbuddha; possessing the three types of clear knowledge, he is named Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna;
not returning again, he is named Sugata; knowing the realms of sentient beings and lands, he is named Lokavid;
being without equal, he is named Anuttara; taming the minds of others, he is named Puruṣadamyasārathi; and as the eye for all sentient beings, he is named...

The Teacher of Gods and Humans who knows the three groups is called a Buddha; possessing these ten titles, he is named the World-Honored One. This explanation concerns the ten titles of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
As for the ten titles of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body), the text is found in the second volume of the *Fuxingji* (Supplementary Record).
The *Jinyin miàozōng chāo* states: "Why is it called 'hú yán' (Hu-language)? 'Shēng xiàng' (raw image) is translated here as 'jīnyín' (gold and silver).
In the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, it is translated as 'shēngsè' (raw color). 'Sì' (resembling) means 'xiàng' (image); that is to say, gold is naturally yellow, while silver is dyed to resemble gold;
therefore, it is called 'shēng xiàng. Now, if 'shēng xiàng' is a term from this region [China], why is it called 'hú'? It says:
In the northern regions of the Five Indias, the languages and sounds of the Hu people have elements that overlap with those of Han China;

thus, it is said that the "living image" (the original form) of the Hu people was translated again into Chinese, thereby preserving Hu phonetics. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Gold comes from within sand.
The *Book of Jin* records that gold was produced in Poyang and Le'an; by digging the earth for over ten *zhang*, one would uncover the sand and find gold, the larger pieces being as big as beans.
Small as a grain of millet, the *Bencao* (Classic of Materia Medica) states that gold is found in great abundance where it is produced; it is also found in Goryeo and Funan.

Ancient texts refer to gold as "Yellow Gold," silver as "White Gold," and copper as "Red Gold. The *Shuowen* (Explanations of Characters) says: "Gold possesses five virtues: it is yellow in color, heavy in weight, malleable, fusible, and bright. Yellow gold is the foremost among them:
it does not grow mold even when buried for a long time, it does not become light even after being refined a hundred times, and it conforms to any alteration without resistance."
The journey to the West originates from within the earth. The *Erya* states: "White metal is called silver; its finest variety is called liao.
The *Wulei xianggan zhi* says: "When the essence of gold remains in the earth for a thousand years, it travels day and night, its radiance brilliant and dazzling, transforming into a yellow dragon."
Regarding the seven treasures, as listed in the sūtras and śāstras, their presence or absence is not fixed; this is because they vary according to different worldly preferences and inclinations.

Consequently, there are differences in the Buddhas' teachings. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* identifies gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, and red pearl as the seven treasures, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* lists gold, silver, glass (kācaka), musaragalva, agate, and ruby (*māṇikya*).
The *Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation* (Guan jing shu) lists gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, agate, and tridacna shell as the seven treasures;
the *Sub-commentary on the Practice* (Fu xing zhuan) lists gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, coral, and amber as the seven treasures;
whereas the scriptural text here lists gold, silver, pearl, lapis lazuli, and coral.
Agate, jade, and horse-trappings made of jade constitute the seven treasures; some say that because the ancients did not value rare goods, they ensured the people would not engage in theft.
Why, then, do the Buddhist scriptures frequently mention the seven treasures? It is said: the Buddha accords with the capacities of beings to save the world through these treasures.
As Vimalakīrti stated: "First, one uses desire as a hook to entice them, and afterwards leads them into the Buddha-way."
How much more so, then, regarding the seven treasures described in various sutras, which are all without exception inherently possessed by the single nature (*ekaprakṛti*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that pearls are produced from within the bellies of fish, from within bamboo, and from within the brains of snakes; however, it is only the pearl from the oyster that exclusively receives the name "pearl.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* states that the red pearl (*lohitamukti*) is produced by a red insect, or [refers to] the substance of the pearl itself.
Regarding "red" (赤): "Red pearls. The *Erya* states: "Among the beauties of the West, there are the pearls and jade of Mount Huo.
Guo Yi-gong’s *Guangzhi* says: "There is a pearl named 'Night-light' (*yèguāng*); those that are perfectly round, when placed on the ground, will not stop moving throughout the entire day.
The *Weilüe* states: "The Kingdom of Daqin produces bright pearls, night-light pearls, and white pearls. The *Book of the Later Wei*.

The *Yunhe Jiaoguo* states that the kingdom of Qiang produces gold and pearls. The *Huayang Guozhi* says that in Bonan County there is a "Luminous Pearl Cave" (*guangzhu xue*) from which luminous pearls emerge.

The *Shenyi Jing* states that in the desolate wastes of the northwest there is a golden gate containing a bright moon pearl (*mingyuezhu*) two feet in diameter, whose light illuminates two thousand li. The *Hanshu* states that pearls are the yin-essence of oysters, appearing at night.
Because it is beautiful, women take it as an ornament; because it can ward off fire disasters, the world regards it as a treasure.
When Mengchangjun served as the Governor of Hepu, the officials of the previous two thousand-stone rank had been greedy and corrupt, causing all the pearls to flee.
Upon Mengchangjun’s arrival, he maintained integrity and purity; within one year, the pearls all returned to the bay. (From the *Hutong*).
It is said that when virtue reaches the profound abyss, the sea produces the bright pearl.
Regarding *lǚlí* (瑠璃), the *Mìtuo shū* (Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra) states: "The character *liú* (琉) does not appear in the standard lexicons; its correct form is written as *lǚ* (瑠).

The *Jīng yīnyì* (Phonetic Explanations of the Sūtras) says that some add the character *fèi* (吠) or add the character *pí* (毗); others say it is called *pítóulí* (毗頭棃) and is named after a mountain. Thus [it is explained].
"Far Mountains are jewels; 'Far Mountains' refers to Mount Sumeru. This mountain’s southern side is made of blue lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*).
All these jewels are indestructible and cannot be melted or cast by smoke or flames;
only spirits and deities possessing supernatural powers can destroy them. It is further said that the shell of the *garuḍa* egg is also lapis lazuli."
Spirits and deities obtain it and sell it to humans. The *Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* by [Zhi]yi states:

"Lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*)—this term means 'not far from the mountain. Because there is a mountain in the Western Regions not far from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī that produces this gem, it is named after it.
Thus, the two commentaries point to different mountains; it is unknown which is correct.

Regarding *shān hú* (coral) [pronounced *shānsī'ān*]: the *Qiáwénjì* states that in the kingdom of *Pǔsū*, two thousand *lǐ* from the capital city, there is a flying bridge across the sea by which one travels west to the kingdom of *Qièlán*.
To the south of the piled-up stones of Qièlán lies a great sea;
within this sea, coral grows on the seabed. Large ships carry iron nets and sink them into the sea when the coral is first emerging.
Resembling fungi, they emerge from within the mesh after one year, transforming into yellow branches with crisscrossing nodes;

the small are three feet tall, while the large reach over ten feet. After three years, their color turns blue. Seafarers use iron hooks to unearth their roots and hoist them out using capstans and nets;
thus, the place is named Coral Isle (*sān-hú zhōu*). If they remain there for too long...
If one gathers it, it immediately becomes worm-eaten and decayed. The *Shuyiji* states that in Yulin Commandery there was a "Coral Market," which was the place where sea merchants traded coral.
Coral is emerald-green in color and grows at the bottom of the sea; a single stem has dozens of branches, and between the branches there are no leaves.
In the second year of the Yuanfeng era of Emperor Yuan’s reign, the commandery presented coral to the Empress Dowager. The Emperor ordered it to be planted before the palace hall, calling it...
The coral tree of Lady Shān'hú suddenly became lush with branches and leaves;
when it died during the time of Emperor Ling, everyone considered it an omen that the House of Han was about to fall into ruin. The *Zadu zaji* states:
"In the Jicao Pond within the Han palace, there was a coral tree one zhang two chi high, with three main branches and four hundred and sixty-three twigs upon them."
This was presented by Zhao Tuo, the King of Nan Yue, and was called the "Fenghuo Tree" (Fire-Signal Tree). At night, its luster would often appear as if it were burning.
The *Book of Jin* states that Shi Chong and Wang Kai vied with one another in their extravagance;
whenever Emperor Wu favored Wang Kai, he would grant him a coral tree two feet high. When Kai showed it to Chong, Chong struck it to pieces with an iron *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk).
Zhi Kai sighed with regret and said to Huichong, "It is not worth much lamentation. He then ordered his attendants to fetch six or seven branches, each three or four feet long;
when they arrived, Zhi Kai was suddenly struck with a sense of profound loss.
Amber, in Sanskrit *aśmagarbha*, is translated as "amber. The *Hanshu* states that there is amber in the mountains of the kingdom of Kāpiśī.
The *Shanhaijing* says that when the Yellow Emperor slew Chiyou, he cast away the latter’s shackles, which transformed into the resin of the *feng* tree;
after entering the earth for a thousand years, it becomes amber. The *Bowuzhi* states that pine resin enters the earth for one thousand...
After a thousand years, it transforms into *fuling* (poria cocos); after another thousand years, it transforms into amber, also known as *hongzhu*.

The *Guangzhi* states: "Amber is produced within the earth; no grasses or trees grow upon its surface or alongside it. It is found at depths of eight or nine feet and can be as large as a *hu* (a measure of capacity).
When the outer skin is pared away, the amber remains inside. It possesses a resinous juice that initially resembles peach gum, which hardens and solidifies."
Furthermore, it is processed by the local people for medicinal use as a secret preparation. According to its name and meaning, it is said that where amber is found, there are no pine trees;
thus, it is a treasure of the ancient country of Lolo in the South Sea. This account is not yet fully detailed. The poem by Li Qiao of the Tang dynasty says:
"It once was aged *fuling* fungus, originally the essence of cold pines; when mosquitoes and gnats fall into it, they remain there even after a thousand years."
I have recently observed several mosquitoes frozen within amber; this truly confirms the accuracy of the verse by [Liu] Qiao.
This is recorded in the *Xiangshan yalu*. Regarding "jade discs" (*biyu*), the *Erya* states:
"A jade disc six inches in diameter is called a *xuan*. The commentary notes: "This refers to what is described in the *Hanshu* as 'xuanyu' (the *xuan* jade)."

When the thickness (the "flesh") is twice the diameter of the hole (the "beauty"), it is called a *bi*. The commentary states: "The 'flesh' refers to the edge; the 'beauty' refers to the hole. Kings used it for sacrifices to Heaven.

The *Rituals of Zhou* states that the azure *bi* is the ritual implement for Heaven. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says that the character for "jade" (*yù*) is identical in form to the character for "king" (*wáng*), though their meanings differ;
originally there was no dot, which was added by later generations. The *Jingzhao Ji* states that beautiful jade is produced in Lantian.
Because it resembles lapis lazuli, it is called "lapis-jade. In the *Book of Rites*, Zengzi asked Confucius:
"May I venture to ask why the gentleman prizes jade and treats basalt as cheap? The Master replied: "As for jade, the gentleman compares its qualities to his own virtue.
It is warm, smooth, and lustrous—this is benevolence (*ren*). It is fine-grained and firm—this is wisdom (*zhi*). Its edges are sharp yet do not cut—this is righteousness (*yi*). When suspended..."

Its falling away from the ritual vessel represents propriety (*li*). When struck, its sound is clear, penetrating, and long-lasting—this is music (*le*). Its flaws do not conceal its virtues, and its virtues do not conceal its flaws—this is loyalty (*zhong*).
Its luster and purity radiate outward everywhere—this is trustworthiness (*xin*). Its vapor is like a white rainbow across the sky—this is heaven (*tian*).

Its spiritual resonance appears in the mountains and rivers—this is earth (*di*). That the *gui* and *zhang* jade tokens are presented alone and directly—this is virtue (*de*). That all under heaven holds it in high esteem—this is the Way (*dao*).
*Kē* (珂) [is pronounced with the *bó* and *gài* finals]. It is an alternative name for *kē*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "The *bèi* is a marine crustacean.
The *Lingbiao Luyi* states: "The *zijù* is the same as the *yáluó*; it is harvested along the shores of Dān, Zhèn, Yí, and Lí and used as currency.
The *Erya* states: "Those dwelling on land are called *bì*; those in water are called *hán*. This represents its form. In ancient times, cowries (*bèi*) were used as currency.
The *Baogui yupian* states: "The *dabei* (great shell) is like a *cheshu*; its body is like a *kedou* (tadpole), possessing only a head and tail.

This means from one to ten, the conclusion of the numerical sequence of sounds. What the present sutra refers to as "verses and phrases" (*zhangju*) is this.
"Chapters" (zhang) refer to sections, and "sentences" (ju) refer to phrases.
Since the words of all divine mantras (*dhāraṇī*) are secret and not to be explained or analyzed, the translators established fixed protocols by annotating them with sentence counts;

this was intended to prevent the loss of the texts through errors in transcription during later generations. It is incorrect for people transcribing sutra scrolls to write out the mantra verses as single, unbroken strings.

The sounds of the mantra are: *khu* (pronounced with the *qiu* and *jia* finals), *ni* (pronounced with the *nu* and *li* finals), *ta* (pronounced with the *ding* and *ke* finals), *hou* (pronounced with the *hu* and *dou* finals), *lei* (pronounced with the *ji* and *ji* finals),
*po* (pronounced with the *bi* and *ge* finals), *xi* (pronounced with the *hu* and *ji* finals), *si* (pronounced with the *so* and *yi* finals), *xi* (pronounced with the *xiang* and *yi* finals),
*a* (the vowel *a* with the entering tone), *ta* (pronounced with the *tou* and *he* finals), and *na* (pronounced with the *nu* and *kou* finals).

Regarding "beings of equal practice" (*samavartin*) and "those with middling roots of goodness," the *Fourfold Record* states: "Equal practice" refers to those who perform all various practices, while "middling roots of goodness" refers to those who practice a single practice.
Based on this interpretation, the character "practice" (*xing*) should be pronounced with the level tone (*ping sheng*).

Regarding the observance of the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*), according to the *Bāguānzhāijìng* (Sūtra on the Eightfold Fasting Precepts), one adds to the five precepts the following three: not wearing flowers, perfumes, or fine clothing;

not watching or listening to music and entertainment; and not sitting on high or wide beds. These eight constitute the precepts, while abstaining from eating past midday constitutes the fasting (*upavāsa*).
The *Miaozongji* commentary explains that these are established as the eight precepts by initially opening up [the prohibitions on] perfumes and clothing, as well as not sitting on high or wide beds.

If the fast (*upavāsa*) is reckoned as being outside the eight [precepts], then by combining the incense, robes, and bed, they become seven; with the addition of "not eating past midday," they become eight.
Thus, the fast is inside the eight. In the Dharma, there is no increase or decrease; the number is subject to opening and closing. The *Āgama* states:
"The height of the legs of a bed is one chi and six cun; this is not high. Its width is four chi; this is not broad. Its length is eight chi; this is not large."
If one exceeds this measure, it is called breaking the precepts. Someone may ask: "Since you do not wear flower garlands or incense, what kind of clothing do you wear?
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "One wears the garments used for daily activities. The *Womb Sutra* (*Garbha-sūtra*) states:

"The Eightfold Fasting Precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla*) mean that the 'gates' (*āṇi*) prohibit sentient beings from committing the eight offenses. The *Four Clarifications Record* (*Sishiming ji*) states: "The Eight Fasting Precepts apply specifically to laypeople."
"Day and night" refers to the precepts. Han Kangbo’s commentary on the *Zhouyi* states: "To wash the mind is called *zhāi*; to guard against calamities is called *jiè*.
Regarding the term *āranya*, some say it is *ālanya*, while others say *lianjū* or *lián'ér*; these are all variations of the Sanskrit sound *ra*, differing only in their phonetic transcriptions.
The term *Araṇya* is translated as "place of tranquility," or "absence of contention," or "secluded and quiet place.
The *Yīngyì* (Explanations of Sounds and Meanings) states: the character *ā* means "non-existence. Regarding *araṇya*, there are two meanings:

first, it refers to sound, meaning there is no sound of human voices nor sounds of clamor and noise; second, it refers to cutting (*chā*), meaning there is no sound of felling trees or bustling commotion. It is great.
The *Śāstra* states that an *araṇya* (forest hermitage) is a secluded place at least two *li* away; the further, the better.
The *Vinaya* specifies that this means five hundred *dhanus* from a village, which is precisely two *li*. The *Dvādaśa-dhūta-sūtra* records the Buddha saying:
"The various Buddhas of the ten directions all together praise the *araṇya* place; immeasurable merits are all born from it. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* [also confirms this].
The Treatise states: "An araṇya bhikṣu must be fully endowed with the fifty dharmas of power to be capable of dwelling [there];
otherwise, he must seek out a teacher and inquire after the Way—how could he permit himself such arrogance?
Regarding the term *sengfang* (monastery): the *Zilin* says, "A *sengfang* is a separate building for the Saṃgha," while the *Yunlin* says, "*Fang* means a district or enclosure."
This refers to a walled enclosure. Su’e’s *Yanyi* states: "A 'fang' (ward) is a square area;
one dwells according to their kind, and those who live together must seek out their own kind. Now, monks dwell there as a community."
Regarding money, the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states that in the Western Regions there are coins made of copper, lead, tin, gold, and silver;

their shapes also differ, being square, round, long, or short, and their inscriptions vary according to the time and place. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that one who steals five coins incurs a grave offense.
The *Guanzi* says: "In the year of Tang, there was a seven-year drought; in the year of Yu, there was a five-year flood."
Tang [the founder of the Shang dynasty] used the gold from Mount Zhuang, and Yu [the founder of the Xia dynasty] used the gold from Mount Li; both cast coins to relieve the distress of the people.

It was not until the Duke of Zhou established the "Nine Treasuries" and the "Circular Law" that they were first designated as *qián* (coins). These coins were circular with square holes, and their weight was measured in *zhū*.
This practice originated with Yu and Tang. Later, during the Northern Wei, Gao Qianzhi maintained that Yao, having encountered a great flood, cast coins, as did the Former Han.

The *Shihuozhi* (Annals on Food and Commodities) states: "Tāigōng established the Nine Treasuries and the *yuánfǎ* (round law) for Zhōu. The commentary notes: "The officials who managed the wealth of Zhōu had nine treasuries;
the fifth was named *Quánfǔ* (Spring Treasury). Regarding "benefiting through knives" (*lì yú dāo*), the commentary notes:

"Money is called 'knives' because it is beneficial to the people. Regarding "flowing like a spring" (*liú yú quán*), the commentary notes: "It circulates like a spring. Regarding "spreading through cloth" (*bù yú bù*), the commentary notes: [The term *bù* refers to the *bù* coin].

It was said that [the currency] was distributed among the common people. The *Zhou yu* states: "During the reign of King Jing of Zhou, the state suffered from the debasement of coinage and subsequently cast large coins.

The commentary notes: "The diameter was one inch and two fen, and the weight was twelve zhu; the inscription read 'Baohuo' (Precious Goods), intended to encourage agriculture and provide for those in want.
The *Tongdian* states: "When Wang Mang reformed the Han currency, the common people all found it inconvenient."
The *Huayang Guozhi* states: "Gongsun Shu abolished the use of copper coins and established iron coins, yet the common people found it difficult to conduct trade.
The *Qianshen Lun* says: "Gold is the father and white silver is the mother; lead is the eldest son and tin is the eldest daughter-in-law.
By nature they are firm and hard, requiring fire to complete their cycle. Their circular form corresponds to Heaven, while their square holes emulate Earth."

Regarding sheep and oxen, the *Youyang zazu* states that when the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty reached the foot of the Great Snow Mountains in the Western Regions, he saw villagers raising sheep as large as donkeys.
The *Yiwuzhi* states that the country of Yuezhi had large sheep which were occasionally used to entertain guests.
Regarding the three sacrificial animals—ox, sheep, and pig—the *Jili* states: "In all sacrifices to the ancestral temples..."
In ritual texts, the ox is called "the Great Hoof of the Primordial Unity" (*yīyuán dàwǔ*), the pig is called "the Firm Mane" (*gāngliè*), and the sheep is called "the Soft Fleece" (*róumáo*).
Cui Bao’s *Gujīn zhù* states: "The sheep is also known as 'The Registrar with a Beard' (*ránxū zhǔbù*).
Its name is also [associated with] "Tathāgata Treasure Victory" (*Bǎoshèng Rúlái*). Below this, the scriptural text lists the names of seventeen Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The *Shuji* (Commentary) does not provide an explanation; following the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), it is judged that the term is applied based on the essential nature of the *dharmatā* itself.

Thus, that text states: "Because *dharmatā* is venerable and precious, *dharmatā* is named 'Gold' (*suvarṇa*); because *dharmatā* is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, it is named 'Light' (*prabhā*);

because great compassion can bring manifold benefit, it is named 'Radiance' (*prabhāsvara*). When a Bodhisattva enters this Dharma-gate of these three characters, they take the Dharma as their basis."
Regarding the names: there are Bodhisattvas such as Suvarṇaprabhāsa who have reached the ultimate realization of this Dharma-gate, and Tathāgatas such as Suvarṇajvālāprabha.
As for "mountain marsh" (*shanzhe*):
*zhe* refers to a broad expanse of water or a marshy basin. The *Shiming* states: "When there is water at the foot of a mountain, it is called a marsh (*ze*)."
The people of Yanzhou called it *zhǎngyán* (palm-speech), meaning that the water stagnates there like the palm of a hand.

It was also commonly used for *sùwèi* (night guard), meaning to stay overnight for protection. Wang Bi’s commentary on the *Yījīng* states: "Guardian (*wèi*) means to protect. According to the *Guǎngyùn*, "guardian" (*wèi*) also means to augment.
This refers to the various guards established by the present dynasty, such as the Palace Guard Cavalry (*shìwèi mǎjūn*) and the Palace Guard Infantry (*shìwèi bójūn*).
Furthermore, this great earth is sixteen thousand eight hundred thousand *yojanas* deep, from the adamantine base (*vajratala*) up to the surface of the sea.
The *Loutan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra) states: "The land of Jambudvīpa is two trillion *li* deep;
beneath it is golden grain for another two trillion *li*, beneath that is adamantine for another two trillion *li*, and beneath that is the water-limit."
Eighty billion *li* below, there is a great wind with a depth of five hundred and twenty billion *li*.
The *Huguo ji* (Record of Protecting the State) states that from the "Vajra-limit" (*vajrānta*), water solidifies to form the golden earth; thus, at its furthest extent, there is a Vajra-limit.
"Extending life, physical vigor, eloquence, and tranquility—these are the five kinds of superior fruits obtained in the present life by those who propagate this Mahāyāna sūtra.

That which receives retribution throughout a single lifetime in an uninterrupted succession is called 'life' (*āyuṣ*); that the complexion is bright and pure is called 'color' (*varṇa*); that one possesses courageous diligence is called 'vigor' (*bala*);
that one delights in unhindered preaching is called 'eloquence' (*pratibhāna*); and that the six sense faculties are well-adjusted is called 'tranquility' (*praśrabdhi*). This Great Sūtra is pure..."

By making the final offering to the Buddha Dharmadhātu, one obtains five fruits; these are identical to the five fruits obtained through the bestowal of food in the *Śrāddhabhojana-sūtra* (Yan-kou-jing).
"Ying" (應) is pronounced with a departing tone (qu-hu), as in the phrase "obtained upon thought" (*ying-nian ji-de*). According to the *Guangyun*, "shi" (適) means "to follow" or "to accord with."

It is also "joy" (*yào*). Laozi said: "Without speaking, there is a spontaneous response; without summoning, they come of their own accord. This refers to what is called responding to the mind and finding contentment.

Regarding the land of Jambudvīpa, it is seven thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth. [The character] *zòng* (縱) is pronounced with the *rù* (入) tone when combined with *róng* (容). The *Han Shi Waizhuan* says: "South..."
The north is called vertical (*āyāma*), while east and west are called horizontal (*vistāra*). The *Rituals of Zhou* (*Zhōu Lǐ*) states: "Regarding the dimensions of the lands of the nine provinces:

the commentary notes that 'wheel' (*lún*) refers to the vertical, and 'broad' (*guǎng*) refers to the horizontal. The *Dīrgha Āgama* says: "The topography of the southern continent is narrow in the south and broad in the north;
its length and breadth are seven thousand *yojana*. The human face is broad at the top and narrow at the bottom, resembling the shape of the land. This is stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā*.
Regarding the characteristics of the great continents therein, Jambudvīpa in the south is like a chariot; its three sides are each two thousand [yojanas], while its southern side is three and a half.
The commentary explains: this means that the east, west, and north are each two thousand yojanas, while the south is only three and a half yojanas.
Calculating by these numbers, it totals six thousand three hundred and five hundred yojanas. This sutra states seven.
"One thousand *yojanas* is stated as a general approximation.

Regarding trees, groves, and gardens: the *Pianyun* lexicon states that the general term for all trees is "tree" (*shu*). The *Shuowen Jiezi* defines a "grove" (*lin*) as a cluster of trees on level ground;
a "garden" (*yuan*) is a park for raising birds and beasts, such as the "Deer Park" (*Mrgadāva*) mentioned in the Buddhist scriptures."
Regarding rivers, ponds, wells, and springs, the *Huainanzi* states: "Bo Yi invented the well. The commentary notes: "Bo Yi assisted Shun and was the first to construct wells. The *Shiben* states:
"The Yellow Emperor standardized the names of all things and was the first to dig wells. The *Shiming* explains: "Well (*jing*) means 'clear' (*qing*);
it refers to that which is pure and clean among springs. The *Fuxing* says: "The character for 'well' should have a dot in its center, with the four sides representing the railing within."
The term "point" (diǎn) refers to the pictographic form of a jar.

A single four-line verse, or even a single line—such as the *Ekottarika-āgama*’s description of taking any essential four-line verse from within the sūtras, like those concerning the Four Noble Truths—is what is meant here.
Now, it is said that these merely express the convergence of actual meanings; as for the "one" [line]...

Regarding "phrases" (*pada*) and "sections" (*varga*), the *Vajra-artha-yuan* states: "The ancient masters discuss four types of phrases: textual phrases (*vyañjana-pada*), meaning phrases (*artha-pada*), textual-and-meaning phrases, and [the phrase as] the completion of a verse.
Textual phrases refer to cases where four lines complete a full verse, such as the numerous verses in the *Avataṃsaka*.
Two lines completing a half-verse refers to cases such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, where the youth of the Snowy Mountains sought a half-verse. Meaning phrases refer to those that explain everything."
Taking the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) as a half-gāthā and further explaining that all phenomena are not empty constitutes a full gāthā.

This is like the ten wonders in the *Fahua xuanyi*, where the first five describe one's own practice (*sva-caryā*) as a half-jeweled wish-fulfilling gem, while the latter five further explain transforming others (*parārtha*) as the full wish-fulfilling gem;
this is precisely its analogy. Even a single phrase contains much meaning, yet it is forcibly divided into halves and wholes.
The Great Sūtra states: "When the Tathāgata expounds a single verse, even after immeasurable kalpas have passed, its meaning is not exhausted.
At that time, the Tathāgata does not give rise to the thought, 'I am speaking' or 'he is listening. Rather, he merely speaks a four-line verse in accordance with worldly convention.
Furthermore, the nature of all dharmas is such that there is no speaking; yet, by virtue of his sovereign mastery, the Tathāgata expounds it."
The mind is always firm and steadfast because it possesses deep faith in the Three Jewels as the eternally abiding true mind that cannot be obstructed or destroyed;

thus it is called "firm. Because it is a perfect, constant, and correct faith, it is called "deep" faith. There are three kinds of the Three Jewels: first, the Buddha, who is represented by images, statues, and paintings;
the Dharma, which consists of the *pātra* leaves and yellow scrolls; and the Sangha, who are those with shaven heads and dyed robes. Second, the distinct [Three Jewels]...
The Buddha of the marks refers to the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body; the Dharma refers to the teaching, wisdom, principle, and severance;
and the Sangha refers to the stages and ranks of the Three Vehicles. These three are of one essence: the Buddha is true suchness and awakening; the Dharma is the totality of the sustaining norm;
and the Sangha is the harmony of phenomena and principle. Therefore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra says: "The Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Assembly."
Within the palaces of the six heavens of the desire realm up to the celestial palaces, there are seven classes of goddesses belonging to the six heavens of the desire realm:
first, the Four Great Kings; second, the Trāyastriṃśa; third, the Yāma; fourth, the Tuṣita; fifth, the Nirmāṇarati; and sixth, the Paranirmitavaśavartin.
Within the palaces of these six heavens, each has its own abundance of goddesses; for now, let us take Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa, as an illustration.
Regarding this, the *Lokaprajñapti-śāstra* states that the abode of Śakra consists of one hundred jeweled towers in total at its four sides;
within each tower dwell seven celestial maidens (*apsaras*), and each celestial maiden has seven handmaidens.
Within these jeweled towers there are seventeen thousand rooms, and within each room there are seven celestial maidens, each of whom has [seven] handmaidens.
The women are likewise seven, all of whom are the principal consorts of Śakra; together with their handmaidens, there are a total of three billion nine hundred and fifty-nine thousand two hundred.
The *Lokadhātu-sūtra* states that when Śakra experiences sensual pleasure, his faculties merely touch one another and he emits only a wind-like breath.
Regarding states, capitals, and walled cities, the *Wuyue Chunqiu* states: "Gong built walls to protect his ruler and constructed outer enclosures (*guo*) to guard the people;

the records consider this the beginning of city walls and outer enclosures. The *Guanzi* says: "That which is inside is called the city (*cheng*), and that which is outside is called the outer enclosure (*guo*).
Mencius says: "There are cities of five *li* and outer enclosures of seven *li*. The *Fengsu Tong* says: "The character for 'city' (*cheng*) signifies 'to contain' (*chēng*)."
The term "guō" (郭) means "kuò" (廓), signifying vastness and spaciousness; it refers to that which contains and receives.
The two words "wéirán" (唯然)—where "wéi" is pronounced with the *qiè* (切) rhyme of "shuǐ" (水)—are sounds used in response.
If one discusses "wéi" and "nuò" (諾) from the perspective of ritual propriety (*lǐ*), "nuò" is a lax form of responding, whereas "wéi" is the proper sound of response.

Because of this reverence, the *Book of Rites* states: "When a father summons one, one does not say 'Yes' (*nuò*); when a teacher summons one, one does not say 'Yes,' but responds with 'Eh' (*wéi*) and rises.
The commentary notes: "'Eh' is a word of response; it expresses greater reverence than 'Yes. For instance, when Confucius responded to Yang Huo, he said 'Yes';
however, when speaking with those of superior rank, one uses 'Eh' instead of 'Yes,' as was the case when Zengzi responded to Confucius. Thus it is.
The *Yupian* explains that "shi" (是) corresponds to the sound of assent, meaning "yes. If we speak in terms of ritual propriety (*li*), this is a term used in response to equals;
it is like Confucius responding to Zi Gong or Mencius responding to Cao Jiao.

The *Shuzhu* (Commentary on the Sub-commentary) states: "Right understanding (*samyag-jñāna*) can manifest the essence (*tattva*), and the manifestation of the essence is called right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). The *Siming Ji* (Record of Siming) says:

"Because it contemplates and penetrates fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), it is called 'right contemplation. According to this, the character 'contemplate' (*guan*) should be pronounced with the level tone (*ping sheng*)."
Regarding the ritual of taking refuge and paying homage: *namo* is the correct Sanskrit term; in the Tang language it means "I pay homage," and is also translated as "taking refuge and paying homage.
It is further rendered as "delivering me," meaning that sentient beings are submerged in the river of craving, and by recollecting [the Buddha] who rescues them, they attain liberation.
In the *Sudarsana-vinaya*, it is translated as "taking refuge in life" (*guiming*). The *Karunapundarika-sutra* states: "Namo refers to the certainty of all Buddhas."

The name of the World-Honored One is his vocal sound. A passage in the *Lotus Sūtra* states that at the time of his death, Devadatta uttered "Namo" but had not yet pronounced the word "Buddha" when he fell into hell.
The Buddha prophesied that upon emerging from hell, he would become a pratyekabuddha named Namo.

The *Commentary on the Chapter on the Correct Discourse* (*Zhenglun pin shu*) states: "Correct" (*zheng*) refers to the "sage" (*sheng*). There are two kinds of sages: first, worldly sages; second, supramundane sages.

"Discourse" (*lun*) means to investigate and verify reality. It investigates the reality of phenomena and principles. This chapter contains the ancient laws of the former kings, transmitted from generation to generation.

The former kings transmitted them through the power of their dignity; the sovereign king transmitted them through the sign of his trustworthiness; and the Crown Prince [received] the laws of the former kings.

It is said that when a king practices this Dharma, the Yin and Yang are thereby harmonized, the sun and moon are thereby made regular, the hundred grains are thereby abundant, the myriad people are thereby joyful, the altars of soil and grain are thereby secure, and the governance and transformation of the world are thereby beautiful. This is the excellence of the present age;
it is the essential flow of the Golden Light, which is the supreme virtue and the vital path of the former kings. (From the *Wenxin diaolong*)
The Dragon said: "Lun" (論) means "order" (倫). It signifies that when ethical principles are without error, the intention of the Sages does not fall into decline.
The *Guangya* states: "Lun is the Way. The *Shuowen* states: "Lun is righteousness.
The King had a son named Śraddhālakṣaṇa (信相), who before long was to receive the position of consecration (*abhiṣeka*). [This is recorded in] the third fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

Nineteenth: It is said that when the crown prince born of a Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses the full marks of his body, the king has the prince sit upon a precious golden throne of a white elephant, spreads a great net-like canopy, erects a great Dharma banner, burns incense, scatters flowers, and plays various musical instruments;
he then takes the waters of the four great oceans and places them within a golden vase, which the king holds as he performs the consecration.
At that time, the Crown Prince was named Shouwang (Receiver of the Throne); he was immediately able to fully practice the ten paths of wholesome action and was called a Cakravartin King.
He addressed his own son, Xinsiang. The Han Shi Waizhuan says: "The Five Emperors governed the world; the three houses ruled by lineage."
The lower house transmits its lineage through the son, while the office of state transmits it through the worthy;

therefore, from the time of the dynasties of Tang and Yu upwards, the classics and commentaries contain no designation for the "Crown Prince" (*taizi*). Although the sovereigns of Xia and Yin transmitted their succession, the records are brief.

It was only under the Zhou that the regulations for the "Son of the King" (*Wenwang Shizi*) first appeared. The *Baihutong* asks: "How do we know that the sons of the Son of Heaven are called 'generations' (*shi*)?"
The *Zuozhuan* on the Spring and Autumn Annals states: "The King’s Heir Apparent attended the meeting at Shouzhi.
How do we know that the son of the Son of Heaven is called the Crown Prince (*taizi*)? The *Shangshu* says: "The Crown Prince Fa ascended the boat.
Some say that the sons of feudal lords are called crown princes; thus, the *Zuozhuan* mentions that Jin had a Crown Prince Shen-sheng and Zheng had [a Crown Prince].

In the *Huāqí*, it states that the Crown Prince was called *Guāng*; viewed from this perspective, the regulations regarding the Crown Prince (*tàizǐ*) and the heir apparent (*shìzǐ*) under the Zhou system were also not fixed.

Under the Han system, the legitimate successor of the Son of Heaven was titled the Imperial Heir (*huángtàizǐ*), while the legitimate successor of a feudal lord was called the Heir Apparent (*shìzǐ*).

"Never for a single thought-moment have I acted according to what is not the Dharma"—the word "xing" (行) is pronounced flatly, meaning that never for even a single instant between thoughts has one practiced what is contrary to the Dharma.
As the *Classic of Filial Piety* says: "I did not dare to speak unless it were the lawful speech of the former kings;
I did not dare to wear anything unless it were the lawful attire of the former kings."
The various kings gathered together and fashioned Mount Vajra (Vajraparvata). According to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the heart of the four great divine continents is Mount Sumeru;

outside of this mountain, it is surrounded by eight mountains and nine seas. Among these eight mountains, with the exception of the Cakravāḍa (Iron Encircling) Mountains which are composed of iron, the remaining seven are composed of gold.
Collectively, they are called the Seven Golden Mountains; thus it is stated in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
The verse states: "The first seven are composed of gold," which refers to the following seven mountains:
(1) Yugandhara, (2) Īṣādhara, (3) Kālaparvata, (4) Sudarśana, (5) Aśvakarṇa, (6) Vinataka, and (7) Nimindhara.

These are collectively referred to here as the "Vajra Mountains," a term that generally encompasses the aforementioned seven. The *Pumen pin* (Universal Gate Chapter) speaks of "falling onto the Vajra Mountains."
This is also merely that.

It should be read as the fourth tone (dàn) for me; in the rhyming dictionary, it signifies "decisive judgment" (*juéduàn*). If it were made the third tone (*shàngshēng*), it would mean "to sever," which is not the intended meaning of the scripture.

Because he governs the territory of a state, he is called a "Human King" (renwang). The term "Son of Heaven" (tianzi)—the character *tian* being pronounced with a departing tone—refers to a "Sovereign King" (bawang).
Han Kangbo’s commentary on the *Yi Jing* states: "The 'King' (Wang) signifies flourishing; it is the ultimate flowering of virtue throughout the world. The *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) says:

"One whose virtue mirrors Heaven and Earth is titled 'Emperor' (Di); one who gives birth to benevolence and righteousness is titled 'King' (Wang). The *Baihutong* (Comprehensive Discussions by the White Tiger Hall) states: "A 'King' (Wang) is one who moves forward (*wang*) throughout the world..."
