It is that to which all turn for refuge. Dong Zhongshu said: "In ancient times, when characters were first created, three strokes were drawn with their center connected;

this was called 'Wang' (the King). The three strokes represent Heaven, Earth, and Man. Connecting the center signifies the unification of their Way. It takes these Three Powers and brings them into harmonious communication."
Because he is protected by the devas, he is further called the "Son of Heaven" (*devaputra*). The *Suyin ji* states: "In Buddhist scriptures, the name 'Son of Heaven' is explained;
this text is the most explicit [on the matter], yet it does not set forth three meanings: first, protection by devas while in the womb; second, protection by devas after birth;
third, that the devas share in his own virtues—these can be seen in the sutras. The *Yiwei* states: "The Son of Heaven succeeds Heaven to govern all things and reform the administration."
Unifying all so that each attains its proper place, with Heaven as father and Earth as mother to nourish humanity—this is the title of the Most Supreme.
The *Yuanshen qi* says: "Heaven covers and Earth bears; therefore he is called the Son of Heaven. The *Shuowen jiezi* says:
"In antiquity, a divine sage was born as a son through the inspiration of Heaven; therefore he is called the Son of Heaven. When Confucius composed the *Chunqiu*, he [treated] the Son of Heaven...
The title "Heavenly King" (Tianwang) refers to what is called "the Heavenly King hunting at Heyang. The *Lengyan jing shu* states:

"In the past, when the House of Zhou declined, the rulers of Wu and Chu all usurped the title of 'King. Confucius rectified their titles by referring to the Son of Heaven of Zhou as the 'Heavenly King' in order to distinguish him from them."
Because each [of the gods] bestows a portion of their own merit upon this person, he is called the Son of Heaven (*tianzi*). The *Zuisheng jing* (Sūtra of Supreme Excellence) states:

"The Lord of the Thirty-three Heavens divides his power to assist the human king. The *Huguo ji* (Record on Protecting the State) notes that the character "divides" (*fen*) should be pronounced with a level tone (*pingsheng*).
"Half are called Kings of Men and half are called Musicians; this is also explained as a pair: half are called Kings of Men and half are called Musicians.
(The character for *lè* [music] is pronounced *jì* when reversed. The *Shū* (Commentary) states: "The King upholds ritual and music (*lǐyào*), causing the world to be peaceful and harmonious.

If it winds once every five days and rains once every ten days, who would not submit to his virtue? Therefore, the name 'Musician' applies to the King. This is from the "Treatise on Ritual and Music" (*Lǐyuè zhì*) in the *Hànshū*.
It is said: "The Way of the Six Classics leads to the same end, yet the application of ritual and music is the most urgent.
For one who governs a state, if ritual is absent for even a moment, violence and insolence will enter; for one who rules a nation, if ritual is lost for a single morning, it will become desolate.

Since human beings contain the qi of heaven and earth and yin and yang, and this qi possesses the emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure, the Sage therefore modeled himself after Heaven and Earth."
The establishment of rites and music is for the purpose of communicating with the spiritual intelligences and instituting the human relations. The *Classic of Filial Piety* says:
"If they are guided by rites and music, the people will become harmonious and respectful.
As for the *Luo-sha*, *Kui*, and *Kuai*, they are able to ward off various evils; the Great Scripture states that the women of the *Rākṣasas* give birth to children according to their own kind.
Having devoured the children until none remained, she next devoured her husband. The *Yìshù* (Commentary on Meanings) states: "The *rākṣasa* is a man-eating ghost;
if a person has died and their body is putrid, they can use incantations to preserve it so that it remains fresh.
This is the ghost presided over by Vaiśravaṇa. The commentary further states: "The title 'Executioner' (*guīkuài*) refers to those who command military forces and restrain malevolent ghosts. Ghost.
They fear the military commander and dare not act in disorder. The *Xinji* (New Record) states that "leader" (*kuí*) means chief or head;

"mincing" (*huài*) refers to finely slicing meat. Although the King possesses great power—like a rākṣasa leader who minces human flesh, causing all people to dare not commit wrongs—these two phrases in the sutra text employ an inferior example to illustrate a superior one.

The phrase "superior, hidden, and difficult to see" should be understood as having the two characters "also named" (*yì míng*) applied above them; when these are further applied over the term "rākṣasa," the meaning becomes manifest.

Furthermore, it is "also named" the *Sāṃkhyakārikā-sūtra* (or *Sāṃkhyasaptati*), which says that a king is the father of his people. It is also taught in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* that one should cultivate goodness through the instructions of one's parents. The *Sāṃkhyakārikā-sūtra* states: "A king is the father of the people."
A mother regards her people as her own infant, turning toward the dry and following the wet without waiting for their words. The *Shu* says:
"Since the King has established ritual and music, who would not turn to his virtue? Therefore, parents name him "King. The *Shi* says:
"The gracious and harmonious lord is the parent of the people. The commentary states: This means that when a ruler possesses the virtue of harmony, joy, simplicity, and ease, then...
The *Zuǎnzǐ* says: "To regard one's subordinates as a father regards his son, or as a mother regards hers. The *Zuǒzhuan* says: "To view the people as one's own children.
Regarding the mutual plundering of wealth and treasures, the *Shuowen Jiezi* says: "'Jie' (plunder) means when a person wishes to depart, another uses force to detain them.
The *Suo Yin Ji* says: "Where there is much gold and treasure, there will inevitably be thieves. Mencius says: "Those who prize pearls and jade..."
The calamity will surely reach one’s own person.
It is like a mad elephant trampling a lotus pond. As the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: "It is like a drunken elephant, wild, unruly, and violent, killing many;
yet when a tamer of elephants uses a large iron hook to pierce its forehead, it immediately becomes subdued and compliant."
Sentient beings are likewise; because they are intoxicated by the three poisons, they commit various evils.
Bodhisattvas and others, using the hook of hearing the Dharma, pierce them and immediately subdue them—"piercing" (còu) means to prick or stab.

"Bad rains fell repeatedly. (The character *lǚ* [屢] is pronounced with the *qiè* [切] rhyme of *liángyù* [良遇]. The *Shàngshū* says: "Repeatedly inspecting, one achieves success. Kong’s commentary states: "Lǚ means 'frequently'.
The *Hánshū* of the Former Han records that in the third year of the Jiānsì era of Emperor Chéng, there was heavy rain (*línyǔ*) in the Three Commanderies for over thirty days;
nineteen commanderies and kingdoms suffered, resulting in more than four thousand deaths and the destruction of eighty-four thousand government offices and private dwellings.

The *Tianwen zhi* (Treatise on Astronomy) in the *Hanshu* states: "Sudden thunder, high winds, strange clouds, and anomalous vapors occur when governance fails in this realm, and thus transformations manifest there.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler beholds them, he adorns his person and attends to affairs of state, reflecting upon their faults and repenting for his transgressions;
thus calamities are removed and blessings arrive."
Regarding the five grains and fruits, the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" (*Guishenpin*) states: "The hundred grains and fruits are now presented together.
The *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*) says: "The sun and moon are attached to heaven; the hundred grains, grasses, and trees are attached to the earth. Gao’s *Minor History* (*Xiaoshi*) says:
"Because the God of Fire (*Yandi*) cultivated the five grains, he was called Shen Nong. The *Book of Zhou* (*Zhou Shu*) says: "All millet and wheat reside in the east; panicled millet resides in..."
In the south dwell the rice-planters; in the center dwell the millet-growers; in the west dwell the bean-cultivators; and in the north dwell those who grow the *zhou* grain. The *Zhouguan* states:
"The Grand Steward employs the ten thousand people through nine occupations; the first is the three types of agriculture that produce the nine grains. Zheng’s commentary says:

"These are *ji*, *shu*, *shu*, rice, hemp, large and small beans, and large and small wheat. Regarding the King’s dietary provisions, he uses six grains; Zheng’s commentary says: [the same list applies].

Rice, millet, broomcorn millet, sorghum, wheat, and beans. Yang Quan’s *Treatise on the Nature of Things* says: "When the qi of grain overcomes the primal qi (*yuanqi*), the person becomes fat but does not live long.
The art of nourishing one's nature consists in always ensuring that the qi of grain is minimal, so that illness does not arise.

*Liang* (sorghum) is the general name for *shu* (millet) and *ji* (broomcorn millet); *dao* (rice) is the general name for crops grown by irrigation; and *shu* (beans) refers to the various types of legumes.

Collectively termed the "Three Grains," each consisting of twenty varieties, they constitute sixty; the fruits and vegetables that assist the grains are likewise twenty each, totaling one hundred grains.
As the *Shi* (Classic of Poetry) says, "Sow forth the hundred grains"—this is the grand designation for the multitude of grain species.
Fanzi’s *Jiren* states: "The five grains are the lifeblood of the myriad people and the precious treasure of the state. [End of] Mount Xiang.
The *Yalu* states: Emperor Zhenzong heard that the rice of the kingdom of Champa was drought-resistant;

he dispatched an envoy with precious treasures to request its seeds, which were then sown everywhere. It was first planted in the Rear Garden (*Houyuan*). Today, it is erroneously called "Jincheng" (Golden Achievement), but this is incorrect.
Because the king was tyrannical—*niè* (魚約切, *yúyuèqiè*)—the *Shangshu* says: "King Shou of Shang did not revere the High Heaven; he brought down calamities upon the people below.
He was immersed in and addicted to wine, and dared to act with tyranny. He punished the guilty by extending it to their clans, and filled offices based on hereditary lineage.

He burned and roasted loyal and virtuous men, and cut open pregnant women. The commentary states: "To be 'immersed' (*shěnmiǎn*) means to be addicted to wine; 'to dare' (*gǎnxíng*) means to act recklessly toward the colors of women."

Regarding cruelty and violent slaughter, the *Lunyu* states: "To kill without having provided instruction is called tyranny (*nüe*); to demand success without prior warning is called violence (*bao*).
The *Erya* states: "Hunting is tyranny (*nüe*)," with the commentary noting: "To hunt down and oppress is violent tyranny."
"Brothers and sisters, orphaned and scattered in exile. The *Erya* states: "Among men, the elder-born is called the elder brother (*xiong*) and the younger-born is called the younger brother (*di*);
among men, one refers to the elder-born woman as the elder sister (*jie*) and the younger-born woman as the younger sister (*mei*'). *Beng* (迸) is pronounced with the *bei* and *zheng* finals;
dictionaries define it as "to disperse. The *Mencius* says: "Fathers and sons do not see one another; brothers, wives, and children are scattered and dispersed."
When a highly esteemed minister departs this life and passes away, the *Baihutong* states: "To *hūng* means to suddenly cease; it refers to passing away abruptly. The *Jiulilü* states:
"The death of a Son of Heaven is called *bēng*; the death of a feudal lord is called *hūng*; the death of a Great Officer is called *zú*; the death of an officer is called *bùlù*;
and the death of a commoner is simply called *sǐ*. The *Erya* states: "To *bēng*, *hūng*, *wúlù*, *zú*, *cú*, *luò*, and *yì* [are all terms for death]."

"Death. The commentary states: "In antiquity, the term for death was used identically by both the noble and the humble; thus, in the *Shangshu*, Yao is said to have 'descended and fallen' (*cúlù*), while Shun is said to have 'ascended toward the four quarters and then died' (*zhìfā nǎi sǐ*).

Regarding "elephant-drawn carriage" (*xiàngmǎ chēchéng*), the pronunciation of *chē* is *chíyá*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "'Chē' is the general name for a carriage, its body, and its wheels. The *Shiming* states: [The definition of *chē* follows].

The ancient pronunciation of *che* (車) was *ju* (居). It signifies that speech and action are what cause a person to dwell; if one says it means "a carriage" (*she*), then speech and action are the place where one resides, like a dwelling.
*Sheng* (乘) is pronounced according to the *zheng* (證) rhyme. The *Zhou Li* states: "Four horses constitute a *sheng*"; *sheng* means to carry. The *Gushi* states:
"The Yellow Emperor invented the carriage to pull heavy loads and reach distant places. From the time the Yellow Emperor invented the carriage until the time of Shao [Huang].
In the time of Emperor Hao, oxen were yoked; in the time of Yu, Xi Zhong yoked horses. During the era of the Lord of Tao Tang, the vermilion chariot with white horses was established.
The Lord of Youyu followed the vermilion chariot to fashion the luan-chariot. The Xia Hou followed the luan-chariot to fashion the hook-chariot (gouche).
Xi Zhong yoked oxen and erected the banner (zhao) to distinguish the regulations between ruler and subject. In the Shang, it was called the hook-chariot and was further refined.
The great chariots have been used down to the present imperial court, where five types of chariots are still displayed during the suburban sacrifices (*jiaoli*).
Regarding the descent of hail, the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Hail is ice from rain; the character is composed of 'rain' (雨) and the phonetic 'bao' (包). The *Zuo Zhuan* says:
"All hail is caused by excessive warmth in winter and latent cold in summer. The commentary notes: "Excessive warmth refers to the warmth of winter; latent cold [refers to the cold of summer]."
It is cold in summer. When a Sage occupies the highest position, there are no hailstones;
even if they should occur, they do not cause calamity. The *Hongfan Wuxing Zhuan* says: "When Yin and Yang constrain each other, hail and sleet form.

When heavy Yin causes snow and rain to congeal and freeze, and the Yang qi strikes them so that they cannot penetrate one another, they are transformed into hail. Sleet is Yang constraining Yin; hail is Yin [constraining Yang]."
The *Hixiang* (Lateral Yang) states that in the twelfth month of the third year of the Yuancheng era of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty, hail fell as large as horse heads.

In the fifth month of the fourth year of the Dijie era of Emperor Xuan, hail fell in Shan-yang and Ji-yin like chicken eggs, two chi and five cun deep, killing two thousand people and causing all flying birds to die. The *Tang Wuxing Zhi* records this for the sixth year of the Qianfu era.
In the fifth month, rain and hail fell like bird eggs; when a ruler believes in slander and executes the innocent, the hail destroys tiles and breaks carts, killing oxen and horses.

The *Shenyiji* states: On the first day of the fourth month of the summer in the second year of the Guangming era of the Tang dynasty, a great wind uprooted trees and rain and hail fell as large as cups and bowls, causing all birds and beasts to die; thereafter, the Yellow Turban rebels entered.
When the Eastern Capital fell and the Son of Heaven entered Shu, the lands of the Central States were thrown into turmoil.

Shen Cunchong’s *Bibatang* states that during the Xining era, hail fell in Hezhou; the large pieces were like chicken eggs and the small like lotus seeds or gorgon fruits, all of which possessed human heads complete with eyes, ears, mouths, and noses.
The following year, the imperial army pacified Hezhou, and many of the barbarians were decapitated.
[The term] *zhòng* (assembly/mass). Regarding "lazy" (*lǎnduò*) and "indolent" (*xièdài*): the *Ěryá* states, "To be lax (*xiè*) is to be indolent (*dài*); to be indolent is to be lazy (*lǎn*).
The *Shìmíng* states, "To be lax means to be relaxed; it refers to the loosening and slackening of the bones and joints. The *Benxíng jīng* says: "Now, as for the indolent..."
The accumulation of various practices is hindered by the indolence of householders who fail to provide for their food, clothing, and livelihood;
the indolence of renunciants prevents them from escaping birth and death. Both the mundane and supramundane realms arise through diligence.

"To instruct according to the Dharma" means to admonish all the luminaries. The *Yuanshimao* says: "Heaven hangs down its literary patterns and images; humans perform their affairs accordingly—this is called 'instruction' (*jiao*).
The word 'instruction' (*jiao*) signifies 'to emulate' (*xiao*). The *Baihutong* says: "'Instruction' (*jiao*) means 'to emulate' (*xiao*);
the superior acts as a model, and the subordinates emulate them. The *Zilin* says: "'Admonition' (*zhào*) means 'to announce' (*gào*). The *Erya* [explains it similarly].

*Zhào* (詔) means to instruct. According to the *Shiming*, *zhào* means to illuminate. When people are obscured by darkness and fail to perceive the principles of affairs, they may commit transgressions;
this [instruction] is shown to them so that they may see clearly.
*Hào míng* (好名) and *shàn yù* (善譽): *yù* is pronounced with the initial *shèng* (余恕切). The *Guǎngyùn* states that to praise is called *yù*. The *Mao Shi Zhuan* says it means to extol beauty.
Regarding this, the *Yugu shi* (Eulogy of Ancient Poetry) states: "A beautiful reputation spreads through the ears of the multitude; a fine name startles the gaze of the masses.

The *Shanshi pin* (Chapter on the Accumulation of Goodness) in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* refers to King Śubhavyūha. The commentary (*shu*) says: "This Wheel-Turning King accumulated the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

By giving away the four great continents with his wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), he accumulated the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*); by listening to the Dharma preached by Ratnagarbha, he accumulated wisdom (*prajñā*)."
The name "Cakravartin" (Wheel-Turning King) is derived from his conduct. There are four types of Cakravartins; this refers specifically to the Golden Wheel-Turning King.

This is because he is said to renounce the four continents filled with precious jewels. The *Dharaṇīśvara-rāja-sūtra* states that a Bodhisattva on the first stage (*bhūmi*) acts as a Golden Wheel-Turning King, transforming the world through the ten wholesome paths of action at the beginning of the eon.
Regarding the *Nirvāṇa Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of Nirvāṇa) concerning the period after Parinirvāṇa: it states that in the five regions of India, the languages differ in five ways.
In the three directions of northeast, east, and center, the *śa* and *qie* sounds are slightly different; in the two directions of northwest and west, they are greatly different.
For example, when one says *mahāmaha-ni-ri*, it is *nirvāṇa*; this is how it is spoken in the three directions. When one says *huan-li-pa-na*, it is *parinirvāṇa*.
Now, these two terms are merely like the dialectical differences between the "Chu" and "Xia" regions of this land; according to the Sanskrit original, it should be called *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Here, "Great" (*mahā*) is translated as "Great Extinction" (*parinirvāṇa*). "Great" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); thus this sutra says:
"That which is called 'Great' has a nature as vast and expansive as empty space; its nature is the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the Dharma-nature is..."
The Dharma-body is such that its extinction is liberation; liberation is the freedom from the two kinds of afflictions and birth-and-death.
To be exempt from these causal and karmic sufferings and entanglements is liberation. "To cross over" refers to *prajñā*. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Faith is that which enables entry; crossing over is that which enables deliverance. These three characters are alternative names for the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*).
Question: Regarding the term "Venerable" (*bhadanta*), the *Vinaya* states that junior *bhikṣus* should address their seniors as "Venerable.
The *Zenghui ji* (Record of Augmented Radiance) notes: "One whose practice is perfected and virtue is lofty is called a 'Venerable.

This title first appeared during the Jin dynasty at Cudong Monastery, where there were over a thousand 'Venerables' who lectured on the sutras; this was the beginning of the custom of calling someone a 'Venerable' in this land."
The *Yinyuan lu* states that since the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, monks and Daoists have frequently been titled "Dade" (Great Virtue); having obtained this appointment by chance,
it became a formal title used by each to precede their name according to their specific field of study, even resulting in titles such as "Wen-zhang Dade" (Great Virtue of Literature and Rhetoric).

Regarding the phrase "Is there perhaps... (*pō yǒu*), the *Yīnyì* (Explanations of Sounds and Meanings) states that the character *pō* is originally pronounced *pǔgē* (普歌), but is here borrowed as *pǔwǒ* (普我).
The *Guǎngyá* (Extended Lexicon) says: "‘Pō’ means ‘few’ or ‘not. Shen Zhi’s supplementary note states: "'Is there perhaps' is equivalent to saying 'is there still.'"

In a cave, the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) and the cave of dhyāna; the *Mysterious Meaning of the Profound* (*Xuanyixuanyi*) likens it to shifting the spirit from a dragon’s lair to a rabbit’s burrow.
The *Erya* states that the place where a rabbit rests is called a "cave" (*ku*). Ma Yuan said, "A clever rabbit has three burrows.
According to the *Guoyu*, a "cave" (*ku*) is a hollow or hole.
"Hanging silk banners and canopies" (*xuán zéng fān gài*). "Zéng" (silk) is pronounced *jí líng qiè*. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Zéng refers to woven silk. The *Erya* states:
"The five colors combined are all called zéng. The *Sancang* states: "Woven silk of various colors is called zéng."
The *Manjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "It rained down *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, and *mahāmañjuṣaka* flowers, as well as various precious and exquisite blossoms.

All other sūtras speak of the heavens raining four kinds of flowers; this text merely omits the phrase "mañjuṣaka flowers" but includes the phrase "various precious and exquisite blossoms," thereby encompassing all types of flowers.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "intentional flowers (*manas-puṣpa*), great intentional flowers (*mahā-manas-puṣpa*), *pūrṇa* flowers, and great *pūrṇa* flowers."
The *Supplement to the Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Buxiang Hua Da Banruo) states: "Pleasant-flower" (*shiyi hua*), "Great Pleasant-flower," "Soft-flower" (*rouduan hua*), and "Great Soft-flower.

The *Fahua Jujing* (Verses on the Lotus Sutra) says: "The heavens rain four kinds of flowers: the old translations call them small white flowers, great white flowers, small red flowers, and great red flowers.
The *Miaole Ji* (Record of the Wondrous Joy) states: "Although various sūtras establish different names for these, their texts generally list [them as follows]."
The *Four Great Treatises* (*Sida lun*) states that the exquisite celestial flowers are called *mandārava* flowers;
the *Aśoka-rāja-sūtra* states that when the *mandārava* flowers bloom, their fragrance is smelled for forty *li*.
Regarding "sitting in the full lotus posture" (*paryaṅka-bandha*), one should understand that *jia* (跏) is used here; it originates from the ritual protocols of our own [Chinese] scriptures.
The *Yili* (Book of Rites) states: "The *qi* (棋) is tied at the *fu* (趺); the *fu* is the top of the foot. Lexicons define "sitting in the *fu*" as the "great sitting" (*dazuo*).

This is because this region [China] did not previously understand the characteristics of the full lotus posture, and thus referred to it merely as the "great sitting. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "As for 'tying the *jia*,' first the left, then the right, with both..."
Regarding the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it states that one places the two feet upon the two thighs, like the coiled body of a dragon;
one should know that this sitting posture is called *jiǎzuò* (armour-sitting) in Jiangdong, while in Jiangnan it is called *pánkua* (cross-legged).

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* further states that when the Buddha sat beneath the Bodhi tree in this manner, binding his legs in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*), he displayed such a majestic demeanor that the armies of Māra were thereby repelled. This is distinct from other postures.

Because it is the seat of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and because it accords with the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the *Mahā-śāstra* asks: "Since there are many methods of sitting, why do you only command the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*)?
The answer is: This sitting is the most secure and peaceful; it holds the hands and feet so that the mind does not scatter; it strikes terror into the Māra kings;
and it differs from the secular sitting or the non-Buddhist practice of standing on one foot. Therefore, in the Buddha’s teaching, one sits cross-legged to keep the body and mind upright.

Because the *Yì* (Book of Changes) establishes the correct order, the *Niansong jīng* (Sūtra on Recitation) states: "The full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) is that upon which Buddhas sit; the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*) is that upon which Bodhisattvas sit.
Regarding the mournful tone of the passage, "mournful" (*dào*) means to grieve or to fear. In ancient times during the Qin and Jin periods, it was used to express grief.
"To grieve for the wounded is to cause damage.
Regarding "xiyi" (熙怡), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states it is the appearance of harmony and joy; the *Fangyan* states that "yi" means "joy.
In the regions of Tan and Xiang, people use "fenxi" (紛熙) for "joyful celebration," or they say "xihua" (熙華). Both the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* state: [text continues]
The Tathāgata smiled with a joyful countenance.
At that moment, he took up the *cintāmaṇi* gem (and so forth, until) it rained down immeasurable varieties of precious jewels. The *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"The *cintāmaṇi* is the relic of an ancient Buddha; after the Dharma has perished, it transforms into the *cintāmaṇi* wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*)."
Having obtained it, one can rain down various treasures according to people's wishes; some call it the "Garuda-heart" because it remains within Mount Cakravāṇa.
Śakra obtained it and named it the "Wish-fulfilling Jewel" (Cintāmaṇi). In the clarity of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, one contemplates the inconceivable realm:
the mind of a single thought-moment is like the Wish-fulfilling Jewel, a supreme treasure of the heavens, resembling a mustard seed in size yet possessing great functional power.

If even the abundance or scarcity of rain falls in profusion without increasing or diminishing, and this is true even for material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), how much more so for the spiritual and wondrous mind, which does not lack any dharma?
The *Bie xing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Separate Practice) states: "The wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) not only rains down treasures but can also eliminate illness;
for example, when Prince Mahātyāga entered the ocean and obtained the jewel, he healed the eyes of his parents. This is precisely that.
It is indeed so; the Prince entered the sea to seek jewels and underwent hardships beyond description, as fully detailed in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the "seven precious gems" (*saptaratna*): in the *Yùpiān*, *guǐ* (古回切) refers to jade, and *qí* (渠羈切) is defined in the *Běicāng* as *guī*.

"Wěi" (瑋) means rare and precious. Regarding the "celestial crown" (*tiānguān*): the *Guǎngyùn* states that a "crown" (*guān*) is head ornamentation; the *Shuowén* states it is a binding, so called because it binds the hair; it is the general name for the *biàn* and *miǎn* headdresses. "Ěr" (珥) refers to ear pendants. The *Guǎngyùn* says: "A crown is head ornamentation. The *Shuowén* says: "It is a binding, used for binding the hair;
it is the collective term for the *biàn* and *miǎn* [headdresses]."
Regarding the practice of giving (*dāna*), there are two meanings: first, that giving encompasses the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); second, that giving gathers in sentient beings.

As Vasubandhu states in the *Vajracchedikā-śāstra*: "The meaning of giving encompasses the six: the gift of material goods, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Among all the Buddha-dharmas, giving is the initial gateway, for it is capable of gathering in sentient beings. Moreover, the other five perfections cannot [function] without it."

If *prajñā* (wisdom) were merely submerged within the world of finite phenomena, then one would not attain *bodhi* through the single perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) unless one realizes that these three factors are all empty and cannot be apprehended through the four logical alternatives (*catuskoṭi*). These three factors are: first, the object;
second, the giver; and third, the recipient.
In the *Mahāśatasahasrapuṇyavyūha-śāstra*, it is asked: "How much constitutes one merit (*puṇya*)? The answer is given:

some say that the sovereignty of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) over the four continents constitutes one merit; some say that the sovereignty of Śakra over the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*) constitutes one merit;
and some say that whatever a person—other than those in their final birth (*caramabhavika*)—accomplishes constitutes one merit.

Regarding merit, some say that all sentient beings within a great trichiliocosm attaining a single blessing constitutes one unit of merit; some say that curing the blindness of all blind people within a great trichiliocosm constitutes one unit of merit;
some say that saving all those who have died within a great trichiliocosm so that they may live constitutes one unit of merit;
and some say it is beyond comparison. This is because when a Bodhisattva enters the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, their mind contemplates great practices and plants the seeds of causal characteristics.

Because its merit is immeasurable, only a Buddha can know it, let alone a bodhisattva. When one cultivates the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*), each consists of five mental states—namely, the inferior, the middling, the superior, the superior-superior, and the superior-middling.

From the initial arousal of these five minds up to their full perfection, there are thus one hundred such mental states, which are called the "hundred merits" (*śata-puṇya*). These hundred merits then constitute a single mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, [regarding] the new...
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that "one hundred merits" refers to one hundred volitions (*cetanā*).

This means that when a Bodhisattva increases the karma for the marks of a Great Man (*lakṣaṇa*), they first give rise to fifty volitions to purify the vessel of the body. These consist of five volitions for each of the ten paths of action:
(1) the volition of abstaining from killing, (2) exhortation, (3) praise, (4) sympathetic joy, and (5) dedication. These are called the fifty volitions; this refers to the subsequent mind.
Furthermore, by generating fifty volitions (*cetanā*) to bring [the merit] to completion, it is called "one hundred blessings" (*śata-puṇya*).
This sūtra is profound and excellent in its beginning, middle, and end; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* explains seven kinds of virtuous meanings within its beginning, middle, and end.

Regarding "excellent in its beginning, middle, and end," this refers to the three divisions of the introduction (*nidāna*), the main body (*śarīra*), and the dissemination (*parivarta*), which are termed "excellent in terms of timing. If one follows the Hīnayāna...

Within the [Hīnayāna] vehicles, the three trainings of morality, concentration, and wisdom constitute the three virtues; whereas within the Mahāyāna, the initial, middle, and final moments of mind constitute the three virtues.

Regarding the term "parable" (譬喻): if one explains the meaning of these two characters according to the common convention, they have the same sense; however, if the two characters are analyzed separately...

As stated in the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary: "To employ analogies through comparison is called a 'parable' (*paryāya*); to provide an explanation that leads to awakening is called a 'simile' (*upamāna*).
Since both terms are presented together, there ought to be some distinction between them.

[For instance,] if a pit were filled with fire and one were to pass through it from the center, the *Sūtra of Supreme Excellence* says: 'Suppose there were a mass of great fire filling a hundred *yojanas*..."
Śāṇakavāsin passed straight through [the flames] without uttering a word of complaint for the sake of hearing this sutra. The *Sijiming* (Record of the Four Clarities) states:

"Passing through fire means sacrificing one's body for the Dharma. This is precisely the event described in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, where Sudhana visits the Brahmin Jvalanāntara and casts himself into a mass of fire.
The character "shèng" (盛) is pronounced level-tone (píngshēng) and signifies "to receive."
The *Mahā-śāstra* states regarding the lotus throne: "All types of seats may be used for sitting; why must it be a lotus? The answer is:

"Various seats are the conventional practice for sitting among laypeople of the world. Furthermore, because the lotus is soft, pure, and delicate, one who wishes to manifest supernatural power can sit upon it without causing the flower to wither. Moreover, it serves to provide magnificent adornment."
Alternatively, one may see Buddha images; as the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:

because King Udyāna had not seen the Buddha return for three months after the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma to his mother, he requested Maudgalyāyana to use his supernormal powers to bring Viśvakarman up to the celestial palace.
There, they observed the Buddha’s physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), carved a sandalwood image five feet high, and brought it down to the human realm. Furthermore—
The *Ekottarika-āgama* states that King Prasenajit heard that the King of Udyāna had cast a statue using purple-polished gold (*cāmīkara*), and this marks the very beginning of image-making.

The *Chuiyu ji* quotes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which says: "If one does not give rise to thoughts of difficulty regarding clay or wood, how could one know that the nature of the image is equal to the realm of empty space?
The three bodies (*trikāya*) are manifest therein, and the four virtues (*catvāri guṇāni*) are complete."
Non-decrease is the state where the mind that follows these characteristics is itself the True Buddha.
The *Sūtra of the Flower of Compassion of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva* says: "I vow to practice the bodhisattva path in a defiled and evil world so as to make it pure and adorned.
The Buddha Ratnagarbha said: "By these causes and conditions, I shall now change your name; your name shall be..."
The *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) states that the Sanskrit term *Samantabhadra* is translated here as "Universal Worthy" (*Puxian*).

His cause is called "universal" (*pu*) because it pervades everywhere; he is called "Worthy" (*xian*) because, following the severance of the path [of afflictions], he is adjacent to the ultimate sage. This is not the "Worthy" of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Furthermore, the *Puxian guan jing* (Sutra on the Visualization of Samantabhadra) names him "Pianji" (Ubiquitous Auspiciousness); "pian" means universal, and "ji" means auspicious.
He is the Worthy One (*Bhadra*).
Mañjuśrī, this Bodhisattva’s name appears differently in various scriptures; he is sometimes called Pūrṇa, sometimes called Kāśyapa, or Vajramati, and so forth.
In older translations he was rendered as "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*), hence the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "He clearly perceives the Buddha-nature. Just as...
Regarding Mañjuśrī and others, the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:

"Mañjuśrī" is translated here as "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (*Miaojixiang*), because when this Bodhisattva was born, he brought about ten auspicious occurrences: first, light filled the chamber; second, nectar overflowed the courtyard;
third, the earth surged forth with the seven treasures; fourth, deities opened hidden treasuries; fifth, chickens gave birth to phoenixes; sixth, pigs gave birth to... [the text continues].
1. A dragon gave birth to a pig; 2. Seven horses produced a qilin; 3. Eight oxen gave birth to a baize; 4. The granary transformed into golden grain;

5. An elephant was endowed with six tusks. The eighth fascicle of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Shiqian) clearly explains that in the past, Mañjuśrī was the Bodhisattva *Prabhāsa*, who taught the eight princes of Buddha *Dīpaṃkara*.
They received their predictions of enlightenment in succession, the last of whom was named *Dīpaṃkara*. This *Dīpaṃkara* is Śākyamuni.
The master who bestowed the prophecy upon Kāśyapa was Mañjuśrī-miṭhā-prabha (Mañjuśrī Wondrous Light), who thus became the ninth-generation patriarch of Śākyamuni;

therefore, in the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*, Mañjuśrī himself says, "I am originally the teacher of the Benevolent One (Maitreya), yet now in my manifested trace, I am the foremost disciple of Śākyamuni.

Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* states that Mañjuśrī is the past Buddha Dragon-Seed Supreme Honored King (*Nāga-jāti-agra-rāja-buddha*), while the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* [describes him as]... [text fragment].
The *Māra-sūtra* states that Mañjuśrī is the Buddha Joy-Treasury Maṇi-Ratna-Heap of the Northern Quarter, who will become a Buddha in the future under the name Samantadarśin;
thus, both his original essence (*honji*) and his manifested trace (*suijaku*) are sublime.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* by the Great Being Maitreya states: "Maitreya is the Great Teacher who will succeed the Buddha in the future.
Regarding the name 'Maitreya,' some say it was established from his clan name (*gotra*); however, I maintain this is not a clan name but rather a personal name.
Why? 'Maitreya' translates as 'Maitreya' (the Compassionate One). In the past, he was Dhammaruci; because he compassionately nurtured the people of the country, [he was known] by that [epithet]."
From that time until the present, Maitreya has always been known by the name Maitreya and the clan name Ajita (translated as "Unconquerable").

Some say that Ajita is the name; however, since one has not personally seen the original text, it is not appropriate to adhere to this definitively. (The above is from the commentary. The *Xiyuji* states:
"In the Sanskrit language, Maitreya; in the Tang language, 'Compassionate One' (*Cishi*). This is his clan name. [Maitreya] below..."
The *Sheng jing* (Sūtra on Birth) states that King Śuddhodana Brahmā gave his son the name Maitreya;
that same sūtra further clarifies that the bhikṣus at the three assemblies under the Dragon-flower tree will all bear the clan name Cishi (Maitreya).
"Valiant and possessed of great strength. The *Zhuangzi* states: "To be valiant, resolute, and daring, gathering the masses and leading troops—this is the lowest form of virtue (*xiàdé*).

The *Shìfǎ* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) says: "To know death yet not avoid it is called 'valiance' (*yǒng*); to risk one's life for others is called 'valiant resistance' (*yǒnghàn*, pronounced *hàn*).

According to the *Guǎngyùn*, "hàn" means to resist or oppose, as well as to be fierce and bold. Upon careful examination, both characters are applicable; however, I take the character "hàn" as the correct reading here.
The term "lower" (*xià*) contains the meaning of strength derived from the character for "hand.

"Renown" (*míngwén*) refers to its wide dissemination; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, "name" (*míng*) means one's own appellation. The character is composed of "evening" (*xī*) and "mouth" (*kǒu*): at evening, people do not see one another, so they announce themselves by mouth.

"Wén" (to hear) is pronounced with the *qièyùn* rhyme *máng yùn*; the *Guangyun* states that when a name reaches others, it is called "renown. This is as described in the *Mao Shi*: "Illustrious renown."
This means that one’s reputation for virtue within is heard far and wide without.
The *Yanmalowang jing yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning of the Sūtra on King Yama) states that Yanmaluo is the general superintendent of the ghost officials;
alternatively, it is said that Yanluo, Yanmo, and Yanma are all phonetic variations. In full, it is called Yanmaluoshi, which is translated as "The Pair."
The King’s elder brother and sister both served as lords of the hells; the brother presided over the affairs of men, while the sister presided over the affairs of women.

Thus they are called the Twin Kings (*Yama-rāja*), a name derived from their being two individuals joined together. Alternatively, it is said they are called "twins" because they experience both suffering and pleasure simultaneously.
As the *Dīrgha Āgama* states: "The palace of Yamarāja is six thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth; the king and his ministers remain there throughout the night."
At three times of day, there appears before him a cauldron of natural copper; a great hell-warden seizes the king, lays him upon hot iron, and pours molten copper into his mouth.
His throat and belly are scorched and rotted as he undergoes this punishment. Once the retribution is finished, he returns once more to his pleasures.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the realm of Yama is beneath Jambudvīpa, while the *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra* states it is outside the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* both state that Yama is subsumed under the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*).

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* maintains that he is categorized within the path of the hells (*naraka-gati*). The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states that in a former life, Yama was King Viśāla, who fought against King Vituśi;
being defeated, he made a vow that in a future life he would become the presiding judge of the hells. These various [accounts]...
The king of men has eighteen great ministers and their retinues, all of whom share his same aspiration; the King Vaiśravaṇa is now Yama.
These eighteen great ministers and their retinues are now the various minor kings, the Ox-Headed Ābhangas, and so forth.
A scholar of the Jin dynasty named Yan An once remarked that when he served as the Governor of Jingzhao, he was renowned for his strength and clarity among the people and officials.
One day, while Wei was fearful, he saw a divine being who, with quiver and scabbard at his side, paid him profound obeisance and said, "I am the General of the Five Paths;
I come today to pay my respects and to present a celestial mandate to welcome you as King Yama, to replace King Han. Wei remained composed that night, and indeed passed away.
The *Mingbao ji* (Records of Karmic Retribution) states: "King Yama is like the Son of Heaven in the human world; the Lord of Mount Tai is like [the Chancellor]."
The Minister of State and others established nine palaces; this was based on what the monk Tang Daoming saw when he entered the underworld, as it had not yet appeared in the sacred teachings.
Regarding the various deities of wind and water, as well as the fire deity, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that there are four great deities named Earth, Water, Fire, and Wind.
The Earth Deity said, "Within the earth there is no water, fire, or wind. The Buddha said, "Do not harbor such thoughts; all [elements] must be present.
It is simply because the element of earth is predominant that it is called 'earth. Upon hearing the Buddha's teaching, she attained the pure Dharma-eye.
The Wind Deity also said, "Just now, as I was sporting with my supernatural powers and thinking these thoughts, winds and waves immediately arose."
The deity Veda: this deity’s surname is Wei and his given name is Kun; he is one of the eight generals under the Southern King Virūḍhaka.

Among the thirty-two generals under the Four Kings, Veda is the foremost. This deity is born with innate knowledge and wisdom, having early on departed from the dust of desire to cultivate the practice of perpetual celibacy (*kumārabhūta*).
Having received the Buddha’s entrustment, he protects those who have left the household life.
Although I have committed many transgressions of the precepts, the foul odor from my person rises up through the air for four hundred thousand *li*, such that there is no one who does not loathe it;
fearing that I might violate the Buddha’s regulations, I must come here. Furthermore, regarding the *vinaya* established by the Buddha, I have heard and received them all in their entirety.

In the past, the Vinaya Master of the Southern Mountain was so pure and strict in his observance of the precepts that he moved the venerable devas to provide him with protection and service; thus, each and every rule—
The matters concerning the teachings and the Vinaya are fully recorded in the two biographies, *Gantong* and *Linggan*, and are not recounted here in detail.
Formerly, the four masters of India each composed their own *Guangming Chan* (Prabhāsa Repentance) rituals, none of which included the Vedic Deity (Weitian).

During the Xining era, Master Mingzhi traveled to study at the residence of Master Zhong in Yongjia. One day, as he was preparing to return home, Zhong said to him, "Upon your return, you must surely carry on [this tradition]."

Regarding the Dharma assembly at Yanqing, I once dreamed that the deity Mārīcī intended to take a seat within the ritual arena; it was likely because the two deities were already occupying positions in this monastery.

From then on, for the sake of the repentance rites, I additionally invoked the images of these deities throughout the world, following this precedent as recorded in the *Mingzhi Ta Ji* (Record of the Mingzhi Stupa).
However, while the names of the various deities in this sutra are all clearly manifest, [the deity] alone is not...
Regarding the deity Mārīcī, I have now included her here so that those who venerate her may obtain the true reality of her nature.
"Mārīcī" is translated here as "mirage" (*marīci*); because this deity is invisible and cannot be compared to anything, being neither combustible by fire nor floatable by water, she is like a mirage.
Thus, there was formerly a *Mārīcī-sūtra* within the Chinese Tripiṭaka.
When this scroll reached the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Great Song, it was newly translated as the *Mahāmāricī Sūtra* in seven fascicles.
It states: "There is a bodhisattva named Māricī who constantly travels before the sun and moon; the sun and moon cannot see her, nor can they seize her.
Water cannot drown her, and fire cannot burn her. She is free from all fears, and none dare to treat her with contempt. If a person recites [her mantra]..."
By holding this divine mantra, one can become invisible; on the road, neither water, fire, kings, calamities, thieves, nor military arrays shall find an opportunity against them.
The practitioner should visualize the Honored Deity seated upon a golden boar, wearing white robes and bearing a jeweled stūpa upon his head.
His left hand holds a branch of the *aśoka* tree, and he is surrounded by a multitude of boars. (From the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha*).
It is said that if one wishes to make offerings to the goddess Mārīcī, one should fashion an image of the goddess out of gold, silver, red copper, or sandalwood.
Her left arm is bent forward toward her breast, holding a celestial fan;

the fan is shaped like the Indian *svastika* with its inner curve forming the shape of four suns, and upon the fan there is the form of a flaming halo. Her right arm is extended, with the five fingers hanging down.
Her lower body was one or two inches long, up to about one cubit; she acted as an attendant and appeared like a celestial maiden. An old sutra contains a later record stating:
"A person in Xiangzhou dreamed at night of a ghost pulling a cart surrounded by a pack of pigs.
The cart was filled entirely with written documents. When someone asked the reason for this, the ghost replied: 'These are the military weapons destined for slaughter.'"
Upon examining the registers, they were all names of people. The ghost said, "If you wish to escape being killed, you must uphold the *Mārīcī Sūtra*.
Consequently, that person requested this sūtra and received it with sincere devotion; within no more than a few months, when a military conflict actually broke out, he alone was able to escape harm.
As for Viṣṇu (毗紐天), the *Shu* (疏) [commentary] transcribes it as "Niǔ" (紐) with the phonetic gloss "jiǔqiè" (九切). It is translated as "Pervasive Victory" (*Biànshèng*, 徧勝).

The *Āgama* identifies him as a deity of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), while the *Abhidharmakośa* identifies him as the deity at the summit of the Third Dhyāna. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that a thousand-petaled lotus grew from the navel of Viṣṇu.
The *Guānyīn yìshū* (觀音義疏) states: "Vaiśravaṇa (韋紐天); this is translated as 'Pervasive Hearing' (*biànwén*, 徧聞). His body has four arms."
Those who hold weapons, carry wheels, and ride upon *garuḍas* are the generals of the devas; as for Maheśvara,
the *Sūtra* commentary states that this Maheśvara is translated as "Great Sovereign" (*Dàzìzài*), "Majestic and Spiritual Emperor" (*Wéilíng Dì*), and so forth—
this refers to the Tiantai school’s identification of Maheśvara as the Lord of Devas, the Great Sovereign Heaven (*Mahādeva*).
However, the *Zhoutian zhuan* (Biographies of the Various Heavens) by Master Ying does not base itself on this explanation;
rather, it states that within the sutras there is another Maheśvara who is a yakṣa deity and not a lord of the heavens. This is as the *Mayūra-sūtra* says:
"The yakṣa Maheśvara dwells in the country of Jālandhara," and within the "Chapter on Radiant Ghosts and Spirits" (*Guishen pin*), it first mentions Īśvara.
This is Maheśvara, the Lord of the Devas. It is further stated that he is the powerful ghost-king Nārāyaṇa and others; Maheśvara is a yakṣa deity.

As described in the *Sūtra on the Past Deeds* (*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*), when the Buddha was Prince Siddhārtha, he went together with his retinue to pay homage at a temple of the gods.
Maheśvara is a deity who is both malevolent and possessed of spiritual power; when the Prince arrived there—

When the body being carried descended the steps, he first prostrated before the Prince; thinking that since the deity was malevolent, it could not have been a celestial lord (deva), those of antiquity have therefore depicted his image with indecision:
one version shows him in the form of a Bodhisattva with three eyes and eight arms, palms joined and holding a fly-whisk (*cāmara*);
another version shows him in the form of a yakṣa with disheveled hair, three eyes, and eight arms.
Regarding the holding of bows, arrows, and so forth, Master Rán-tíng has provided this explanation; let later scholars examine it further.

Regarding the term "five hundred followers" (*wǔbǎi túdǎng*), the *Shìmíng* states that five hundred households constitute a "party" (*dǎng*), which refers to the leader of a party, or the one honored by a single group, or a generation.
The *Lúnyǔ* contains the chapter titled "The Master’s Conduct in His Native Village" (*Fūzǐ xiāngdǎng*).

The *Pūrṇabhadra-mahāsūtra* states: "When the Bodhisattva was first born, the great general of the spirits, Pūrṇabhadra, grasped and shook immeasurable and boundless Buddha-worlds, which were filled with a golden radiance that pervaded empty space.
(In a loose translation, *pūrṇabhadra* is rendered as "Accumulated-to-Perfection.")
Furthermore, the *Kumbhīra-māyā-sūtra* states: "The deity Kumbhīra presides over all ghosts and spirits;
he is a subordinate minister under the Heavenly King of the East. The golden-haired deity is a subordinate minister under the Heavenly King of the North."
Nārāyaṇa is translated here as "the wrestler with the iron chain. Piṇḍola-bharadvāja is translated as "standing immovably.
Carpaṭa is translated as "attaining liberation through patience. Dharmabhadra is translated as "the learned king.
Makarapa is translated as "removing crookedness of mind. Śrīmitra is translated as "possessing meritorious achievements. Rāṇaviśa.
*Chao-hui-p'ien-chien-mo-she-ti*: translated as "Taming and Pacifying the Sword-Māṣadeva. *Fu-chung-ken-shê-lo-mi-ti*:
translated as "Subduing the Multitude of Faculties Śarabha-deva. *T'u-ch'u-kuai-hsieh-mo-p'o-to*: translated as "Delighting in Solitary Abode Haimavata. *Ying-she-chu-sa-to-ch'i-li*:
translated as "Lord of the House Sātāgiri. *Ta-li-t'ien-po-ho-li-tzu*: translated as "The Mighty and Majestic Vāhlika. *Chiu-lo-t'an-ti*: translated as "Warrior."
The names of those above the rank of Invincible (Ajita) are abbreviated and all appear in the commentary (*śāstra*). They are:
Dhyāna-ṛṣi, Āravāṭī, Mahādeva Pītamauli, Citrasena, Nārāyaṇa, Kinnara, Śiva, Maṇicandra, Gandharva, and Mahākāla. Half... [text ends].
I pray to the spirits and deities: the spirit Bana-li, the needle-haired spirit, Mahābana, Gundaka, Mauci, Gandha, Caṇḍa, Caṇḍālī, and the great female spirits such as Kaurava.
These nineteen names of spirits have not been translated [into Chinese] in the commentaries; neither the ancient nor the modern translators have provided translations for these Sanskrit terms.

According to the summary in the sutras, which states that "all are great bodhisattvas and so forth," one knows that these are all manifestations of Dharma-body bodhisattvas appearing provisionally to protect the Teaching.

Regarding King Mucilinda, the *Lotus Sutra* refers to him as Mount Mucilinda, while the supplementary commentary translates it as "Stone Mountain" (*śaila-parvata*), and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* [refers to it as]... [text truncated].
The *Jīngyīn* (Sound of the Sūtras) states: "Mucilinda" is translated as "Liberation," and "Nāga-rāja" is translated as "Abode. This dragon attained liberation through hearing the Dharma;
it is thus the "Abode of Liberation.
King Elāpattra is called Upala in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, while the *Tiānpǐn Fǎhuá* (Addendum Chapter of the Lotus Sūtra) calls him Utpala. The *Fǎhuá* [Sūtra]... [text continues].
The phrase "Uppalavaṇṇā" translates as "Dark-Colored Lotus Pond. The dragon dwells in this pond and thus acquired its auspicious name.
Regarding the Dragon King Nanda and the Great Dragon King Upananda, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that when the Bodhisattva first descended into birth, the Dragon King Nanda...
The King and Upananda used their supernatural powers to bathe the Bodhisattva’s body. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to the dragon Upananda as being "without ears yet able to hear.
Zhang Wujin’s commentary states: "The dragon's ears were deaf, yet through its spiritual power it was able to hear.
A passage from the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Nanda translates as 'Joy' (歡喜), and Badda translates as 'Good' (善). These two brothers are dragons."
He constantly protected the kingdom of Magadha so that it never suffered from famine due to lack of rain.

King Bimbisāra held an annual assembly to repay his debt of gratitude, which brought joy to the common people; from this, he gained the name "The Two Dragons. At first, he did not believe in the Buddha.
When the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother and resided on the edge of Mount Sumeru, [the king] remarked, "How can this shaven-headed man ascend above me?"
The dragon immediately released flames; Maudgalyāyana subdued it by manifesting as a fourteen-headed dragon that encircled Mount Sumeru fourteen times.
When the dragon encircled it seven times, [Maudgalyāyana] again released thunderbolts. Maudgalyāyana said, "If I were also like this, all of Jambudvīpa would be harmed.
Thereupon, he transformed himself into a small insect and bit the dragon; the dragon then conceived the aspiration for renunciation and left the household life. Maudgalyāyana manifested [this].
While walking upon the eyelashes of a dragon, Maudgalyāyana asked, "Why do you trouble me with such suffering? The dragon replied, "Why do you call me 'bald'?
Maudgalyāyana said, "I wish to become your disciple. The dragon went to where the Buddha was, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for him. And so forth.
Pāli-rahu is the name of this asura; the phrase from the *Lotus Sūtra* translates it as "Obstructor" (Zhangchi), for he is the one who obstructs the sun and moon.
His species is that of an animal, and his body is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length.

When the sun emits its radiance and shines upon his eyes, he raises his hand to block the sun, whereupon people of the world all say, "The sun is eclipsed. His obstruction of the moon is likewise. Sometimes he takes on a great [form].

The people of the world all said that the celestial beast was roaring, terrifying the sun and moon; it doubled its body size and hissed at them with its breath, causing the sun and moon to lose their radiance.
It then came to inform the Buddha, who commanded it; its limbs and joints trembled, and it subsequently released the sun and moon.
The *Pimozhidu jing yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning of the Vemacitra Sūtra) states: "Vema" is translated as "pervading the void," and "citra" is translated as "variously equipped.
This refers to when this asura fought with Śakra, his military equipment was arrayed throughout the sky.
The *Guanfo sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha) states: "Beings born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven cause those with desire to enter the ocean."
While bathing, some impurity fell into the mud and transformed into an egg. After eight thousand years, it gave birth to a daughter with one thousand heads, twenty-three hands, and one hand missing.
While this girl was playing in the water, water-essence entered her body;
after eight thousand years, she gave birth to Vemacitra, who had twenty-four heads and one thousand hands, one hand missing. He took a Gandharva maiden as his wife, and they fathered Śakra.
The consort Śacī married Śakra Devendra. One day, she slandered her father, claiming he was at war with Śakra;

however, by the power of Prajñā, Śakra was unable to cause him harm. The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states that beneath the eastern ocean of Mount Sumeru lies the country of Cīna, measuring eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth.

Regarding *Śyāmāvatī*: in the commentary, it is translated as "Heroic Virtue" (*yingxiong de*); various celestial transmission texts identify her as Mārīcī, which is a regional variation of the Sanskrit sound.
Examining this explanation now reveals three points of inconvenience: first, the Sanskrit term is incomplete and one must not recognize it erroneously;
second, according to Tiantai’s translation of the name, he does not mention "mirage" (*yángyàn*); third, based on the following... [text continues].
The concluding text of the sutra itself states: "All these are asura kings.
In the commentary (*śāstra*) on *Khara-karṇa*, it is translated as "Roaring like Thunder. A phrase from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"*Khara-karṇa* is translated as 'Broad Shoulders,' and also as 'Evil Shadow. This asura has the power to surge up the waters of the great ocean."
To "plant" (zhòng) means to establish; it is also written as "to cultivate" (zhí). The *Zuǒchuán* states: "I have fields and plots which Zǐchǎn cultivated. The *Huìtōng* says:
"The *Xiàzǐ* states that planting by transplanting roots is called 'establishing' (zhí); 'establishing' (zhí) means to set up. The *Shuōwén* says:
"A place for fruit trees is called a garden (yuán); a multitude of trees is called a forest (lín)."

It can cause the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) to emerge entirely upon the surface of the ground. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that at the beginning of the kalpa of formation, the essence of the earth arose like thin honey;

there were sentient beings with past habitual tendencies who became addicted to its flavor and took it as food. At that time, these sentient beings were called "the first to receive solid food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

Subsequently, the "earth-skin" (*pṛthivī-tvac*) and "earth-cakes" (*pṛthivī-piṇḍa*), and so forth, arose. However, this sutra explains that the essence of the earth does not belong to the [present] kalpa.
The initial matter now cites the preceding passage to clarify that beneath the earth there is "earth-flavor" (*pṛthivī-rasa*) and so forth.
Regarding the various hundred-grasses and trees, the *Huainanzi* states: "Shennong tasted the flavors of the hundred-grasses," and the *Zhuangzi* states:
"When the spring breath issues forth, the hundred-grasses grow."

There is no slanting or crookedness. The character *li* (戾) is pronounced with the *ji* (計) and *qiè* (切) finals; the *Zilin* (字林) states that this character is derived from a dog exiting a door with its body bent and crooked, serving as a pictographic representation.
Regarding the *utpala*, *padma*, and *kumuda* flowers, the *Jingyinyi* (經音義) states that "utpala" is the correct [transliteration].
*Nīla-utpala* is translated as "blue lotus. *Utpala* is translated as "lotus.
In the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra*, the flesh protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) on the crown of Avalokiteśvara’s head is like an *utpala* flower;
it is correctly called *padma*, also known as *padma*, which is translated as "red lotus. *Kuvalaya* is translated as "yellow lotus. (Tang Dynasty).
The *Shihuo lu* (Record of the True History of the Taizong Emperor) states that the kingdom of Kaśmīra presented *kumuda* flowers whose fragrance could be smelled for several li.
Regarding the *puṇḍarīka*, the *Miaoxuan* (Mysterious Profundity), fascicle 7, records that Master Rui said: "That which has not yet blossomed is called *kumala*;
that which is about to fall is called *kamala*; and that which is in its full, prime bloom is called *puṇḍarīka*. Master Yuan further stated: "*Puṇḍarīka* is the lotus."
The metaphor of the blooming flower illustrates that the physical body shifts with time and its name changes according to its color; thus, there are three names. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Among humans, he is like a lotus, a *puṇḍarīka* flower. Since these two names are listed side by side, there must be both a general and a specific designation.
Here, we take "lotus" as the general name and "puṇḍarīka" as the specific epithet. Master Lang said: "Alternatively, it is translated as 'fresh white color,' or..."

The Buddha did not explain to Ānanda that his elder brother had bestowed upon him the discourse on supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). He spoke to King Ajātaśatru, saying: "I am the new Buddha; you are the new king.
From this point on, King Ajātaśatru killed his father and murdered his mother. He seized a stone thirty cubits long and hurled it at the Buddha, but a forest deity caught it with her hand.
A small fragment splintered off and injured the Buddha’s foot. Furthermore, he instructed King Ajātaśatru to release a drunken elephant to trample [the Buddha].
The Buddha’s fist killed the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā; furthermore, he placed poison on his ten fingernails and went to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, wounding the Buddha.
From this act, he fell into hell. Because those who commit these five heinous crimes experience a burning heat in their hearts at the time of birth, it is called "Heavenly Heat" (Tianre).
Now, regarding Gopī, according to the *Jātakamālā*, Prince Siddhārtha had two wives:
the first was named Gopikā, a woman of noble birth who was barren; the second was Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula.
Gopī is translated here as "Bright Woman" (Ming-nü) and was the Prince’s principal consort. The Prince’s maternal family lived at a distance...
The city was eight hundred li in circumference, and the clan name was Gopī. There was an elder named Śreṣṭhin-jala-prabhā (Water-Light), whose wife was named Candra-nidhi (Moon-Treasury).
They lived near the edge of the city; when their daughter was born, the sun was about to set, and the remaining light illuminated their entire home.
Therefore, she was named Gopī.

Regarding the current five bhikṣus, the *Dharmapada* states: "When Prince Siddhārtha entered the mountains to study the Way, his father the King, filled with longing, dispatched five men to follow and attend him:
first, Kauṇḍinya; second, Aśvajit; third, Bhadrika, also known as Mahānāman;
fourth, Vāṣpa-Kāśyapa; and fifth, Gavāmpati. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) commentary on the *Prince* [text] states: "Aśvajit, Mahānāman, and Gavāmpati."

These [first] two are the father’s, while the other two are the mother’s. If one follows the phrasing of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, chapter five, it lists Cunda, Aśvajit, Bāṣpa, Daśabala-Kāśyapa, Mahānāman, and the Prince Kauliya;
however, if this text were to list Bāṣpa, Mahānāman would have to be excluded, because the preceding passage states that these are alternative names for him. If one relies on the [list of] five...
If one divides the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha*, Mānava is the son of Droṇodana and Bāṣpa is the son of Amṛtodana;
since these are two distinct individuals, they would thus constitute six [princes]. Given such differences and similarities, it is unknown which account is correct.
Furthermore, regarding the passage on Śāriputra in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "Śāriputra" is translated here as "Jewel.
His mother was the foremost among women in intelligence; since the mark of such intelligence resides in the eyes, and because [the eyes] are like jewels, he is called "Jewel-born" (珠子).
Moreover, his body was well-proportioned; because he was born from such a body, he is called "Body-born" (身子).
Because she gave birth to a son who was so exceptionally radiant, she was given this title. The Venerable One’s clan name was originally Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, a lineage of the Brahmins.
According to the *Huayan yinyi* (Phonetics and Meanings of the Avataṃsaka), it should be called Śārikāputra;
"Śārikā" translates as "śārika bird" (a kind of waterfowl), and "putra" translates as "son. The Venerable One’s mother had eyes with black and white clearly distinguished and flowing [with luster].
His name, Śāriputra, means "Eagle-Eyed" (Śāri), derived from his mother's name; the old translation "Body-Son" (Shenzi) is an error.
The translation "Cloud-Interval" (Yunjian) renders the Sanskrit as *Śakuntaka*; one version translates it as "Body-Son" and another as "Eagle-Eyed," thus encompassing both traditions.
Maudgalyāyana is a term from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; "Maudgalyāyana" is his clan name, which translates as "Praised Reciter.
In the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, it is translated as "radish," while Paramārtha translates it as "mudgara," which translates as "mung bean.

Because ancient seers were fond of these two things, they used them to name their clans. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the Buddha addresses Maudgalyāyana as "Maudgalyaputra," which is how the Buddha calls him.

Maudgalyāyana’s *Chuiyu ji* (Record of the Bequeathed Benefits) states: "Lái (萊) is pronounced with the initial *lì* (力) and the final *hé* (何); fú (茯) is pronounced with the initial *pú* (蒲) and the final *běi* (北).

Those in the world who do not understand this often call it by the pronunciation 'Làifú' (來伏), which is truly laughable. It should correctly be pronounced 'Lúbó' (蘆菔), which matches the preceding [phonetic analysis].
The characters currently used to write it as 'Luóbò' (蘿蔔) are merely vulgar forms. A detailed explanation of these names and characteristics can be found therein."
Yajña collected the *śarīra* and immediately erected a stūpa made of the seven precious substances at this very spot. The *Jātaka of the Starving Tiger* states:

"After the Prince had fed the tiger, the ministers addressed the King, saying: 'It is fitting to collect the remains, bring them out from the mountain onto level ground, cremate them, and collect the *śarīra*.'"
The construction of this stūpa for making offerings is that very stūpa erected in the past.

Regarding the passage at the beginning of this chapter concerning those who emerged from the earth, the *Record of the Tripitaka Master Faxian* states: "In the Western Regions there is a kingdom named Takṣaśilā;

traveling two days to the east, one arrives at the place where the Bodhisattva threw himself to feed a tigress. There is a stūpa at this site, adorned with various precious jewels. The King... [continued].
The subject’s offerings have continued without interruption. Furthermore, the *Postscript to the Sūtra of the Starving Tiger* states:
"At that time, having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, the King immediately erected at this very spot the Bodhisattva Tower of the Body-Sacrifice to the Starving Tiger.

This tower still exists today on the eastern side of the mountain, containing a vihāra where more than five thousand monks reside. The tower seen by the two masters mentioned above is precisely this one.
The stupa erected by the king today is not the same as the one from when he sacrificed his body in the past;
for although that former stupa was said to have emerged from the earth, the end of the chapter itself states that it immediately sank back and disappeared.

Regarding the prostration with the five limbs touching the ground, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that the two elbows, the two knees, and the head constitute the "five wheels" (*pañcamaṇḍala*), where "wheel" (*maṇḍala*) carries the meaning of circular rotation.
The *Zhulin* (Pearl Forest) records: "I have observed that when monks from the Western Regions perform prostrations, they lift their robes to expose their knees;
first, these touch the ground, and then they press their elbows against the earth while supporting their palms in the air, thereby demonstrating the act of receiving [the feet of] the honored one."
This is the meaning of "prostrating with the five limbs. The *Commentary on the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* states: "The 'ground' is the ground of the single true reality (*eka-lakṣaṇa*).
To be in accord with *sarvajñā* (omniscience) is called 'prostrating to the ground.'"
Regarding "Mount Zijing" (Purple Gold Mountain), the *Erya* states: "Gold is called *tang*; that which is beautiful among it is called *liu*. The commentary notes:

"*Liu* is precisely purple-polished gold (*zimo jin*). The *Chuxue ji* says: "The finest gold is purple-polished; its color is transparently bright, fresh, and pure, and it is also called *yangmai jin* (soaring gold).
The *Sutra on Invoking Avalokiteśvara* states: "All Buddhas appearing in the world shine with brilliant illumination."
The body of the Sun and Moon emits the light of great wisdom, like the blazing of a mountain of purple gold.
There are six kinds of pure and subtle, wondrous sounds; according to the *Dharmadhātu-krama*, eight kinds of sounds are enumerated, though the "six" mentioned here need not be sought far away:
first, the sound is clear and penetrating; second, it is wondrous like the voice of Brahmā; third, it is the lion’s roar.
1. The sound of the four great elements; 2. the sound of thunder; 3. the voice of the *kalaviṅka* bird; 4. the voice of the peacock; 5.

as described in the *Avataṃsaka*, the Brahmā-voice is so pure and subtle that every member of the Brahma assembly thinks, "The Brahmā King is speaking to me alone," and whether near or far, it is heard equally; 6.
as stated in a verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, Maudgalyāyana perceived the Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice from afar as if he were right by the Buddha's side.
If one wishes to know whether the Buddha’s voice remains as it was and does not differ when it reaches lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to the west, [it is like this].
*Kalinga* (or *Karavinka*) is translated as "Wondrous Sound" (*miao sheng*);
the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* calls it the "Kalinga's immortal voice" that pervades the worlds of the ten directions. The *Huayan Yin Yi* states that this bird originally comes from the Snow Mountains.
While still within its shell, it is already able to sing; its voice is harmonious and elegant, such that listeners never tire of hearing it.
Its form resembles that of a magpie, and it often dwells in flocks within bamboo groves. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"The *kalaviṅka* produces a wondrous sound that no other voices—whether those of devas, humans, or *kiṃnaras*—can equal, with the sole exception of..."
The voice of the Tathāgata:
"exhausting thought and measurement" (*jin si du liang*). "Exhaust" (*jin*) means to end, to deplete, or to terminate.

"Thought" (*si*)—the character is pronounced *xi zi*—the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that "to plan deeply and consider afar is called 'thought'. "Measurement" (*du*)—the character is pronounced *tu ge*—the *Guangya* states that "measurement means to gauge or to assess."
"Also measure" (yě liàng) means to deliberate or calculate.
Regarding "brilliant radiance" (guāng míng hè yì): the *Guǎng yǎ* states that "hè hè" means brightness; the *Guǎng yùn* states that "yì" means great, flourishing, or abundant.
There are some editions of the scripture where "yì" is written as "yì," which is incorrect; it is likely a scribal error for the character used in "chess" (bó yì).
"Rare, rare! The *Huguo ji* states that repeating "rare" is the ultimate expression of praise, identical in meaning to the repetition of "well done" (*sādhu*).
For example, the *Udumbara* flower appears but once in a great while. The *Miaole ji* notes that the *Udumbara* is newly called the *Utpala*.
"Luó" (羅) is translated here as "Auspicious Response Flower" (*ruiyinghua*), also called the "Numinous Auspicious Flower. This flower appears once every three thousand years;
when it appears, a Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*) emerges in the world. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Within Jambudvīpa there is a sovereign tree-king named Udumbara.
This tree has fruit but no flowers; only when its golden flowers bloom does a Buddha appear. If the Buddha does not [appear], [the flowers do not bloom]."
Upon emerging, there is immediately a Golden Wheel-Turning King who rules the world.
He then enters again the Great City of Sublime Tranquility. A great sutra states: "It is like a great city that has but a single gate;
its guardian is wise and intelligent—he allows those who should be let in, and he bars those who should be barred. The city is a metaphor for Nirvana, and the gate is a metaphor for [the path].
The "guardian of the Eightfold Path" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata.

When one investigates their fundamental nature and characteristics, they are all empty and quiescent, and wondrously blissful. It is said that upon the principle of the single reality, both nature and characteristics are empty;
the emptiness of nature means there are no four natures, and the emptiness of these non-natures is itself the emptiness of characteristics.
The *Mahāvaipulya-māyājāla-sūtra* states: "When children see a mirage in the heat, they call it water;

a person of wisdom, seeing it, never gives rise to the thought that it is real water. For example, when a magician conjures an illusion of the fourfold army, or even mountains, forests, rivers, and wells, children perceive them as real, while a person of wisdom knows they are the power of illusion deceiving people."
Just as a valley produces an echo due to sound, and a child hears it and thinks it truly exists, whereas a person of wisdom understands it has no fixed reality;

the *Dharmadhātu-krama* states that those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are able to perform transformations, creating beings who are free from birth, old age, sickness, and death, because these are empty. The *Guxiang chao* says: "The Buddha constantly uses flames..."
Regarding the use of illusions and the like as metaphors: because sentient beings do not understand that the phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *āśrita*) are empty,
illusions, mirages, and so forth are employed as easily understood metaphors for emptiness to enable them to realize that body and mind are unreal,
just like illusions, mirages, and the like.

Just as the moon in the water appears in succession to the moon in the sky reflected upon the water, so too within the water of the ordinary person’s mind, the signs of "self" and "what belongs to self" appear. Therefore, it is like the moon in the water:
when a child sees the moon in the water, they rejoice and wish to seize it; when an adult sees it, they laugh.
It is like what is seen in a dream; the sequence is as follows: there is no reality within the dream, yet upon waking one laughs at oneself. People are also like this:

while asleep amidst the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), reality is absent, yet they cling to existence; only when they awaken through the attainment of the Path do they realize it is unreal and laugh at themselves.

Regarding the five supernatural powers of the *ṛṣis*, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "There are those who do not rely on perfect enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead cultivate deluded thoughts to preserve their forms through visualization, roaming in mountain forests and remote places inaccessible to ordinary people, living for ten million years.
There are ten kinds of such immortals, namely: earth-walking immortals, flying immortals, light-walking immortals, and so forth. These, too, are merely the delusions of saṃsāra."
When the retribution for their transmigratory flow is exhausted, they return to the various realms of existence.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that among all the Buddha’s teachings, sound is supreme;

or, because one hears the verbal teachings from teachers and friends and progressively cultivates and realizes them to seek supramundane minor practices and minor fruits, it is called "Sound" (*Śrāvaka*).

I have heard it said in the *Sarvapratyeka-buddha-mahā-śāstra*: "Pratyekabuddha" is translated here as "Awakened by Causes and Conditions" (*yin-yuan-jue*) and is also called "Solitary Awakened One" (*du-jue*).

Those who appear during the era of a Buddha hear the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and are thus called "Conditionally Awakened Ones" (*yuan-jue*); those who appear in an era when no Buddha exists awaken spontaneously.
One who has attained the Way is called a Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer).
Regarding the term *samādhi*, the *Jingyinyi* (Meanings of Terms in the Scriptures) states: "The correct Sanskrit term for *samādhi* is *samāpatti*.
