This is translated as 'equanimous maintenance' (*samādhi*), meaning to maintain all meritorious qualities with equanimity; it may also be translated as 'right concentration,' meaning that one remains constantly and correctly concentrated regardless of whatever objects arise."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All states of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are termed *samādhi*; in the language of Qin, this means 'the locus for the correct movement of the mind.

Since this mind has been constantly crooked from time immemorial, when it enters the locus of correct practice, the mind becomes upright and straight—just as a snake that moves in constant curves becomes straight when it enters a tube."
○ Ninth: Questions and Answers Resolving Doubts.

Doubt is the ford to liberation, and liberation is the ferry across doubt. Although the preceding sections have already clarified various phenomena (*dharmas*), they have not yet examined the points where the meanings and implications within the scriptures intersect.
Therefore, following the ancient tradition, questions are set forth hereafter. However—
Subsequently, I shall elaborate upon this by summarizing the text and its essential meaning; such sections total thirty-six.
Should these not serve as the ferry and the ford for this sutra?
First question: Is Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain within the city of Rājagṛha or outside it? If it were outside, it should not...

If it is said that [the Buddha] dwells within, why did Śraddhālakṣaṇa, having dreamed of the golden drum at night, emerge from the city of Rājagṛha at dawn and proceed to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain? The commentary states:
what is called the royal city must be understood as double-layered; first, the mountain range of the five peaks serves as its surrounding wall. Thus, it is a city.

The *Lotus Sūtra* lists the following locations: the Caves of the Heavenly Kings (*Devadaha*), the Seven-Leaf Cave (*Saptaparṇa-guhā*), the Snake God Mountain (*Nāgaśaila*), Mount Ekabala (*Ekabala-parvata*), and Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
Second, the city walls were constructed from a mound of pheasants; this was the place where the king, ministers, and commoners resided. Thus, the *Biography of Tripitaka Master Xuanzang* states:
"The city of Rājagṛha is surrounded on all four sides by mountains that are steep and precipitous as if carved; its circumference is one hundred [yojanas]."
Within fifty-odd *li* there was the foundation of a mountain city, thirty *li* in circumference. Traveling four or five *li* east from the palace city, one reaches Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.

Furthermore, the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that the royal city was surrounded on all sides by lofty mountains serving as an outer wall, and that the inner city was thirty *li* in circuit.
Based on this, we know that what Xinxiang (Śraddhālakṣaṇa) refers to as "leaving the city" [refers to departing from this inner city].
Leaving the city of Rājagṛha and heading toward Vulture Peak Mountain, he traveled four or five *li* until he reached the Buddha’s location.
It appears that while the Buddha was wandering for alms in the royal city, this place was designated as his temporary residence (*sthita*);
however, his permanent dwelling was on Vulture Peak. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because Vulture Peak is near the city, [the Buddha] does not grow weary from begging for alms."

Therefore, the Buddha frequently dwells upon the various mountains and cities of the upper realms; although he does not descend there for sightseeing, it is as clear to him as looking at the palm of his hand.

Second, regarding the explanation of the text and phrases of the sutra: among the five preliminary matters, it is stated that this sutra lacks the fifth item, the assembly of those who heard the teaching together. If...
However, it is not the case that this sutra was spoken by the Buddha solely to Ānanda alone. The commentary states:
"Regarding whether the assembly is listed [at the beginning] of this sutra, two perspectives should be maintained. First, according to Tiantai’s general interpretation of the scripture:

on one hand, although the assembly is absent, on the other hand, it is indeed present. Therefore, the sub-commentary says: "This sutra lacks the 'concurrent audience' (sahā-śrāvaka-saṃgha), meaning that at that time there were five [aspects]."

There are four assemblies at Mount Qi; the assembly at Mount Qi did not hear what was said in the Hall of Faithful Signs (Xinxiang-shi), the assembly in the Hall of Faithful Signs did not hear what was said in the dream, and the assembly that heard what was said in the dream did not hear what was said after waking from the dream. Because these were not a single assembly, they are not listed [in the preface].
Furthermore, the Commentary states: "The devas and nāgas gathered in the Hall of Faithful Signs did not hear the preceding introduction, nor did they hear the subsequent [conclusion]."

The dream was likewise the same; the assembly of those who heard [the teaching] together was also the same assembly of those who heard it together, differing only in that the number of those who heard it together was small and not in sequence.

This is because the original Sanskrit manuscript actually contained the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), which was omitted during the translation; thus, in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), while refuting the old [interpretations], it says:

"Some raise doubts by claiming the case is not analogous to the 'those who heard it together. Yet the Hu (Sanskrit) manuscript still contains much more—how could it be limited to four fascicles? It is simply that the text has not yet been transmitted."
In the Tang dynasty translation of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the assembly of followers is enumerated as consisting of ninety-eight thousand bhikṣus,
hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas, and forty-two thousand devaputras; yet, having distinguished between these two meanings,
whether such an assembly exists or not cannot truly be determined by a single path.
The *Sānwen Chanhui Pin* (Chapter on the Three Questions on Repentance) states: "If one can perform the repentance as described here, one will immediately transcend the sins of sixty kalpas.
Yet, how can a single act of repentance extinguish the sins of so many kalpas?
The commentary states: This is the merit of the contemplation on the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in extinguishing transgressions.
Therefore, the sub-commentary says: "The repentance through contemplating non-arising can extinguish ignorance; it is like overturning the great earth, where both roots and leaves wither away.

How much more so when the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* speaks of the wondrous power to eliminate the sins of birth and death for fifty thousand kalpas? The *Miaozong chao* (Exposition of the Wondrous Principle) clarifies its meaning as follows:
The extent to which offenses are extinguished is all spoken of according to the measure of the Buddha’s wisdom;

therefore, it is not something that can be conceived by those at the initial stage of practice, let alone the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden, wherein there is no distinction between light and heavy offenses, and all are extinguished through repentance. If one understands that intent, then the meaning of these texts will become clear.

Fourth question: This scripture’s Chapter on Praise describes the Tathāgata’s tongue-mark as being exceptionally broad and long; the sutra states that his tongue extends throughout the great trichiliocosm.
Since the Buddha attained such a tongue-mark in the past due to his truthful speech, many people in the world have doubted it as being excessively long.
How is this now to be reconciled?
The commentary states: This should be understood through two meanings. First, it is spoken in reference to the Buddha’s empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*);

as stated in the *Mahā-śāstra*, when the Buddha extended his tongue for the sake of a Brahmin, it covered his face up to the hairline—this was for a minor teaching. Now, because he is preaching the *Prajñāpāramitā*, his tongue covers the great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhatu*).
Alternatively, it is said that what the human eye can perceive does not exceed a few *li*, yet here it is said to cover the great trichiliocosm; this is not a contradiction.

This is a difficult-to-believe response; the Buddha used skillful means to borrow his own supernatural power to empower [the beings] so that they might see him—even animals can perceive this, whereas those with only the ten levels of faith would not know it were it not for the Buddha’s empowerment. Second, regarding what is manifested according to circumstances:
this is because practitioners of the Perfect Teaching cultivate the Middle Way and, through the functioning of their *karmic consciousness*, see the Buddha abiding in the principle of the Middle Way.
Although the sixteen-foot body with its forty-eight marks is individually infinite and free from the characteristics of limitation,
this is precisely the meaning of the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* regarding the principle that whatever is manifested is itself boundless.
Fifth question: This sutra contains the statement that the Dragon Honored One praised the Buddha as having a circular halo one *zhang* in circumference.

If this is so, is the Buddha’s body the Honored and Extraordinary Reward Body (*sambhogakāya*), or is it the inferior Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of one *zhang* and six feet? If you say it is the Honored and Extraordinary [Body], then the statement regarding the one-*zhang* halo would not be large;
if you say it is the inferior Response [Body], why does the commentary state that the circular halo is one *zhang*? Below, in this very sutra, he is clearly praising the Honored [Body].
"Especially so.

The commentary states: "The praise by the Honored Dragon (Nāgarāja) does not exceed the thirty-two marks. Regarding the definitive determination of their superiority or inferiority, there have been slight differences in opinion throughout antiquity and the present;
now, I shall directly manifest the *vairocana* (universal manifestation) through the four clarities to extend this meaning. Thus, the record says: 'Perfect.'"

The radiance on each side is one *zhang*; this term "one *xun*" is spoken in reference to the Buddha. Since this is his constant radiance (*nitya-prabhā*), it is verified that all the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are likewise constant marks.
Thus, when praising the "Venerable Extraordinary Form" (*vairocana-vigraha*), one should know that it does not require a massive body with numerous marks;

rather, when the consciousness of karma (*karma-vijñāna*) relies upon the Middle Principle (*madhyama-tattva*) to perceive, this is precisely what is called the "Venerable Extraordinary Form. One should further understand that if the measurement of the [sixteen-foot] body is...
If crossing over does not involve reaching a limit— just as in the room of Vimalakīrti, which was only ten feet square yet could accommodate thirty-two thousand lion thrones—
is it not likewise the case here that the constant body (dhruvakāya) extols the meaning of the marks of supreme excellence?
Question Six: In the "Chapter on Explaining Emptiness," it is said that he blew the great Dharma conch and struck the great Dharma drum.

Since these conchs and drums were all produced by killing living beings, why did the Buddha command that one should not kill? With what intention, then, did he take these as instruments of the Dharma?
The commentary states: Zhā Ān (釋樝菴) or Duì Cháng (對嘗) extended this meaning, saying that blowing the conch and beating the drum are merely parables;
they represent the vanguard of the army of precepts, which must blow and beat before battle, analogous to the Bodhisattva facing the powerful enemy of the Māra of birth-and-death.
Even if one does not adopt this interpretation, there are naturally those who die from conches and oxen, or there may be none at all.
The Buddha also permitted the use of [implements] that one neither sees nor hears killing, because they are removed from the hand of the killer through successive transmission.
Regarding the seventh question on *huku* (kneeling with one knee): the first section has already concluded its explanation in accordance with ancient precedents.
Former sages once remarked, "In recent times, people alone have come to despise the term 'Hu' (barbarian). If we were to retain it now, would we not incur such censure?
The commentary states: One who wishes to define a term must first rectify its name. The single term "hukui" (half-kneeling) has been incorrect for a long time;
let us now investigate it and find that there are two errors. First, there is the abandonment of the root in pursuit of the branches.

For the posture of kneeling before the Buddha originated in the land of Brahmā (India), as the fourfold assembly established their reverence upon the Buddha’s descent into birth there; thus, this ritual gesture came into being. If one follows...

Regarding the distinction between names and titles: one should properly use the term "Vanda" (Sanskrit) when kneeling. However, because the holy teachings were transmitted to the East by passing through the lands of the Hu (Huns), they have consequently come to be called by Hu names;
this is the error of abandoning the root and pursuing the branches. Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Sifenlü Xingshichao*) distinguishes them, stating:
"To the west of the Pamir Mountains all belong to the Vanda lineage; to the left of the Iron Gate all belong to the Hu region. Based on this principle:
It is certain that "Hu" (Chinese) and "Fan" (Sanskrit) are not the same; one must understand that this adherence to long-standing errors did not begin with us today.

During the Eastern Jin dynasty, Dharma Master Dao’an mistakenly treated Sanskrit sounds as if they were Chinese, and this practice was followed until the Tang dynasty, when the error was finally rectified.
Thus, people of old severely rebuked [Dao’an], calling him "Mitiān" (Heaven-filling).
For what reason do the words "each kneeling on one knee" (hu-gui) still persist today outside of the sūtras and śāstras?
Is this not merely following long-established error?
Question Eight: In this sūtra, the Four Kings petitioned the Buddha six times to circulate the Great Teaching and vowed to protect the nation.
It is not known whether there has been any verification of the protective deities since ancient times. The commentary states:
"The Four Kings vowed to protect the nation; as for their secret and subtle protection of people, individuals certainly cannot perceive it.
For now, I shall briefly record two manifest instances, the first of which is as described in the old *Xiyu ji* (Record of the Western Regions): Long ago, there was one..."
The temple stored many precious treasures with the hope of using them for restoration; thus, the Four Heavenly Kings were sculpted to serve as guardians.

At that time, there was a Turkic king who, coveting the temple’s wealth, intended to launch an invasion. Suddenly, he dreamed that a Heavenly King pierced his heart with a halberd, whereupon he collapsed and died.
In the thirteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, the three kingdoms of West Fan, Dàshí, and Kāngjū came to invade.

During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong in the Western Capital, the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra was summoned by imperial decree to recite dhāraṇīs for the salvation of the realm and to petition the Four Heavenly Kings to protect the state.
Suddenly, the Emperor beheld approximately five hundred spirits and deities upon the palace floor.

When the Emperor questioned Amoghavajra, he replied, "The son of Vaiśravaṇa leads his army to rescue Anxi. Subsequently, when the report from Anxi arrived, it was indeed on that very day, amidst clouds and mist.
Divine soldiers appeared, causing the barbarian tribes to flee in terror; furthermore, golden mice gnawed the strings of their bows and crossbows until they all snapped;

then, a Heavenly King manifested atop the gate tower, leading the barbarian forces into a great rout. [The Emperor] was greatly delighted and issued an edict that images should be established and venerated in all military camps, cities, and watchtowers throughout the realm.
The *Navapraśna-sūtra* states that if a ruler listens to this sūtra while his neighboring enemy nations prepare their fourfold army to destroy his kingdom,
by the power of this sūtra, the troops will not advance from that point. I do not know whether this sūtra is truly capable of thus quelling war.
The commentary states: It is not that one suffers from a lack of divine protection, but rather that one suffers from the world’s lack of such a person.
Formerly, when Dharma Master Mātanga was staying in a small vassal state of India, the King invited him to lecture on this sutra.

Suddenly, a neighboring state raised an army to invade. Just as they reached the border, the lecture was interrupted by an unforeseen obstacle. When he secretly sent someone to investigate, he saw that—
The king and his ministers sat at ease and listened to the sutras from the monks; their hearts were filled with joy, and they immediately came to request peace and further sought the Dharma.
From this, the two nations were spared from conflict. Is it not the case that those who listen to the sutras can thus quell war?

In the *Shiwen shu* (Commentary on the Ten Questions), it is said that when a human king offers incense, he does so by using the fire of wisdom to burn the incense of the true mark (*dharmatā*), from which the smoke of morality, concentration, and wisdom arises;
thus, it shines through all things without obstruction. Yet, does this incense pertain to phenomena (*dharma*) or to principle (*li*)?

If one says it pertains to phenomena, it should not be called "burning the incense of the true mark. If one says it pertains to principle, it should not be called "incense. This is because the golden light [of the Buddha] pertains to phenomena.
I request that you attempt to resolve this according to principle.
The commentary states: "The principle apart from phenomena is coarse; phenomena that fully embody the principle are subtle. The subtle essence is fundamentally fused, such that the two are non-dual.
This refers to the practitioner of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), who uses perfect understanding to expound the perfect principle, and perfect oneness to [realize] reality.
Contemplating the three [truths] as the substance of the great vow, one is led to realize that principle and phenomena are unified; thus one advances through all realms.
Fragrance is itself the Dharma-realm, and the Three Jewels offered therein are likewise the Dharma-realm. There is only one Dharma-realm and no second Dharma-realm.
Not a single mote of dust moves, yet the myriad dharmas are in full bloom—all are the eternally quiescent light and nothing is not the Dharma.
Regarding the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), when a practitioner performs the threefold offering of body, speech, and mind, they must be free from the notion of substantial reality.
Whether it be incense or flowers, their essence is the *dharmadhātu*; the nature of both the offering and the recipient of the offering is fundamentally empty space.
When one realizes that this measure pervades everywhere and gives rise to the inexhaustible, and understands this principle, one will vaguely perceive the all-pervading.
Question 11: This sutra lists all the devas who protect the Dharma;
if we inquire as to who the Lord of Devas refers to, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is the Great Brahmā Śikhin, the Lord of the Sahā World.
However, according to Zhan’an’s commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, Maheśvara is taken as the Lord. Thus, he says: "Maheśvara has one face and three eyes."

The Brahma King who presides over the Great Thousandfold World System actually governs only a Small Thousandfold World; it is merely because he has already mastered his own household that he is praised as the "Lord of the World.
[In private discourse, it is said that this refers to one who attains the status of lord within a Great Thousandfold World, and those below this level do not qualify.

(The phrase "in private discourse" and what follows is the explanation of Jingxi. Since the descriptions of the Celestial Lord differ between these two passages, to whom does the ultimate authority belong?
The commentary states: To establish a point of reference, two meanings must be clarified. First is that which serves as the sovereign ruler, namely Brahmā.

This is because this deity dwells within the first dhyāna; internally possessing *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought), and externally possessing speech and commands, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* therefore designates him as the lord. In the second dhyāna and above, there is no speech, nor are there *vitarka* and *vicāra*.
Regarding "attaining the status of a ruler," the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains: "Mahābrahmā is the ruler of the three realms; all others belong to him as subjects. This refers to that point.
Second, regarding "being a ruler by virtue of superior retribution": this refers to those from the second dhyāna upward who further cultivate the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).

This is called being a ruler by virtue of superior retribution, and thus lacks the sense of a sovereign king. It is because of this meaning of superior retribution that [the Buddha] takes [Nirvana] as his own.
Śiva is the principal [subject], and thus his retribution is superior; because Brahmā’s retribution is inferior, the sūtra author uses words of praise for him.
To argue definitively that the sovereign returns to Brahmā is a statement that Jingxi (Zhiyi) would not accept.
By distinguishing these two meanings, the subject finds its proper place of return.
The Twelve Questions, based on the *Zhun suoyin ji* (Record of Unveiling the Obscure), provide an exegesis of the *Vajrapāṇi-rahasya-sūtra*.

Quoting from the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, it states that Prince Dharmamati vowed to become Vajrapāṇi to protect his thousand elder brothers and the teachings; according to the sūtra, he is uniquely the one at the gateway.
Second, his manifestations are boundless and manifold. Furthermore, the Indian master who translated this [text] refers to Ucchuṣma within the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
The two masters [Zhili and Zunshi] explain that Vajrapāṇi is also the one who acts as the counterpart to the Dharma-protecting Guhyapada Vajra;
is this interpretation still appropriate?
The commentary states: The interpretations offered by Gushan exist but are not followed. Furthermore, regarding the Vajras listed in various sutras—

To include slightly more [deities] would require artificial adaptation, such as the *Mayūra-vidyārājñī-sūtra* which lists five types of *vajras*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* which mentions eight hundred *vajras*, or the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* which speaks of *vajras* as numerous as the sands of ten *gaṅgā* rivers. Furthermore, when the Buddha attained enlightenment, he was moved by the appearance of five hundred *vajras* and others;
yet these are merely names pointed out in the Sanskrit originals that were not originally present [in the context], yet were forcibly employed. Moreover, regarding the *Śūraṅgama*...
Although Uṣṇīṣacakravartin Vajra is described as a protector of the Dharma, there is no mention of him acting as a gatekeeper.
Those who deliberate on this matter today should know that Guhyapada Vajra is a deity who protects the Buddha-dharma wherever it may be;
he is certainly not a figure fixedly assigned to the three gates. As for the circumstances regarding the installation of images at the gates, they must be based upon...
According to the *Pinaiye* (Skt. *Vinaya*), when the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada asked the Buddha upon the completion of his monastery, the Buddha replied:
"On both sides of the gate, you should paint yakṣas holding staffs. Since this was personally ordained by the Buddha, how could one fail to comply and instead insist on using something else?
In the thirteenth chapter, "The Questions of the Four Kings," three types of treatises are enumerated, namely those such as the "Discourse on Renunciation" spoken by the Brahmā deities.
However, these three treatises are merely worldly dharmas of the Western Regions;

compared with this sutra, which is a supramundane dharma, it is said that this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the most excellent among them. If this is so, why does the subsequent text speak of "worldly treatises that have been composed"?
"Is it all because of this sutra? The commentary states:
If one does not say that this sutra is the most supreme, then the Buddha-dharma would be no different from worldly dharmas;

yet if one does not say that all worldly treatises derive from this sutra, then the essence of the Dharma-nature would lack universal pervasiveness. Only when these two aspects are maintained together can one truly grasp [the truth].
This is most subtle. However, regarding the meaning of "pervasive penetration," the original commentary does not explicitly state it.
The sixth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* states: "The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says that all worldly treatises derive from this scripture; thus, worldly dharmas are themselves Buddha-dharmas.

For example, the ten wholesome acts of a Wheel-Turning King correspond to the five precepts of the Buddha. The Five Constants and the Five Elements also resemble the five precepts in their essential meaning, though they differ in name."
Ordinary fools do not realize that the Sage has manifested traces [in the world] to preach this; furthermore, the *Weimojie xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Vimalakīrti) states:
"Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas are born among humans and devas to compose scriptures. This is precisely the establishment of all dharmas from the root of non-abiding (*anālaya*).
If one understands this principle, then the subsequent "Chapter on the Correct Discourse" is likewise a worldly dharma that is itself a supramundane dharma.
This explains the sequence of the thousand followers.
Regarding the fourteen questions on the Great Eloquence (Mahāprajñā) as the Lord of Dharma Gates: in the "An" chapter (*Anpin*) of the sutra, Great Eloquence is placed first;
in the arrangement of positions for the ritual of repentance (*chanyi*), Merit (*Guṇadeva*) is placed first; and in the "Saṃjñeya" chapter, Merit is again placed first. Thus it is.
Is there not still a meaningful principle regarding this lack of fixed order between the former and the latter?

The commentary states that the various celestial beings of the Thunder-Master (Ding-shi) school have once explained this meaning, saying: "If these are the stages of the 'peaceful category' (an-pin), they constitute the sequence of the primary and the auxiliary as mutual provisions;
this is truly because the wisdom of the Great Eloquence Lord (Mañjuśrī) serves as the primary [virtue], while the merit of the Virtue Lord (Śakra) serves as the auxiliary."

The "Assistants" (zhù) serve to assist the "Principal" (zhèng). As for those listed in the *Sanjī Pǐn* (Chapter on Vaiśravaṇa) and the *Chàn Yí* (Ritual of Repentance), they are directly taken as the sequence of merit and wisdom;
this is because both mundane and supramundane realms take merit as their priority.

Question fifteen: Regarding the Great Goddess Guṇakārandavatī, because she is able to provide material wealth and support for those who lecture and recite the scriptures, the Buddha instructed that one should offer prayers to her and present offerings to her.
According to the *Mahāsāhasrapramardani Sūtra*, it clarifies that wherever the Goddess Guṇakārandavatī goes, she is able to increase one's wealth and treasures.
The text continues: "Furthermore, outside the gate, there is another sister whose form is ugly and who is named Andhāvatī."
Even if it were possible to cause them to disperse, the two women dwell together and have never parted;
since they are said to dwell together without separation, what benefit would there be now in inviting their sisters to follow and scatter them?
The commentary states: Regarding this meaning, those who have explained it since ancient times have been numerous. The *Sijimingjie* (Record of the Four Clarities) says:

"The manifestation of forms by great skillful means is not of a single kind. That [manifestation] facing darkness symbolizes that birth must lead to death; this [manifestation] facing Great Eloquence symbolizes that merit provides the resources for wisdom.
Now, through the mind that seeks to propagate the sūtra while having transcended both birth and death, he moved Guṇakārandavatī (Gongde Tian), whereby he obtained material wealth."
"Since she has detached from self and what belongs to self, even her elder sister does not cling [to her]; how could her younger sister possibly come? Or, some say:
"One should know that the merit invited by the light is indeed a reality. If those two women follow one another in the Great Sūtra, it is because birth is being contrasted with death;
when a Bodhisattva employs contemplation, both are simultaneously discarded; therefore, the sūtra says 'there is'."
The Master of Wisdom says that both [the sisters] are not accepted; although those two women—one beautiful and one ugly—are indeed parables established as metaphors, in reality there are no people.
Thus, Zhiyi’s *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the initial exchange, although they appear to exist, there are actually no persons engaging in the dialogue;
the guest and host are merely assumed, and thus there are no sisters. Siming composed [this].
That it exists yet does not come is explained next through the use of parables and metaphors; whether this accords with principle, one should perhaps attempt to discern it.
Regarding the sixteenth question: "These meritorious and honored devas and humans have all that is required; among these, there is mention of 'like an ox'."

If sheep are like grain and rice, and oxen can be used for plowing and sowing, yet sheep serve only as food, would the heavenly deities provide sustenance for human mouths by causing people to kill living beings?
The commentary states: "Whether it be *zhā* or *ān*, this is merely an extension of the argument; does this not mean that Heaven is without mind, yet responds to the myriad things? If so...
If there is someone who can master the Buddhist scriptures but lacks the necessities of life, Heaven will also provide for them by granting cattle and sheep.
This is like the account in the sutras where the Buddha manifested fish and rice on Mount Yu to relieve those suffering from hunger.

During the period of the pseudo-Tang dynasty, when the people were starving, they took the large lake mollusks and clams to eat; though the harvest was bountiful the following year, they continued to gather them without ceasing until suddenly one was obtained [that was not edible].
A clam spat out a single image of the Buddha, and only when it was taken up did [the pain] cease; this was a manifested transformation intended ultimately to prevent killing.
The story of Devadatta and the sheep is also of this same category.
Question seventeen: The *Dṛḍhadharmaparyāya* states that if one hears even the meaning of a single verse of this sutra, at the time of death, one will follow [it].
If one intends to be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, why is it that merely hearing this sutra results in birth in heaven,
given that this sutra is that which all Buddhas have traversed and where Bodhisattvas practice?
The commentary states: The Buddha’s intention was firmly to cause people to enter directly by a single leap;

however, because sentient beings were burdened by their own karma and lacked sufficient merit, he could not help but employ gradual transformation. Therefore, he first causes those who hear this sutra to give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and subsequently leads them to ultimate liberation.
Thus, at the end of this chapter, it says: "Having heard this sutra, in future ages they shall encounter..."
To encounter the Buddhas and swiftly attain Bodhi is precisely this. How much more so when it comes to hearing the sutras and being born in heaven—all great teachings are like this.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that by copying this scripture, one shall be born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* says that those who receive and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts shall be born among humans or in the heavens. If one understands the present text, one will fully grasp the intent behind all such passages.
Eighteenth Question: According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, it is stated that anger (*dveṣa*) does not occur in the upper realms;
yet why does this scripture, in its "Chapter on Correct Discourse" (*Saddharma-paryāya*), state that the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens each give rise to resentment?
The commentary states: According to the divisions of the Three Realms (tridhātu) in the Buddha’s teachings, the thirty-three heavens belong to the lower Realm of Desire (kāmadhātu).

The *Abhidharmakośa* speaks only of the Form and Formless Realms (rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu) as being free from anger (*dveṣa*). If this is so, why does the *Miaole lun* (Treatise on Sublime Joy) state that anger pervades all three realms? The answer is:

The debate regarding the presence or absence of anger in the two upper realms is merely a difference in the calculations of the Hīnayāna schools. If one follows the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, [anger is indeed absent].
The school clarifies that anger exists throughout all three realms; however, the Sarvāstivāda school maintains that anger is absent in the two higher realms.

Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "The Sautrāntikas clarify that there is no hindrance in the first dhyāna. Furthermore, according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, greed and anger both extend throughout the two higher realms.
Moreover, one must understand that the presence or absence of anger in the two higher realms is merely a conventional teaching within the period of the Hīnayāna.
If one considers this according to the Mahāyāna teachings, there is nowhere it does not reach; thus, the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) commentary states:

"Although the various afflictions differ in their degree of gravity, they still extend up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*); how could they be excluded from the Formless Realm? This is precisely the text [referred to].
Question 19: In the "Chapter on the Correct Discourse" (*Saddharmaviniścaya*), it is stated that because human kings are tyrannical, three anomalies arise simultaneously in the world.

New records and the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā* both explain these by means of the three calamities of water, fire, and wind, and further explain them by means of the three types of anomalies involving the sun, moon, and stars.
Are the meanings of these two explanations consistent with one another?
The commentary states: Regarding the principle of "taking the long," one does not take it according to the literal sentiment;

one should know that the explanations of the two masters are acceptable as a rough interpretation for the passage on the three calamities of sun, moon, and stars, but they are not so for the different interpretations of the three [calamities] of fire, water, and wind.

This is because throughout the preceding and following sections of the sūtra text, these three are never mentioned. Therefore, observing the context of the text, the "knife" (the logical point) must be applied here.
Regarding the elimination of the three calamities—famine, pestilence, and warfare—the phrasing of the text is elegant and harmonious; thus the Sūtra says:
"Because the king abandons the Right [Dharma], even if the country suffers famine and the people are hungry, and there are many pestilences where they plunder one another and die by the sword.
These three disasters arise because kings and ministers act contrary to the Way and纵容 (indulge) evil.

The temporary arising of calamities during the period of excellence (*śubhakāla*) is thus fundamentally different from the enumeration of the three minor calamities at the end of a single *antarakalpa* as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*.

According to the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" (*Guishen pin*), those listed there are all members of the eight classes of beings, such as devas and nāgas; how could they [the calamities] abandon them?
Is it appropriate for the superior to be distinguished from the inferior solely by the term "ghosts and spirits" (*guishen*)?
The commentary states: Shi Zi says, "The spirits of heaven are called *ling*; the spirits of earth are called *qi*; the spirits of humans are called *gui*.

According to this, the single character "spirit" (*shen*) is also applicable. As for the phrase "distinguishing the category by means of ghosts and spirits," this refers to the text of the sub-commentary (*shu*).

It is said: This chapter lists universally the various deities of the heavens, dragons, rivers, seas, sun, moon, and so forth; since the section on the heavens has already been concluded above, there is no room for them to appear again.
Although it lists beings from all realms universally, because the texts concerning ghosts and spirits are numerous, this is the reason the chapter is named as such.
This is precisely the intended meaning.
Question 21: Since the Buddha takes great compassion as his primary principle, he established the precept against killing.
If this is so, why does the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" state that one feels joy in one's heart upon achieving victory when entering a battle?
The commentary states: This objection was also once debated by Zhā Ān, who managed to provide some degree of clarity; therefore, I shall now employ his arguments in full.
He may say: "Confucius stated that he had not yet studied the affairs of military campaigns, and Laozi said that weapons are instruments of ill omen.
Since even these two sages were ashamed to speak of warfare, how can the Buddha, on the contrary, claim victory upon entering the fray?"

"Does this mean that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni incited people to kill? He replied: "In Jambudvīpa, there have been a hundred thousand wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) who governed by means of the ten wholesome paths;

they all laid down their spears and ceased military prowess. Long ago, when Zhonglian of Lu dissuaded the Qin army with a mere laugh and conversation, he repelled them forty li away without harming a single soldier.
A skilled warrior does not need to form battle lines; to enter the ranks and achieve victory is what is meant by 'excellence in combat.'"
It is likewise so; the Buddha’s words are rich with profound implications, speaking only of waging war against the demonic armies of birth and death.

Taking the precepts as the vanguard, meditative concentration as the strategy, and wisdom as the shield and breastplate, he captures the six thieves alive and strikes them down with the sword of insight, allowing the King of the Mind to find peace.
One should not claim that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni incited people to kill.
In the twenty-second chapter, "Questions on Ghosts and Spirits," it is said that the ritual for repentance of Hārītī, Mother of Demons, and others is based upon these two lines.
Consequently, sculptors and painters depict Hārītī in male form and the Mother of Demons in female form.
Is such a representation consistent with their actual names and natures?

The commentary states: This was fabricated by one who is unacquainted with the holy teachings. One should know that although two phrases are listed in the sutra, they actually refer to only one person;

this is merely a case of citing both the Chinese and Sanskrit names together. Therefore, translating from the Sanskrit, the Sanskrit term *Hārītī* means "Mother of Ghosts" (*Guǐzǐmǔ*) in the Liang dynasty Chinese language.
Such instances of citing both meanings are common in the sutras and treatises, as it is said:
*Camana* is translated here as "repenting one's transgressions" (*huìguò*); the current term *chànhuǐ* (repentance) is used as a synonymous designation.

To understand why the Mother of Ghosts is named *Hārītī*, see the detailed account in the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings," specifically the note under the entry for Guǐzǐmǔ (Mother of Ghost Children).
Question 23: This chapter, "Eliminating Illness," represents the way of the ancient sages who practiced extensive charity to relieve the masses.
If this is so, why does the *Śāriputra-parinirvāṇa Sūtra* (Yíjiào jīng) stipulate that bhikṣus should not engage in activities such as compounding medicinal decoctions?
The commentary states that the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra-ṭīkā* (*Yijiao jing shu*) also once raised this objection, to which it was replied:
"The detailed account of treating illness in the *Liu-shui-jing* (*Sutra of the Flowing Water*) accords with the medicinal prescriptions and techniques found here;

yet this sutra prohibits them because longevity or premature death depends upon karmic retribution and does not reside in medical art. Generally speaking, these points do not exceed three intentions, the first being that they would impair wisdom."
"Because it pertains to the nature of life, it contains much falsehood; this is the teaching of Mount Gushan.

To further demonstrate this now, one should know that although this chapter concerns medical treatment, its underlying intent contains the medicine of the Dharma, as will be seen in the subsequent text.

If one were to discuss it solely from the perspective of worldly medical practice, it would indeed be an external method; however, for a follower of the Mahāyāna who manifests in the provisional world to transform sentient beings, it serves a different purpose.
Within this, if one can forget hope and abandon both grasping and rejecting, then matters will not be fixed or constrained.

Thus, during their causal stage, the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja) and the Superior Medicine (Bhaiṣajyasamudgata) tasted all manner of herbs and plants to save the sick; through this, they attained realization of the Perfect Penetration (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa).

Furthermore, the preface to the *Bencao* (Pharmacopoeia) records that the Medicine King was Wei Gu-yuan, a man from the kingdom of Shule, who wore a coarse woolen robe and carried a sword at his waist.

During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, when hundreds of gourds were entangled [in the trees], many people suffered from illnesses; he administered medicinal decoctions to all who encountered him, and they were all cured.
Furthermore, the *Shenxian zhuan* (Biographies of Divine Immortals) states that since the time of Yao and Shun, the Medicine King has manifested in five incarnations to rescue the poor and the sick.
Subsequently, a black dog transformed into a black dragon and carried the Master away; beholding this divine marvel...
How could this be anything other than the conduct of a Great Being (mahāsattva) benefiting others?

If one considers the intent established in the *Śālistambasūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching), this represents the teaching of the Hīnayāna concerning solitary cultivation for one's own liberation; therefore, practices such as those involving medical prescriptions and the like should not be undertaken.
Question 24: This sutra removes illness; since it employs ordinary medicines for treatment, it is a worldly physician.

If we follow the Great Sutra, wherein the Buddha treats the mental illnesses of sentient beings, he is a supramundane physician. Ultimately, does this sutra also possess the qualities of a supramundane physician?
The commentary states: In this chapter, my ancestor’s sub-commentary first relies on Paramārtha’s extensive exposition of methods and medicines for treating the diseases of the world.
It continues by stating that the "equal distribution of the three poisons" and so forth are the diseases, while "counting the breaths" and "contemplating impurity" and so forth are the medicines.

However, these medicines and diseases still merely rely on metaphorical events to discuss medicine; they do not yet constitute a definitive clarification of the medical prescriptions for practice. Therefore, [the discussion] now proceeds to the cessation [of suffering].

The contemplation that extensively demonstrates the ten objects and ten vehicles as the remedy for the maladies of the three delusions and two deaths is precisely what this chapter cites as proof, stating:
"Upon merely hearing these words, the illness was immediately cured. This refers to the contemplative method of the first vehicle, which is the contemplation of the inconceivable realm.

Furthermore, the passage regarding those with more severe illnesses going to an elder to have medicine prepared to treat their disease refers to the meaning of the contemplative methods of the subsequent nine vehicles.

How wondrous! That the "Divine Prescription in the Physician’s Sleeve" of the Buddhas and Patriarchs contains such a teaching—how many people in future generations will be able to take it as their medicine?

The twenty-fifth question, following the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) in its analysis of the phases of doctrinal classification, cites the *Liu-shui pǐn* (Chapter on the Flowing Water), where a certain bhikṣu was reading...
Having recited the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, you have consequently classified this scripture as belonging to the third period, the Vaipulya period;
however, regarding the term "vaipulya," there is both a phenomenal aspect and a noumenal aspect—please point out its essential meaning.

The commentary states: "The four teachings all speak of phenomena; this is the *vaipulya* (extensive) in terms of phenomena. The three truths are discussed together; this is the *vaipulya* in terms of principle.
Since Tiantai’s classification of the teachings cites this passage, we know that *vaipulya* refers to the extensive [teachings] regarding phenomena. "Vaipulya" means equal and level.

This is because the *Avataṃsaka* speaks only of the Separate and Perfect [vehicles], the Deer Park [teachings] are merely the Tripitaka, and the *Prajñāpāramitā* teaches the three [vehicles]—all of which belong exclusively to the third period.
Because all four teachings are discussed therein, it is called "Broad and Level" (*guǎngpíng*);

as for its principle being "Square and Equal" (*fāngděng*), since it discusses the three truths together, it exists in all five periods except for the Deer Park [period]. Thus, in terms of principle, it is pervasive and not restricted;
yet, because the Perfect teaching exists within all four periods, in terms of phenomena, it is restricted and yet pervasive—referring here to the "Square and Equal" in terms of phenomena.
"Round" refers to the principle (*li*), because it is equal to the square.

Question twenty-six: The twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as taught in various sutras speak of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) immediately upon mentioning the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), such as that which was turned by the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Yet, in this sutra, the Elder’s Son Flowing Water (*Jalavāhana*) saves the fish...

If one speaks only of the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) and does not discuss the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), how then can the fish understand arising and cessation so as to attain rebirth in a higher realm?
The commentary states: The sub-commentary (*śū-jì*) does not mention this; I shall now answer by means of two points. First, it is a matter of the brevity and essentials of the translation.

Knowing that the Sanskrit original must have contained [these sections], yet fearing that Master Xun Chen might have omitted them and thus failed to translate them—just as the *Sishen* (Four Manifestations) indicates omissions—it is clear from the statement in the *Sanguizhong* (Within the Three Refuges):

"Although the original for the *Chanyan* lacks the Three Refuges, the *Zuisheng jing* (Most Victorious Sutra) does contain them"—that not only were the Three Refuges omitted, but furthermore, they were not translated;
this clearly demonstrates the nature of the causes and conditions for such omissions. Second, because their faculties were sharp, these matters were not discussed.
Generally speaking, the preaching of the Dharma is adapted to the capacities and circumstances of beings; for this reason, it is not presented exhaustively.

This is largely because, in the past, certain beings possessed great karmic conditions such that upon hearing the Ten Epithets of the Buddha, they immediately realized non-arising and non-ceasing, wondrously awakening to the fundamental emptiness of all things, and thereby attained transcendence.
This is what is meant by "hearing one and knowing two," or as the saying goes, "the swift horse seeing the shadow of the whip."

Furthermore, in the twenty-seventh question of the *Śāsanaprakāśanaviniścaya-śāstra*, it is stated that because drinking alcohol leads to transgressions and the retribution for such offenses, the Buddha prohibited even a single drop from being consumed.
If this is so, why did the Buddha, in the past as the youth Jalavāhana, save the fish, and after having saved them, return home to entertain his guests while drinking wine?
"While lying down, one observes that this [act] results in great compassion for saving sentient beings; why then is it a fault to drink alcohol and break the precepts?
The commentary explains: This objection has been raised since ancient times. Now, I shall extend the response through two points. First, regarding the facts:

at that time, our Buddha manifested traces identical to those of ordinary people. Since ordinary people in the world cannot escape worldly conventions (*saṃvṛti*), he therefore had to attend to his guests.
The act of drinking alcohol is manifested here as an inclusion through "sameness of kind. Regarding these two points from the perspective of principle:
if one discusses the Sage Vairocana’s long-standing realization, he acts upon what is considered a non-path to penetrate the Buddha-way.

This is what is meant by "filling a vessel of true emptiness with the wine of real marks. Since real marks are signless, who is it that drinks? Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "He enters into wine."
To establish one's own resolve and also to establish the resolves of others is precisely his intention.
Regarding the twenty-eighth question: once a *sattva* suddenly entered a mountain forest and saw a tigress that had recently given birth to seven cubs;
after seven days, as she was frozen by the cold snow and tormented by hunger, he then sacrificed his body. Since the tigress cannot speak, how did the Prince know she had given birth?
"Seven days after birth.
The commentary states that Tiantai has already clarified this difficulty; the text contains four points:

first, it cites the *Shanhai jing*, which says that when a tiger is born, one spot appears on its head on the first day; now that there are seven spots, we know it must be seven days old. Furthermore, [it refers to] another seven days.
It is said that his eyes opened because they had not yet opened before; furthermore, he would have died after seven days without food, as the tiger cubs were on the verge of death.
Alternatively, it is said that spirits revealed them to him, such as when a tree spirit manifested its upper body or when the number of fish was shown toward the flowing water.
Question Twenty-nine: Tigers are ferocious beasts that do not eat anything except flesh and blood. Now, the Prince has sacrificed his body to feed a tiger;
yet on other days, tigers harm living beings with great frequency. Why did the Prince not consider this?
The commentary states: Sentient beings devour one another; why should it be the tiger alone?

If the Prince had witnessed the starving tiger and yet failed to rescue it, how could he be called compassionate? This was merely done because he wished to fulfill the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), and thus he extended his salvation.
The *Thirty Questions* states, according to the biography of the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty:

To the southeast of North India, there is a great rocky mountain which is the place where the Bodhisattva sacrificed his body. The ground and its vegetation have been stained by the blood of the Prince’s body and remain a deep crimson even today.
Furthermore, at the time the Prince sacrificed his body, he himself said in the sutras: "In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas..."
After such a vast number of kalpas, when the great tri-calamities arise, the world no longer exists;
how then can it be said that the grasses, trees, and earth are still crimson?
The commentary states: In the past, Master Nanshan also doubted this and once questioned a celestial deity. The deity replied:

A certain master said: "This is due to the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata; because of the bodhisattva’s resolve and conduct, the three calamities (*trayo 'ntarakalpa*) cannot destroy it.

Furthermore, another raised a difficult objection, saying: "In the transformation of the three calamities, even the *paramāṇu* (the most subtle atom) is exhausted; now you say the stupa remains—does this not contradict [the teachings]? He replied:
"It is simply that no *paramāṇu* whatsoever can abide unless it is a site of the Sage's traces. Now, through the empowerment of the Sage's power, [it remains]."
This causes those of future generations to aspire and look up toward it so that they may attain the Way.

Once the world has been established, all the vestiges left from past kalpas are manifested one by one in the sequence of each successive Buddha. This is the "inconceivability of the Buddha's power" among the five inconceivables;
the text is found in the *Linggan Zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance).

Chapter Thirty-one: Praising the Buddha. It is said: At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas departed from this world for the land of the Tathāgata Golden Jewel Canopy Mountain King. Having arrived in that land, they offered praise, saying:
"Is this the collection of words? There are two doubts: first, having already reached that land, could this not be a praise of that Buddha? Second, [doubt].
One might wonder: since the Buddha-lands are exceedingly numerous, why is it that the assembly listed here proceeds specifically to that land?

The commentary explains: "This is not a praise of that Buddha, but a praise of Śākyamuni. Therefore, the sub-commentary (*śū*) clarifies this intent, stating: "A single sūtra maintains its excellence from beginning to end;
thus, from the initial to the middle and finally to the conclusion, all the bodhisattvas extol the Teacher. The record states: "Reaching the Golden..."
Regarding the land of Ratnacchattra: it is intended to magnify the assembly, for the bodhisattvas therein all praise Śākyamuni.

How could there be any doubt that this commentary is not obscure? Why then would they praise that Buddha? As for the statement that the assembly extends as far as the land of Ratnacchattra, this refers to the land where [the Buddha] will surely attain Buddhahood in the future. The reason the assembly is listed as extending to that place is, first, to signify...

Within the section on the causes of the signs of faith, the two fruits are explained; this indicates that those who attain the prediction [of enlightenment] based on the signs of faith will not fail to acquire a Buddha-land.
People do not understand this meaning and needlessly produce forced interpretations, saying:

"In the thirty-second question, it is stated that in the introductory section of this sutra, the Buddha 'roams in the dharma-nature,' which refers to entering meditative absorption, and that he subsequently finished preaching the sutra."
If it is said that [the Buddha] arose from samādhi, this indicates that this sutra is taught entirely within a state of meditative concentration from beginning to end.
If that is so, why does the Buddha arise from his seat in the "Chapter on Casting Off the Body" to pay homage to the Sattva-hōtā (Sattvadhātu) stūpa?

The commentary states: Since it has already been said that arising from meditation to perform prostrations is not fixed, one should further raise the objection: "How can a sutra be preached while in a state of meditative concentration? I shall now address this together.
The reason for this objection is that the small is used to challenge the great. This is because the teachings of the Hīnayāna are characterized by limited practice and lack the Middle Way;
since they do not accord with the fundamental principle, as soon as one speaks of entering concentration, movement and stillness are deemed incompatible.
The "Dharma-equality" (dharmasamatā) and other matters refer to what is called the "mark of the cessation of all dharmas" in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

Now, because the concentration (*samādhi*) of the Mahāyāna is characterized by the identity of movement and stillness, dispersion and concentration, permanence and impermanence, and going and coming, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
"In tranquil meditation, with palms joined, they praise the King of Dharmas with ten million gāthās. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* likewise states: "All Buddhas are constantly in right concentration."

To universally and extensively expound the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings within the midst [of existence] is precisely to manifest all majestic deportments without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation;
yet this realm is what the dragon-elephants can swiftly traverse, not something a donkey is capable of enduring.
Question 33: Among the various Mahāyāna sūtras spoken by the Buddha, there are instances where he does not mention entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) when teaching;
for what reason does this particular sūtra specifically state that he entered absorption?

The explanation says: If one discusses the Buddha’s own practice, there is no distinction between entering and emerging from, or being in a state of stillness and distraction; however, it is solely for the purpose of accommodating...
Because the dispositions of those to be converted have a particular affinity for this, it differs from the ordinary path;

it is precisely because those of the Vaipulya class find their mental inclination toward meditative concentration that they attain entry into the Way, and thus the Buddha, the Great Sage, stoops down to accord with them.
Question thirty-four: Is this sutra concerned with the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) entered by the Tathāgata, or with its principle (*tattva*)?
If it is said to concern the matter (*vastu*), the text itself states that "the Tathāgata dwells in the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*.

If it is said to concern the principle, why does the commentary state, "Because the Buddha wishes to respond to the capacities of sentient beings, he manifests ritual protocols"? Is this not indeed a matter?
The commentary states: Master Cao’an once thoroughly understood this meaning and said, "Generally speaking, there are three types of 'concentration' (samādhi):
first, phenomena; second, principle; and third, that which is principle manifesting as phenomena. The concentration of light is precisely that which is principle manifesting as phenomena.

One must understand that in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), phenomena and principle are not such that if one mentions phenomena alone, there is no principle outside of phenomena, nor if one mentions principle alone, is there [no phenomenon outside of it]."
Because there is no external phenomenon with which it can be identified, the Buddha accords with the capacities of sentient beings to manifest the *dharmatā* in its entirety as a model of conduct;
yet outside this model of conduct, there is no separate *dharmatā*. As the Patriarch said: "The Great Enlightenment is suddenly perfected, illuminating while remaining eternally quiescent.
The present practice of entering meditative concentration is merely a manifestation of this model of conduct to cause people to delight in concentration; it is truly its textual expression.
Regarding the thirty-fifth question: It is already clear that the meaning of this sutra was proclaimed by the Buddha while he was in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, in the preface to the *Paramasaṃyukta-sūtra* translated during the Tang dynasty, it says: "At that time, the Bhagavān arose from samādhi at the hour of late afternoon, surveyed the great assembly, and then spoke these verses.
Since this refers to a different translation of the same sutra, why is there such a discrepancy—one version mentioning [the arising] and the other omitting it?
"Is this not a discrepancy?

The commentary states: "One should know that in that sutra as well, from beginning to end, [the Buddha] was in meditative concentration; yet, though they were but a few inches apart, they were a thousand li distant, such that people could not perceive it.
Therefore, the preface to that [other] sutra says, "The realm of purity is where the Tathāgata dwells," while the preface to this sutra says, "This is..."
At that time, the Tathāgata dwelt within the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*; the passages describing the Buddha’s entry into meditative concentration in these two sūtras are identical.
At the end of that [other] sūtra it says: "I only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on me and always allow me to behold his body of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
At the end of this sūtra it says: "I only pray that, out of compassion, you will manifest your body for me. In both sūtras, the tree spirit...

The passage requesting the Buddha to emerge from meditative absorption is identical in both [texts]. Comparing them in this way, the Buddha remains in samādhi from beginning to end in that sutra as well, with no difference in the fundamental teaching.

As for the statement in that sutra that he "arose from samādhi at the hour of late afternoon," this is what Tiantai referred to as the Tathāgata entering to roam within the *dharmatā* and emerging to expound the meaning of the King of Sutras. Siming said:
The statement regarding "emergence" (chū) actually indicates that emerging from meditative absorption does not obstruct illumination; thus, it is called "emergence.
The Sūtra says, "Arising from samādhi," while Tiantai speaks of "entering and roaming" and "emerging and narrating," and Siming speaks of "stillness not obstructing illumination.

Although these three modes of expression differ, their underlying meaning is identical. Thus, although both Tiantai and Siming propagated the *Lunji jing* (the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*), [their views were consistent].
This work simultaneously subverts [false views] and accords with the pure essence, harmonizing with the sūtras;
it is not merely the lofty discourse of "Mitiān" (Daoan). Regarding these thirty-six questions, this sūtra has been most widely circulated from ancient times to the present.
Among its contents, may we hear of instances of efficacy and miraculous traces?
The commentary states: The teaching is not established in vain; its principle must surely evoke a responsive resonance.

Since this sutra was proclaimed by the Buddha and subsequently translated by the masters of prophecy (śāstrins), it is truly the sun and moon for those lost on their path and the bridge for crossing the sea of suffering.

Its divine efficacy and magnificent traces are recorded in the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*) and secular classics; there is nothing that does not bear witness to them. However, to exhaustively record all that has been heard, these matters must be separately compiled here. Now...
In response to your inquiry, I have briefly recorded one or two instances. In the "Essay on Prohibiting Killing" written by Qin Shaoyou, it is said:
Zhang Judo of Wenzhou died for three days and then revived. He was initially led away by a spirit, who said to him, "Your lifespan is not yet exhausted;

however, you must face the karmic retribution for the living beings you have killed. Judo sought to be exempted from this, and the messenger instructed him to produce a copy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

A monk named Judo was staying at a monastery. After a short while, he arrived at the king’s residence. When the king summoned those who were facing charges as his accusers, not a single person appeared.
An official said, "Today, the auspicious registrar reported that Judo has come to the assembly where the scriptures are being recited; because of this, all the accused have been released.
The king was delighted and said, "You may return at once; do not kill living beings ever again. This is recorded in the *Leishuo ji* (Classified Accounts) under Chen Yaozi’s entry.
At the piers of the Three Mountains, an old man said, "Tomorrow afternoon there will be a great wind; the boat will surely capsize, so you must be cautious.
The next day the sky was clear and cloudless, and the boatmen requested that the mooring ropes be cast off. The Master delayed them.
While the accompanying boats left the shore at the same time, suddenly at noon, black clouds and a violent gale arose, and the raging waves were like mountains. The [other] boats went... [lost].
Many of the boats capsized, and the official again saw the old man from before, who said, "I am truly not a human being; I am a patrol commander of the Yangtze River.
Since you are currently serving as a prime minister, I must inform you. The official asked, "How may I repay your kindness?
The old man replied, "I wish to obtain a copy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*; by its power, I hope to achieve a slight promotion in rank. The official granted his request.
Once he had arrived at the capital, he sought three copies of the scripture and sent someone to cast them into the Three Mountains Shoal.
He then dreamed of the old man from before, who said, "I originally prayed for only one copy, yet you have granted me three blessings; you shall ascend through several volumes in succession.
Thereupon, he bowed twice and departed. The *Yijian Zhi* states that toward the end of the Shaoxing era, there was a commoner in Huaiyin whose daughter died during the cold season.
Bereaved by her mother’s death and lacking the means to offer a memorial service, she cut off her hair and sold it for six hundred coins.

Just as she was about to invite monks to recite the sutras, five monks happened to pass by her door; she immediately invited them, but they all declined one after another. After a long while, one monk finally consented.
He went to neighboring households to borrow a copy of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, and as he read from it during the meal, he expounded the commentary.

As he was walking along the street, four monks happened to encounter him and invited him to a wine shop. Just as they were taking their seats, he suddenly heard a woman outside the window calling the monk’s name as he recited the sutras.
When the monk asked who she was, the woman wept and said, "I am the deceased daughter of the family where you were reciting the sutras.
For a long time I have been lingering in the dark realms of the netherworld, but thanks to the master’s recitation of the sutras, I have finally been able to escape."

"The officials of the underworld have already issued an edict regarding his place of rebirth; if you, Master, drink wine and break your fast, this merit will be utterly nullified—this is truly lamentable.
I pray you show me compassion. Having spoken, he vanished from sight. The monk withdrew in shame.

Regarding the cultivation of the contemplation on the ten realms, Master Jingxi said: "Those who are stubbornly obstructed [by delusion] find the profound subtlety of principle-contemplation difficult to penetrate; they can only interpret the text through phenomenal appearances, yet those who claim to propagate the Lotus Sūtra in such a manner are far removed from its true intent.
I have synthesized various scriptures to assist in the exegesis of this sūtra, deeply reflecting upon the instructions of my predecessors, for whom there is no substitute.

I, Zili, have carefully examined this brief exposition of the essentials of the method for contemplating the mind (*guanxin fayao*) according to the teachings of the Mountain School (Tiantai), and have personally verified it within my own mind.
Might there be those who, upon seeing or hearing it, are able to rejoice in it?
To begin with, the principle of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) in this scripture is that which the Tathāgata has traversed; it is the fruit of realization attained by the Sage.

Regarding the Dharma: if one wishes to open up one's own treasure store, one should aspire to emulate the "thought of the steed" (the aspiration for enlightenment) and practice contemplation upon hearing [the teaching].
Only when the principle is manifested through its completion will it be truly excellent and beautiful. Thus, the Master of Siming said:

"Although the mind is fundamentally wondrous, as long as contemplation is not yet perfected, it is merely termed the 'aggregates' (skandhas) and 'entrances' (āyatanas). Now, those who are beginners wishing to engage in cultivation should employ the Buddha-eye and the seed-wisdom (bīja-jñāna).
To understand that the three-character dharma-gate of *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is the Dharma itself and not a mere metaphor is my own present sixth consciousness.
This mind is both the object of contemplation and the contemplation itself;

in this very place, it is inconceivable, subtle, wondrous, and most noble—this is precisely the Middle Way. Within this, quiescent yet ever-illuminating, it is able to give rise to wisdom that illuminates principle. This is...

The light of the dharma-nature is what is called the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Once this principle is illuminated, the practitioner’s complexion naturally becomes full and pure;

this is because the dharma-nature is capable of providing manifold benefits, causing both the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) to become luminous. This constitutes the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).

These three contemplations are distantly received from the World-Honored One Śākyamuni and proximately inherited from Nāgārjuna. They arise entirely from one's inherent nature and are not achieved through artificial cultivation. Only...

Within a single mind there are, as it were, three functions: first, "all is empty," wherein both the provisional and the middle are equally empty, such that the three contemplations all manifest the eradication of characteristics;
second, "all is provisional," wherein both the empty and the middle are equally provisional, such that the three contemplations all clarify the establishment of phenomena;
third, "all is the middle," wherein both the empty and the provisional are equally the middle, such that...
The three contemplations are thus all perfected as being beyond all dependence. One who cultivates in this manner spends the whole day dispelling and purifying, yet all dharmas are fully realized;

spends the whole day establishing dharmas, yet not even a speck of dust remains; spends the whole day transcending dependence, yet the two truths remain distinct and clear. With emotional deliberation extinguished, the dualistic and the particular are simultaneously shattered.
To realize that all phenomena are identical with all dharmas, one contemplates in accordance with the nature of reality (dharmatā), such that in profound stillness there is luminous illumination.
When both subject and object have subsided and one contemplates their non-duality, having attained this realization, one should illuminate all objects with this contemplation;
establish all practices by leading them through this contemplation; accomplish all tasks by perfecting them through this contemplation;
and expound all teachings by unfolding them via this contemplation. To abandon this is to become one with the various māras.

Apart from this, the various external [phenomena] have not yet arisen; thus the *Mahā-śāstra* says: "Excluding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, everything else falls into the works of Māra.
Kāśyapa said: "Prior to hearing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, all were people of false views.
How great indeed is the wondrous principle of the single mind and the threefold contemplation! A person such as this can practice within the three characters of *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
There is nothing to be cultivated, yet one cultivates the three contemplations; there is nothing to be destroyed, yet one destroys the three delusions;

there is nothing to be revealed, yet one reveals the three truths; there is nothing to be realized, yet one realizes the three virtues. For one's own practice and for the transformation of others, one dwells peacefully within the Tathāgata’s secret treasury, reaching ultimate perfection therein.
Since this is so for the general title, it is likewise so for the specific text; its essence, doctrine, function, and teaching are thus appended.
The *Dharmāloka-cittarāja Śrīśaila-śāstra*: One Volume, Eighteen Chapters on Contemplating the Mind by Means of Phenomena. With every single phrase heard, affairs are gathered to form contemplation;

with every word, one faces the Dharma-nature, and with every character, one realizes the King of Sutras. This is what is called the practice of clarity and stillness and its profound, deep-reaching realm;
it is something that only individuals can attain for themselves, and only when they have realized the Way will they become intimate with it.
The Golden Light Sutra: Illuminating Explanation, Scroll Lower (End)
